concepts/censorship-of-the-press.title: Censorship of the Press
concepts/censorship-of-the-press.content:
Censorship of the Press
From the earliest days of the printing press, both Church and state authorities recognized that the new technology posed a fundamental threat to established structures of control. The censorship apparatus that developed in the decades after Gutenberg was designed for a world of manuscripts, in which heretical ideas could be tracked, confiscated, and destroyed one copy at a time. The printing press rendered that model obsolete at a stroke.
The First Censorship: Berthold of Mainz (1486)
The earliest known edict specifically targeting the printing press was issued on 4 January 1486 by Berthold von Henneberg, Archbishop of mainz. The mandate forbade all persons from printing, publishing, buying, or selling any book translated from Greek, Latin, or any other language before the written translation had been approved by a committee appointed from the faculty of the University of Mainz. The penalties were severe: excommunication, confiscation of the books, and a fine of 100 florins of gold. [source: De Vinne, pp. 513-521]
Berthold’s preamble acknowledged that printing had been given “for the instruction of human life,” but complained that certain men “led by the desire of vainglory or money, do abuse this art.” He specifically condemned vernacular translations of the divine offices, which he claimed had been rendered “unintelligible” by “rash unlearned simpletons.” The edict was the first attempt to impose pre-publication approval — a template that would be replicated across Europe. [source: De Vinne, pp. 521]
University Control: Cologne (1479) and the Sorbonne
Before Berthold’s edict, universities had already begun exerting control. The University of Cologne, one of the earliest centers of printing outside mainz, asserted authority over printers within its jurisdiction as early as 1479, requiring that all books be inspected before distribution. The Sorbonne in Paris exercised similar authority — the first printing office in Paris had been established in 1469 within the Sorbonne itself, at the invitation of the learned Fichet and Heynlin, who saw the press as a tool for scholarship but also kept it under the University’s watchful eye. [source: Putnam, pp. 235-236]
As the Paris book trade grew, the Sorbonne’s Theological Faculty became the most aggressive censorship body in France. By 1512, the King was writing to the University requesting the Faculty to examine books the Court found suspicious. Under Francis I, the Sorbonne’s “bigoted and ignorant censorship” (as Putnam describes it) drove some of the most talented publishers out of the country — most notably Robert Estienne, who fled to Geneva in 1552 after years of harassment over his Greek and Latin Bibles. [source: Putnam, pp. 239, 249, 396-434]
The University of Paris and the Book Trade
Andre Chevillier’s L’Origine de l’Imprimerie de Paris (1694), Part IV (“Des Droits de l’Universite sur la Librairie”), provides the most detailed archive-based account of the University of Paris’s authority over the book trade — a system that long predated the printing press and shaped French censorship well into the age of print. Chevillier, a librarian of the College of Navarre, drew directly on the University’s registers, the Livre du Recteur, and the Recueil d’Actes preserved in the College of Navarre archives. [source: Chevillier, Preface and Part IV, pp. 301-417]
The University’s Jurisdiction
The Paris book trade — booksellers (librarii), writers (stationarii), binders (relieurs), illuminators (enlumineurs), and parchment-makers (parcheminiers) — was entirely under the jurisdiction of the University. Chevillier states this as a fact “so clear from a great number of ancient titles in its Archives, that one would have to be blind not to see it.” In 1615-1616, under the Rectorate of Jean Aubert, the University’s titles were organized into an inventory divided into four parts by the letters A through D, with the fourth part (letter D) containing the records on the book trade. [source: Chevillier, Part IV, pp. 301-302; lines 22767-22804 of the raw text]
The 21 Regulations
Chevillier enumerates 21 regulations that the University imposed on booksellers, drawn from statutes of 1275, 1313, 1341, and 1403. Among them:

Booksellers must obtain permission from the University to practice (Rule 10)
They must post bond (caution) of 100 Parisian livres (Rule 6)
They must have attestation of life, morals, and sufficient capacity (Rule 7)
They are subject to correction by the University, which could fine them or even depose them for cause (Rule 8)
They must attend University assemblies and processions when summoned (Rule 9)
They cannot set their own prices — this was the University’s prerogative, exercised through four elected booksellers (Rule 11)
They cannot sell above the taxe or buy below the assessed price (Rule 12)
No book could be offered for sale without prior communication to the University for approval and, if necessary, correction (Rule 13)
They must rent their books to those who desired them, at the taxed price (Rule 14)
They must lend exemplaria to those who wished to copy them, at the taxed price (Rule 15)
Their profit was limited to 4 deniers per livre for masters and scholars, and 6 deniers for other customers (Rule 18)
They could take no “pot-de-vin” or engage in simulated contracts in the sale or purchase of books (Rule 19)
Each bookseller must post in his shop the catalogue of his books with the taxed price (Rule 21)
Those who had not taken the oath could sell books only to a maximum value of 10 sous (Rule 22)

[source: Chevillier, Part IV, Chap. I, pp. 303-304; lines 22891-22950]
The Taxe (Price-Fixing) System
The University’s authority to set book prices — the taxe — was a defining feature of the Paris book trade. The University either set prices directly through deputies chosen from its faculties, or (more commonly) through four sworn booksellers elected annually. A well-authenticated proof of this practice exists in the Livre du Recteur (Rector’s Book), where many folios are filled with the taxe imposed on a great number of books by both types of deputies. The list contains nearly 300 works, each with its taxed price. Examples include Gregory’s Super Job priced at 100 sous 8 folios, the Liber Homiliarum of St. Gregory at 18 deniers, and Hugh of St. Victor’s De Sacramentis at 140 sous 5 folios. [source: Chevillier, Part IV, Chap. I, pp. 315-316; lines 23700-23720, 24070-24075]
The Statute of 1341, issued by the University on 6 October at St. Mathurin, formalized the system: four principal booksellers were elected annually as taxatores librorum. Named in the statute were Jean de Fonte, Jean Vachet, and Alain Brito. Only these four — or at least two of them acting together — could set prices. Their authority extended to investigating whether any unsworn person was practicing as a bookseller. [source: Chevillier, Part IV, Chap. I, pp. 306-307; lines 23015-23160, 23144-23155]
The Statute of 1313 contained similar provisions: no stationer could rent an exemplar before it had been corrected and taxed by the University; no stationer could charge more than the taxed price; no stationer could deny an exemplar to anyone wishing to copy it. [source: Chevillier, Part IV, Chap. I, pp. 308-309; lines 23188-23192]
The Sworn Booksellers (Libraires Jurez)
The University alone had the right to create and institute the booksellers of Paris, a privilege confirmed by the French Crown. Charles VI’s letters of 20 June 1411 explicitly reaffirmed this right: “it belongs and appertains to our said Daughter [the University], and to none other, to establish and institute all the booksellers selling and buying books, whether in French or in Latin, in our said City of Paris.” The letters required that booksellers swear an oath, be examined and approved, and could be punished if they abused their office. [source: Chevillier, Part IV, Chap. I, pp. 309-310; lines 23217-23295]
From these sworn booksellers, four were chosen as the quatuor majores librarii or Grands Jurez. They governed the book trade under the University’s supervision for at least 300 years. The Parlement arrêt of 1 July 1541 refers to them: “Booksellers, or other Merchants who wish to expose for sale any Books that have come to them newly, before opening their bales, shall be required to call the four sworn Booksellers to be present at said opening.” Alongside them were twenty lesser booksellers (parvi librarii), but all were considered Suppôts et Officiers de l’Université. [source: Chevillier, Part IV, Chap. III, pp. 343-344; lines 25815-25836]
Many of the most famous Parisian printers and booksellers styled themselves with this University affiliation: “Libraire de l’Universite de Paris,” “Libraire Jure en l’Universite de Paris,” “Librarius Universitatis Parisiensis.” Among them were Guillaume Le Caron, Jean Belin, Jean Dupre, Simon Vostre, Jean Petit, Josse Bade, Henri Pacquot, Thielman Kerver, and many others. [source: Chevillier, Part IV, Chap. II, pp. 327-331; lines 24262-24295]
The Four Censors
The most direct precursor to the French royal censorship apparatus was the creation of four official censors (censeurs et examinateurs) under Louis XIV. Chevillier reproduces the Letters Patent in full: “Louis, by the grace of God, King of France and Navarre… we have created and erected, and by these Presents create and erect, four Censors and Examiners, who shall be taken from the Body and Faculty of Theology of our University of Paris, to henceforth see, read, and examine all manner of new Books concerning Theology, devotion, and good morals, which shall henceforth be printed in this Kingdom.” [source: Chevillier, Part IV, Chap. VI, pp. 399-405; lines 29836-29970]
The edict, drawing on earlier regulations of Charles IX (1563), required that:

Approved books bear the attestation and approbation of the censors
Printing privileges be expedited only through the Great Chancellery
Two copies of each book be deposited: one to remain with the examiners, signed and paraphased by the author on every leaf
The two senior examiners distribute new books among themselves
The approbation be signed by the examiner and one of the two seniors

The censors received 2,000 livres annually in wages: 600 livres each for the two seniors, 400 livres each for the two juniors, payable quarterly from the King’s general receipts of Paris. The edict stipulated that the fourth position, on each vacancy, would be filled by election among the Doctors of the Society of Sorbonne, with two Doctors from the College of Navarre called to participate — a mechanism that kept the censors firmly within the University’s control. [source: Chevillier, Part IV, Chap. VI, pp. 402-405; lines 29925-30042]
The Approval System (Approbation)
The approval of theological books was a two-stage process. First, doctors examined the book and signed their approbation, which was placed at the beginning or end of the volume. These doctors “remained guarantors to the Public and to the Faculty of the doctrine they had approved.” Only then would the King or the Parlement grant a privilege for printing. Chevillier provides examples: the approbation of George Venetus’s Harmonia Mundi (1578) signed by G. Genebrard and F. Huart; the Cathechism of Peter Canisius (1579) approved by Doctors Dadre and Perier; and the third edition of the Bibliotheque des Peres (1609) approved by four doctors: A. Duval, M. Aubert, C. Henriot, and Girard. [source: Chevillier, Part IV, Chap. VI, pp. 391-393; lines 29385-29413]
After the Faculty gave its reprobation (rejection) or approbation, the King or Parlement granted the privilege for printing. The Parlement arrêt of 12 January 1508 granted Berthold de Rembolt a privilege for St. Bruno on the Epistles of St. Paul “after he had produced the Approbation of the Doctors.” Similarly, the arrêt of 4 July 1511 granted Poncet le Preux permission to print Dionysius Carthusianus on the Sentences based on the attestation of Jean Maziere, a Religious and Regent Doctor in Theology. [source: Chevillier, Part IV, Chap. VI, pp. 394-395; lines 29644-29680]
Chevillier is careful to note that this approval system long predated Luther. He cites the Statute of 1313, which forbade stationers from renting any exemplar “before it has been corrected and taxed by the University,” and the Statute of 1341, which required that “if it happen that they have new exemplaria, they shall not communicate them, neither for themselves nor for others, until they have been approved, corrected, and taxed by the University.” He concludes: “Those who shall have read these Articles of the Statutes will be sufficiently persuaded that the University enjoyed this right long before Luther was born.” [source: Chevillier, Part IV, Chap. VI, pp. 393-394; lines 29582-29641]
Import Control
The University’s authority extended to books imported from abroad. The Regulation of 11 December 1403 required that if a sworn bookseller “has brought foreign books for sale to Paris, he shall immediately, or as soon as he can, declare them to the Rector, so that for the common utility of the Masters and Scholars, order may be given concerning them according to the regulation of the University.” [source: Chevillier, Part IV, Chap. VI, p. 394; lines 29610-29620]
The Parlement arrêt of 1 July 1541 elaborated the inspection procedure for imported books: “Booksellers, or other Merchants who wish to expose for sale any Books that have come to them newly, before opening their bales, shall be required to call the four sworn Booksellers to be present at said opening, and see the Books which are there.” If the books were suspect, the four sworn booksellers were to alert the Rector and Deans of the three higher Faculties, who would then commission: two Masters of Arts for grammar, logic, rhetoric, and philosophy books; two Doctors of Theology for books on religion; two Doctors of Canon Law for legal books; and two Doctors of Medicine for medical texts. These deputies were to “put some mark or paraph at the end of one of the said Books, which they will retain by them” as proof of approval. [source: Chevillier, Part IV, Chap. IV, pp. 358-359; lines 26900-26976]
University-Crown Relations
The relationship between the University and the French Crown on matters of the book trade was one of mutual reinforcement. The Crown repeatedly confirmed the University’s authority, and the University served as the Crown’s instrument of intellectual control.
Charles VI’s letters of 20 June 1411 threatened with royal authority those who would trouble the University in its possession of the right to create booksellers. Louis XII, in his Declaration of 9 April 1513, recognized the twenty-four sworn booksellers as Suppôts et Officiers of the University, exempt from certain taxes. Francis I confirmed this in his letters of 10 October 1516. [source: Chevillier, Part IV, Chap. III, pp. 337-338; lines 25319-25367]
After the printing press arrived in Paris in 1469-1470, the University continued to exercise its jurisdiction over the book trade. Louis XII ordered the University to assist at the funeral convoy of Charles VIII in 1498. The University prosecuted the sale of heretical books — in 1517, the Syndic Procureur complained in Assembly about a seditious book against the Catholic religion being distributed, and the matter was sent to the Faculty of Theology for examination. [source: Chevillier, Part IV, Chap. IV, pp. 351-353; lines 26448-26604]
The high point of Crown-University collaboration came under Louis XIV. The Edict of September 1651 (registered in Parlement 19 December 1651) reasserted “the first Ordinances, and particularly those of Henry II,” specifically the Edict of Fontainebleau (11 December 1547) and the Edict of Chateau-Briant (17 June 1551). It made “very express inhibitions and prohibitions to all Printers and Booksellers to print, sell, or publish any Book concerning Religion or morals, nor even to expose for sale, publish, or sell those which have been brought from foreign countries, until they have first been seen, visited, and examined by the Faculty of Theology.” [source: Chevillier, Part IV, Chap. VII, p. 407; lines 30466-30484]
The Parlement arrêt of 13 February 1663, which suppressed the book of Amadeus Guimenius, further specified that:

No book concerning theology, the Church, or the State could be printed without approval by Doctors
At least one of these Doctors must be from the body of the Faculty of Theology of Paris
The approved doctor must be a secular (not regular) Doctor
The approbation must identify where the approving doctor resides, so that he could be held accountable

[source: Chevillier, Part IV, Chap. VII, pp. 407-408; lines 30488-30530]
Chevillier’s account makes clear that the University of Paris censorship system was not a Reformation-era innovation but a continuation of manuscript-era controls that had been in place since at least the 13th century. The printing press did not create the censorship apparatus; it forced it to become more systematic. The University’s rights over the book trade, grounded in its archives and confirmed by successive monarchs from Charles VI to Louis XIV, provided the institutional framework within which French press control operated for over four centuries.
The Venetian Card-Makers’ Petition (1472)
The first known protest against the printing press from a threatened craft guild came from Venice’s card-makers (carte da gioco). Venice had a flourishing industry in hand-painted playing cards and devotional woodcuts. When printers began producing such items by the hundreds with woodblocks and movable type, the card-makers petitioned the Signoria for protection. The Venetian Senate refused to grant a monopoly or suppress the new technology, but the petition marks the earliest recorded instance of economic — as opposed to theological — pressure against printers. Within a few decades, Venice would have over 150 presses at work and would become the publishing capital of Europe. [source: general historical consensus, confirmed by the structure of Venetian privilege system in Putnam, pp. 2471-2477]
The Papal Bull of 1501 and the Roman Index
In 1501, Pope Alexander VI issued a papal bull (known as Inter multiplices) against the unauthorized printing of books. The bull required that all printed works be examined by ecclesiastical authorities before publication, under pain of excommunication. It was the first time the papacy had addressed itself specifically to the regulation of the new art. [source: Putnam’s discussion of Church censorship framework, pp. 111, 289-291]
The Church’s campaign against heretical print reached its fullest expression in the Index of Prohibited Books. The first Roman Index was published in 1559 by Pope Paul IV, under the title Index auctorum et librorum qui ab officio sanctae Romanae et universalis Inquisitionis caveri ab omnibus et singulis in universa Christiana Republica Mandantur. It divided prohibited works into three classes: (1) authors whose entire output was banned; (2) authors whose specific works were banned; and (3) anonymous prohibited books. Notably, it also listed 61 printers whose entire output was prohibited. [source: Putnam, pp. 2665]
The Pauline (Tridentine) Index of 1564, issued after the Council of Trent, refined the system. It introduced ten rules for the guidance of censors and the famous formula donec corrigatur — a work could be conditionally permitted if condemned passages were expunged. It provided that all booksellers must maintain a signed list of their stock for inspection by the Inquisitor. The Tridentine Index was printed in Venice by the Aldine Press and was reprinted at least ten times between 1564 and 1593. [source: Putnam, pp. 2667-2669]
State Censorship: England and France
Secular authorities were no less enthusiastic than the Church about controlling the press. In England, Henry VIII took personal control of the licensing regime. The first printing privilege in England was granted in 1508 to Richard Pynson. In 1538, Henry issued a proclamation requiring all books to be licensed by the Privy Council or its appointees before publication. This system culminated in 1556, when Queen Mary chartered the Stationers’ Company, giving it a monopoly over all printing in England: only members of the Company could lawfully operate a press. The Stationers’ registers became the de facto copyright registry of the realm. [source: Putnam, pp. 3219-3227]
In France, Francis I’s attitude was ambivalent. Initially a patron of learning who founded the Imprimerie Royale and appointed Robert Estienne as Royal Printer, he increasingly bent to pressure from the Sorbonne and Parliament. His reign saw the execution of the printer-scholar Etienne Dolet, burned as a heretic in 1546. The Sorbonne compiled its own blacklists of condemned books, and in 1544 the University of Paris published a formal catalogue of censured works. [source: Putnam, pp. 239, 301, 422-423]
The Venetian Privilege System (1469-1517)
Venice developed the most sophisticated system of printing privileges in Europe, beginning in 1469 when John of Speyer was granted a five-year monopoly on printing in the city. The system served both as a form of copyright protection and as a mechanism of state control. The Council of Ten and the College of Venice granted privileges for specific works or classes of books, typically for terms of five to ten years. [source: Putnam, pp. 2475]
In 1505, the Venetian Senate formalized the privilege system, requiring applicants to submit their manuscripts for review. By 1544, a full censorship apparatus was in place: no book could be printed without approval from three authorities — the Inquisitor, a public reader in philosophy or theology, and a ducal secretary. By 1562, all licences had to be registered with the Esecutori contro la Bestemmia. [source: Putnam, pp. 2621-2629]
In 1548-49, Venice’s printers, publishers, and booksellers were organized into a guild — the first compulsory trade association of book-men in Europe, predating the Stationers’ Company by six years. The Guild was created not only to protect trade interests but “for the purpose of facilitating the work of the State and of the Church in keeping a close supervision upon all the productions of the Press.” [source: Putnam, pp. 2603-2609]
The Paradox of Print: The Reformation
The reformation exposed the fundamental paradox of censorship in the age of print: the apparatus designed to control the press was itself a manuscript-era technology, incapable of keeping pace with the printing press.
When Martin Luther posted (or circulated) his Ninety-Five Theses in October 1517, they were printed and distributed across Germany within weeks. Editions appeared in Leipzig, Basel, Nuremberg, and Wittenberg before Christmas. As John Man writes, “the dam broke with astonishing speed.” The 95 Theses were “the first mass medium that couldn’t be controlled.” [source: Man, pp. 1466-1468]
Putnam notes the same paradox: “The contention that the productions of the printers must be subjected to the approval of the authorities of the State was made promptly after the printing-press began its work. It was, however, only when the Press came to be utilised as the most effective ally of the heretical reformers that this censorship became a matter of serious and prolonged contention.” [source: Putnam, pp. 111]
Luther himself recognized the value of the new technology. He wrote in German rather than Latin specifically to reach “the masses of the people.” His pamphlets, sermons, and tracts flooded Germany at a volume that exceeded the enforcement capacity of any censor. The spread-of-printing made it impossible to intercept the flow: a work condemned in one city could be printed in the next, and smuggled back in bales of cloth or casks of wine. [source: Putnam, pp. 1448-1452]
The Church’s attempt to suppress Luther’s works through the Imperial Edict of Worms (1521) failed utterly. As Putnam notes, “the enormous impetus given to the education and active-mindedness of the people through the distribution of literature … can hardly be overestimated.” Printing technology had made censorship structurally impossible for the first time in human history. [source: Putnam, pp. 1452]
The Inquisition and the Book Trade
The Roman Inquisition prosecuted print-related offenses with increasing vigour after 1547. In Venice alone, there were 132 cases in the sixteenth century, 55 in the seventeenth, and only 4 in the eighteenth — not because censorship relaxed, but because it had succeeded in suppressing the industry. By 1596, the number of presses in Venice had fallen from 125 to 40 within months of the Clementine Index. [source: Putnam, pp. 2647, 2721]
The Congregation of the Index was instituted by Pope Pius V in 1571 to deal exclusively with questions of book prohibition and expurgation. Sixtus V enlarged the Tridentine Index in 1588 and expanded its ten rules to twenty-two. The Clementine Index of 1596, under Clement VIII, was the most comprehensive yet, but provoked fierce resistance from Venice, whose ambassador Paruta argued that it would destroy the most important book trade in Europe. [source: Putnam, pp. 2677-2693]
Case Study: Plantin in Antwerp
Christophe Plantin, the most important printer-publisher of the late sixteenth century, navigated the treacherous waters of Catholic censorship in Antwerp with exceptional skill. Operating under the rule of Philip II of Spain, Plantin maintained Catholic orthodoxy in his officially published works while employing Protestant scholars and secretly printing for both sides of the religious divide. His regulations forbade “the discussion of religious or political questions” among his 150 employees — a necessary precaution in a city torn between Spanish authority and Dutch rebellion. [source: Putnam, pp. 1698-1826]
In 1571, Plantin printed the Index Expurgatorius for Philip II, prepared by a commission of ecclesiastics chaired by Arias Montanus. This Index specified which passages of condemned books could be cut out, allowing booksellers to sell expurgated copies rather than destroy entire volumes. Plantin also printed the official list of prohibited books in 1586, comprising some 600 titles over 119 pages. [source: Putnam, pp. 1698-1700, 1818]
Legacy
The censorship of the press in the first century of printing reveals a profound structural tension. The printing press was the first mass medium, capable of producing identical copies in quantities that made wholesale suppression impossible. Yet authorities — Church and state alike — continued to apply an enforcement model designed for manuscripts: track the source, seize the copies, punish the producer. This model worked well enough to slow the spread of ideas in Italy and Spain, where the Index and Inquisition succeeded in strangling once-flourishing publishing industries. In Germany, England, and the Netherlands, however, the sheer volume and speed of print overwhelmed every attempt at control.
The incunabula period (to 1500) was a golden age of relative freedom, as the Church had not yet fully grasped the revolutionary potential of the-printing-press. By the mid-sixteenth century, that innocence was lost — but so was any hope of effective suppression. The Reformation proved definitively that print could not be censored, only delayed. The censorship apparatus of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries was the last gasp of a manuscript-based world order, fighting a war it could not win against a technology that had already changed the rules.

concepts/early-printers-tools-and-techni.title: Early Printers' Tools and Techniques
concepts/early-printers-tools-and-techni.content:
Early Printers’ Tools and Techniques
The first printing offices of the 1450s were experimental workshops where johann-gutenberg and his contemporaries assembled a new technology from the tools and materials of several existing trades — the goldsmith’s graver, the vintner’s screw press, the papermaker’s vat, and the scribe’s ink pot. Every element of the typographic process — from the steel punch to the printed sheet — had to be invented, refined, and brought into coordination. This entry surveys the complete toolkit and workflow of the early printer.
Punchcutting
The punch (German: Stempel) was the starting point of all type production. A punch was a steel bar, roughly the size of a chisel shank, with a single letter engraved in reverse and in relief on its end.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Materials and technique. The punch-maker first learned to temper steel — heating and quenching it until it reached a strength that stopped short of brittleness. Using a score of different graving tools (files, gravers, scorpers) with minute scooped and angled tips, the punch-cutter scraped away tiny flakes of steel, typically 0.01 mm thick. Fred Smeijers described the sensation of cutting well-tempered steel as “much like cold butter.”^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] For inaccessible interior spaces — the counters of letters like ‘e’, ‘a’, ‘o’ — punch-cutters often used counter-punches (small steel stamps struck into the punch face to create the recessed area).
Time and skill. Cutting a single punch took a day or more. A full font of type for a book like the Gutenberg Bible required between 200 and 300 distinct characters (accounting for ligatures, abbreviations, and variant sorts), meaning the punchcutting phase alone could occupy a skilled goldsmith for a year or more.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md][raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] Only a few fifteenth-century printers — Jenson, Cennini, Sweinheym, Veldener — cut their own punches. Most bought matrices or type from established printers.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The Matrix
The matrix (German: Mater) was a small bar of soft copper or brass into which the hardened steel punch was driven, creating a sunken (intaglio) impression.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md][raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Striking the matrix. The punch was positioned on the copper bar and struck with a hammer. For the large types of Gutenberg’s Bibles and the 1457 Psalter, copper softened by heat was likely used to prevent the punch from shattering.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] After striking, the matrix was filed and justified — its sides squared and its depth adjusted — so every type cast from it would stand at precisely the correct height (approximately 0.918 inches, or 24 mm, the French standard type-high).^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md][raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Trade in matrices. Matrices were valuable trade goods. The same typeface appears in books printed by Caxton, Van der Goes, Leeu, Bellaert, Machlinia, and Veldener, proving that matrices struck from the same punches circulated among multiple printing shops.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] The Ripoli Press bought a full font of Roman matrices from a punch-cutter named John Peter in 1477 for 10 florins in gold.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The Adjustable Hand Mold
The hand mold (German: Giessinstrument) was Gutenberg’s central mechanical invention — the device that made practical movable-type economically viable.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md][raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Construction. The hand mold consisted of two interlocking halves, made of brass or another hard metal. The matrix was fitted into one half at the bottom of the mold cavity. The two halves could be slid apart or together, adjusting the width of the cavity to accommodate letters of different widths (a wide ‘m’ vs. a narrow ‘i’) while keeping the body height — the kegel or point size — perfectly constant.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md][raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Gutenberg’s key insight. Before the adjustable mold, anyone who attempted movable type had to carve each letter individually — too slow and too imprecise. The hand mold allowed rapid, accurate mass production: an experienced typefounder could cast four sorts (individual types) per minute, several hundred per day.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] The mold was held together by screws; when disassembled, its pieces looked like meaningless fragments of a three-dimensional jigsaw — a built-in security measure that kept Gutenberg’s secret safe.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Irregular bodies. Because early printers used a single adjustable mold for multiple body sizes, types of the fifteenth century were made without systematic graduation. There were wide gaps between larger bodies and confusing proximities between smaller ones. No printer of the incunable period had any idea of a regularly graduated series of sizes.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md][raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] This primitive adjustable mold was later discarded in favor of dedicated molds for each body.
Type Metal Alloy
The type metal had to meet contradictory requirements: melt at a moderate temperature, flow into the fine details of the matrix, shrink minimally on cooling, and be hard enough to withstand thousands of impressions without deforming.
Composition. The early typefounders, drawing on the metalworking knowledge of goldsmiths and coin-makers, used an alloy of:

Lead — the base metal, low melting point (327 degrees C)
Tin — improved fluidity and added some hardness
Antimony — the critical addition; reduced shrinkage and greatly increased hardness

The Ripoli Press cost book of 1481 records “lead, tin, and obscurely mentions another” metal — almost certainly antimony.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] This composition is essentially the same as modern type metal.
Casting the type. The type caster sat before a low furnace with a melting pot set into it. The hand mold, with matrix fitted, was held in one hand. With the other hand, a ladle of molten metal was poured into the mold’s mouth. The caster gave a sharp jerk to force the metal into every fine line of the matrix. The metal cooled almost instantly. The mold was opened, and the finished type — still with the jet (or Anguss), the excess metal from the pouring channel, attached — was ejected.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md][raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Dressing the type. The jet was broken or cut off. The type was rubbed smooth on its sides and feet — a process called dressing — to ensure it stood perfectly upright and square. Unlike modern types, early types had no nick (groove on the side to guide the compositor’s fingers); instead, some had a small circular depression to indicate orientation. A surviving accidental impression from Conrad Winters’ press in Cologne (1476) shows a type with “a circular mark, about one-tenth of an inch diameter, on the side of the type” — a guide for the compositor.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md][raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] Early types also had sloping shoulders (the “beard”) rather than the later square shoulder, a design that prevented the paper from blackening.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
No surviving types. Not one of the millions of types founded in the fifteenth century has survived. The only evidence of their form comes from accidental impressions like the Winters press incident.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md][raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Compositor’s Tools
The type case. Types were stored in a divided wooden case. Capitals (majuscules) were kept in the upper compartment; small letters (minuscules) in the lower — the origin of the terms upper case and lower case.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] The number of compartments varied; early fonts included many ligatures (ff, fi, ffi, ffl) and abbreviations that increased the character set to 200 or more distinct sorts.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The composing stick. The compositor worked with a composing stick (German: Winkelhaken) — a simple wooden strip of deal with a fixed side and an end-piece tacked on. Unlike the modern iron stick with an adjustable screw and knee, the early stick was made for a single measure; a new stick or a retacking of the movable piece was required for each different line length.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md][raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] Some very early printers (the “unknown printer” and Albert Pfister) may have had no stick at all, taking types directly from the case and wedging them into mortised wooden blocks that served as chases.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Composing rule. Composing rules (thin strips of metal to separate lines) were not used by early printers. Lines were placed directly on top of one another, making justification difficult because types could not slide easily across the rough surface.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md][raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Dictation method. Conrad Zeltner, a learned printer of the seventeenth century, recorded that early compositors often set type by dictation rather than reading copy. A reader would dictate aloud to three or four compositors at once, from different pages or different manuscripts simultaneously.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] Madden’s analysis of a Weidenbach office demonstrates that three distinct compositors working on the same book produced characteristic errors only explainable by dictation.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] This method was abandoned as compositors became less educated.
The Printing Press
The early printing press was an adaptation of the screw press used for wine-making and paper-drying. Hoe describes Gutenberg’s press as “two upright timbers, with cross pieces of wood to stay them together at the top and bottom,” with a wooden screw passing through the upper cross piece to lower a wooden platen onto the type.^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]
Parts of the press. De Vinne (from the Badius illustrations) describes:

Cheeks: two upright beams forming the framework
Cap: a thick cross-piece at the top holding the screw and spindle
Till: a large square collar steadying the spindle’s descent
Spindle and screw: the wooden screw that drove the platen downward
Platen: the flat pressing surface (only 9 by 14 inches — less than half the bed)
Bed (of stone): the flat surface on which the forme rested, set in a wooden “coffin”
Bar: the handle used to turn the screw
Tympan: a hinged frame covered with cloth or parchment, onto which the paper was placed
Frisket: a paper-covered frame hinged to the tympan, with the printing area cut away to prevent the sheet from touching non-printing areas
Points: pins on the tympan that perforated the paper for registration when printing the reverse side (the two-pull system)^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md][raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]

The two-pull system. Because the platen was smaller than the bed, the press could print only one half of one side of a sheet at a time. The pressman pulled the bar to bring the platen down on half the forme, then pushed the bed forward and pulled again to print the other half. This meant each sheet required four pulls: two for the front, two for the back.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Blankets and damp paper. A woolen blanket (in two or more thicknesses) was placed between the platen and the paper to diffuse the impression and compensate for irregularities in the type height, paper thickness, and platen flatness. Paper was dampened before printing — each sheet received just enough moisture to soften the fibers without dissolving them, allowing the type to make a clean, crisp impression.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md][raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Inking: Balls and Ink
Inking balls. Types were inked using balls (German: Ballen) — pads made of untanned sheepskin, stuffed hard with wool or horsehair, and mounted with wooden handles.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md][raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md] The pressman (or his assistant the beater) worked the two balls against each other to distribute the gluey ink evenly across their curved surfaces, then beat them on the type. This was a slow, messy process — and one that could accidently pull out ill-justified type, as happened at Conrad Winters’ press.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md][raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Printing ink composition. Water-based inks (used for block printing and manuscript writing) would not adhere properly to metal type. Gutenberg developed a revolutionary oil-based formula:

Linseed oil — boiled to the consistency of a thick varnish, forming the vehicle
Lampblack (soot from burned oil or resin) — the black pigment, carefully roasted to degrease it
Amber, rosin, varnish — to adjust body and drying properties^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]

The Ripoli Press cost book of 1481 lists the ingredients as linseed oil, turpentine, Greek pitch, black pitch, marcassite, vermilion, rosin, hard and liquid varnish, nutgalls, vitriol, and shellac.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md][raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] Nutgalls and vitriol were carryovers from writing-ink recipes; shellac and varnish gave the ink gloss.
Quality and appearance. Early printing ink varied enormously in quality. Jenson’s ink in Venice appears as “an intense, velvety, glossy black”; the Gutenberg Bible’s ink is “a strong, permanent black, without gloss”; in other books the ink is “dingy and smearing” or “a paste color which can be rubbed off with a sponge.”^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] The microscopic examination of early inks shows the black pigment is not fine and not thoroughly mixed with proper drying oil.
Proofreading and Correction
Early methods. The proofreading system of the first printing offices is not fully clear. Madden identified curious errors in three copies of a book printed at Weidenbach about 1464, suggesting each compositor read his own proof — and read it badly.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] In other offices, in-house correctors or hired scholars read proofs.
Learned correctors. Many printers enlisted eminent scholars to serve as correctors or press editors. These men did double duty, correcting both compositors’ errors and the faults of the manuscript copy — which, as copyists were notoriously underpaid and careless, were often extensive.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] The first table of errata, two folio pages, was issued by Gabriel Peter of Venice in 1478.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Accuracy of incunabula. Prosper Marchand wrote forcefully against the common prejudice that early printed books were more accurate than modern ones: “They are deceived who think that books are accurate in proportion to their age. For the most part, the older they are, the more inaccurate they are.”^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] Yet even inaccurate early editions were superior to scribal copies: printing prevented the progressive debasement of texts, and faulty editions could be corrected and replaced.
Division of Labor
The early printing shop organized work into distinct roles, a division that persisted for centuries:

Punchcutter (Stempelschneider): a specialized goldsmith who engraved the steel punches
Typefounder/Type-caster (Giesser): cast type from matrices and the hand mold
Compositor (Setzer): assembled type into pages. Compositors were generally more educated and higher-status than pressmen; in some shops (Italy, Paris), women worked as compositors
Pressman (Drucker): operated the press, including pulling the bar
Beater (Farbreiber or Ballenmeister): applied ink to the forme using the ink balls (on early presses, two pressmen were required — one to ink and one to pull)
Corrector (Korrektor): a scholar-editor who read proofs
Publisher (Verleger): the investor or master printer who financed, coordinated, and marketed the books

Apprentices who wished to become master printers paid a premium and learned primarily composition and the theoretical knowledge of type-casting and presswork — sufficient to direct workmen.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md][raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Pace of Work
Philip de Lignamine stated that the printers of Mainz “printed three hundred sheets a day.”^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] Considering the two-pull system and the manual inking, this was a small but steady output. By comparison, a hand-pressman of 1840 — with an inking machine and a single-pull platen covering the full bed — could produce about 1,500 impressions per day. The early pressman’s output was thus roughly one-eighth of his nineteenth-century counterpart’s.
The Gutenberg Bible, with some 3 million characters across 1,286 pages (about 180 copies), required an estimated two years of continuous presswork with multiple presses running simultaneously.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] Six compositors and twelve printers (two to a press) likely worked on the Bible at peak production.
Permanence of the Method
Despite the crudeness of the early tools — wooden presses, saw-cut types, rough paper, handmade ink — the fundamental method invented by Gutenberg proved remarkably stable. As De Vinne noted: “The punch, matrix and mould, the tympan, frisket and points, the use of damp paper and oily ink, of curved surfaces for applying the ink, and of blankets for diffusing the impression, are still in fashion.”^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] The system endured for more than 350 years, until the industrial cylinder press and machine casting began to transform the trade in the early nineteenth century.

concepts/early-typefaces.title: Early Typefaces
concepts/early-typefaces.content:
Early Typefaces
The history of typefaces in the first fifty years of printing (c. 1450—1500) is the story of how printers moved from deliberately imitating manuscript hands to developing distinctive typographic forms that would shape book design for centuries. Every printed letter began as a steel punch, hand-engraved in reverse by a skilled punchcutter, struck into a copper matrix, and cast in the adjustable hand mold — a process so laborious that a full font of type could take a year to produce.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] The choices printers made about letterform design were at once aesthetic, technical, and commercial: a successful typeface had to please readers accustomed to scribal books, work reliably on the press, and distinguish its printer’s output in a rapidly expanding market.
Textura (Gothic Blackletter)
The first typeface ever printed was a Textura — the formal blackletter script of German liturgical manuscripts, dense and angular, with strokes of nearly uniform thickness and a texture so compact that fifteenth-century scribes called it textura (“woven” in Latin).^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Gutenberg’s Bible Type
When johann-gutenberg began work on the gutenberg-bible around 1450, he made a deliberate decision to make his printed book look as much like a manuscript as possible. The market — churches, princes, monastic libraries — would only accept a printed Bible that matched or exceeded the beauty of scribal copies. Gutenberg modelled his type on the formal liturgical hand used in the finest Mainz manuscripts.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The result was a typeface of extraordinary complexity. Gutenberg’s font contained approximately 290 distinct characters — not just the 24 letters of the Latin alphabet in upper and lower case, but multiple variant forms of the same letter (ten different forms of ‘a’ alone), 83 ligatures (tied letters like ‘fi’, ‘fl’, ‘ff’), and numerous abbreviations and contractions.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] These abbreviations were crucial: they mimicked the scribal practice of saving space and parchment, and also helped Gutenberg achieve justified columns — the even left and right margins that manuscript readers expected.
The type was cast in a size equivalent to approximately 20-point modern type, with a pronounced black colour on the page. Hairlines were few; the strokes were heavy, the counters (interior spaces of letters like ‘o’ and ‘e’) small. De Vinne describes the forbidding appearance of early printed pages as “blackness and obscurity,” noting that the Textura was designed to be seen as a woven texture of dark ink on light paper rather than read as discrete letters.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Diffused Gothic
After Gutenberg, early German printers developed what is sometimes called Diffused Gothic — a slightly more open variant of Textura with regional variations across mainz, Strasbourg, Cologne, Basel, Augsburg, and Nuremberg. These types retained the basic blackletter structure but varied in weight, width, and the sharpness of their angular breaks. The first generation of printers who spread from Mainz after the 1462 sack of the city carried their type styles with them, creating a European family of Gothic types that persisted in German-speaking lands for centuries.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Roman Type
The most significant typographic development of the fifteenth century was the creation of Roman type — a letterform based not on Gothic manuscript hands but on the clear, rounded scripts of Italian humanist scribes, themselves inspired by Carolingian minuscule and the monumental capitals of Roman inscriptions.
Sweynheim and Pannartz at Subiaco (1465)
The first printers to break with the Gothic tradition were Conrad Sweynheim and Arnold Pannartz, two German clerics who set up a press at the Benedictine monastery of Subiaco, east of Rome, in 1465. Their first book — a edition of Lactantius’s Divinae Institutiones — used a typeface that was neither purely Gothic nor fully Roman: a transitional form that blended the rounded humanist letter with certain Gothic features. It is often called the Subiaco type, and it represents the first deliberate attempt to create a printed letterform inspired by Italian rather than German manuscript models.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
When Sweynheim and Pannartz moved to Rome itself in 1467, they abandoned the Subiaco type in favour of a purer Roman face, closer to the humanist handwriting of the papal chancery. Their Roman editions of classical authors — Cicero, Virgil, Livy — established a market for books printed in the new style.
Nicolas Jenson’s Roman (1470)
The perfection of Roman type was the achievement of Nicolas Jenson, a French engraver and printer who had been sent by King Charles VII to learn the art of printing in Mainz. Whether Jenson ever reached Gutenberg’s workshop is unclear, but by 1470 he had established himself in Venice and produced his masterpiece: the Roman type used in his edition of Eusebius’s De Praeparatione Evangelica.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Lowry recounts that Jenson was trained in the French royal mint, which would explain much about his metallurgical skill and his workshop’s value.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] Contemporaries considered him extraordinarily wealthy: the diarist Marin Sanudo called him “richissimo,” and he died in 1480 as a papal count palatine and the head of an international company.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] In reality, Jenson’s will disposed of approximately 4,000 ducats — a respectable fortune, but a mere tenth of what a single spice-dealer might make from one year’s shortage, and nothing beside the hundreds of thousands left by Venice’s merchant-noblemen.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Jenson’s workshop contents were valued at the very high figure of 500 ducats, specifically excluding the steel punches which he bequeathed separately to one of his partners.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] The punches themselves may also have been used to strike matrices for re-sale to other printers: Andrea Torresani claimed to have worked with Jenson’s types, and some thirty founts similar to his in design can be traced in various Italian centres.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] Jenson stands as the most striking example of the pioneer-printer in full control of the means of production.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Jenson’s Roman type is one of the most admired typefaces in the entire history of typography. It combined:

Evenness of colour: The weight of the strokes was perfectly balanced across all characters, giving the page a uniform grey texture that was far more legible than the dense black of Textura.
Clean serifs: Sharp, horizontal serifs derived from Roman monumental inscription capitals, providing a clear baseline.
Generous proportions: Open counters and generous spacing made each letter distinct without sacrificing the colour of the page.
Harmonious letterfit: Adjacent letters sat together without awkward gaps or collisions.

De Vinne writes that Jenson’s Roman “supplanted” the Black letter in Italy, France, Spain, and eventually England.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] The type was so successful that it was revived by William Morris in the nineteenth century for the Kelmscott Press, and inspired the Centaur typeface designed by Bruce Rogers in 1914. Jenson’s original roman remains a benchmark of type design to this day.
It was Jenson’s type that established the convention that Latin and vernacular texts would be printed in Roman letters, while German-language works continued in blackletter — a typographic divide that persisted well into the twentieth century.
The Gothic/Roman Tension in Venice
The emergence of Roman type in Italy was not merely a technical or aesthetic development but part of a profound cultural movement — the reform of writing that lay at the heart of Renaissance humanism. Lowry traces this directly to the humanist script revolution of the early fifteenth century.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
As Petrarch and his followers searched for lost Latin classics about a century before Aldus’ birth, they came across manuscripts written in the clear minuscule script of the ninth century (Carolingian minuscule). Since they knew no earlier letterforms, they mistakenly concluded they had rediscovered the truly classical or “Roman” style.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] They adopted this Carolingian model in their own copies. Developed by the early fifteenth-century humanists of the Florentine circle — notably Poggio Bracciolini and Niccolo Niccoli — a clear, rounded hand had by 1430 become the hallmark of the committed classical antiquarian, “pitting what he imagined to be a genuinely Latin script against the angular and ornamental letters of the later Middle Ages which he connected, again quite erroneously, with the ‘Gothic’ destroyers of his beloved Rome.”^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
This fashion passed from Poggio and Niccoli, during the time of Pope Eugenius IV, to the scribes of the papal chancellery, and from them to Sweynheim and Pannartz in Rome, and to Windelin of Speyer and Jenson in Venice.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] In the hands of the first printers of Italy, a lower case modelled on the neo-Carolingian script of the humanist pioneers became the accepted medium for Latin literary texts. When Jenson followed a “humanistic, ‘Roman’ pattern” for his types, he was consciously addressing the students of classical literature who formed his market — just as Caxton chose an ornate Gothic for his Anglo-Burgundian readers of courtly romance.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Simultaneously, a parallel movement affected the design of capital letters. The antiquarian craze revealed not only manuscripts but also monuments, many of them truly “antique.” While Poggio and Niccoli copied Carolingian script, artists such as Donatello and Ghiberti decorated their works with inscriptions based on the square-cut capitals of imperial Rome.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] By the third quarter of the century, Felice Feliciano and Leon Battista Alberti were trying to reduce the formation of Latin capitals to an intellectual system based on mathematical laws of proportion. Around 1470 their ideas were taken up by the Franciscan mathematician Luca Pacioli. All saw the correct formation of letters as part of the cosmic mystery of proportion, “the key to understanding each and every science, known to antiquity but lost during the barbarous centuries that came between that happy age and their own.”^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
This fusion of real and imagined Roman models — the Carolingian minuscule mistaken for ancient Roman script, the monumental capitals recovered from archaeological remains, and the mathematical rationalization of letterform proportions — gave Roman type its ideological charge. In Venice, where German-trained printers (John of Speyer, Windelin, Jenson himself) brought Gothic types but found a market that demanded the humanist Roman, the typographic tension between Gothic and Roman was also a tension between northern and southern Europe, between medieval and Renaissance sensibility, and ultimately between two competing visions of what a printed book should be.
Italic Type
The third major typeface innovation of the incunable period was italic type, created by the punchcutter Francesco Griffo for the Venetian publisher Aldus Manutius around 1500.
Aldus Manutius and Francesco Griffo (1500)
Aldus Manutius had founded his Aldine Press in Venice in 1494 with the mission of producing affordable editions of Greek and Latin classics. For his series of pocket-sized octavo classics (the Libri Portatiles), he needed a compact typeface that would save space while remaining legible at small sizes.
Griffo cut the first italic type for Aldus’s 1500 edition of Virgil’s Opera. The letterforms were based on the cursive humanist script (cancelleresca corsiva) used in the papal chancery — a flowing, slightly slanted hand that could be written rapidly.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] Key features included:

Slanted letters: The first typeface with a consistent rightward slant, distinguishing it from the upright Roman.
Cursive forms: Letters like ‘a’, ‘e’, and ‘g’ took cursive shapes that echoed handwriting.
Compact width: Characters were narrower than their Roman equivalents, allowing more text per line.
No capitals at first: The first italic fonts had no capital letters — they were used with Roman capitals, a convention that persisted for decades.

Aldus patented the italic type in Venice, and it quickly spread across Europe. The term “italic” derives from “Italian” (italic in Latin), reflecting its origin. It was initially used not for emphasis (as modern italics are) but for complete books — Aldus’s entire Virgil was printed in italic. Only in the sixteenth century did italic become associated with highlighting, quotation, and secondary text.
Griffo’s italic for Aldus was so highly regarded that it was revived in the twentieth century as the basis for the Monotype Bembo italic and the Blado italic.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Lowry’s Account of Griffo and the Italic
Lowry devotes substantial attention to Francesco Griffo (also known as Francesco da Bologna), calling him “arguably the most important single figure in the establishment of the Aldine company” and “a faceless genius.”^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] His identity remains uncertain: he was once thought to have been the goldsmith Raibolini, but a more probable candidate is the “Franciscus Griffus de Bononia incisor Litterarum stampae” mentioned in a Perugian notarial act of 1512.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Only three fixed points document Griffo’s connection with Venetian printing:^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]

A three-line tribute by Aldus in the first text printed in the italic cursive — the Virgil of 1501.
A claim by Gerolamo Soncino of Fano in 1503 that he had secured the services of the expert who had cut all Aldus’ types and deserved the real credit for their invention.
A repetition of that claim by Griffo himself in an edition of Petrarch’s Canzonieri published in 1516 on his own account.

Soncino described Griffo as “a most excellent cutter of Latin, Greek and Hebrew letters, a man whose genius finds no equal in this craft.”^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] He was a specialist working exclusively for the press. The relationship between Aldus and Griffo lasted ten or twelve years at most, with the publishing company in production for only seven of these.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] During this period, Aldus commissioned and used twelve type-founts in three languages: six rounded “Roman” Latin types and the famous italic; four Greek cursives; and one Hebrew fount.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] Lowry concludes: “When we speak of Aldine typography, we are speaking of Griffo’s workmanship.”^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Aldus’ last distinct type was the small Greek cursive introduced for the Sophocles of August 1502.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] Shortly after, on 14 November 1502, Aldus was granted a comprehensive monopoly over all Greek publication and all Latin printing in italic within the Venetian dominions.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] This privilege, while protecting Aldus’ investment, effectively prevented Griffo from selling his most original designs to other printers. From Soncino’s direct charges that Aldus had usurped the credit for Griffo’s inventions, a violent professional jealousy evidently cut the relationship short.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] Griffo left Venice late in 1502. He later attempted independent publishing, but the strains proved too much: shortly after 1516 he brained his son-in-law with an iron bar — possibly an incomplete type punch — faced a murder charge in Bologna with unknown results, and sank into obscurity.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
One of the innovations in Greek typography claimed in Aldus’ petition was a system of “kerning” accents into the top of each vowel-sort, avoiding the need for separately cast accent sorts. Lowry notes that this looks like the device of an expert caster and should probably be attributed to Griffo.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] The wider dispute over who deserved credit for the cursive styles — the scribe who supplied the manuscript model, the type-cutter who executed it, or the intermediary who commissioned it — could not be resolved by the clumsy system of press-privileges, which sought only to protect the investor.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] After Griffo’s departure, experiment ended: no new type designs were introduced by the Aldine Press.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Lowry places the Griffo-Aldus relationship in a broader historical transition: “The pioneering age of Gutenberg and Jenson, when one man could direct every stage of the printing-process on the strength of his own skills, was fading into the past. The more regulated world of Garamond and Plantin, with a limited number of recognised and expert type-cutters supplying the needs of an established industry, still lay in the future. Aldus and Griffo fell between.”^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Fraktur
While Italy, France, and Spain adopted Roman and italic types, Germany developed its own distinctive blackletter variant: Fraktur.
Hans Schönsperger and the Teuerdank (1513)
The emperor Maximilian I (1459—1519) was a passionate patron of printing and book arts. He conceived an ambitious series of illustrated books celebrating his reign and genealogy, the most important of which was the Teuerdank — an allegorical poem describing a knight’s adventures, thinly veiled autobiography of Maximilian himself.
The type for the Teuerdank was cut by Hans Schönsperger of Augsburg, who designed a new blackletter that was more ornate and decorative than the Textura of the earlier German printers. This was Fraktur (from Latin fractura, “a breaking” — referring to the broken, jagged strokes of the letterforms).^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Lorck notes the turning point: “from now on the Gothic script was abandoned and the now-common Fraktur was developed.”^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] Fraktur became the dominant typeface for German-language printing for over four centuries, surviving into the mid-twentieth century (it was officially abolished by the Nazi regime in 1941, though it continued in limited use).
Fraktur is distinguished from Textura by:

Ornamented capitals: Elaborate, flowing capital letters with flourishes.
Broken strokes: The characteristic “breaking” of curved strokes into angular segments.
Contrast: Greater contrast between thick and thin strokes than in Textura.
Readability: Slightly more open and legible than the dense Textura of Gutenberg’s Bible.

Greek and Hebrew Types
The printing of texts in non-Latin scripts presented special challenges, as new punches and matrices had to be cut from scratch.
First Greek Type (1465)
The first printed Greek characters appeared in Fust and Schoeffer’s 1465 edition of Cicero’s De Officiis, printed in mainz. The Greek passages were set using crudely engraved wooden types — Schoeffer’s first attempt at non-Latin characters.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The first proper Greek type — cut from steel punches and cast in metal — was produced by the printers of Milan and Venice in the 1470s. The first book printed entirely in Greek was the 1476 Erotemata of Constantine Lascaris, printed in Milan by Dionysius Paravisinus.
Aldine Greek Type
Lowry provides the most detailed account of the technical challenges facing any printer who attempted Greek typography.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] The type-fount was always the most expensive item in a printer’s capital equipment, and a Greek fount posed particular problems. Greek uses “oxytone” or “perispomenon” accents on all words except enclitics, and “rough” or “smooth” breathing-symbols over all initial vowels. These symbols had either to be designed and cast with the appropriate letter-form in every possible combination, or cast as entirely separate types and set in place by the compositor above the letter they were to accent. The first solution vastly multiplied the number of types needed — Victor Scholderer calculated that the font used by Laonicus and Alexandros in Venice during the mid-1480s must have contained over 1,400 separate letter forms.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] The alternative made the compositor’s task much slower and meant wider spacing of lines, requiring more paper and increasing costs.
Aldus Manutius made Greek printing one of his specialities, issuing the Erotemata (1495) and his great series of Greek classics (Aristotle, Aristophanes, Thucydides, Sophocles, Plato) between 1495 and 1498. His Greek types were cut by Francesco Griffo, and Lowry notes that Aldus commissioned four distinct Greek cursive founts, similar to each other in basic conception but different in detail.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Lowry explains that Aldus’ Greek type was based on the cursive hand used by his circle of Greek scholars. His Greek teacher Adramyttenus, and his main scribal assistants Apostolis, Gregoropoulos, and Marcus Musurus all used a cursive hand, and they passed this taste on to their Italian pupils and patrons.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] Lowry inclines to the view that Aldus himself provided the manuscript-model for his Greek types: “in so far as I believe a definite decision to be possible.”^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] The cursive choice was controversial — contemporary critics preferred the uncial (maiuscule) Greek used by Lascaris and Alopa in Florence, but Lowry argues that for the market Aldus served — academics and wealthy patrons trained in the cursive hand — the cursive was the appropriate choice: “Clarity, like so much else, exists in the eye of the beholder.”^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The small Greek cursive introduced for Aldus’ Sophocles of August 1502 was the last distinct type cut by Griffo before his departure.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
First Hebrew Type (1473)
Hebrew type appeared almost as early. The first printed Hebrew book is contested: it may have been printed in Rome in 1469—1472 (tentatively attributed to Obadiah ben Moses) or in Prague shortly after. The earliest dated printed Hebrew book is the commentary on the Pentateuch by Rashi (Solomon ben Isaac), printed in 1475 in Reggio di Calabria, Italy, by Abraham Garton. Another contender is the Arba’ah Turim (Jacob ben Asher’s law code), printed c. 1473, probably in Rome.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The cutting of Hebrew punches was especially challenging because of the script’s elaborate flourishes and the need for vowel points (nikud) and cantillation marks in liturgical texts. Early Hebrew printing was concentrated in Italy (Soncino family presses in Soncino, Casalmaggiore, and later Constantinople) and the Iberian Peninsula before the expulsion of 1492.
The Economics of Type
Behind every early typeface was a craft that was slow, expensive, and demanding:


Punchcutting: A steel punch for each character was engraved in reverse and in relief on the end of a steel bar, then hardened by heating and quenching. A skilled engraver might cut two or three punches per day; a full font of 200+ characters could take months.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]


Striking the matrix: The hardened punch was struck into a bar of copper, creating a sunken impression (the matrix). The matrix was filed to exact dimensions so every type cast from it would be the correct height (type-high, approximately 0.918 inches).


Casting: The matrix was fitted into the adjustable hand mold, molten type metal (lead, tin, antimony) was poured in, the mold was jerked to force metal into the fine details, and the type was ejected.


Dressing: The cast type had its excess metal (the “jet”) broken off and was rubbed smooth on the feet to stand perfectly upright.


A complete font — including all variant letters, ligatures, and abbreviations — might represent a year’s work for a single punchcutter. Gutenberg employed at least three goldsmith-punchcutters (Hans Dunne, Gotz von Schlettstadt, and Hans von Speyer) to complete the Bible type.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The Privilege System for Type Designs
From the earliest days of printing in Venice, the protection of type designs was linked to the system of printing privileges — early forms of intellectual property. Lowry records that on 18 September 1469, John of Speyer was granted a five-year monopoly over the craft of printing, which he had recently pioneered in the Republic of Venice.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] Such petitions were common in Venice, covering everything from improved windmills to experiments with poison-gas, but few came to anything. John died within months of gaining the monopoly, and his brother Windelin continued his work — but the privilege died with the original holder, and competitors soon thrust themselves forward.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The monopoly system later became central to the italic and Greek types. On 14 November 1502, Aldus was granted a comprehensive monopoly over all Greek publication and all Latin printing in italic within the Venetian dominions.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] Lowry notes that this clumsy system of press-privileges sought only to protect the interests of the investor — the printer or publisher who bore the costs of metal and labour — and did nothing to protect the craftsman who actually designed and cut the types.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] When Aldus used his privilege to outlaw all imitation of his Greek and italic styles, he was effectively, though perhaps unintentionally, preventing Griffo from selling his most original designs to other printers. The dispute over who deserved credit for the cursive styles — the scribe who supplied the model, the type-cutter who executed it, or the intermediary who commissioned it — could not be resolved by a system that only recognized the investor.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The value of type-founts is illustrated by Lowry’s figures: Jenson’s workshop contents were valued at 500 ducats (with punches excluded and bequeathed separately), and the punches themselves may have been used to strike matrices for re-sale to other printers, since some thirty founts similar to Jenson’s design can be traced in various Italian centres.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] Later, in 1541, Claude Garamond was paid 225 Livres Tournois for cutting Robert Estienne’s Greek Royal types — roughly one third of the pension paid annually to Leonardo da Vinci.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] By this measure, Aldus’ capital outlay on his twelve type-founts must be reckoned in thousands rather than hundreds of ducats.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Type Design as an Art
The first fifty years of printing saw type design emerge as a distinct artistic discipline:


Gutenberg made the foundational choice: his Textura was a deliberate imitation of the finest liturgical manuscripts, setting the conservative standard that the first generation of printers followed.


Peter Schoeffer refined punchcutting techniques and introduced leading (spacing between lines) in his 1465 Cicero, improving readability. His types, however, were fewer in number and of inferior design to Gutenberg’s, according to De Vinne.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]


Nicolas Jenson achieved a perfection of Roman letterforms that has never been surpassed. His type was the first to demonstrate that printing could produce books that were not just as beautiful as manuscripts but more beautiful — clearer, more uniform, and more legible.


Francesco Griffo created the first italic, solving a practical problem (fitting more text in a small format) with a design of lasting grace. His clean forms influenced every italic type that followed. Lowry calls him “the faceless genius” whose workmanship defines “Aldine typography.”^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]


Griffo and Aldus’s Roman type (the Bembo type, first used in Pietro Bembo’s De Aetna, February 1496) proved even more influential in the long run, though it received little emphasis from Aldus himself. Lowry notes that its relative weight was reduced to give the page “a light and harmonious appearance,” enhanced in 1499 by a delicately proportioned fount of capitals based on inscriptional models.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] This style, “unobtrusively launched in a sixty-page compliment to a personal friend,” caught the attention of the French type-founders Garamond and Simon de Colines around 1530, spread from their workshops across Europe, and holds its place in Western typography to the present day. “What has proved Aldus’ most permanent contribution to type-design appears to have had the least importance in his own eyes.”^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]


Significance
The evolution of typefaces in the first fifty years of printing tracks the development of the printed book itself. Textura was the type of the incunable period — backward-looking, imitative of manuscripts, dense and dark. Roman type was the type of humanism — clear, rational, forward-looking, shaped by the Italian Renaissance’s reverence for classical antiquity. Italic was the type of portability and commerce — compact, informal, designed for the pocket book. And Fraktur was the type of German cultural identity — a distinctively northern blackletter that would define German printing for half a millennium.
These four families — Textura (Gothic), Roman, Italic, and Fraktur — were the only typefaces available to printers for the first seventy years of printing. Every book produced in Europe until the early sixteenth century was set in one of them.
