concepts/manuscript-to-printed-book-trad.title: From Manuscript to Printed-Book Trade
concepts/manuscript-to-printed-book-trad.content:
From Manuscript to Printed-Book Trade
The first century of printing (c. 1450-1550) was not just a story of technological invention. It was a story of how the book trade re-invented itself. Gutenberg’s press created a flood of identical copies, but the distribution system that could move those copies from printer to reader had to be built from scratch — partly by adapting the infrastructure of the manuscript trade, partly by inventing entirely new institutions. The process took a full century. By 1550, the printed-book trade had guilds, regularized fairs, specialized publishing houses, and a geography of production that would remain stable for 200 years. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Before Print: The Manuscript Book Trade
The manuscript book trade before Gutenberg was more organized than is often assumed. Three distinct systems coexisted:
The University Pecia System
In the university cities of Bologna, Paris, and Padua, the production and distribution of textbooks was controlled through the pecia system. Licensed stationarii rented out manuscript quires (peciae) to students for copying. The system was tightly regulated: prices fixed by the rector, commissions capped at 2.5% (Bologna statute of 1259), quality inspections with fines for defective texts. The stationarius was a university officer, enjoying privileges (freedom from military service, a guaranteed salary) in exchange for compliance. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
The Paris Guild of Booksellers
In Paris, the university exercised even tighter control. The four sworn booksellers (les quatre grands libraires) supervised the entire trade. No one could sell books without being a libraire jure, examined for scholarly competence and moral standing. By 1368, there were 14 registered libraires and 11 registered scribes. The system governed manuscript production, pricing, and sale for over a century before printing arrived. When the first printers came to Paris in 1470 (Gering, Friburger, Crantz), they were rapidly absorbed into this existing guild structure. “As early as 1476, one of the four officials of the guild was the printer Pasquier Bonhomme.” ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
The Fairs
Manuscripts were traded at the Frankfurt and Nordlingen fairs from the early fifteenth century. Between 1445 and 1450, fortune-telling books and illustrated almanacs were among the most important items. The fairs concentrated buyers and sellers from across Europe, creating a marketplace that the printed-book trade would inherit. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Phase 1 (1450-1480): Print Arrives, Trade Chaos
The first generation of printers had no organized distribution for their products. They sold from their own workshops, through direct correspondence, or through travelling agents. The results were often disastrous:

Sweynheym and Pannartz in Rome printed 28 editions of classical and patristic works, then went bankrupt. Their warehouse filled with unsold copies. They had no way to reach buyers beyond Rome.
Gutenberg himself struggled: even the Bible, his masterpiece, did not return a profit. His financial collapse led to Fust’s seizure of the workshop in 1455.
Aldus Manutius, as late as the 1490s-1500s, was “dependent upon direct correspondence with scholars” because “in Italy prior to 1550, bookselling hardly existed as an organised trade.” ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]

The established manuscript-dealer guilds did not know what to do with printed books. In Paris, printers were absorbed into the guild, but this meant they operated under the same rules as scribes — rules designed for manuscript production, not for mass-producing editions of hundreds of copies. The tension between the two groups was considerable: “there must have been, during the earlier years at least, not a little rivalry and bitterness between the two groups of dealers.” ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
The Frankfurt Fair recorded its first sale of printed books in 1480. Before that date, the fair dealt primarily in manuscripts. The transition was gradual. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Phase 2 (1480-1500): The Trade Begins to Organize
The last two decades of the fifteenth century saw the emergence of the first systematic distribution networks for printed books.
Koberger’s Agent Network
Anton Koberger of Nuremberg built the first pan-European distribution system for printed books. His correspondence reveals agents or representatives in Frankfurt, Leipzig, Vienna, Basel, Strasbourg, Cologne, Paris, Budapest, Warsaw, Venice, Florence, Rome, Antwerp, Bruges, and Leyden. He was “the first bookseller in Germany, and possibly in Europe, to issue a classified catalogue of current publications.” Koberger’s network demonstrated that a printer-publisher could reach buyers across the continent — but it was tied to his personal management and collapsed after his death in 1513. The network was a person, not an institution. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Frankfurt Fair Takes Hold
Printed books appeared at the Frankfurt Fair from 1480. Peter Schoeffer became a citizen of Frankfurt in 1485, a sign of the city’s growing importance to the print trade. By 1500, the fair was established enough for the German publishers to organize it as a regular institution. But the fair system had a critical weakness: it depended on personal attendance. A publisher who could not travel to Frankfurt could not sell. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
City Specialization
By 1500, different cities had developed distinct publishing specializations, creating a division of labour that required trade between them:








































CitySpecializationKey PrintersVeniceClassical texts, Greek editions, law, vernacularAldus, Jenson, GiuntiParisTheology, university texts, liturgical worksGering, Estienne, BadiusLyonLaw, medicine, cheap reprintsMultiple German printersBaselHumanist editions, Reformist worksFroben, Amerbach, PetriNurembergIllustrated works, Bibles, chroniclesKobergerCologneSmall-format innovations, signatures/paginationKoelhoff, Zell
A scholar seeking Greek texts went to Venice; a lawyer needed a commentary went to Lyon; a bishop ordering a missal went to Paris or Mainz. This specialization made inter-city trade necessary and created the demand for fairs and agents. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Phase 3 (1500-1550): Institutionalization
The first half of the sixteenth century transformed the book trade from a collection of individual arrangements into an institutionalized industry.
The Frankfurt Book Fair Becomes a Regular Institution
The German publishers organized the Frankfurt Fair “as early as 1500” as a dedicated book fair within the general trade fair. Twice a year (Lent and Michaelmas), publishers and dealers gathered from across Europe. The fair served as:

A marketplace for buying and selling stock
A clearing house for settling accounts between distant correspondents
An intelligence network for learning what competitors were printing
A credit mechanism that allowed trade on trust between publishers who met only twice a year

The fair’s importance was such that when wars blocked the Alpine passes and Venetian books could not reach Frankfurt in 1510, a professor lamented that his lectures could not proceed because the books had not arrived. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
The Leipzig Alternative
Leipzig developed as a rival to Frankfurt. “By the year 1495, the book-trade of Leipzig had assumed very considerable proportions, not only in connection with printing and publishing, but in the organisation of machinery for collecting and distributing the publications of other cities.” The Leipzig booksellers’ association was organized in 1525 and became “the most effective and intelligently managed trade organisation that the world has ever known.” Leipzig’s rise was accelerated by the Reformation: Catholic-controlled Frankfurt became less hospitable to Protestant publishers, while Leipzig, in Protestant Saxony, offered a more favourable environment. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Guilds Are Formed
The first half of the sixteenth century saw the creation of formal trade organizations for printers and publishers:























YearCity / CountryOrganizationSignificance1548-49VeniceGuild of Printers and PublishersEarliest trade association of book-men in Europe. Lasted 250+ years.1556EnglandStationers’ CompanyChartered by Queen Mary. Monopoly on printing; copyright registration.
These guilds gave the trade legal standing, self-regulation, and the power to enforce rules against unauthorized editions. Before the guilds, a printer had no institutional protection against piracy. After the guilds, a publisher could register his title and — at least in theory — prevent others from reprinting it. The Venetian guild was created because printing was “the only important trade in the city that was not already so organised.” ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Reformation Transforms the Market
The Reformation (1517 onward) did not merely increase demand for printed products; it changed the structure of the trade:


New distribution channels: Luther’s pamphlets were sold not through book-shops but by pedlars, colporteurs, and travelling students in market-places. “Thousands of copies were sold in the market-places by dealers of all kinds, many of whom had never before handled books.” This created a parallel distribution system alongside the established trade. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]


Censorship creates parallel networks: Catholic territories blocked Protestant books; Protestant cities banned Catholic works. The trade fractured along confessional lines. Publishers in Geneva manufactured Catholic works for illicit sale in France; Lyon printers used heresy accusations to block Geneva’s shipments. Trade routes became ideological. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]


Mass-market economics: A Lutheran pamphlet sold for one groschen (2.5 cents). At this price, volume mattered more than unit profit. The Reformation proved that printing could be profitable at low price points with high circulation — a lesson that would later shape the Elzevir small-format revolution. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]


The Limits of Organization in 1550
Despite these advances, the book trade in 1550 was still far from the sophisticated system that Plantin and the Elzevirs would build. The Frankfurt catalogue — the first printed list of available books — did not appear until 1564. Aldus had died without ever solving his distribution problems. Koberger’s network had collapsed with its founder. The Venetian guild was new, its effectiveness unproven. International copyright did not exist: a book printed in Venice could be reprinted in Lyon the same week with no legal recourse.
What did exist by 1550 was a framework: regular fairs, guild structures, established trade routes, recognized specializations, and a market that had proven it could absorb editions of thousands of copies. The next generation — Plantin, the Estiennes, the Elzevirs, the Blaeus — would build the superstructure on this foundation.
Beyond 1550: From Infrastructure to Industry
By 1550 the printed-book trade had the institutions it needed. What followed was not another fundamental reorganization but the growth and refinement of those institutions:


1564: The first printed Frankfurt Fair catalogue (George Willer of Augsburg) transformed the trade by making it possible to order books without attending the fair. (See book-trade)


1555-1589: Plantin in Antwerp built the largest and longest-lived publishing house of the early modern era, demonstrating what the new institutional framework could support at scale. (See christopher-plantin and antwerp)


1576: The Spanish Fury destroyed Antwerp’s printing dominance. The centre of gravity shifted from the Catholic south to the Protestant north. (See antwerp and amsterdam)


1580s-1650: The Elzevir family created a federation of book-selling agencies across Europe — the first multi-city publishing network built on the fair and guild system. (See elzevir-family and book-trade)


1600-1700: The Dutch Republic’s press freedom made Amsterdam and Leyden the world’s printing capitals. The Blaeu atlas dynasty, the Elzevir cheap classics, and Joseph Athias’s Hebrew Bible all flourished under conditions no Catholic city could match. (See amsterdam, blaeu-family, and seventeenth-century-printing)


1648-1700: The Frankfurt Fair declined and Leipzig emerged as the new centre of the European book trade, a shift cemented by the Thirty Years’ War and the changing politics of the empire. (See book-trade)


1710: The Statute of Anne created the first statutory copyright, ending the era when trade practices and guild rules were the only protection a publisher had. (See literary-property-and-copyright)


By 1700, the trade had become the industry that would persist, with only technological changes (the steam press in the 19th century, digital in the 21st), until the present day. The institutions built between 1450 and 1550 — the fair, the guild, the catalogue, the geography of specialization — proved remarkably durable.



































PeriodState of the TradeKey DevelopmentsPre-1450Manuscript trade organizedPecia system, Paris guild, Frankfurt manuscript fair1450-1480Print arrives, no trade for itDirect sale, bankruptcies, manuscript guilds absorb printers1480-1500First distribution networksKoberger’s agents, Frankfurt printed-book sales, city specialization1500-1520Fairs institutionalizedFrankfurt organized as book fair, Leipzig rises, Koberger network collapses1520-1550Guilds and parallel networksReformation creates mass market + confessional divisions, Venetian guild (1548), Stationers’ Company (1556)
The arc is clear: the manuscript trade was localized and regulated by universities; the printed-book trade had to become continental and self-regulating. It took a century to build the institutions that made that possible.

concepts/map-making-and-the-printing-pre.title: Map Making and the Printing Press
concepts/map-making-and-the-printing-pre.content:
Map Making and the Printing Press
Map making and printing developed in a tight symbiotic relationship in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. The printing press made possible the mass reproduction of maps, while the technical demands of map publishing drove innovations in printing technique — especially in copperplate engraving, colour printing, and large-format presswork. At the same time, the rediscovery and printing of Ptolemy’s Geography transformed European understanding of the world by making ancient geographical knowledge available to every scholar with access to a printed book. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Maps Before Printing
Before the press, maps were rare, expensive, and non-standardised. Manuscript maps in the European tradition included the mappa mundi tradition (world maps oriented to the east, combining geography with biblical history), portolan charts (practical navigational maps of Mediterranean coastlines, used by sailors since the thirteenth century), and a small number of regional maps based on Ptolemy’s coordinates. Fewer than a thousand manuscript maps survive from the entire Middle Ages. A single manuscript of Ptolemy’s Geography might cost as much as a small farm. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Manuscript maps were typically unique: each copy was drawn by hand, and copies of the same source could differ substantially. There was no mechanism for standardisation, no way to correct errors systematically, and no means of reproducing a map in quantity. The printing press changed all of this. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The Printed Ptolemy: Cartography’s Foundational Text
The Geography of Claudius Ptolemy (second century AD) was the most important geographical text of antiquity. It provided a systematic method for locating places by latitude and longitude and included instructions for map projection. The text was rediscovered in Byzantium in the late fourteenth century, translated into Latin by Jacopo Angeli da Scarperia around 1406, and circulated in manuscript through the fifteenth century. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Printing transformed Ptolemy’s work from a rare scholarly treasure into a widely available reference. The key printed editions were:







































































YearPlacePrinterDescription1475VicenzaHermannus LichtensteinFirst printed edition of Ptolemy’s Geography (Latin text, no maps) ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]1477BolognaDomenico de’ LapiFirst edition with maps — engraved copperplates ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]1478RomeArnold Bucking (after Sweynheym)Copperplate engraved maps by Sweynheym; landmark of map printing ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]1482UlmLeonhard HollFirst woodcut maps for Ptolemy, engraved by Johann Schnitzer; combined woodcut maps with inserted type ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]1486UlmJohann Reger (after Holl)Second Ulm edition; maps re-cut ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]1490Rome—Reissue of the 1478 Rome Ptolemy ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]1507Rome—New edition including seven modern maps ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]1525StrasbourgJohann KobergerWaldseemuller’s edition with new maps1540BaselHeinrich PetriMunster’s Ptolemy edition with 48 maps ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]1578Duisburg—Mercator’s Ptolemy edition with 27 maps ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Each edition added modern maps (called tabulae modernae) alongside the Ptolemaic ones, so that the same book showed both the ancient and the contemporary world — a juxtaposition that made the progress of geographical knowledge visible. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Woodcut vs. Copperplate for Maps
The choice between woodcut and copperplate engraving was the central technical decision in early map printing. Each method had distinct advantages and limitations that shaped the evolution of cartographic publishing.
Woodcut Maps
Woodcut (xylographic) maps were cut from a single block of wood, with the map and any text carved together. The block was a relief surface — raised lines took ink, recessed areas were white — and could be printed on the same press as movable type. This meant woodcut maps could be integrated into books and printed in a single pass with the text. The Ulm Ptolemy of 1482, with its thirty-two woodcut maps by Johann Schnitzer, was the first printed Ptolemy to use woodcut. Leonhard Holl, the printer, “was the first to print a work with woodcut maps into which type could in part be inserted” (der erste, der ein Werk mit in Holz geschnittenen Landkarten, worin zumteil Typen eingesetzt werden konnten, druckte). ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The hybrid technique of inserting type into woodcut maps — cutting recesses into the woodblock for individual letterforms or lines of type — allowed place-names to be set in movable type and locked into position before printing. This was a significant innovation: it meant that text changes (corrections, additions, translations) required only recomposition of type, not recarving of the woodblock. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Copperplate Maps
Copperplate engraving (intaglio) produced much finer lines and more detail. The map was incised into a copper plate with a burin, then the plate was inked and wiped — ink remained only in the incised lines — and printed under heavy roller pressure. Because copperplate was an intaglio process, it required a separate rolling press rather than the screw press used for type. This meant copperplate maps could not be printed alongside text and had to be bound in as separate sheets. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]
Copperplate was superior for maps because it allowed:

Much finer lines for coastlines, rivers, and mountains
More lettering per area
Delicate hachuring and stippling for terrain
Clearer differentiation between land and water

Conrad Sweynheym made “the first attempts to produce maps for the printing press in high-cut copper” (die ersten Versuche, Landkarten für die Buchdruckerpresse in Kupfer hoch geschnitten herzustellen) for the 1478 Rome Ptolemy. His letter-punch technique — individual capital letters punched into the copper plate rather than cut with a graver — was a unique technical innovation that linked typefounding and map engraving. The same punches appeared on the Eichstatt map of Nicholas of Cusa and the Rome Ptolemy, suggesting Sweynheym may have engraved both. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
The Shift to Copperplate
By the mid-sixteenth century, copperplate had decisively won for high-quality map work. Giacomo Gastaldi in Venice, Abraham Ortelius in Antwerp, and Gerard Mercator in Duisburg all used copperplate exclusively. The shift was driven by reader demand for detail and by the growing market for atlases, where the higher cost of copperplate was offset by premium pricing and larger edition sizes. Woodcut maps persisted in cheaper productions (school texts, cosmographies like Munster’s) but disappeared from serious cartography by 1600. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
The Atlas as a New Book Genre
Before Ortelius’s Theatrum Orbis Terrarum (1570), maps were sold as single sheets, as loose collections, or as illustrations bound into books. There was no standardised format, no uniform size, and no systematic organisation. The atlas — a collection of maps designed to uniform specifications, bound as a book, and sold as a coherent work — was a new category of printed artefact. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
The atlas required:

Standardised plate sizes so that all maps in the book matched
A consistent design language (borders, typefaces, scales, compass roses)
Scholarly apparatus (descriptive text on the verso, a catalogue of sources, indexes)
Commercial distribution through the same book-trade networks that sold other printed books

Ortelius’s Theatrum succeeded because it was not only a cartographic achievement but a publishing achievement: Plantin’s printing, the Antwerp distribution network, and the Frankfurt Book Fair made it a European bestseller. The atlas genre — with Ortelius, Mercator, and then the Blaeu family — became one of the most prestigious and profitable branches of the printing trade. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
The Business of Map Publishing
Map publishing shared the economic structure of book publishing but added the costs of copperplate engraving. A single engraved plate might take months to produce and cost the equivalent of a year’s wages for a skilled worker. The capital tied up in plates was substantial and had to be recovered over multiple editions. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
This high fixed cost created several dynamics:

Plate inheritance: Map plates were bought, sold, inherited, and re-used across generations. The Blaeu firm’s atlases incorporated plates originally engraved for Ortelius and Mercator. The Eichstatt map’s plate, originally owned by Conrad Peutinger, was still being used for printings as late as the 1560s or 1570s. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Privilege protection: Map publishers sought exclusive privileges (early forms of copyright) to protect their investment. The Venetian Senate granted Gastaldi the title of cosmographer and protected his rights. Ortelius obtained privileges from the King of Spain and the Emperor. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Commercial risk: Leonhard Holl’s Ulm Ptolemy “had no financial success; first he had to pawn the work, later sell it” (Pekuniären Erfolg hatte Holl davon nicht; erst musste er das Werk versetzen, später verkaufen). It took a Venetian buyer, Justus de Albano, to revive the edition through his factor Johannes Reger. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Piracy: Successful maps were immediately copied. Ortelius’s Asia map (1567) was copied in Venice by Donato Bertelli. The Antwerp printer-publisher Gerard de Jode tried to compete with Ortelius’s Theatrum with his Speculum Orbis Terrarum (1578), but failed commercially, partly because Ortelius’s privilege protection gave him a head start.

Key Cartographers and Their Printing Connections

































































CartographerDatesCentreConnection to PrintingNicholas of Cusa1401–1464GermanyMap engraved with Sweynheym’s punches; link between Mainz printing and Roman cartographyConrad Sweynheymd. c. 1475RomePrinter-turned-map-engraver; 1478 Rome Ptolemy; letter-punch techniqueLeonhard Hollfl. 1480sUlmPrinter of the 1482 Ulm Ptolemy; map-card factory; combined type with woodcut mapsJohann Schnitzerfl. 1480sUlmWoodcut map engraver for the Ulm PtolemySebastian Munster1488–1552BaselHebrew scholar turned cosmographer; Cosmographia (1544); worked as proofreader in Petri’s shopGiacomo Gastaldic. 1500–1566VeniceLeading Italian cartographer; copperplate specialist; cosmographer to VeniceAbraham Ortelius1527–1598AntwerpFirst modern atlas; published by Plantin; Catalogus auctorumGerard Mercator1512–1594DuisburgMercator projection; coined “atlas”; engraver, printer, and instrument-makerBlaeu family1571–1672AmsterdamAtlas dynasty; press improvers; inherited Ortelius-Mercator map plates
Maps in the Broader Printing Revolution
The printing of maps contributed to the broader transformation of European knowledge in several ways:

Standardisation of geographical knowledge: For the first time, readers in different cities could consult the same map. Errors could be identified, reported to the publisher, and corrected in the next edition. The cumulative improvement of map accuracy over successive editions was a direct consequence of print. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Integration of text and image: Maps required the combination of image (coastlines, rivers, mountains) with text (place-names, legends, titles) on the same sheet. This pushed the technical boundaries of both woodcut and copperplate printing. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Scientific collaboration across distance: Munster’s network of 120+ collaborators, Ortelius’s Catalogus auctorum, and Mercator’s correspondence all used print to build a geographically distributed community of knowledge. Cartography was one of the first sciences to rely systematically on the printed book for its development. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Popularisation of geography: Munster’s Cosmographia (written in German as well as Latin) and the many vernacular editions of Ortelius’s Theatrum brought geographical knowledge to readers beyond the scholarly elite. This had practical consequences for navigation, trade, and colonial expansion. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
The first reference-work genre: The atlas, as the first standardised, systematically organised printed reference work, established a model that would be followed by dictionaries, encyclopaedias, and other reference genres. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]

concepts/maritime-publications.title: Maritime Publications
concepts/maritime-publications.content:
Maritime Publications
From the 1530s onward, the printing press produced a distinct and commercially significant category of works specifically for mariners and navigators: pilot books, navigation manuals, island books, and sea atlases. These maritime publications were practical tools — often written in the vernacular, illustrated with coastal profiles, and priced for working seamen — and formed a genre quite different from the scholarly geographies and luxury atlases produced for the same presses. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md] ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
Pilot Books and Rutters: The Dutch Leeskaarten
The earliest printed maritime publications in Northern Europe were the Dutch leeskaarten (literally “reading-maps”) or pilot books — practical guides for coastal navigation that gave compass bearings, depths, and descriptions of harbours, accompanied by coastal profiles showing what the land looked like from the sea.
The first known printed Dutch pilot book was De Kaert vader zee, published in 1532 by Jan Severszoon. An enlarged and revised edition by Jan Jacobszoon followed in 1541. Neither survives in any known copy. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Cornelis Anthoniszoon (c. 1507-1553), a Dutch painter and cartographer, produced the next landmark. In 1543 he published the Caerte van Oostlant, a large wall map of the eastern navigation (the Baltic and North Sea). In the note to readers on this map, he promised “a little book” that would have “pictures of the land as seen from the sea and other things useful and pleasurable to mariners.” That book was his Onderwijsinge vander zee (Instruction concerning the Sea), a treatise on navigation — the first in the Dutch language — probably first published in 1544. The book consisted of two parts: the Onderwijsinge proper (a theoretical navigation treatise) and the Caerte van die Oosterse See (Chart of the Eastern Sea), which included dozens of woodcut coastal profiles by Anthoniszoon himself. Unlike the earlier pilot books, which treated both the western (Atlantic) and eastern (North Sea) navigations, Anthoniszoon covered only the eastern navigation, as a companion to his map. The earliest surviving edition is the third (1558), printed in Amsterdam by Jan Ewoutzoon. A second edition (c. 1551) and the first (c. 1544) are lost. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
A later anonymous pilot book, the Leeskaartboek van Wisbuy (1566), and its English translation The Safegard of Sailers (1584), borrowed heavily from Anthoniszoon but included additions by another hand. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
The Scottish Rutter
The Scottish pilot Alexander Lindesay compiled a manuscript rutter (a sailing guide) describing the coasts and harbours of Scotland, including the Hebrides and Orkney Islands. This manuscript fell into the hands of the French cosmographer Nicolas de Nicolay (1517-1583), who took it back to France in 1547 after a spying mission to England and Scotland. The rutter was put to immediate practical use: in June 1547 a French fleet under Admiral Leone Strozzi, with Nicolay as pilot, used it to besiege St. Andrews. Lindesay’s original manuscript is lost, but Nicolay had it translated from Scots into French by Johannes Ferrerius, added his own section on navigation derived from his translation of Pedro de Medina (see below), and eventually published it in 1583 as La navigation du roy d’Escosse Jacques cinquiesme (Paris: Gilles Beys), with a fine copper-engraved chart. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Navigation Manuals: The Spanish and Mediterranean Tradition
The most influential printed navigation manual of the sixteenth century was the Arte de Navegar (Art of Navigation) by Pedro de Medina (1493-1567), a Spanish mathematician, cosmographer, and instrument maker. Medina arrived in Seville and discovered that many of the instruments and charts produced by the Gutiérrez family (who had a near-monopoly on navigational tools under the Casa de Contratación) were faulty. He complained to the Council of the Indies and was granted a licence in 1538. The Arte de Navegar was published in Valladolid in 1545 (with a second, expanded edition in 1546), and Sebastian Cabot, the aged pilot major of Spain, publicly impugned its accuracy in a dispute that required the adjudication of a special court of the Casa. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
The work was an international success. It was translated into French by Nicolas de Nicolay as L’Art de naviguer (Lyons: Guillaume Rouille, 1554, with a title page reading 1553), including a copper-engraved map centred on the Atlantic. The French edition was republished repeatedly: Lyons (1561, 1569, 1576), Rouen (1573, 1577, 1602, 1607, 1628), and La Rochelle (1618). The Rouen editions used woodcut maps; the Lyons editions used copperplate. An Italian translation also appeared. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
In addition to his translation of Medina, Nicolay himself produced a manuscript on comparative naval organizations (1582), titled Extraict des observations… touchant la diversité des navires, galleres, et autres vaisseaux de mer, describing the different types of ships used in the Ocean, Baltic, and Mediterranean seas. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Isolarii: Printed Island Books
A distinctly Italian (and especially Venetian) genre, the isolario or island book was a printed collection of maps and descriptions of the world’s islands — part geographical reference, part travel narrative, part illustrated book. The genre existed in manuscript before printing, but print turned it into a commercial success. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
The most famous printed isolario was that of Benedetto Bordone (c. 1450-1539), a Paduan miniaturist, woodcut artist, and cartographer active in Venice. Bordone had applied to the Venetian Senate for permission to publish maps as early as 1508, but his great work, the Libro di Benedetto Bordone nel qual si ragiona de tutte l’isole del mondo (Book of All the Islands of the World), appeared only in 1528, printed in Venice by Nicolo d’Aristotile, detto Zoppino. He had been granted permission to print in 1526, and there is a preparatory manuscript in Florence dating from before 1524. The work consisted of 108 woodcut maps of islands and views of port cities, each with a double-line border and lines indicating the eight winds radiating from a central point. It began with three large maps (Western Europe and the Mediterranean, Southeastern Europe, and an oval world map — the earliest known printed oval world map, though Bordone probably borrowed the projection from Francesco Rosselli). ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
The Libro was a great success. A second edition, retitled Isolario di Benedetto Bordone, appeared in 1534 (also from Zoppino), adding only the text of Pizarro’s letter describing his conquest of Peru. A third edition followed from Francesco di Leno (c. 1537), and a fourth from Frederico Toresano (1547). All editions used the same woodblocks. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Bordone’s Isolario “firmly established the genre as an Italian and particularly Venetian specialty.” Tommaso Porcacchi’s L’Isole piu famose del Mondo followed in 1572, and as late as 1697 Vincenzo Maria Coronelli published an Isolario in the form of a world atlas. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Bordone was also a miniaturist who may have done the woodcut illustrations for the Aldine Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (1499), and his interest in the press is documented by applications for privileges on translations of Lucian (1494), illustrations of the “Triumph of Caesar” (1504), and a world map (1508), though none of these survive. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Sea Atlases and Mariner’s Guides
The late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries saw the rise of the printed sea atlas — a collection of navigational charts designed for use at sea, distinct from the geographical atlases of Ortelius and Mercator.
Lucas Jansz Waghenaer (c. 1533-1606), a Dutch navigator and cartographer from Enkhuizen, published the Spieghel der Zeevaerdt (Mariner’s Mirror) in 1584-1585, the first printed sea atlas. It contained navigational charts, coastal profiles, and sailing directions for European waters, and was quickly translated into English, Latin, French, and German. The term “waggoner” entered the English language as a generic name for a book of sea charts. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
In Amsterdam, Willem Jansz Blaeu (1571-1638) built a substantial business around maritime publications alongside his better-known atlases. The Blaeu review documents that he “onderscheidde hij zich ook met de uitgave van veel boeken op het gebied van de wiskunde, navigatie en astronomie” (distinguished himself also with the publication of many books on mathematics, navigation, and astronomy), and that a chapter of Van Netten’s study is devoted to “zijn zeemansgidsen” (his seaman’s guides) and his collaboration with the mathematician Adriaan Metius. Blaeu disguised his Copernican convictions in these mariners’ guides, presenting a conventional Ptolemaic world picture to avoid frightening practical sailors. ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
His competitors Willem Janssonius and Jacob Aertsz Colom also produced pilot books and sea charts. All three firms were located on the Damrak in Amsterdam, in direct proximity to one another, and their competition extended to the maritime publishing market: Janssonius and Colom regularly reprinted Blaeu’s successful navigation titles in cheaper formats. ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
The Business of Maritime Publishing
Maritime publications shared several economic characteristics that distinguished them from other printed products:
Vernacular audience. Unlike most scholarly publishing, which remained in Latin, pilot books and navigation manuals were written in the vernacular (Dutch, Spanish, French, English, Italian) because their users were working mariners and ship captains, not university-educated scholars. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Illustration costs. The signature feature of these works — coastal profiles showing the appearance of the land from the sea — required woodcut or copperplate illustration. Anthoniszoon’s Caerte van die Oosterse See was built around dozens of such profiles. The cost of cutting these blocks or plates was substantial but could be amortized across multiple editions. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Low survival rates. Pilot books and rutters were carried to sea, used in salt spray, and literally read to pieces — a fate they share with cheap school texts and ephemera. Of Anthoniszoon’s Onderwijsinge vander zee, the first and second editions are entirely lost; the only surviving copy is of the third (1558) edition, preserved in a library. The same fate befell the early Dutch pilot books of Severszoon and Jacobszoon. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
International market. Successful navigation manuals crossed linguistic borders rapidly. Medina’s Arte de Navegar was translated into French (1554) and Italian within a decade of its Spanish publication, with editions in five French cities across the next seventy years. Waghenaer’s Spieghel der Zeevaerdt appeared in four languages within a decade of its Dutch publication. The Leeskaartboek van Wisbuy was translated as The Safegard of Sailers in English. This multilingual diffusion was driven by the practical needs of international shipping. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
State involvement. Navigation manuals were entangled with state-sponsored monopolies and colonial administration. In Spain, the Casa de Contratación in Seville controlled the production and licensing of charts and navigation texts. Medina’s Arte de Navegar emerged from a dispute with the officially sanctioned Gutiérrez family of instrument makers and chart producers. The Venetian Senate granted privileges for map and island-book publication. In the Dutch Republic, the States-General granted seven-year privileges to competing publishers. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Relation to Other Printed Genres
Maritime publications fit into the spectrum-of-printed-output as a middle-tier product — more expensive than ephemera (because of illustration and navigational expertise) but considerably cheaper than the prestige atlases of Ortelius or Mercator. They belong alongside school texts, practical manuals, and professional reference works as a category of applied printing: books made not for contemplation or display, but for use.
They also connect directly to the maritime trade routes that distributed printed books across Europe. Venice, the leading fifteenth-century printing capital, was also a maritime republic whose commercial fleet carried books along with other goods. The Blaeu firm’s location on the Damrak in Amsterdam — the city’s main harbourfront — was no coincidence: sea captains and ship owners were customers as well as subjects. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md] ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]

concepts/medieval-libraries.title: Medieval Libraries
concepts/medieval-libraries.content:
Medieval Libraries
Based on Putnam, Books and Their Makers in the Middle Ages, Vol. I, Chapter II (“Some Libraries of the Manuscript Period”), lines 1510–1700+.

Earliest Ecclesiastical Libraries
The earliest ecclesiastical library was probably that collected by Bishop Alexander in Jerusalem at the beginning of the third century. Fifty years later, a library was founded at Caesarea by Origen, described as extensive and important 1. Collections were also made at an early date at Hippo, at Cirta, at Constantinople, and at St. Peter’s and the Lateran in Rome. All of these earlier libraries were connected with churches, and in most cases places had been found for them within the church walls. Clark quotes from a narrative of the persecution of 303–304: the officers “went to the church where the Christians used to assemble, and spoiled it of chalices, lamps, etc., but when they came to the library (bibliothecam), the presses (armaria) were found empty” 2. This indicates that vessels and books were in different parts of the same building.
The library of St. Augustine was bequeathed to the church of Hippo, and preserved within the church building.
In the Greek Church, the Patriarch of Constantinople had a library in Thomaïtes said to be of considerable importance, often referred to in Synod transactions. It was destroyed by fire in 780 but speedily replaced 3. The monastery of Mt. Athos possessed one of the most important Greek collections, with some treasures preserved to the present day. During Basilius Macedo (867–886), much scribal work was done there 3. In Egypt, literary activity in monasteries continued until the Arab conquest; the monastery of St. Catherine of the Sinai preserved early manuscripts, most notably the Testament discovered by Tischendorf.
Benedictine Library Regulations
The regulations of libraries in all Benedictine monasteries were based upon the Rule of St. Benedict. As new Orders were founded, care for books steadily developed. St. Benedict gave only general directions for study. The Cluniacs prescribed the selection of a special officer to take charge of the books, with an annual audit and assignment to each Brother of a single volume for the year’s study. The Cistercians and Carthusians provided for loans to outsiders under certain conditions, a practice later adopted by the Benedictines. The Augustinians prescribed the kind of press (armarium) for keeping books, and both they and the Premonstratensians permitted books to be lent on receipt of pledges of sufficient value.
The Mendicant Friars, who originally restrained themselves from holding possessions, found books indispensable, and their libraries came to excel those of most other Orders. Richard de Bury, in his Philobiblon, said of the Mendicants: “These men are as ants, ever preparing their meat in the summer, or as ingenious bees continually fabricating cells of honey… although they lately at the eleventh hour have entered the Lord’s vineyard, they have added more in this brief hour to the stock of sacred books than all the other vine-dressers.”
Armarius System
Clark points out that the word “Library” was used by the Benedictines long before any special room was assigned for book storage. Until the 13th and 14th centuries, books were mostly kept in the cloisters (the only areas except the refectory and occasionally the califactorium where monks could congregate). Books in the cloisters were shut up in presses called armaria — the same term used by the Romans for their book-cases. The monk charged with the care of the books took his name not from the books but from the presses, and was generally styled armarius.
In the Customs of the Augustinian priory of Barnwell (late 13th century): “The press in which the books are kept ought to be lined inside with wood, that the damp of the walls may not moisten or stain the books. This press should be divided vertically as well as horizontally by sundry partitions, on which the books may be ranged so as to be separated from one another: for fear they be packed so close as to injure each other, or to delay those who want them.”
The catalogue of the House of the White Canons at Titchfield in Hampshire (dated 1400) shows books kept in a small room on shelves called columpnae set against the walls — a closet of storage, not a working place. By the early 15th century, larger monasteries had accumulated many hundred volumes, and separate rooms were constructed for collections. The presses in the cloisters were still used for books in daily reference.
Annual Audits
A statute of Archbishop Lanfranc for the English Benedictines (dated 1070), based on general monastic practice, gives the following regulation: “On the Monday after the first Sunday in Lent, before Brethren come into the Chapter House, the librarian [here called custos librorum , not armarius] shall have a carpet laid down and all the books got together upon it, except those which the year previous had been assigned for reading. These the Brethren are to bring with them, when they come into the Chapter House, each his book in his hand. Then the librarian shall read a statement as to the manner in which Brethren have had books during the past year. As each Brother hears his name pronounced, he is to give back the book which had been entrusted to him for reading; and he whose conscience accuses him of not having read through the book which he had received, is to fall on his face, confess his fault, and entreat forgiveness. The librarian shall then make a fresh distribution of books, namely a different volume to each Brother for his reading.”
Two classes of volumes are evident: one for distribution for separate reading, and one reserved for reference in a separate room (first called armarium, later bibliotheca), where books were fastened with iron chains to lecterns or reading-desks.
The statutes of Oriel College, Oxford (1329) borrowed directly from monastic customs: “The common books (libri communes) of the House are to be brought out and inspected once a year, on the feast of the Commemoration of Souls (November 2d) in the presence of the Provost or his deputy, and of the scholars (Fellows). Each one of the scholars, in the order of seniority, may select a single book… This he may keep until the same festival in the succeeding year.”
Similarly, the Brothers of Common Life ordered that at least once a year all books not out on loan should be called in and inspected in the presence of the Brothers.
Carrells
In monasteries where literary studies were pursued with special ardour, readers and scribes were provided with small wooden compartments or studies called carrells. The Rites of Durham describes them:
“In the north syde of the cloister, from the corner over againste the church dour to the corner over againste the Dorter dour, was all fynely glased from the hight to the sole within a little of the ground into the Cloister garth, and in every window iij Pewes or Carrells, where every one of the old monks had his carrell, several by himselfs, that, when they had dyned, they dyd resort to that place of Cloister, and there studyed upon these books, every one in his carrell, all the after nonne, unto evensong tyme… In every carrell was a deske to lye there books upon, and the carrell was no greater than from one stanchell of the wyndowe to another, and over againste the carrells againste the church wall, did stande certain great almeries (or cupbords) of waynscott all full of bookes (with great store of ancient manuscripts to help them in their study) wherein did lye as well the old anncyent written Doctors of the Church as other prophane authors, with dyverse other holie men’s wourks, so that every one did studye what Doctor pleased them best, havinge the Librarie at all tymes to goe studye in besydes there carrells.” 4
Chained Library System
The system of chaining, as adopted in England, allowed books to be readily taken down from shelves and placed on a lectern for reading. One end of the chain was attached to the middle of the upper edge of the right-hand board or cover; the other to a ring which played on a bar set in front of the shelf. The fore-edge of the books, not the back, was turned to the front. A swivel, usually in the middle of the chain, prevented tangling. Chains varied in length according to the distance of the shelf from the desk 5.
A copy of Locke’s Treatise on the Epistles (printed 1711) bears an inscription complaining about thieves in libraries, noting that chains were necessary “to secure the innocent books, and even the sacred volumes themselves” 6.
At Clairvaux, the library (described in 1723) was “stocked with a large number of manuscripts, fastened by chains to desks.” At Bordesholm (1477), Brother Liborius gave over his works on jurisprudence “with the provision that they were to be placed in chains and to remain forever in the reading-room” 7.
At the Sorbonne (statutes of 1321), all books were chained to the wall or reading-desks. Books not protected by chains were called libri vagantes and could, under restrictions, be loaned out; Wattenbach believed only duplicates were placed in this class.
The College of Plessis statutes of 1455 prescribed that all books except Missals must be chained, and unchaining required authorisation of the master of all bursars.
Cataloguing Practices
Isidore, Bishop of Seville (c. 560–636) possessed probably the largest collection of books in Europe at the time, contained in fourteen presses or armaria, each ornamented with a bust and inscribed with verses.
The monastery of Vivaria (founded by Cassiodorus) classified writings according to contents, arranged in a series of armaria.
At Reichenau, librarian Reginbert prepared in 821 an exhaustive catalogue of the collection, with notes showing many manuscripts were his own work. Only five sheets of one book and a portion of the catalogue remain.
The first catalogue of St. Gall includes beneath the titles various critical notes, with record of loans to Emperor Charles III., Frau Rickert, and Liutward, Bishop of Vercelli 8.
At Pomposa, Henricus Clericus (writing in 1093) prepared a catalogue of the library and at the close found it necessary to apologise for the abbot including heathen books. These libri scholastici were by no means exceptional; copies of Virgil, Ovid, and Cicero were found in many monastery collections. A separate catalogue of libri scholastici was made in 1297 for the cathedral library of Lübeck. An inventory of Neumünster (near Wurzburg, 1233) includes a special list of Classics.
At St. Père-de-Chartres, a catalogue inscribed in four rolls (1367) gave titles of 201 volumes 9. At Admunt, the library was catalogued in 1380 by Brother Peter of Arbonne. At Bordesholm, a catalogue prepared in 1498 contained more than five hundred titles 7.
Great Monastic Collections
Bobbio
After the beginning of the 7th century, the most noteworthy collection was that of Bobbio. A portion remained as late as 1618 and was taken by Paul V. for the Vatican Library; another portion went to Turin. Bobbio received books from wandering Irishmen, as indicated by an inscription recording that Dungal bestowed a book upon St. Columba 10.
Reichenau
In Germany, the monastery of Reichenau was noted as early as 821 for its excellent collection of manuscripts. Librarian Reginbert prepared an exhaustive catalogue in 821.
St. Gall
Of nearly as early a date is the first catalogue of St. Gall, with various critical notes beneath titles and records of loans.
Pomposa (Lombardy)
Abbot Jerome brought together in the 11th century a great collection of manuscripts, despite grumblings from the monks. Henricus Clericus wrote in 1093 that in no church, not even in Rome, could such a wonderful group of books be found 11.
Christ Church, Canterbury
As early as the 14th century, the collection comprised as many as 698 books. A library at Canterbury was built about 1425 by Archbishop Chichele 12.
Clairvaux
One of the two great Cistercian foundations in France. The Queen of Sicily (who visited in 1517) described: “On the same side of the cloister are fourteen studies, where the monks do their reading and writing, and over these studies, one mounts by a broad spiral staircase to the new library. This library is 189 feet long by 17 feet wide. It contains 48 seats (bancs) and in each banc four shelves (poulpitres) furnished with books on all subjects, but chiefly theology; the greater number of the said books are of vellum and are written by hand, richly storied and illuminated.”
A 1723 description from the Voyage Littéraire speaks of “fifteen little cells, all in a row, where the Brethren formerly used to write books, for which reason they are still called the writing rooms. Over these cells is the library, the building for which is large, vaulted, well lighted, and stocked with a large number of manuscripts, fastened by chains to desks; but there are not many printed books.”
St. Germain des Prés
The library dates from 1513. The collection was one of the earliest in France; as early as the beginning of the 13th century, there is record of it being consulted by strangers. At the time of the French Revolution, it contained 7000 manuscripts and 4900 printed books 12.
Citeaux
The library was placed over the scriptorium and dates from 1480 12.
Durham
The library at Durham was built about the same time (c. 1425) by Prior Wessyngton 12.
Corbie
The library existed throughout the lifetime of the monastery. After 1350, the monks gave up the work of writing. Étienne de Conty is recorded as a special benefactor, collecting books and employing special scribes 13.
Fleury
Léon Maitre says each new scholar was expected to present at least two codices.
St. Père-de-Chartres
Abbot Alveus (died 955) presented a book Pro Vita Æterna 14. His successor Fulbert instituted a new room for the collection and kept the monks working; a 1367 catalogue in four rolls listed 201 volumes 9.
Scottish Monastery (near Vienna)
A record of gifts kept in the 13th century includes a long list of book presents. The monastery degenerated later and presents ceased. In 1418, Scottish monks were driven out and Germans took possession; from this date, gifts of books resumed. In 1453, it received the entire library of Dr. Johannes Polzmacher as a bequest 15.
Evesham (Worcestershire)
A statute enacted in 1215 provided that certain tenths should be reserved for buying parchment and increasing the library. The following year, the amount available was five solidos, eighteen deniers 16.
Ely
Account books show that in 1300, the monks purchased five dozen sheets of parchment, four pounds of ink, eight calf-skins, four sheep-skins, five dozen sheets of vellum, and six pairs of book clasps. They paid six shillings for a Decretal and two shillings for a Speculum Gregor. In 1329, the Precentor received six shillings and seven pence to go to Balsham to purchase books; four shillings were paid for twelve iron chains. Between 1350 and 1356, purchases included no less than seventy dozen sheets of parchment and thirty dozen sheets of vellum 17.
San Giovanni in Naples
Not an old monastery collection; its origin, according to Blume, was with Janus Parrhasius. The Augustin monks presented it in 1729 to Emperor Charles VI to avoid visits from zealous scholars 1819.
Admunt
Catalogued in 1380 by Brother Peter of Arbonne.
Leyden — Chapter of S. Pancras
Received in 1380, through a bequest of Philip of Leyden, a collection of 80 manuscripts, whose catalogue has been preserved 20.
St. Ulrich (near Augsburg)
The Benedictine monastery retained its importance until the invention of printing; in 1472 a printing office was instituted in connection with it.
Sponheim
Abbot Trithemius presented in 1480 the sum of fifteen hundred ducats for the enlargement of its library.
Beuggen (near Rheinfelden)
A library was founded in 1345 through the exertions of Wulfram of Nellenberg, who directed that all books left by deceased Brothers throughout Elsass be brought there, and urged living Brothers to present their own books 21.
Dargun (Rostock)
Prince Borwin of Rostock in 1240 presented a hide of land, the proceeds to be used for the repairing and preservation of books 22.
Penfont (Rennes)
Adam, treasurer of the Chapter of Rennes, in 1231 presented his library to the abbey, with the condition that books never be diverted and that copies be lent only against adequate pledges.
Other Notable Collections

Verona (library of the Town Hall): one of the most important Italian collections where old manuscripts have been preserved to the present (Wattenbach).
Hexham (England): originally collected by Bishop Acca in the year 700; referred to by Bede 23.
York: first described by Alcuin 24.
Lupus of Ferrières wrote to Pope Benedict III (855) begging for loan of texts including Jerome on Jeremiah, Cicero de Oratore, Quintilian, and Terence 25.

Brothers of Common Life Libraries
The Brothers of Common Life planned their collections expressly with reference to the service of students in their schools. These libraries contained a much larger proportion of books in the vernacular than were found in other monasteries. In some Brotherhood Homes, the library was divided into a collection for the Brothers and a collection for the students. It was ordered that at least once a year, all books not out on loan should be called in and inspected in the presence of the Brothers.
Monastery Reform
The Monastery Reform, instituted at the beginning of the 15th century, exercised a decided influence on interest in books and the development of libraries.

Tegernsee: The once noted library had fallen into ruins. Abbot Casper (1426–1461) reorganised it, restored manuscripts, bought new codices, and put hired scribes to work. His successor Conrad V purchased for eleven hundred pounds heller no less than 450 volumes, in addition to securing gifts 26.
Salzburg: Archbishop Johann II (1429–1441) caused a new library building to be erected and collected many beautiful manuscripts.
Bergen (near Magdeburg): Abbot Bursfelder (1450–1478) organised a library, utilising an old chapel.
Bordesholm: Prior Martin instituted a library in 1477. Brother Liborius (professor in Rostock) gave over his works on jurisprudence in 1405, with the provision that they be chained and remain forever in the reading-room. A catalogue of 1498 contains more than 500 titles 7.

Imperial Library of Constantinople
Of the libraries of antiquity, only a single one — the Imperial Library of Constantinople — continued in existence as late as the Middle Ages.

Founded in 354 by Emperor Constantius.
Largely added to by Julian the Philosopher.
Under Emperor Basiliscus, the original library — said to have contained no less than 120,000 volumes — was destroyed by fire.
Afterwards reinstituted by Emperor Zeno, with Julian (prefect of the city) giving personal supervision.
References are made to it in 1276, and again early in the 14th century, when John Palæologus was able to present from it certain manuscripts (probably duplicates) to the manuscript dealer Aurispa of Venice.
It is probable that the manuscripts were to some extent scattered before the fall of the city in 1453. Manuscripts that escaped destruction during the siege were hidden by scholars in various monasteries and out-of-the-way corners, from which they were brought out by degrees during the following two or three centuries.
Large quantities found their way promptly to Italy, chiefly through Venice. Not a few Greek scholars driven from Byzantine territories brought into Italy collections of manuscripts as their sole valuable possessions, used as texts for lectures or for transcribing for sale.

Gifts and Bequests
While the principal increase in monastery libraries came through scribal work, exchanges, and occasional purchases, a considerable proportion came through gifts or bequests. The gift a novice customarily made on entering a monastery very frequently took the form of books.

1055: Priest Richlof, placing his son with the Benedictines, gave a farm and books; his mother gave a copy of a treatise of St. Ambrose 27.
Tegernsee (late 11th century): A noble cleric entering as a monk brought so many books that, when placed by the principal altar, they covered it from top to bottom 28.
Dietrich Schreiber of Halle gave in 1239 to the preaching Brothers of Leipzig a canonistic manuscript, with the condition that either of his sons could redeem it for five marks 29.
Robert of Lille (died 1339) left in his will to his daughters an illuminated calendar, with the condition that after their death it go to the nuns of Chikessaund 30.
Bequests of annual income: The Abbot of St. Père-de-Chartres ordered in 1145 that tenants must take up each year for the support of the library eighty-six solidos 31.

Public and University Libraries in the Monastic Tradition
The collections in Western monasteries, brought together for the requirements of the monks and restricted (at least in theory) to devotional or doctrinal books, were in large measure placed at the disposal of scholars outside the monasteries as literary interest extended beyond the class of ecclesiastics. Long after monks and ecclesiastics ceased to exercise control over books, the most convenient space for collections was still found in church buildings; many came to be known as cathedral libraries.
The provisions of the statutes affecting the libraries at Oxford and Cambridge colleges were borrowed directly from the customs of the monasteries. The Sorbonne (dating from 1253) had its librarium instituted in 1289, specified for common use of instructors and students; a catalogue of 1290 contained 1017 titles 32. The Sorbonne also took the initiative in inviting the first printers to Paris in 1469, with the prior and librarian finding work and support for two printers from Mayence; the first book printed in Paris was the letters of Gasparin of Bergamo (1470), bearing the imprint in aedibus Sorbonnae 33.
