concepts/reformation.title: Reformation
concepts/reformation.content:
Reformation
The Reformation was not caused by printing alone, but it became the first great European religious movement to exploit print at scale. movable-type made it possible for arguments, sermons, vernacular Bibles, pamphlets, broadsides, and polemics to circulate faster and farther than manuscript culture allowed. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Printing as an Accelerator
By the early sixteenth century the infrastructure described in spread-of-printing was already in place: presses, publishers, paper supply, book fairs, distribution routes, and a reading public. Reformers entered a communication environment that Gutenberg could not have foreseen. A theological dispute could now become a public controversy across cities and principalities. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Luther was prompt to recognise the value of the new art for his work. He understood that if the fight against Rome was to secure popular support, it was necessary to reach not only the limited circles of the educated but the masses. For that purpose he put forth his sermons, tracts, and controversial pamphlets at once in the language of the people. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1450] For thousands of Germans, the first practical knowledge of the existence of the printing-press came with the sight of the sheets of the Wittenberg pamphlets or of the volumes of the Wittenberg Testament. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1450] The greater number of the pamphlets were issued at once in two editions, one Latin and one German. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1496]
Luther himself was amazed at the extent of the public he was able to reach when, after 1518, his tracts and sermons came to be printed in German; up to this time they had been originally issued in Latin and only in part translated. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1578]
Flugschriften: The Pamphlet Economy
The revolution in publishing methods brought about in connection with the Reformation was not restricted to the introduction of German as a language for popular publications. Of almost equal importance was the change in the form and price of books: costly folios and quartos were replaced by comparatively inexpensive twelvemos and sixteenmos, and by far the larger proportion of the writings that exercised the most immediate influence on the thought of the time were issued in the form of pamphlets. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1576] These pamphlets, sold in market-places, along highways, and from house to house, by pedlars working for gain and by colporteurs having a missionary purpose, took the place which in modern times is filled by the magazine or weekly paper. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1576] The German term Flugschriften — literally “fly-leaf literature” or “flying writings” — captures their ephemeral, rapidly circulated character. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1498] Every pfennig that came in from the fly-leaves or pamphlets appears to have been at once expended in further printings and in instituting further distributing machinery. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1620]
Statistical Explosion (1513-1523)
According to the statistics of book-production collected by Panzer, Weller, and Kuczynski, and tabulated by Kapp, the total number of separate works (principally pamphlets, Flugschriften) printed in German rose dramatically: ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1576]

























YearGerman-language works151390151814615205711523944
The aggregate for the decade 1513-1523 was 3,113. Of that total, no fewer than 600 were printed in Wittenberg — a place which before 1517 had not possessed a printing-press. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1576]
Edition Sizes and Speed of Sale
One of the more important of the earlier Flugschriften of Luther was the Address to the Nobility of Germany, printed in August 1520, of which 5,000 copies were sold in five days. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1498] Of the pamphlet containing his controversial address against Eck, printed in 1518, 1,400 copies were sold in two days at the Frankfort Fair. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1498]
Kostlin estimates that by 1520, more than one hundred editions had been printed of the German versions of Luther’s sermons and tracts, including all unauthorised issues as well as the editions printed at Luther’s Wittenberg Press. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1514] During the lifetime of the Reformer, not less than 100,000 copies of Luther’s New Testament were printed in Wittenberg alone. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1548]
Price Point
The usual price for the Protestant tracts was one groschen, equal to two and a half cents, or in purchasing power to perhaps twelve cents today. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1604]
Distribution Networks
The distribution of Luther’s pamphlets was effected only in part through the regular book-trade. Thousands of copies were sold in the market-places by dealers of all kinds, many of whom had never before handled books. Large supplies were distributed among readers out of reach of book-shops and market-places by travelling pedlars and by colporteurs. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1514] Many of the colporteurs were travelling students who were working not for gain but in the cause of the Reform. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1514]
The habit of circulating books and pamphlets by means of pedlars and colporteurs in districts far beyond the reach of the book-shops had both an immediate and an abiding effect upon the reading habits of the German people and did much to bring about the development of the publishing and bookselling business in Germany. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1452]
The circulation of the Lutheran tracts was taken charge of not only by book-pedlars and colporteurs but by a large number of travelling preachers (Pradikanten) — in part old-time priests, in many cases laymen of very varying degrees of education. The Wittenberg tracts gave a supply of ammunition that even the most ignorant preachers could make effective. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1608]
Under the pressure of the widespread interest in the writings of the Reformation, publishing business was done in a number of out-of-the-way little towns that would today hardly support a printing-press. Lutheran tracts were printed in places such as Grimma, Zwickau, and Eilenburg, principally for sale through the pedlars, very frequently without imprint or date. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1598]
The effective circulation of Luther’s pamphlets was very much multiplied by the practice of reading such pamphlets out loud in the market-places to all who might be interested. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1592] Each tract reached, as a rule, a number of readers or hearers, for the old Oriental and Greek practice of reading aloud to an audience was carried on in hundreds of market-places, shops, and other informal auditoriums. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1604] After the Lutheran writings had been put under interdict, such public readings had to be discontinued in towns and districts that remained under Catholic control, but the pamphlets were still widely (though surreptitiously) sold by pedlars and colporteurs, and the readings continued in places less liable to interruption than the inns and market-places. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1592]
Effect of the Bull of Leo X (1520)
In 1520, a Bull of Leo X excommunicated Luther, condemned his works individually and collectively, ordered existing copies to be burnt, and prohibited, under severe penalties, the printing, sale, distribution, or even possession of any of his writings. The immediate effect of this Bull was to cause a largely increased sale throughout nearly all parts of Germany for everything that Luther had written, and to bring about also a very considerable demand for them from other countries. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1514]
As an evidence of the very general distribution secured for Luther’s writings, the publisher Froben wrote to Luther from Basel on February 14, 1519, speaking of large supplies of the Basel editions being called for not only in Germany but in France, Spain, Italy, Brabant, and England. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1590]
Unauthorised Reprints and Luther’s Response
Luther and his associates were greatly troubled at the inaccuracy and incompleteness of much of the material sold over their names by unauthorised printers. In September 1525, Luther wrote to inquire whether his printers had been heedless in permitting sheets to be stolen for use in unauthorised printing elsewhere. “It is bad enough for these rascals to get the advantage, through theft, of my labour and pains, but with that I would be patient, if it were not for the shamelessly false and blundering form in which they issue books described as mine.” ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1554] He closed his complaint not with a contention for complete control of his material but with a moderate suggestion that the reprinters ought, as a matter of Christian feeling, first to wait a few months to give the original edition a fair chance, and second, to print their own issues with a decent regard for correctness and completeness. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1556]
Luther’s principal annoyance about reprints was in connection with inaccurate and incomplete texts. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1526] He wrote to the magistrates of Nuremberg in September 1525 complaining that proof-sheets of a volume of his sermons had been stolen from his printing-office in Wittenberg and used in Nuremberg for a piracy volume. He asked them to induce local printers to delay bringing out reprints until seven or eight weeks after the publication of the original editions. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1558]
Vernacular Religion
Printing strengthened vernacular religious culture. Texts in German, English, French, Dutch, and other languages reached readers who did not command Latin. This mattered not only for Protestant reform but for Catholic response, censorship, devotional literature, and education. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The popular interest excited by the writings of Luther and his associates brought about a great change in the trade of the book-shops. Editions of the Fathers and of the lives of the Saints were pushed aside from the counters or the book-shelves, or stored away in the warehouses, and even the classics were neglected. All the demand was for the writings of the Reformers. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1498] The jurist Scheurl wrote from Nuremberg to Cardinal Campeggi on March 15, 1524: “Every common man is now asking for books or pamphlets, and more reading is being done in a day than heretofore in a year.” ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1594]
The Catholic-Protestant Publishing War
The Reformation did not simply create a Protestant publishing industry. It created a confessional publishing war in which both sides used the press to fight for the same audiences, and the competition reshaped the economics of European printing.
Catholic Repression and the Protestant Advantage
The Catholic authorities responded to the pamphlet flood with censorship — the Index of Prohibited Books (1559), the Roman Inquisition, the Paris Parlement, and the English Stationers’ Company. But censorship had a paradoxical effect. The Bull of Leo X (1520) excommunicating Luther and ordering his works burned “caused a largely increased sale throughout nearly all parts of Germany for everything that Luther had written.” Condemnation acted as advertising. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md L1514]
In Catholic-controlled territories, the repression of Protestant printing created a two-way squeeze. Duke George of Saxony, a Catholic, “seriously hampered” Protestant printers in Leipzig with rigorous censorship. But “the writings of the Romanists found few buyers” — the Catholic market was smaller than the Protestant one in most German cities, and printing for an unpopular minority was commercially unattractive. The result was a depressed book trade in Catholic cities and a boom in Protestant ones. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
The Geneva-Lyon Rivalry
The most dramatic example of cross-confessional publishing competition was the relationship between Geneva (Protestant) and Lyon (Catholic). Lyon was the larger and more established printing centre, but Geneva’s Calvinist printers developed a specialized strategy: they manufactured cheap editions of Catholic works — missals, breviaries, books of hours, even Jesuit publications — for illicit sale in Catholic territories. The Lyonese printers retaliated by using “the brand of heretic to secure the confiscation at the frontier of a good many shipments of the books from Geneva” — even when those books were perfectly orthodox in content. The charge of heresy was a trade weapon as much as a religious one. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Catholic Printers Fight Back
The Catholic Church did not rely solely on repression. It also built its own printing infrastructure:


The Jesuit press in Vienna (1559). Ferdinand I called the Jesuits to Vienna in 1551, and the rector Johann Victoria established a press “zum besten der Religion und armer Studenten” (for the benefit of religion and poor students). Its main product was the catechism of Peter Canisius, commissioned by imperial order, translated into many languages and still in use in Austrian schools centuries later. The press operated until 1565. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]


Jesuit missionary presses. Jesuits operated secret presses in Cordoba (17th century), and presses in Japan (Amacusa, Nagasaki from the late 16th century) and China (Peking, Nanjing) for printing Christian texts in local languages. In Constantinople, Jesuits successfully prevented a Greek Orthodox press from being established. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]


The Congregation de Propaganda Fide (1622). Rome established a missionary press attached to the Vatican, equipped with oriental types by the punchcutter Stefano Paoli, printing New Testaments and devotional books “in many languages” — though Lorck notes it “never developed effectiveness commensurate with its considerable resources.” ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]


The Blaeu Paradox
The most striking example of how confessional competition distorted normal publishing economics was the Blaeu firm in Amsterdam. Willem Jansz Blaeu was a convinced Copernican and Protestant who disguised his views in his mariners’ guides. Yet his firm’s most reliable revenue stream — alongside atlases — was the “semi-clandestine production of missals and other Roman Catholic literature” for export. When Blaeu’s printing house burned on 22 February 1672, “strict Protestants called it divine punishment because Blaeu printed many breviaries and missals for Catholics.” ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Protestant Conversion of Gutenberg
John Man summarizes the ideological reversal neatly: “Gutenberg, once the darling of the Catholics, now became a Protestant hero. Printing, Luther said, was ‘God’s highest and extremest act of grace, whereby the business of the Gospel is driven forward.‘” The technology that had been invented to produce standardized Catholic liturgical texts became the engine of the movement that shattered Catholic unity. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]

concepts/seventeenth-century-printing.title: Seventeenth-Century Printing
concepts/seventeenth-century-printing.content:
Seventeenth-Century Printing
The sixteenth century made printing an industry. The seventeenth century made it a medium.
By 1600, the press was no longer a new technology. The basic processes — punchcutting, matrix-striking, typecasting, composition, impression — had been stable for over a century. What changed in the 1600s was not how printing was done but what it was used for, who controlled it, where it was centred, and how far its reach extended. The newspaper, the scientific report, the novel, the children’s book, the systematic atlas, and the first copyright laws all belong to this century. The wooden hand press reached its mature mechanical form, typefounding became an independent industry, and the geographic centre of European printing shifted definitively to the Dutch Republic.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]
The Press Reaches Maturity
The wooden screw press that Gutenberg had adapted from the winepress remained essentially unchanged for nearly 170 years. The first significant improvements came around 1620, when Willem Jansz Blaeu (1571-1638), the Amsterdam printer and instrument-maker, introduced a series of mechanical refinements. Hoe describes the Blaeu press: the spindle passed through a square block guided in the wooden frame, the platen was suspended by wires and cords from this block, preventing twist and ensuring equal motion across the entire impression. A device for rolling the bed in and out was added, along with a new form of iron hand lever for turning the screw.^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]
Lorck notes that Blaeu, described as “a skilled mechanic” (ein tuchtiger Mechaniker), built nine presses of this improved construction, named after the nine Muses. The Blaeu press became the standard throughout Europe and remained so until the Earl of Stanhope’s iron press in 1798. It was substantially the same press that Benjamin Franklin worked on as a journeyman in London a century later.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]
Blaeu’s printing house on the Damrak in Amsterdam, opened in 1637 and enlarged in 1639, was considered the most significant and beautiful in Europe, regularly employing over forty workers. It was destroyed by fire on 22 February 1672 — strict Protestants called it divine punishment because Blaeu printed many breviaries and missals for Catholics. The firm continued under his sons Peter and Johann, but the 1672 disaster, combined with the general Dutch economic decline of the late seventeenth century, ended its pre-eminence.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
Typefounding Becomes an Independent Industry
In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, printers cut their own type. By the seventeenth, typefounding had become a distinct trade, and the Dutch typefounding industry supplied all of Europe. The key figures:
Christoffel van Dyck (c. 1600-1669) was described by contemporaries as “the first punch-cutter of his time.” He cut the types used by the Elzevir family, whose clean, sharp letterforms defined the look of the scholarly duodecimo. Van Dyck also cut types for Joseph Athias, a Spanish Jew who printed in Amsterdam and produced a celebrated Hebrew Bible whose types “still count among the best.”^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Enschedé family in Haarlem became the most famous typefounding dynasty of the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Isaak Enschedé (born 1681) opened a printing house around 1703. His son Johannes acquired the Wetstein foundry in 1743 and later the Blaeu and Elzevir foundries, assembling the largest collection of historic types in Europe. The Enschedé Specimen de caracteres typographiques anciens preserved type specimens that no longer survive in their original matrices.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The separation of typefounding from printing was a quiet industrial revolution: it meant that a printer in London could buy the same Dutch types as a printer in Paris or Copenhagen, creating a standardisation of typography across Europe that had not existed in the sixteenth century.
The Dutch Republic Becomes the Printing Capital of Europe
The centre of gravity that had shifted from Venice to Antwerp in the sixteenth century moved again in the seventeenth — to the Dutch Republic. The fall of Antwerp to Spanish forces in 1585 sent Protestant printers, scholars, and capital north to Amsterdam, Leyden, Utrecht, and Haarlem. The Dutch Republic offered what no other European state could match: relative religious toleration, a highly literate urban population, excellent trade networks, and a legal system that — while far from granting full press freedom — was more permissive than the Index-controlled Catholic states or the Star Chamber-controlled English press.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
Four cities dominated:

Amsterdam: The largest. Home to the Blaeu firm, the Janssonius firm, Joseph Athias (Hebrew printing), and dozens of smaller presses. Amsterdam printed everything: Bibles for export, scholarly works in Latin, newspapers in Dutch, maps for the East India Company, and clandestine Catholic liturgical works.
Leyden: The university city. The Elzevir family established their press here, securing the post of university printer and bookseller. The Elzevirs’ duodecimo classics were known across Europe for their elegance and affordability.
Haarlem: The Enschedé typefoundry. Also the centre of the Coster legend — the claim that Laurens Janszoon Coster, not Gutenberg, invented printing. Lorck devotes substantial space to refuting this claim, which was a matter of Dutch national pride.
Utrecht: A smaller but significant academic and theological printing centre.

The dominance of the Dutch Republic meant that Dutch became a major European print language for the first time, and that the format and typography of Dutch books — especially the Elzevir duodecimo and the sharp van Dyck types — set the standard that the rest of Europe imitated.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Newspaper is Born
The most consequential new product of the seventeenth-century press was the newspaper. Before 1600, news had been transmitted through occasional pamphlets, handwritten newsletters, and word of mouth. The idea of a regularly published serial giving current news was an invention of the early 1600s.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The first regularly published newspapers appeared almost simultaneously across Europe: Strasbourg (1605), Berlin (1615, printed by Christoph Runge), Antwerp, London, Paris, and Copenhagen. Lorck notes that by the first quarter of the eighteenth century, London alone had three daily newspapers, ten published three times weekly, and five weeklies, supported by seventy-five printing offices in the capital and twenty-eight in the provinces.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The newspaper created new pressures on the press:

Regular deadlines demanded faster production and a larger workforce.
Subscription economics replaced single-sale book economics — a publisher needed a steady subscriber base, not one-off buyers.
Censorship became harder because newspapers reported on current events that could not be anticipated or pre-approved.
The news trade created a new relationship between print and power: governments wanted to control the news, but they also wanted their own version printed.

The first English newspapers appeared during the Civil War period: the Mercurius Aulicus (Royalist) and the Mercurius Britanicus (Parliamentarian) in the 1640s. The London Gazette (1666) became the first official government newspaper. The Tatler (1709) and the Spectator (1711) by Steele and Addison created the English periodical essay, which influenced European journalism for a century. The 1712 stamp tax — a halfpenny per half-sheet — doubled newspaper prices and reduced circulation, establishing a pattern of taxation-as-censorship that lasted into the nineteenth century.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
In the American colonies, the Boston News-Letter (1704) was the first newspaper, followed by the Boston Gazette (1719), printed by James Franklin. The newspaper as a genre was now a global phenomenon: Mexico and Peru likely had newspapers from the end of the seventeenth century, and issues of the Mexico-Gazette from 1728-1730 survive.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Atlas Reaches Its Peak
The sixteenth century had invented the atlas (Ortelius 1570, Mercator 1595). The seventeenth century made it monumental. Johann Blaeu’s Atlas Maior (1662-1665), eleven volumes in the grandest edition, was the largest and most expensive printed book of its century. Lorck describes it as “a magnificent Atlas in 12 large folio volumes” followed by several equally grand works.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
The Atlas Maior represented the integration of cartography, copperplate engraving, and commercial publishing at the highest level. It included maps of every known region, city views, and extensive descriptive text. The cost of production — the copperplates alone represented a huge investment — was so great that it burdened the Blaeu firm’s finances. The 1672 fire that destroyed Blaeu’s printing office was the final blow.^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
The atlas market was intensely competitive. Blaeu competed directly with Willem Janssonius and Jacob Aertsz Colom, both of whom worked within sight of Blaeu’s shop on the Damrak. The same map plates were bought, sold, and reused across firms. The atlas was the prestige product of the seventeenth-century press — too expensive for most readers, but essential for any printer who wanted to be taken seriously.^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Bible Printing in the Vernacular
The seventeenth century saw the printing of the two most important English and Dutch Bibles.
The King James Bible (1611) was the work of fifty-four scholars appointed by James I, divided into six companies working at Westminster, Cambridge, and Oxford. It replaced the Geneva Bible as the standard English translation. The first edition was printed by Robert Barker. Lorck records the details of the commission and the 1611 publication.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The “Wicked Bible” of 1632, printed by George Baker and George Lucas, famously omitted the word “not” from the Seventh Commandment (“Thou shalt commit adultery”). The edition was confiscated and the printers fined 3,000. The fine money was used to purchase Greek matrices and types for the royal printers — a remarkable example of a printing error shaping the typographic resources of the English press.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Dutch States Bible (1637) was the first official Dutch translation authorised by the States General, serving the same consolidating function for Dutch Protestantism that the KJV served for English. It was printed by several presses in large editions.
Bible printing was the most capital-intensive and politically sensitive branch of the trade. A large Bible edition required months of press time, expensive paper, and careful correction. The profit on a successful Bible edition was substantial, but the risk of error or political offence was severe.
The Novel and the Shakespeare First Folio
Two literary landmarks belong to this century.
Miguel de Cervantes’ Don Quixote (Part I, 1605; Part II, 1615) was printed in Madrid by Juan de la Cuesta. It is often described as the first modern European novel — a sustained work of vernacular prose fiction with developed characters and a unified narrative. It was translated into every major European language within decades and became the most influential work of fiction of the century.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
William Shakespeare’s First Folio (1623) was printed by Isaac Jaggard and Edward Blount. The first collected edition of Shakespeare’s plays, it preserved thirty-six plays, eighteen of which had never been printed before. Only about 750 copies were printed; the fact that two editions sufficed until 1664 (barely 1,000 copies total) tells us how small the market for English drama was in the seventeenth century, compared to the hagiographic status of the playwright today.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Other notable literary publishing: John Bunyan’s The Pilgrim’s Progress (1678), continuously reprinted; Daniel Defoe’s Robinson Crusoe (1719), which had forty-one editions in its original form. Lorck also notes that at the end of the seventeenth century, Robert Clavel’s General Catalogue of Books (1676, continued to 1700) provided the first systematic English-language book trade bibliography.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The English Press and the Struggle for Control
The seventeenth century in England was the great age of press control and the beginning of press freedom.
The Stationers’ Company (chartered 1556) had given the Crown effective control over English printing. Under Elizabeth I, all books required official approval. The Star Chamber decrees of 1637, under Archbishop Laud, reduced the number of London printers to twenty, type foundries to four, and limited each to two apprentices. Only London could print, except for the university presses at Oxford and Cambridge.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Civil War and Interregnum (1642-1660) temporarily broke this system. Parliament and the Crown each tried to control the press, and both failed. The number of presses expanded rapidly. John Milton’s Areopagitica (1644) was the most eloquent defence of press freedom of the century, though even Milton did not advocate complete freedom — he excluded Catholics and Unitarians.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
After the Restoration (1660), the Licensing Act of 1662 restored pre-publication censorship and required the registration of all books. Three copies of every work had to be deposited in libraries. But the system was leaky, and enforcement was inconsistent. When the Licensing Act lapsed in 1694, it was not renewed. Lorck states: “1694: the last restrictive measures against the press were lifted — England can be considered to have a free press from this time.”^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Copyright and the Statute of Anne
The first exclusive privilege for a printed book had been granted to Richard Pynson in 1518. But throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, “copyright” was a right of the publisher, not the author. It was protected by the Stationers’ Company register and enforced by the Crown. The author had no legal right in his own work.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Statute of Anne (1710, referred to in the sources as 1709 under old-style dating) changed this. For the first time, copyright was recognised as the author’s right, not the publisher’s. The term was fourteen years, renewable for another fourteen if the author was still alive at the end of the first term. Putnam describes it as the foundational copyright legislation of Europe. Lorck notes that “in these privileges are found the first traces of recognition of intellectual property rights, though more in the material interest of the publisher than the author.”^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
In the Dutch Republic, the situation was different. Privileges (printing patents) were granted by individual provinces and were only effective within the issuing jurisdiction. An expired privilege made a book “vogelvrij” (fair game) for reprinters. Blaeu could not obtain a privilege for Grotius’s De iure belli ac pacis (1631) due to political sensitivities — a reminder that copyright was never merely a legal question but a political one.^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
The Frankfurt-Leipzig Book Fair Shift
The Frankfurt Book Fair had been the centre of the European book trade since the late fifteenth century. In the seventeenth century, it was supplanted by Leipzig.
The first Leipzig fair catalogue appeared in 1594. In 1595, Leipzig listed 68 works against Frankfurt’s 117. By 1604, Leipzig had overtaken Frankfurt. The Thirty Years’ War (1618-1648) accelerated the shift: by 1632, Leipzig had 221 works to Frankfurt’s 68. Leipzig’s advantage was partly geographical (central Germany, out of reach of the Catholic censorship that constrained Frankfurt) and partly commercial (a more efficient fair organisation).^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The total Leipzig press output between 1641 and 1740 was 19,711 items, with the strongest year being 1698 at 401 works. By 1689, Leipzig listed 310 works to Frankfurt’s 90; by 1699, 319 to 109. The Thirty Years’ War also brought a general decline in book quality — poor type, sloppy proofreading, bad paper — from which the German trade recovered only at the very end of the century.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Stereotyping: The First Attempt at Mass Production
The idea of making a single cast of an entire page — stereotyping — was experimented with around 1700. J. van der Mey and the German preacher Johann Müller in Leyden produced several “stereotyped” works, including a Bible in folio and quarto, a New Testament in English and Greek, and a Syriac dictionary. Four of their plates survived to be exhibited at the Caxton Jubilee in London in 1877. The Enschedé firm printed a Bible in folio in 1727 using the van der Mey-Müller process.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
William Ged in Scotland experimented with stereotyping in partnership with the typefounder Thomas James around 1710. But printers viewed stereotyping with suspicion, seeing it as a threat to their compositors’ livelihood. Ged’s experiments brought James “direct and indirect losses,” and the technology was abandoned for nearly a century. True economic stereotyping had to await the mass-demand for Bibles and newspapers of the nineteenth century.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Copperplate Illustration Becomes Standard
In the sixteenth century, woodcut was the standard technique for book illustration. In the seventeenth, copperplate replaced it for all serious work. Lorck notes the decisive shift: “From the Papillons onward, woodcut declined completely and only copperplate engraving was used for book illustration” — not just as separate plates but also for vignettes printed in the text.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Jean Papillon (1660-1710) was the founder of a wood-engraving family, but even his work could not reverse the trend toward copperplate. The Dutch in particular excelled in copperplate engraving and etching. The Plantin-Moretus Museum’s collection of 7,000 to 8,000 copperplates testifies to the scale of the copperplate trade. The integration of copperplate illustration with letterpress text — requiring separate presses and careful planning — was now standard practice for any ambitious book.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Children’s Books and Education
John Amos Comenius (1592-1670), the Czech educational reformer, published his Orbis Sensualium Pictus (The Visible World in Pictures) in 1658. It was the first children’s picture book — a Latin-German illustrated encyclopaedia designed to teach language through labelled woodcut scenes. It was reprinted for two centuries and translated into every European language. The idea that children needed books designed specifically for them was itself a product of print culture. Comenius’s earlier treatise on language teaching was published by the Elzevir press in 1642 and “had a great popularity.”^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The French Royal Printing Office and State Patronage
Under Louis XIII and Cardinal Richelieu, the Imprimerie Royale (Royal Printing Office) was founded in Paris. In 1631, Richelieu assigned the printing of liturgical and sacred texts in Oriental languages to a Paris consortium. Under Louis XIV, the press was patronised but also restricted. The Revocation of the Edict of Nantes (1685) drove French papermakers and printers to emigrate to England and the Netherlands, boosting English papermaking but devastating the French trade.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Moxon’s Mechanick Exercises (1683)
Joseph Moxon’s Mechanick Exercises on the Whole Art of Printing (1683) was the first complete textbook describing the printing process in detail. Moxon, a London printer and maker of globes, described the hand mould, the press, the process of composition, and the organisation of the workshop. John Man notes that Moxon’s book was the first to explain the hand mould in over two hundred years — no one had bothered to describe it in writing since Gutenberg. It remained the standard reference for a century.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Legacy
The seventeenth century is the century in which printing became recognisably modern. The physical press reached its mature mechanical form. Typefounding became an independent industry. The newspaper, the atlas, the novel, and the children’s book all appeared as new genres. Copyright was defined as an author’s right for the first time. The centre of the trade shifted to the Dutch Republic and remained there for a century. And the first successful arguments for press freedom were made — arguments that would shape the eighteenth-century Enlightenment and the American and French revolutions.
Lorck called the period 1500-1750 the “Glanzperiode und Verfall” — the period of splendour and decline. For the seventeenth century, it was more splendour than decline. The press was still a wooden hand press, but it was now printing newspapers, novels, atlases, and scientific reports for a reading public far larger and more diverse than anything the sixteenth century had known.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]

concepts/sixteenth-century-printing.title: Sixteenth-Century Printing
concepts/sixteenth-century-printing.content:
Sixteenth-Century Printing
The year 1500 is an artificial boundary. The incunable period did not end on 31 December 1500 because anything suddenly changed in the trade. It is a bibliographic convenience, imposed by Johann Saubert’s catalogue and accepted by scholars ever since. But the sixteenth century was genuinely different from the incunable period in almost every dimension of printing: the content of what was printed, the format and price, the organisation of the trade, the technology of typefounding and illustration, and the political relationship between print and authority.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
This page synthesises the major shifts that transformed European printing between 1500 and 1600.
The Reformation and the Vernacular Explosion
The single most transformative event for sixteenth-century printing was the Reformation. In the incunable period, 77% of editions had been in Latin, and 45% of output was religious — mostly liturgical books for priests (missals, breviaries, psalters) and patristic theology for scholars. The Reformation changed all of this.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Luther’s Ninety-Five Theses (1517) were printed in German, not Latin, and they spread through pamphlet networks, not through the established book trade. In the years 1517-1525, Luther published over 300 pamphlets, many in editions of 4,000 copies that sold out in days. Putnam notes that the Reformation “gave employment to the presses of Germany for a generation.” The Catholic Church responded with its own pamphlets, creating a Europe-wide polemical literature that had no precedent in the manuscript age.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
This had lasting structural effects:

Vernacular printing became a major market. German, French, English, Italian, and Spanish all grew from small shares to substantial print languages. The reader was no longer necessarily a Latin-literate cleric or scholar.
Pamphlets became the dominant format for new ideas. Cheap, short, fast to produce, easy to distribute. The Reformation was, in John Man’s phrase, “the first movement in history to be powered by print.”
Censorship became systematic in response. The Index of Prohibited Books (1559), the Roman Inquisition, the Paris parlement, the English Stationers’ Company (1557) — all were attempts to control the flood of vernacular religious printing.^[raw/articles/censorship-of-the-press.md]
Vernacular Bibles became the norm. Tyndale’s New Testament (1526, 18,000 copies through six editions), Luther’s German Bible (1534), Coverdale’s English Bible (1535), the Geneva Bible (1560). The printed vernacular Bible, once rare and suspect, became ubiquitous.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]

The Book Gets Smaller and Cheaper
In the incunable period, most serious books were folios. The Aldine octavo (from 1501) pioneered smaller formats for classical texts, but it was the Elzevir family in the early seventeenth century who perfected the duodecimo — a format small enough to hold in one hand, priced low enough for a student or merchant to afford. Lorck calls the Elzevirs “the heirs of Aldus” in the small-format market.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The format shift was also a price shift. A folio Bible or law commentary might cost several ducats — a year’s wages for a labourer. An Elzevir duodecimo of Virgil or Horace cost a fraction of that. The personal library, once the preserve of princes and monasteries, became accessible to scholars, professionals, and the literate middle class. This expanded the market for printing far beyond what the incunable period had known.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
By the late sixteenth century, the small-format book — octavo, duodecimo, even sextodecimo — had become the standard format for most reading matter. The folio was reserved for reference works, liturgical books, and prestige projects. The “portable book” that Aldus had pioneered became the norm.
Typography Becomes a Profession
In the incunable period, printers cut their own type. The punchcutter was a craftsman within the printing shop. By the mid-sixteenth century, typefounding had become a separate trade.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Claude Garamond (c. 1510-1561) was the first type designer to sell his types to multiple printers rather than working for a single shop. His Roman types, cut for Robert Estienne’s Greek Royal types (commissioned by King Francis I of France), became the standard across Europe. Lorck treats the Estienne family as “the generation that reached the highest typographic honours” alongside the Aldi.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The separation of typefounding from printing was an industrial development: it meant that a printer in Lyon could buy the same typefaces as a printer in Antwerp, which contributed to the standardisation of book design across Europe. It also increased specialisation — a punchcutter could focus on perfecting his letterforms while the printer focused on production and sales.
Other typographic developments included:

Italic type became standard for certain genres (poetry, prefaces, annotations).
Fraktur became the standard German typeface after Schonsperger’s Theuerdank (1513) and remained so into the twentieth century.
Greek types improved dramatically, notably through the Aldine press and the Estienne foundry, enabling the printing of Greek classics and the New Testament in its original language.
Hebrew types were developed for scholarly and missionary printing.

Music Printing Becomes Viable
Before 1501, music could only be printed from woodblocks or left blank for hand-rubrication. Ottaviano Petrucci in Venice (1501) developed a method of printing polyphonic music from movable type using three impressions: staves, text, and notes were printed separately, requiring precise registration. This was technically brilliant but slow and expensive.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Later innovators — notably Pierre Haultin in Paris and the Plantin press in Antwerp — developed single-impression music type, which could print staves, notes, and text in one pass. This made music printing commercially viable.
The consequences were significant:

The Catholic Church, after the Council of Trent (1545-1563), could standardise liturgical music across Europe through printed graduals and antiphoners.
The Reformation could distribute printed hymnbooks (Luther’s hymns, the Genevan Psalter).
Secular music could be printed and distributed, creating a market for madrigals, chansons, and instrumental works.

New Genres
The sixteenth century created new categories of printed work that had no real manuscript precedent.
Atlases. The concept of a uniform-format collection of maps was invented by Abraham Ortelius (1570) and named by Gerard Mercator (1595). The atlas was a new kind of book — a reference work designed to be consulted, not read linearly. It required the integration of copperplate illustration with letterpress text, pushing the technical boundaries of both.^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Navigation manuals and sea atlases. The practical needs of European maritime expansion created a new genre of printed works for navigators: pilot books, navigation manuals, island books, and sea atlases, written in the vernacular and illustrated with coastal profiles, compass bearings, and sailing directions.^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
Scientific and medical books with systematic illustration. The landmark work was Vesalius’s De humani corporis fabrica (Basel: Oporinus, 1543), which was impossible in manuscript: its copperplate anatomical plates required a level of precision and standardisation that only print could provide. Vesalius had spent years in Venice commissioning woodcuts from Jan van Calcar, a pupil of Titian, to illustrate human anatomy “with great talent.” He was so concerned about print quality that he sent his own pressman from the famous Bomberg printing shop in Venice to Basel to supervise production. The resulting work — with woodcuts so fine they were mistaken for Titian originals — demonstrated the value of the woodcut “for scientific purpose and the easier understanding of a work.”^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Copernicus’s De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (Nuremberg: Johannes Petreius, 1543) was the other pillar of the scientific revolution in print, its diagrams and tables integrated with the text. The 1617 Amsterdam Astronomia instaurata shows the afterlife of that print event: Mulerius advertises the edition as a restoration of a text damaged by earlier printers and numerical corruption, with notes, tables, errata, and a format suited to Blaeu’s type and companion Frisian tables. John Man notes that printing allowed specialists “to agree on their agendas and feed off each other” for the first time.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]^[raw/articles/copernicus-astronomia-instaurata.md]
Between these two landmarks, the astronomer Regiomontanus (Johann Muller, 1436-1476) was the first to demonstrate how a scholar could use the press for original scientific work. He set up both an observatory and a printing press in Nuremberg in the 1470s and published his own detailed observations of the moon and planets. In 1474 he published a new method for calculating longitude by measuring lunar distance — a system that proved too complex for practical use at sea, but whose observational tradition fed directly into Copernicus’s work seventy years later.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Architectural treatises were another new genre made possible by systematic printed illustration. Vitruvius’s De architectura — the only surviving architectural treatise from classical antiquity — could now be reproduced in all major languages, and architects armed with the printed works of his Renaissance disciples (Vignola, Palladio) could recreate classical forms in building projects across Europe.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Herbals and natural history also demanded accurate plant drawings that only print could standardise and distribute, creating a market for illustrated botanical works that became one of the most commercially successful scientific genres of the sixteenth century.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Travel and exploration narratives. Ramusio’s Navigationi et Viaggi (1550-1559) collected accounts of voyages to the Americas, Asia, and Africa in a single printed work. Hakluyt’s Principal Navigations (1589) did the same for English exploration. These collections had no manuscript equivalent — they were compilations of materials that could only be gathered, edited, and distributed through the print network.^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
The learned journal. The Journal des scavans (1665) and the Philosophical Transactions (1665) were the culmination of a sixteenth-century trend toward periodic scholarly communication, which had begun with the letter-books of humanist scholars and the regular newsletters of the book fairs.
The vernacular novel. Amadis de Gaula (1508), Lazarillo de Tormes (1554), Montaigne’s Essais (1580). These were new forms that print enabled — long-form vernacular prose for a lay readership.
The emblem book. Andrea Alciato’s Emblemata (1531) created a new genre combining image, motto, and epigram. Emblem books became one of the most popular genres of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, endlessly reprinted, translated, and imitated.
Illustration Becomes Systematic
In the incunable period, illustration was optional and expensive. By the late sixteenth century, many genres demanded illustration: herbals (which required accurate plant drawings), anatomical works, travel books, atlases, architectural treatises, and emblem books.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The woodcut remained the workhorse technique for most illustrated books. But copperplate engraving, pioneered for maps by Sweynheym (1478), became standard for high-end scientific and cartographic work. The copperplate press — a rolling press separate from the screw press used for text — became a standard piece of equipment in larger printing houses. Lorck notes that the Blaeu firm in Amsterdam had nine presses “of improved construction, named after the nine muses,” and that their main activity was “the publication of astronomical and map works.”^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The cost of illustration was now a budgeted line item, not an exceptional expense. Plantin’s Polyglot Bible (1568-1572) included engraved plates, ornamental initials, and complex typographic layouts across eight volumes in five languages. The Nuremberg Chronicle’s 1,800 woodcuts (1493) had been exceptional; by 1600, a work of that scale of illustration was merely ambitious.
Censorship Becomes Systematic
The incunable period had seen sporadic censorship — Berthold of Mainz’s 1486 edict against vernacular liturgy, the occasional burning of heretical works. The sixteenth century made censorship systematic.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
The key institutions:

The Index of Prohibited Books (first Roman Index 1559, Tridentine Index 1564) listing approximately 1,000 titles. Expanded steadily through the century.
The Venetian privilege system, which granted exclusive printing rights for periods of ten to twenty-five years, but also gave the state a mechanism for approving books before publication.
The Paris parlement, which controlled printing in France through a system of licensing and inspection. Chevillier documents how the University of Paris exercised authority over the book trade.
The English Stationers’ Company (1557), which gave the Crown effective control over all printing in England.
The Spanish Inquisition, which maintained its own Index and conducted regular inspections of bookshops and libraries.^[raw/articles/censorship-of-the-press.md]

Censorship and printing grew up together. The technology that made the Reformation possible also made the Index necessary. Every advance in the speed or reach of the press provoked a corresponding effort to control it. This dialectic between print freedom and print control is a defining feature of sixteenth-century printing that had no real equivalent in the incunable period.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
The Centre of Gravity Shifts North
In 1500, the centre of European printing was Venice and the German cities. By 1600, it had shifted to the Low Countries. This reflected the broader shift of European trade from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic.
Antwerp became the leading printing city of the mid-sixteenth century. Christopher Plantin (c. 1520-1589) built the largest printing and publishing firm Europe had seen, with multiple presses, a typefoundry, and an international network of agents and correspondents. His Polyglot Bible (1568-1572), commissioned by Philip II of Spain, was the most ambitious scholarly printing project of the century.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Amsterdam succeeded Antwerp after the Spanish sack of 1576 and the fall of Antwerp to Spanish forces in 1585. The Blaeu family and the Elzevir family made Amsterdam the printing capital of the seventeenth century. Blaeu’s Atlas Maior (1662-1665), in eleven volumes, was the largest and most expensive printed book of its century. The Elzevirs’ duodecimo classics set the standard for affordable scholarly publishing.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]^[raw/articles/van-netten-blaeu-review.md]
Leiden became a centre of academic printing through the university and the Elzevir firm. Geneva became a centre for French-language Reformed printing. Frankfurt remained the centre of the book fair system.
This northern shift was not just geographic. It represented a change in the nature of the trade: from the artisanal, scholar-printer model of the incunable period (Gutenberg, Aldus, Froben) to the industrial, capital-intensive model of the seventeenth century (Plantin, Blaeu, Elzevir). The printing firm had become a business that required sustained investment, international distribution, and professional management.
The Book Trade Matures
In the fifteenth century, printing was a risky trade dominated by individuals — Gutenberg needing Fust’s capital, Sweynheym and Pannartz going bankrupt in Rome, Koberger operating more like a merchant than a publisher. By 1600, the book trade had institutional structures:^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]

Regular book fairs at Frankfurt (established by 1500 as the centre of the trade) and Leipzig (beginning to rival Frankfurt in the late sixteenth century). The Frankfurt fair catalogue (first published 1564) listed all new books, creating a Europe-wide awareness of what was being published.
Guilds and companies regulating the trade: the Stationers’ Company in London, the guilds of Frankfurt and Leipzig, the printers’ guilds in Paris and Lyon.
International distribution networks maintained by the largest firms. Plantin had correspondents across Europe; Koberger had branches in a dozen cities; the Giunti firm had offices in Venice, Florence, and Lyon.
The exchange of books between publishers as a standard practice, allowing a publisher in Basel to sell Parisian books without maintaining a Paris office.
The beginnings of copyright through the privilege system. Extended from single-city privileges to empire-wide protections, and from ten-year to twenty-five-year terms.^[raw/articles/literary-property-and-copyright.md]

By 1600, printing was no longer a new technology finding its feet. It was a mature industry with established business practices, professional specialisation, international trade networks, and regulatory frameworks. The essential structure of the European book trade would remain stable from 1600 to the industrialisation of printing in the nineteenth century.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Legacy
The sixteenth century was the period in which printing became what it would remain for the next 300 years. The incunable period invented the technology and proved it could work. The sixteenth century made it an industry. It created:

The genres that printing would sustain for centuries (the novel, the learned journal, the atlas, the travel narrative, the polemical pamphlet, the hymnbook)
The division of labour (typefounder, printer, publisher, bookseller) that would characterise the trade until the Industrial Revolution
The relationship between print and authority (censorship, privilege, licensing) that defined the politics of publishing
The geography of the trade, which shifted from the Mediterranean to the North Sea and then remained remarkably stable until the rise of the American book trade in the nineteenth century
The economic structure of the book as a product: high fixed costs, variable scale, tiered pricing, international distribution

Lorck calls the period 1500-1750 the “Glanzperiode und Verfall” of printing — the period of splendour and decline. The splendour came first, in the sixteenth century, when the press was still new enough to be revolutionary but established enough to be an industry.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]

concepts/spectrum-of-printed-output.title: Spectrum of Printed Output
concepts/spectrum-of-printed-output.content:
Spectrum of Printed Output
The output of early printing presses spanned a far wider range than the word “book” suggests. From luxury vellum folios costing more than a year’s wages to single-sheet indulgences sold for pennies, from scholarly editions of Aristotle to almanacs for shepherds, from copperplate maps to playing cards — the printing press produced goods at every price point, for every conceivable buyer, in formats ranging from monumental to vest-pocket. This spectrum is the organising reality of the early printing trade.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The Six Tiers
1. Luxury Editions
At the top of the spectrum sat a small number of extraordinary works designed to compete with the finest illuminated manuscripts. These were printed on vellum in folio format, with wide margins, generous type, and elaborate decoration. The gutenberg-bible (c. 1455) was the prototype: thirty to thirty-five vellum copies requiring an estimated 5,000 calfskins, printed in a type designed to imitate manuscript Textura, with space left for hand-illuminated initials. The vellum alone cost 300 gulden — roughly a year’s wages for a skilled craftsman.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The 1457 Mainz Psalter followed, the first book to print decorative initials in two colours directly from the press. The Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (1499, Aldus) took luxury to an extreme: a typographic and woodcut masterpiece so deliberately exclusive that “hardly anyone bought it.”^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Economics: Very high capital intensity, very long payback period, very few buyers. Only the wealthiest patrons — churches, princes, and monastic libraries — could afford them. The profit per copy was high, but the total profit was often negative.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Survival rate: High. These books were valued from the start and have been preserved in institutional collections. About 48 of the estimated 180 Gutenberg Bibles survive (including fragments).
2. Prestige Folios
Large-format works on good paper, aimed at institutions and professionals. Law books, massive patristic editions, illustrated chronicles, and multivolume classical editions. The Nuremberg Chronicle (1493) is the archetype: 600 folio pages, over 1,800 woodcuts, printed in editions of 1,500 Latin and 1,000 German copies. Koberger’s investment in the Chronicle was substantial — the woodcuts alone cost 1,000 gulden — but the edition sold out.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Other examples: Sweynheym and Pannartz’s classical editions in Rome (twenty-eight titles, but overproduction bankrupted them), Koberger’s Bibles (thirty-three editions), and the great liturgical works commissioned by religious orders.
Economics: High capital, moderate risk, institutional buyers who paid reliably (if slowly). The market was predictable but limited. Overproduction, as Sweynheym and Pannartz discovered, was fatal.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Survival rate: High. These books filled library shelves and were seldom discarded.
3. Standard Quartos and Octavos
The middle of the market — serious books for serious readers. Humanist editions of classical authors, medical texts, scientific works, scholarly commentaries. Printed on good paper in quarto or octavo format, with standard typefaces, usually without illustration.
Venetian printers dominated this tier. Aldus Manutius’s Greek folios (Aristotle in five volumes, 1495-1498) sat at the upper end, priced at 11 ducats for the set. His octavo Libri Portatiles (from 1501) aimed lower: Virgil, Horace, Ovid in pocket-sized editions at around 1.5 lire (0.234 ducats) per volume.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Economics: Moderate capital, moderate margins, moderate risk. The buyer base was scholars, lawyers, physicians, and the literate bourgeoisie. This was the tier where one Aldine octavo cost “about 4 marcelli” — roughly a week’s wages for a skilled worker. Not cheap, but accessible to a professional reader.^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Survival rate: Moderate. Many survive in library collections, but even more were read to pieces.
4. Cheap School Texts and Practical Manuals
The largest print runs of the incunable period were not for any of the above. They were for school texts — above all the Donatus (Aelius Donatus’s Ars Minor, the standard Latin grammar) and Alexander de Villa Dei’s Doctrinale. These were printed in runs that may have exceeded 1,000 copies, in cheap formats on cheap paper, and sold to schoolboys who literally used them to destruction.
De Vinne describes how school texts “were read to pieces.” John Man notes that the Gutenberg Donatus survives only as “odd pages used for the binding of later publications.” No complete copy of any Gutenberg Donatus exists. Yet between 1450 and 1500, the Donatus was probably the single most printed work in Europe.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Other cheap texts included: vernacular ABCs and primers, arithmetic manuals, medical recipe books, guides to letter-writing, and legal formularies.
Economics: Very low capital requirement (a single small type font was enough), very low per-unit margin, but extremely fast turnover. A printer could produce a run of school texts in a week and sell them at the next market day. These were the cash-flow products that kept small presses alive.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Survival rate: Extremely low — far below 1%. The category that was most printed is the category we know least about.
5. Ephemera: Broadsides, Indulgences, Almanacs, Posters
Single-sheet printing was the volume end of the business. Indulgences — fill-in-the-blank forms authorising remission of sins — were the first mass-produced printed products. Gutenberg printed thousands for Pope Callixtus III in 1454-1455. Only about fifty survive.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Almanacs and prognostications combined calendar, astrology, and practical advice. They were printed in large runs, posted on walls, and thrown away when the year ended. Lorck notes that they survive almost exclusively as binder’s scrap.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Broadsides — single-sheet announcements, proclamations, polemics, and news — were the newspapers of their age. The 1462 Diether manifesto, identified by Lorck as the first political pamphlet, survives in a single copy. Broadsides were posted on church doors and town hall walls, read aloud, and discarded.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Other ephemeral products included:

Posters advertising books for sale (Koberger’s 1471 catalogue, arguably the first printed book advertisement)
Playing cards (printed from woodblocks, hand-coloured, sold in vast quantities)
Saint’s images (woodcut prints for private devotion, often hand-coloured)
Calendars (wall calendars, pocket almanacs)
Blank forms (legal documents, certificates, receipts)

Economics: Minimal capital, minimal skill required. A press, a small supply of type, and cheap paper were all that was needed. The per-unit profit was trivial, but the volume could be enormous. At the 1466 Aachen pilgrimage, 130,000 pilgrim badges were sold.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Survival rate: Below 1%. The vast majority of all printed ephemera from the 15th and 16th centuries has been completely lost.
6. Maps and Prints
Maps occupied a special position on the spectrum. They were not books, but they were printed products that required the highest level of technical skill. As map-making-and-the-printing-press documents, map production ranged from cheap woodcut maps for school cosmographies (Munster’s Cosmographia) to premium copperplate maps for luxury atlases (Ortelius’s Theatrum).
A closely related but distinct category was maritime-publications — pilot books, navigation manuals, island books (isolarii), and sea atlases — which combined cartographic illustration with practical sailing instructions for working mariners.
Single-sheet prints — woodcuts and engravings for decoration, education, and devotion — formed their own market. Albrecht Durer’s woodcuts and engravings, produced in large editions from the 1490s onward, represent the high end of this market; cheap woodcut saints’ images the low end.
What the Spectrum Tells Us
The spectrum of early printed output reveals several things that the standard incunabula statistics obscure:
1. The press was not primarily a book machine. In terms of sheet count, most of what came off early presses was not books at all, but ephemera: indulgences, broadsides, almanacs, posters, forms, cards, and prints. These were the products that paid the rent.
2. The middle of the spectrum was thin. There was a sharp gap between the prestige/luxury tier and the cheap/ephemeral tier. The Aldine octavo was an attempt to fill this gap — and it succeeded, but only after 1500. In the 15th century, most printing was either expensive or disposable.
3. Survival bias distorts everything. Our knowledge of early printing is based on the books that librarians chose to keep, not on what printers actually printed. The “typical” incunable in a special collections library is a large folio in Latin; the typical incunable on a 15th-century market stall was a cheap Donatus or a broadside.
4. Products dictated economics. The economics of a luxury folio (high capital, slow return, high risk per unit) and the economics of an indulgence (minimal capital, immediate return, trivial risk per unit) were so different that they belonged to different businesses. Most printers had to choose: chase the prestige of fine book production or the cash flow of jobbing work. Only the largest houses (Koberger, Aldus, Plantin) could do both.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
