concepts/spread-of-printing.title: Spread of Printing
concepts/spread-of-printing.content:
Spread of Printing

Caption: Spread of printing across Europe from Mainz to major fifteenth-century print centers, 1450-1500.

Caption: Mainz printer diaspora after the sack of 1462, with routes toward early print centers across the Rhine region, France, Italy, and England.
The spread of printing from mainz across Europe between 1450 and 1500 is one of the most rapid and consequential diffusions of a technology in history. Within fifty years of Gutenberg’s first experiments with movable-type, printing presses had been established in roughly 280 cities across Europe, producing an estimated 15—20 million individual volumes. The engine of this diffusion was the Printer’s Dispersal of 1462 — the sack of Mainz by Archbishop Adolph of Nassau — which scattered the journeymen who had learned the art in Gutenberg’s, Fust’s, and Schoeffer’s workshops to every corner of the continent. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The Printer’s Dispersal of 1462
The single most important event in the spread of printing was not a commercial development but a political catastrophe. On the night of October 27—28, 1462, troops of Archbishop Adolph II of Nassau stormed Mainz, murdering hundreds of citizens and plundering the city. Mainz had been the sole center of European printing for over a decade; its master printers — Gutenberg, Fust, and Schoeffer — had maintained the technology as a closely guarded trade secret, and journeymen had sworn oaths of secrecy. The sack shattered this monopoly.
The journeymen printers, suddenly thrown out of employment, “fled panic-stricken to other countries; and considering themselves freed from their oath, the great secret of thirty years was spread abroad.” ^[raw/articles/pearson-gutenberg-and-art-of-printing.md] These wandering printers carried not only their practical knowledge of typefounding, punchcutting, presswork, and the punch-matrix system, but also actual type, matrices, and tools. Lorck describes them as “furchtlose Apostel und vorherbestimmte Verbreiter eines neuen Glaubens” — fearless apostles and predestined disseminators of a new faith. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The dispersal followed the major trade and pilgrimage routes of late-medieval Europe — down the Rhine to Cologne and the Netherlands, up the Rhine to Basel and Switzerland, across the Alps to Italy, westward along the French rivers to Paris and Lyon, and south to Spain. In nearly every city, the first printers were German immigrants. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Spread Within Germany
Printing spread rapidly within the German states after 1462:


Strasbourg: Although Gutenberg himself had worked there in the 1430s—1440s during his years of experimentation, the first established press was that of Johann Mentelin (c. 1458). Mentelin was producing a Bible by 1466 and issued what is thought to be the first printer’s catalogue in 1471. Heinrich Eggesteyn also printed in Strasbourg from the mid-1460s. By 1500, Strasbourg had some fifty printers, making it one of the most productive printing centers in Germany. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]


Cologne: Ulrich Zell, a priest and printer who had probably learned his craft in Mainz, established the first press in Cologne around 1464. Cologne became a center of typographical innovation — the introduction of printed signatures (for binder’s collation), pagination, proper book-titles, and column titles are all associated with Cologne printers. Zell later provided crucial testimony in the Cologne Chronicle of 1499, affirming that “the art of printing was first invented in Mainz, by Johann Gutenberg.” ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]


Basel: Berthold Ruppel (Berthold of Hanau), a workman from Gutenberg’s own shop, brought printing to Basel around 1468. The city’s university, founded in 1460, provided a ready market for scholarly texts. By 1473, Michael Wenssler and Bernhard Richel were producing substantial editions. Basel later became the home of Johann Froben (from 1491), whose press printed the works of Erasmus and set new standards for humanist scholarship. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]


Augsburg: Gunther Zainer, probably a pupil of Fust or Schoeffer, began printing in 1468. Augsburg, a wealthy imperial city and major commercial hub, quickly developed a robust book trade. Zainer’s illustrated editions helped establish the German tradition of the illustrated printed book. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]


Nuremberg: Anton Koberger established his press in 1470 and built it into the largest publishing operation in Europe during the incunable period. Koberger operated twenty-four presses simultaneously, employed over 100 workers, and maintained a network of branches and agents stretching from Paris to Vienna and from Krakow to Venice. His most famous production was the Nuremberg Chronicle (1493), a world history of 600 pages with over 1,800 woodcut illustrations, printed in editions of 1,500 Latin and 1,000 German copies. Koberger’s scale of operation was unmatched: he published more than 230 works in his career. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]  ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]


Other German cities that received presses before 1500 include: Bamberg (Albert Pfister, c. 1461, who printed the first illustrated book Der Edelstein and the first German Bible), Ulm (Johann Zainer, 1473), Lubeck (Lucas Brandis, 1475), Leipzig (c. 1481), and many others. By 1500, over sixty German cities had printing presses, with some 300 individual printing establishments. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Italy
Printing reached Italy remarkably early, and Italy — particularly Venice — surpassed Germany in total output before the end of the century.


Subiaco (1464): Two German printers, Konrad Sweynheym (from Schwanheim, near Mainz) and Johann Pannartz, established the first press in Italy at the Benedictine monastery of Santa Scholastica in Subiaco, some seventy kilometers east of Rome. They may have been encouraged by Nicholas of Cusa, who had close ties to the monastery and to the Benedictine order. In 1465 they printed Italy’s first printed book: the works of Firmianus Lactantius, an early Christian author. They used a semi-Gothic type that blended German and Italian scribal traditions. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]


Rome (1467): Sweynheym and Pannartz moved their press to Rome in 1467, encouraged by Giovanni Andrea de Bussi (Vatican librarian and former secretary to Nicholas of Cusa). They produced twenty-eight titles in Rome, including editions of classical authors. Overproduction eventually ruined them; by 1472 their house was filled with unsold books, and the press failed. Pannartz died soon after, and Sweynheym turned to engraving maps. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]


Venice (1469): Johannes de Spira (John of Speyer), a German printer who had learned his craft in Mainz, received a five-year monopoly on printing in Venice from the Signoria in 1469. His first book was Cicero’s Epistolae ad familiares, printed in a fine roman type. After his death later that year, his brother Wendelin continued the press. Nicolas Jenson, a Frenchman who had been sent to Mainz by Charles VII to learn the art, arrived in Venice around 1470 and perfected the roman typeface that became the standard for the next four centuries. Erhard Ratdolt, a German from Augsburg, introduced the first printed title pages and decorated initials from 1476.


Venice became the printing capital of Europe by 1500, producing over 4,000 editions — more than any other city. Its commercial networks, paper supply from the Alpine valleys, and concentration of humanist scholars created ideal conditions for the industry. The Venetian press of Aldus Manutius (from 1494) revolutionized book production in the 1490s with his octavo-format Libri Portatiles (portable books), printed in the cursive italic type he commissioned. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]


Florence: Printing reached Florence in 1471, brought by Bernardo Cennini, though the city’s most famous printer-publisher was the Giunta family (from 1477). Florence’s humanist culture made it a natural market for classical texts, but it never rivaled Venice in scale.


Milan: The first press in Milan was established by Antonio Zarotto (a native of Parma, not Germany) in 1470. Milan became an important center for liturgical printing under the patronage of the Sforza dynasty.


Other Italian cities with presses by 1500 include Bologna, Padua, Ferrara, Naples, Brescia, and Parma. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
France


Paris (1470): The first press in France was established not by a commercial entrepreneur but by the University of the Sorbonne. Three German printers — Ulrich Gering (from Constance), Michael Friburger (from Colmar), and Martin Crantz (from Basel) — were invited by the professors Guillaume Fichet and Johann Heynlin (also called Jean de Lapierre) to set up a press within the Sorbonne. Their first book was the Letters of Gasparino of Bergamo (1470), printed in a roman type inspired by Venetian models. The Sorbonne press was primarily a scholarly enterprise, issuing classical and humanist texts for the university community. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Chevillier’s L’Origine de l’Imprimerie de Paris (1694), drawing directly on the Sorbonne’s registers, records that Jean de Lapierre (Heynlin) was the one who wrote to Germany to summon the printers, being himself German and having the necessary connections. He was Prior of the Sorbonne in 1470, the year the press was established. Lapierre not only procured the printers but prepared copies for them, read proofs, and helped with their editions. Fichet’s letter prefacing the first book thanks Lapierre for “the great advantage he has procured for the study of the Sciences, by means of the Germans he has brought.” ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
The first Paris editions — eleven known titles printed 1470-1471, preserved in the Sorbonne library — were all printed in the same round Roman type (“gros Romain”) from the same matrices. Chevillier describes them: some letters are half-formed and half-printed, finished by hand; there are no capital letters (spaces left for illumination); no titles, foliation, or signatures; the ink is a beautiful black; some lines are printed in red on vellum. The paper is not very white but strong and well-sized. The books include Gasparino’s letters and orthography, Florus’ epitome of Livy, Sallust, Fichet’s own Rhetoric (on vellum), the Cynic Epistles, Bessarion’s letters, Laurentius Valla’s Elegantiae, and Jacobus Magnus’ Sophologium. ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Around 1473, after Fichet had left for Rome (called by Pope Sixtus IV in 1471) and Lapierre was preparing to enter the Carthusian order, Gering moved his press from the Sorbonne to the rue Saint-Jacques at the sign of the Soleil d’or (Sun of Gold). New types were cast in new matrices — Chevillier identifies three or four distinct characters in these second-press editions, some resembling current handwriting, others a large clear Roman type that he judges as beautiful as the best Venetian work. Gering’s Bible (c. 1475) was the first Bible printed in France. ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
In 1473, the second press in Paris was established by Pierre Caesaris (Keyser) and Jean Stol, two Germans studying at the University who had been instructed by Gering. Caesaris, a Master of Arts, lodged on the rue Saint-Jacques at the sign of the Swan, in a house belonging to the Sorbonne. Their books — in Roman letters but less beautiful than Gering’s first editions — included the Manipulus Curatorum (1473), Seneca’s Epistles (1473), Valerius Maximus (1475), and the Dialogue of Ockham (1474), which Chelvillier attributes to them on typographic grounds. ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Gering continued printing in Paris after his partners departed (around 1477). He died on 23 August 1510 in the Soleil d’or, rue de Sorbonne, after forty years of printing in Paris. The Sorbonne kept an annual anniversary for him. By 1500, Paris had become one of Europe’s largest book-trade centers, with numerous presses in the Latin Quarter. The Estienne (Stephanus) family would later make Paris the capital of classical and biblical scholarship in the 16th century. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]


Lyon (1472): Lyon received its first press in 1472, brought by three German printers. The city’s position at the confluence of the Saone and Rhone, its location on the trade routes connecting Italy, Germany, and France, and its regular fairs made it a natural center for the book trade. Lyon specialized in legal, medical, and humanistic works and had more than fifty printers by 1500. In the 16th century, Lyon would rival Paris in the scale of its publishing industry. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]


The Low Countries (Netherlands)


Utrecht (1470): The first press in the Northern Netherlands was established by Ketelaer and De Leempt in Utrecht around 1470, though some scholars believe there may have been earlier activity in the region.


Deventer: Richard Pafraet established a press in Deventer around 1477. The city, home to the Brethren of the Common Life (whose schools educated Erasmus), became a center for the printing of schoolbooks and theological works.


Louvain (Leuven, c. 1473): Flanders’ university city received its first press from John of Westphalia (Johannes de Westfalia) around 1473. The university, founded in 1425, provided a steady market for scholarly texts. Dirk Martens, another influential printer, began work in the 1470s and later became one of Erasmus’s publishers.


Antwerp: Though Antwerp would become the printing capital of the Low Countries in the 16th century (the Plantin-Moretus house), printing only arrived there in the late 1470s. The city’s commercial importance as a port and financial center made it a natural location for the book trade.


Printing in the Low Countries had a distinctive character: the region’s prosperous towns, high literacy rates (by medieval standards), and strong tradition of manuscript illumination created a receptive market. The so-called “Coster question” — the claim by some Dutch scholars that Laurens Janszoon Coster of Haarlem had invented movable type before Gutenberg — arose from this region. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Spain
Printing reached Spain relatively late compared to Italy and France, but spread quickly once established.


Valencia (1474): The first press in Spain was established by Lambert Palmart, a German from Cologne, who printed the first dated Spanish book, the Obres e trobes en lahors de la Verge Maria, in 1474. The exact date is March 25, 1474.


Barcelona (c. 1475): The first press in Barcelona was set up by two German printers, Johann Gherlinc and Johann of Salzburg (also known as Johannes de San Ciuto). Barcelona quickly developed a significant printing industry, producing Catalan-language works alongside Latin.


Seville (c. 1477): The first press in Seville was established by Meinard Ungut (a German) and Stanislaus Polonus (a Pole). As the gateway to the New World, Seville would later become the center for books shipped to the Americas.


By 1500, printing presses were active in at least a dozen Spanish cities, including Salamanca, Zamora, Burgos, and Zaragoza. The Complutensian Polyglot Bible, printed at Alcala de Henares under the patronage of Cardinal Cisneros (1514—1517), would become Spain’s most famous early printing achievement. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
England
Printing reached England later than any other major European region, introduced not by a German immigrant but by an Englishman who had learned the trade abroad.

Westminster (1476): William Caxton (c. 1422—1492), an English merchant, diplomat, and translator, learned printing in Cologne and practiced it in Bruges (where he printed the Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye, the first book printed in English, in 1473). In 1476, he returned to England and established his press at the sign of the Red Pale in the precincts of Westminster Abbey. His first dated English-printed book was The Dictes or Sayengis of the Philosophres (1477), a translation by Earl Rivers.

Caxton’s press was not a commercial operation on the scale of Venice or Nuremberg, but it was culturally decisive: Caxton printed over one hundred works, many of them in English translation (Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales, Malory’s Le Morte d’Arthur, Aesop’s Fables), and his linguistic choices helped standardize the emerging English literary language. After his death in 1492, his foreman Wynkyn de Worde took over the press and moved it to Fleet Street, establishing the pattern of London’s book trade for centuries. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Oxford received its first press in 1478 (printer: Theodoric Rood of Cologne), and St. Albans in 1479 (a schoolmaster-printer), but English printing remained overwhelmingly concentrated in London until well into the 16th century.
The German Immigrant Printer
A pattern recurs across every region to which printing spread: the first printer was almost always a German immigrant. Sweynheym and Pannartz in Subiaco, Johannes de Spira in Venice, Ulrich Gering in Paris, Lambert Palmart in Valencia, Meinard Ungut in Seville, Theodoric Rood in Oxford — all were Germans or had learned their craft in the German-speaking lands.
This was no accident. The practical knowledge of typefounding, punchcutting, and presswork could not be learned from books; it was transmitted through apprenticeship and hands-on experience. The Mainz workshops, established by Gutenberg in the 1440s and expanded by Fust and Schoeffer in the 1450s, were the only places in Europe where a printer could acquire this training before 1462. After the sack of Mainz, these trained printers carried the technology with them, and their apprenticeships became the seed from which national printing traditions grew. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The German printers did not merely transplant a technique; they adapted it. In Italy, Sweynheym and Pannartz moved from Gothic Textura to a semi-Gothic and then to roman type. In Paris, Gering began with roman type at the Sorbonne, influenced by Venetian models. In Spain, Palmart and Ungut developed hybrid types that blended Gothic and roman characteristics. The technology was standard, but its typographic expression diversified according to local scribal traditions and reader expectations. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]

Significance
The spread of printing was the first large-scale diffusion of an information technology in European history. It transformed a secret art concentrated in one mid-sized Rhenish city into a pan-European industry within a single generation. The Printer’s Dispersal of 1462 — a political catastrophe that destroyed Mainz’s printing monopoly — paradoxically ensured the technology’s triumph.
By 1500, the infrastructure of the modern book trade was in place: typefoundries, presses, publishing houses, book fairs (notably Frankfurt and Lyon), distribution networks, and a literate reading public. The spread of printing laid the material foundation for the Renaissance, the Reformation, and the Scientific Revolution. Every subsequent revolution in communication — from the steam press to the internet — follows a pattern first established by the German journeymen who carried Gutenberg’s invention out of Mainz in 1462. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
George Haven Putnam, whose second volume of Books and their Makers during the Middle Ages (1896) provides the most detailed English-language account of the early book trade, emphasizes that the spread of printing was driven not merely by technical capability but by “the requirement” of a Europe hungry for books: “With the requirement came, as always, the men. The press that Gutenberg had given to the world was not allowed to rust for want of plucky and public-spirited printers to develop its full scope and usefulness.” ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
German Printers Abroad: The First Wave
John Man’s Appendix II (The Gutenberg Revolution, 2002) catalogues the first printing presses established outside Germany by German-trained printers, listing over eighty towns across eight countries or regions with their year of first printing and the printer’s name. The table below captures a representative selection by country; the full appendix lists many more smaller towns, particularly in Italy, where German printers reached nearly three dozen locations within thirty years of the sack of Mainz. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]

The single African entry (Sao Tome, 1494) demonstrates that German printing reached even the Atlantic islands within the first generation. Every town listed in the appendix received its first press from a printer whose name is identifiably German or who trained in the German-speaking lands. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Regional Specialisation of Output
The sources reveal that different printing centres developed distinct specialisations, shaped by local markets, institutional buyers, and available expertise:^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]

This specialisation meant that a scholar seeking a Greek edition went to Venice, a lawyer seeking a law commentary went to Lyon, a bishop ordering a missal went to Mainz or Paris, and a merchant wanting a practical almanac went to the nearest local printer. The printing press was not a uniform technology — it adapted to each city’s economic and intellectual ecology.
Sixteenth-Century Expansion: Beyond Europe
The first generation of printing (1450-1500) had been a European phenomenon confined to the continent. The sixteenth century saw printing cross the Atlantic, penetrate Eastern Europe and Russia, and reach Asia through Jesuit missionary presses. The German printer diaspora that had driven the first wave was gradually supplanted by local printing traditions, but the pattern of itinerant printers carrying the technology to new territories continued. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Scandinavia
Printing reached Scandinavia in the incunable period but took hold only slowly. Denmark received its first book from the traveling German printer Johann Snell, who printed a Latin account of the Siege of Rhodes in Odense (1482). The first Danish New Testament was printed not in Denmark but in Leipzig (1524), reflecting the absence of a mature domestic printing industry. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
In Sweden, Snell also printed the first book, the Dialogus creaturum moralizatus (1483). He was followed by Johann Fabri, whose widow completed the Breviarium Upsalense in 1496. Then came “an interruption of over fifty years, during which no trace of the art is found in Sweden.” Printing revived with the Reformation: the first Swedish Bible was printed in 1521, and the New Testament in Finnish appeared in 1548. King Charles IX established a royal printing press in 1594. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Norway received printing even later. The first book printed in Norway was produced in Christiania (Oslo) in 1643 by a traveling printer, Tyge Nielsen from Copenhagen. A permanently established press arrived only with a German printer, Valentin Kuhn. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Poland and Eastern Europe
Krakow, the seat of Polish learning, had a press from 1491 (Swaybold Frank), who also printed works in Cyrillic script for East Slavic markets. Hebrew printing began in Krakow in 1517 and flourished under Isaac ben Aaron Prostitz (see hebrew-and-oriental-printing). The first Bible in the local language was printed in Brzesc (the Radziwill Bible, 1563), and the Bohemian Brethren printed a six-volume quarto Bible at Kralitz in Moravia (1579-1593). ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Russia
The first press in Russia was established in Moscow in 1553 under Grand Prince Ivan Vasilievich (Ivan the Terrible). The press was operated by the deacon Ivan Feodorov and Timofey Mstislavzoff, under the supervision of the Dane Hans Hannsen. Their most famous production was the Apostol (Acts of the Apostles), printed in Church Slavonic in 1564 — the first dated printed book in Russia. Only a single copy survives, in the library of the Academy of Sciences in St. Petersburg. The Russian press produced primarily liturgical works in Cyrillic type, which required its own typefounding tradition independent of the Latin and Gothic types of Western Europe. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Americas
The Spanish were the first to bring printing to the New World, “a full hundred years before North America had a press.” The first press in the Americas was established in Mexico City around 1539 by Juan Pablos (Giovanni Paoli), an Italian printer working under the sponsorship of the Cromberger firm of Seville. Juan Cromberger, a German-descended printer of Seville, sent Pablos with a press and types to Mexico to supply the colonial market. The earliest surviving Mexican-printed book is the Manual de Adultos (1540), a liturgical work. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The output of the American presses was “mainly religious in content,” but also included historical works and many linguistic books in indigenous languages for missionary use. Printing followed the Spanish colonial administration: presses were established in Lima (Peru) and Santo Domingo later in the century, always under Church and Crown control. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Asia: Jesuit Missionary Presses
The Jesuits brought European-style printing to Asia before any colonial administration did. In Japan, a book on the lives of the Apostles was printed in European type at Tacaco (on the island of Nippon) in 1591, with a vocabulary appended. The Jesuits also printed at Amacusa, and Nagasaki had “a fairly active press” by the end of the sixteenth century. These presses produced Christian texts in Japanese using both Latin characters and Japanese script, for the use of converts and missionaries. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
In China, the Jesuits operated concealed presses in Peking (Beijing) from the early seventeenth century. The oldest known Peking-printed European-style book is a Chinese-language catechism titled Coelestis doctrinae vera ratio (1603). The Jesuit Nicolas Trigault published a Chinese dictionary in three volumes in Nanjing around 1620. These presses were clandestine — the Chinese imperial authorities did not authorize European printing — and their output was limited to missionary materials. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Africa
The only recorded African press from the early period was a brief appearance on the island of Sao Tome (1494), where a printer named Valentin of Moravia produced liturgical works for the Portuguese colonial and missionary presence. There is no evidence of sustained printing on the African mainland until much later. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Significance of the Second Wave
The sixteenth-century expansion of printing meant that by 1600, the technology had reached every continent except Australia and Antarctica. The pattern established by the Mainz diaspora — itinerant printers carrying type and presses to new territories, adapting their output to local languages and authorities — repeated itself in Mexico City, Moscow, and Nagasaki. But the second wave was qualitatively different: printing was now carried not by independent craftsmen but by organized institutions — the Spanish colonial administration, the Russian Orthodox Church, and the Society of Jesus. The age of the wandering German printer was giving way to the age of the corporate press. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Seventeenth-Century Expansion: The Global Press
The seventeenth century extended printing to North America, deepened its presence in Asia, and saw the technology become a truly global medium. The Dutch Republic, the English colonial administration, and the missionary societies replaced the Spanish and Portuguese as the primary carriers of the press to new territories. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
North America
The first press in North America was established in Cambridge, Massachusetts in 1638. The equipment was brought from England by the Puritan minister Joseph Glover, who died during the voyage; his widow carried out the plan and set up the press. The first printer was Stephen Daye (or Day), and the first known product was The Freemans Oath (1639). The press was later moved to Boston and operated by Samuel Green. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
From the start, the North American press was different from its European counterparts. Lorck notes that the press in North America “could not draw its principal nourishment from science and literature as in Europe” because the colonies were “struggling for political and material existence.” Its main task was “the promotion of civil liberty and political education, as well as the strengthening of faith among the adherents of the many religious sects.” ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The colonial authorities were ambivalent about the press. In 1662, Massachusetts appointed official censors and passed a law that “no press other than the one in Cambridge should be set up within their jurisdiction.” Full press freedom did not arrive until around 1755. For most of the seventeenth century, “many books were still printed in England” for the colonial market. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Boston received its first press under John Forster; the second was operated by Samuel Green and continued by his brother Bartholomew Green, who in 1704 started the first American newspaper, The Boston News Letter. In 1709, Green printed a psalter in an indigenous American language. James Franklin (older brother of Benjamin) arrived in Boston in 1717 with a press and types learned in England, and started the Boston Gazette (1719) and later the New England Courant. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Benjamin Franklin (1706-1790) began his career as a printer’s apprentice to his brother James, later establishing his own press in Philadelphia with Hugh Meredith. He published Poor Richard’s Almanack for 25 years and printed the earliest known German-language book in America (1730). Franklin’s press also served as a vehicle for his civic and scientific work; his later political career as a statesman and diplomat made him the most famous printer in American history. His self-written epitaph reads: “The body of Benjamin Franklin, Printer, (like the cover of an old book, its contents worn out, and stript of its lettering and gilding) lies here, food for worms!” ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
German-American printing began with Christoph Sauer (Christopher Sower), a German immigrant who established a press in Pennsylvania. Sauer’s most important undertaking was the German Lutheran Bible (1743), 1,284 pages in royal quarto, printed in 1,200 copies and bound in leather. For this work, he established the first type foundry in America (1740). This was the first Bible in a European language printed in North America; the first English-language American Bible appeared only in 1782, under Oxford University’s monopoly. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
South America
Printing continued to expand in Spanish America. Presses were established in Lima (Peru) and other colonial centres, always under Church and Crown control. A secret Jesuit press operated in Cordoba (in present-day Argentina) in the seventeenth century, producing clandestine religious works. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Asia: India and Southeast Asia
European printing in Asia expanded beyond the Jesuit missions to include Protestant missionary and colonial presses.
In India, the first European-style press was established in Goa (1563), the earliest Portuguese settlement on the west coast. In Tranquebar on the Coromandel Coast, the London Society for the Propagation of the Gospel established a press in 1569, printing a New Testament in quarto, prayer books, and catechisms in Portuguese, English, Danish, and several Asian dialects. When Tranquebar came under Danish control, the Danish mission became active: Bartholomaeus Ziegenbalg and Heinrich Plutschau brought a press and types from Germany. Tamil type was cast at the orphanage press in Halle and brought to India by J.G. Adler, who published the four Gospels and Acts (1714) and the complete Tamil Bible (1723, three parts in quarto). ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
In the East Indies, the Dutch East India Company (VOC) established presses in Batavia (modern Jakarta, Java) at the end of the seventeenth century. On Ceylon (Sri Lanka), Governor G.W. von Imhof ordered a press set up in Colombo in 1737 for printing Gospels in local languages, which later also produced scholarly works. In Manila (Philippines), printing was active from around 1600, and in the eighteenth century Catholic missionaries there competed with the Protestants in Tranquebar for evangelical printing. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Lorck’s Conclusion
Lorck’s handbook closes its survey of the spread of printing with a summary:

“Thus the art of Gutenberg, which in its first hundred years had already made its way across all of Europe and achieved a high level of development… was spread across the entire world. Already by the time which forms our provisional boundary, the words spoken a hundred years later held true:
‘Across the expanse of the Ocean into the farthest regions of the Earth,
Carries, Celebrated one, your Fame, never resting in flight;
You need no stone, nor cast bronze,
For every line of the book proclaims your praise.‘” ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]

concepts/the-coster-legend.title: The Coster Legend
concepts/the-coster-legend.content:
The Coster Legend
The Coster Legend (Dutch: Koster-legende) is the historical claim that Laurens Janszoon Coster (also spelled Koster) of Haarlem invented movable-type printing before johann-gutenberg of Mainz. For nearly three centuries — from the late 1500s well into the 1800s — the legend was accepted as patriotic history in the Netherlands and was debated across Europe. Modern scholarship has rejected Coster priority entirely, but the story remains one of the most instructive episodes in the historiography of printing.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, Chapter XVII, pp. 326-346]
The Junius Account (1588)
The first detailed, named account of Coster’s invention appears in Hadrianus Junius (Adrian de Jonghe), Batavia (1588). Though earlier hints exist — a 1561 preface by Jan van Zuren and Dirck Volckharts Coornhert, and a 1567 description by Luigi Guicciardini — Junius was the first to give the inventor a name, a date, a house, and a printed book.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, pp. 328-331]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md, lines 1196-1206]
Junius writes that about 128 years before he wrote (i.e., c. 1440), there lived in Haarlem, near the market square, a man named Laurentius Joannes, surnamed Coster (from custos, keeper or sexton). The story unfolds as follows:

The walk in the wood: While strolling in the Haarlem woods (het Hout), Coster carved letters from the bark of a beech tree as a pastime. Impressing them on paper, he produced a few lines of text as a keepsake for his grandchildren.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, p. 331]
Development: Encouraged by his son-in-law Thomas Pieterzoon, Coster developed a thicker ink (to prevent blotting), then progressed from wooden letters to lead and finally to tin, which was harder and more durable.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, p. 331]
The printed book: Junius identifies the Spieghel onzer behoudenisse — a Dutch edition of the block-book Speculum Humanae Salvationis (Mirror of Salvation) — as Coster’s first typographic work. He notes that early copies were printed on one side only and the blank pages pasted together.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, pp. 331-332]
The treacherous servant: A workman named Johann — whom Junius insinuates was Johann Fust (Gutenberg’s financier) — stole the equipment on Christmas Eve while the household attended church. He fled to Amsterdam, then Cologne, and finally to Mainz, where he set up shop and began printing, using Coster’s own types to produce the Doctrinal of Alexander Gallus and the Treatises of Peter of Spain around 1442.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, pp. 332-334]

Junius cites as his sources: the bookbinder Cornelis (who had been Coster’s apprentice and told the story weeping, even at age 80), his own tutor Nicholas Gallius, and the burgomaster Quirinius Talesius.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, pp. 333-334]
Earlier Hints
Before Junius, the legend existed as vague civic pride. In 1561, Jan van Zuren and Dirck Volckharts Coornhert — printers opening a shop in Haarlem — published a preface implying Haarlem had invented printing but naming no inventor. In 1567, Luigi Guicciardini, a Florentine resident of Antwerp, wrote in his Description of the Low Countries that “according to the common tradition of the inhabitants” printing was invented in Haarlem, with a servant carrying the art to Mainz after the inventor’s death. Guicciardini cautiously declined to decide the truth.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, pp. 329-330]
Growth of the Legend: The Patriotic Campaign
Once Junius had given the story a named hero, Dutch patriots elaborated on it enthusiastically.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, Chapter XVIII, pp. 347-359]
Scriverius (1628)
Peter Scriverius published Laurecrans voor Laurens Coster (1628), a poetical elaboration. In his version, Coster cut letters from an oak branch, wrapped them in paper, fell asleep in the woods, and was awakened by a thunderclap, discovering that rain had transferred the letters’ impress to the paper. Scriverius moved the date of invention back to 1428 and added the detail that Coster was a sheriff of Haarlem.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, pp. 348-349]
Boxhorn (1640)
Marcus Zuerius Boxhorn pushed the date further back to 1420 in his Dissertation on the Invention of Typography (1640), without producing new evidence — only patriotic confidence.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, p. 350]
Meerman (1765)
Gerard Meerman, a distinguished Dutch scholar, published Origines Typographicae (1765), the most learned defense of the legend. He conceded nothing to mechanics (he knew nothing of typefounding) and proposed a “contributive invention” theory: Coster invented wooden movable type (c. 1428-1430), Johan Gensfleisch (Gutenberg’s brother) cut metal types, Peter Schoeffer invented cast types. Gutenberg and Fust were mere printers who invented nothing. Meerman was warned by the typefounder John Enschede that his wood-type theory was mechanically absurd, but he ignored the advice.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, pp. 354-356]
Koning (1816)
Jacobus Koning won a prize essay competition with The Origin, Invention and Development of Printing (1816). He brought archival research to bear — discovering records of a Laurens Janszoon Coster in Haarlem tax rolls — but he confounded two different men: a civic official named Laurens Janszoon (who died in 1439) with Lourens Janszoon Coster (a tallow-chandler and innkeeper who appears in records until 1483). Koning willfully suppressed evidence that contradicted his case.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, pp. 356-357]
De Vries (c. 1830)
Dr. Abraham de Vries proposed a date of 1423 and argued that Coster invented printing with movable cast letters, giving the example to Mainz. His chronology was as unsupported as the others.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, p. 358]
The Downfall: Van der Linde’s Archival Demolition
The legend’s decisive refutation came from Dr. Antonius van der Linde, a German-Dutch scholar whose research was published in 1870 as The Haarlem Legend of the Invention of Printing. He was subsequently driven out of Holland for his pains.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md, line 291]
Van der Linde examined the archives of Haarlem — town accounts, church registers, and the membership book of the Holy Christmas Corporation — and established the following facts:^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, pp. 360-368]

Lourens Janszoon Coster was a tallow-chandler (candle-maker), supplying the town hall with oil, soap, and candles from 1441 onward.
After 1447, he gave up the chandler’s business and became a tavern-keeper. The tavern (at the same address Junius describes) was consistently known as a drinking-house for centuries afterward.
He was alive in 1483, when he paid ferry toll to leave Haarlem — contradicting the legend that he died in 1439 or 1440.
There is no record — in any archive — that he was ever a printer, a sheriff, a sexton, or a treasurer.
The famous Coster pedigree — a vellum document from c. 1550 describing Coster as the man “who brought the first print in the world” — was shown to have been falsified: the date 1446 had been altered to read 1440. The document was written a century after the events it claimed to record, by Gerrit Thomaszoon, a vain innkeeper who lived in Coster’s old house.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, pp. 361-365]

Van der Linde showed that the legendary Laurens Janszoon Coster the printer was a conflation of two men: (1) Laurens Janszoon, a wealthy civic official who died in 1439, and (2) Lourens Janszoon Coster, the chandler/innkeeper who lived until at least 1483. Neither had anything to do with printing.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, p. 368]
De Vinne’s Typographic Critique
Theodore Low De Vinne, in The Invention of Printing (1876, chapters XVII-XIX), reinforced Van der Linde’s archival work with a typographic critique:^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]

No dated Coster print exists: None of the books attributed to Coster (the Speculum editions, Donatus fragments, etc.) bear a date, a printer’s name, or a place of publication.
The Speculum editions are typographic, but not necessarily pre-Gutenberg: They were printed with cast metal types, not wooden ones as Junius claimed. Their type and paper suggest a date in the 1460s or 1470s, well after Gutenberg’s invention.
Internal contradictions: Junius says Coster used wooden types, but the Speculum types are unquestionably cast metal. The “Cornelis the bookbinder” cited by Junius was born around 1442 — after the alleged theft — and could not have been an eyewitness. The alleged thief’s first books cannot be traced to Mainz; fragments of the Doctrinal were found in the Netherlands, not Germany.
The story of theft is inherently improbable: If Coster had functioning types and trained workmen, the knowledge of the art would not have vanished overnight. Yet Haarlem produced no typographic work between the alleged invention (c. 1440) and the arrival of Jacob Bellaert as the city’s first documented printer in 1483 — a gap of over 40 years.

The Physical Evidence
Portraits of Coster
A revealing anachronism: every known “portrait” of Coster shows him holding a Roman-form matrix of the letter A. But Roman type was not used in the Netherlands in the 1440s — all books attributed to Coster are in Gothic (Textura) letterforms. The portraits were invented long after Coster’s death, based on imagination rather than likeness. Van der Linde suggested the earliest Scriverius engraving might be a portrait of Gerrit Thomaszoon, pressed into service as Coster.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, pp. 371-372]
The Enschedé Typefoundry
The Enschedé family of typefounders in Haarlem played a peculiar role in preserving the legend. John Enschede (the elder) owned a collection of early type specimens, including the Enschede Abecedarium — fragments of an early alphabet that some claimed as Coster types. While Enschede correctly warned Meerman that wood types were unworkable, his collection was later used by patriotic historians as “Costeriana.” The fragments are now recognized as the work of an anonymous Dutch printer working after 1460.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, p. 290, 355]
Monuments and Public Memory
Despite the total lack of evidence, Haarlem erected multiple monuments to Coster:^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, pp. 358-359]

A statue in the Doctors’ Garden (early 1600s), without a date of invention — suggesting even then the authorities were unsure.
A cenotaph in the Haarlem Wood (the Hout), bearing the arms of the sheriff Laurens Janszoon and the year 1423.
A marble tablet in St. Bavo’s Cathedral, placed in 1824 by King William I, acknowledging Coster as the inventor.
A memorial stone on the rebuilt “Coster House” (1851) on the market square.
The grand statue in the Grote Markt (Market Square), unveiled July 16, 1856, the day accepted as the anniversary of the invention. The pedestal reads: “LOURENS JANSZOON COSTER / INVENTOR OF THE ART OF PRINTING / WITH MOVABLE LETTERS / CAST OF METAL / HOMAGE OF THE NETHERLAND NATION / MDCCCLVI.” The date of the invention was deliberately omitted, reflecting unresolved disagreements among the monument committee.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, pp. 360-361]

The Speculum Salutis Editions
The Speculum Humanae Salvationis (Mirror of Human Salvation) editions — four in total (two Latin, two Dutch) — are central to the Coster claim because they are early, undated, and printed in the Netherlands. Lorck notes their importance: “The book is of Lower Rhine origin, and the Dutch declare this late product to be a work printed by Koster with movable types.”^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md, line 461]
De Vinne devotes his entire chapters XIV-XVI to the Speculum. His conclusion: the Speculum editions are genuine typographic works of the 1460s or 1470s, printed by an unknown Dutch printer whose types show affinities with those of Jacob Bellaert and John Brito in Haarlem. They are valuable as early Dutch typography, but they cannot be dated before Gutenberg’s Bible (c. 1450-1455) and therefore do not establish Coster priority.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, Chapter XVI, pp. 308-325]
Why the Legend Persisted
The Coster Legend survived so long for several reasons:^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, pp. 329, 346, 358]^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md, lines 636-656]

National pride: The Dutch Republic, having fought off Spanish rule, cultivated heroes. Coster became a symbol of Dutch ingenuity.
Undated Dutch incunabula: A body of early undated Dutch typography — the “Costeriana” — could not be securely assigned, leaving room for speculation.
The Speculum puzzle: The Speculum editions blur the line between block-books and typography. Early bibliographers struggled to classify them, and their hybrid nature made the Coster claim arguable.
The lack of Gutenberg documentation: Before the 19th century, Gutenberg’s own priority was poorly documented. The 1439 Strasbourg documents and the Helmasperger Instrument were not widely studied until the 1700s.
Civic investment: Haarlem’s monuments, museums, and festivals created a self-perpetuating tradition. The Costerian Museum displayed type fragments and “relics” that, though worthless as evidence, impressed visitors.

Modern Consensus
Modern scholarship is unanimous: Laurens Janszoon Coster did not invent movable-type printing before Gutenberg. The archival work of Van der Linde, the typographic analysis of De Vinne, and subsequent 20th-century research have established:^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md, lines 652-656]

Gutenberg’s priority is confirmed by the 1439 Strasbourg documents (the Dritzehn lawsuit), the 1448 Mainz loan, and the 1455 Helmasperger Notarial Instrument.
The “Costeriana” — early Dutch typographic fragments — represent the work of anonymous Dutch printers working after Gutenberg’s invention spread from Mainz.
The Speculum editions are transitional works of the 1460s-1470s, combining woodcut illustrations with cast-metal type, valuable for understanding the early spread of the-printing-press to the Low Countries, but not evidence of an independent Dutch invention.
Coster himself (the tallow-chandler and tavern-keeper) was an innocent man — he never claimed to have invented printing; the claim was made on his behalf by others a century after his death.

As Haarlem’s chief archivist told John Man: “We know he did not pre-empt Gutenberg. It’s a nice story, nothing more.”^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md, lines 654-656]
Significance in Historiography
The Coster Legend is more than a historical footnote. It illustrates:

How nationalist historiography can create and sustain false claims for centuries.
The importance of archival evidence over oral tradition and family pedigrees.
How typographic analysis — examination of type bodies, paper, ink, and presswork — can date and place printed works with greater precision than textual tradition.
The role of civic boosterism in shaping public memory: Haarlem’s monuments remain tourist attractions, even though the story they commemorate is false.

The Coster Legend is, as De Vinne put it, “a snowball that became a snow-heap” — built from a grain of ambiguous tradition by generations of well-meaning but uncritical patriots. Its demolition is a landmark in historical method.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md, p. 346]

block-printing — the xylographic tradition from which the Speculum emerged
movable-type — Gutenberg’s system of punch, matrix, mold, and alloy
the-printing-press — the mechanical press that made typography practical

concepts/the-indulgence-trade.title: The Indulgence Trade
concepts/the-indulgence-trade.content:
The Indulgence Trade
The indulgence was the first great commercial market for European printing. Before Bibles, before psalters, before any bound book, movable-type proved its commercial viability by mass-producing single-sheet documents that the Church sold to remit sin. This trade—the sale of indulgences—financed Gutenberg’s early presses, provided the earliest dated specimens of typography, and later erupted into the controversy that became the reformation.
What an Indulgence Was
An indulgence was not forgiveness of sin itself (that required confession and contrition) but the remission of the temporal punishment still due after sin had been forgiven. The theological underpinning was the Treasury of Merit—the infinite reservoir of grace accumulated by Christ and the saints, which the Pope could dispense to the faithful. Pope Clement VI formalized this doctrine in the bull Unigenitus (1343), declaring that the Pope held the keys to this treasury and could grant indulgences to the living (and, by 1476, to souls in purgatory). ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
An indulgence, therefore, was a certificate stating that the bearer had performed a specified good work—paid alms, prayed, fasted—and thereby qualified to receive remission of temporal punishment for a defined period (e.g., three months, a year) or, in the case of a plenary indulgence, all punishment whatsoever. The document itself—called a confessionalia in Latin or Ablassbrief (‘reduction-letter’) in German—was a contract between the penitent and the Church, with blank spaces left for the name of the buyer, the date, and the place of sale. Once filled in by hand, it became a personalized ticket to shortened time in purgatory—or, for a plenary indulgence, a straight pass to Heaven. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The First Print Run: Cyprus and the Turkish Crusade
In August 1451, Pope Nicholas V granted King John II of Cyprus the right to issue plenary indulgences for three years (1 May 1452 to 1 May 1455) to raise mercenary funds against the advancing Ottoman Turks. Paulinus Zapp (Chappe), the Cypriot ambassador, appointed John de Castro as chief commissioner for Germany. The Archbishop of Mainz, Theodoric, granted permission to sell within his diocese. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Sales were initially slow. Then Constantinople fell on 29 May 1453. The shock across Europe was immediate. John de Castro, panicking that Cyprus had fallen too, embezzled the collected money and was arrested and imprisoned—a scandal that further injured the market. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
With the indulgence’s expiry date of 1 May 1455 fast approaching, Zappe needed to distribute thousands of documents urgently. Hand-copying was too slow, too error-prone, and too vulnerable to forgery. He turned to johann-gutenberg’s new printing press in mainz. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Gutenberg’s Indulgence Editions
Three distinct editions of the indulgence letter were printed, known today by their line-counts: approximately 30, 31, and 32 lines (De Vinne uses 30, 31; modern scholarship typically refers to the 31-line and 28-line editions). Each was a single sheet of parchment, about 9 x 13 inches, printed on one side only, with movable type, black oil-based ink, and blank spaces for the buyer’s name, the date, and the seller’s signature. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The three editions used different typefaces, cast from different matrices and set by different compositors:

The 31-line edition used a display line in the large Double-pica body type (the same type used for the 36-line Bible and the Donatus), with the text body in a smaller type on English body. The large display types are identifiable as the lettres de forme (Pointed Gothic), the text as lettres de somme (Round Gothic). ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The other editions used types on Paragon body and a Pica body, some of which match the type of the 42-line Bible. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The small text type used in one edition is unique—it appears in no other known work. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]

The presswork is good, done on a properly constructed screw press with damp vellum and oil-based ink, but the typography has blemishes: abbreviations are frequent, lines are unevenly spaced, the capital letters are rudely cut. One surviving copy shows a white gap below the sixteenth line where the types were not securely fastened in the chase. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Surviving Copies and Their Significance
Twenty-three copies of these indulgence letters survive (De Vinne in 1876 counted eighteen; Lorck by 1882 counted twenty-three; modern scholarship counts at least twenty-three, with new fragments occasionally discovered in book bindings). They date from 25 November 1454 to 30 April 1455—the period of the last desperate sales push. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
These surviving copies are historically invaluable because they are the earliest printed documents with a firm date. The 31-line edition carries the printed year 1454 (MCCCCLIIII); the others carry 1455. This makes them the cornerstone of Gutenberg chronology: they prove that by late 1454 Gutenberg not only had a working press but was operating at least two workshops (the Gutenberghof and the Humbrechthof), with two distinct typefaces being run simultaneously. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The indulgences also provide the first solid evidence of a demand for printing—a customer (the Church) needing thousands of identical copies of the same text faster than scribes could produce them. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
After 1 May 1455, the indulgences became worthless. Their parchment sheets were recycled by bookbinders as waste leaves for binding pastedowns, which is how most copies survived to be discovered centuries later. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Financial Engine
The indulgence trade was not a one-off job for Gutenberg; it was a recurring revenue stream that sustained his press between larger projects. John Man notes that by late 1454 indulgences were “flowing from his presses,” churning out by the thousand for sale across the Frankfurt-Mainz-Cologne region. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] The income from indulgences, Donatus grammars, and the Sibylline Prophecies just about covered his costs and paid the interest on the loans from johannes-fust, even as the monumental 42-line Bible was being typeset in the second workshop. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The business model was elegant:

The Church provided the text and the authority (the papal bull).
The commissioner (Zapp/de Castro) handled distribution and collection.
The printer provided the press, the type, the paper or vellum, and the labor.
The product was a blank form—the text was fixed, but names, dates, and places were filled in by hand at the point of sale. This made the document both standardized and individualized, and it meant thousands of copies could be run from a single setting of type.

This “blank form” model—printing identical documents with variable fields—was printing’s first killer app. It was the fifteenth-century equivalent of printing tax forms, banknotes, or contracts. It required no bookbinding, no rubrication, no complex page layout—just speed, accuracy, and volume. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The Business of Selling Salvation
Indulgence selling was a deeply corrupt business even by the standards of the medieval Church. The De Vinne source describes the scandal of John de Castro’s embezzlement and notes that the 1454 indulgences “give us a glimmer of the corruption of some of the men who sold the indulgences—a corruption which, in the next century, brought down upon the sellers and the system the scorn of Holbein and the wrath of Luther.” ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The illustration reproduced in De Vinne—a Holbein satire—shows a canon absolving a kneeling young man while pointing at a money-chest, three Dominicans greedily counting coins at a table, a penniless cripple being turned away, and the Pope enthroned granting commissions. The apparatus of the indulgence trade—commissioners, sub-agents, preachers, collectors—created a sprawling commercial network that reached every parish in Germany. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The Road to Reformation
The indulgence trade that Gutenberg helped launch with his press in 1454 came back to haunt the Church seventy years later. In 1515, Pope Leo X authorized a new plenary indulgence to finance the completion of St. Peter’s Basilica. The marketing was entrusted to Johann Tetzel, a Dominican monk whose sales pitch was legendary: “As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs.” Tetzel’s campaign was backed by printed indulgences—by then a well-established genre of print. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
In Wittenberg, Martin Luther was appalled. On 31 October 1517, he sent his Ninety-Five Theses (strictly, a disputation on the power and efficacy of indulgences) to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz. Within weeks, the theses were printed and circulating across Germany—in Leipzig, Basel, Nuremberg, and Wittenberg itself. As John Man puts it: “The noises that accompanied Luther’s message of doom were probably not hammer-blows; they were the squeaks and bangs of busy printing presses.” ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The same technology that Gutenberg had used to mass-produce indulgences was now being used to mass-produce arguments against them. The reformation became the first great European movement to exploit print at scale: Luther’s writings, vernacular Bibles, pamphlets, and broadsides circulated faster and farther than manuscript culture ever allowed. The indulgence trade, which had proved printing’s commercial viability in the 1450s, proved its revolutionary power in the 1510s.
Summary
The indulgence trade sits at the crossroads of church finance, commercial printing, and religious upheaval:

It was the first large-scale commercial application of movable type.
It produced the earliest dated printed documents (1454-1455), anchoring Gutenberg’s chronology.
It demonstrated the blank-form business model that would later underpin official printing (tax forms, legal documents, papal bulls).
It created the financial bridge that kept Gutenberg’s press running while the Bible was being produced.
Its abuse triggered the Reformation, which in turn proved print’s power to spread ideas faster than any institution could suppress them.

concepts/the-printing-press.title: The Printing Press
concepts/the-printing-press.content:
The Printing Press

Caption: Fifteenth-century wooden screw press, showing the screw, platen, pull bar, bed, tympan, frisket, forme, inking balls, paper, and press frame.
The printing press is the mechanical device used to transfer ink from a composed forme of movable-type to paper or vellum. While the principle of relief printing was known long before the 15th century, the press itself — capable of applying strong, even, and repeatable pressure over a large surface — was the crucial mechanical innovation that turned movable type into a practical system for mass-producing books. The press designed by johann-gutenberg around 1450, adapted from the screw presses used in wine-making and paper-making, remained the dominant form of printing technology for roughly 350 years.^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]
Gutenberg’s Adaptation of the Screw Press
Gutenberg did not invent the press mechanism from scratch. The screw press had been used for centuries in Europe for pressing wine grapes, olives, and linen, as well as in paper-making (squeezing water from freshly made sheets).^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md] What Gutenberg did was recognize that this same mechanism — a heavy wooden screw threaded through a cross-beam, turned by a lever or bar to drive a flat surface downward — could be adapted to apply uniform pressure over a bed of type.
The key difference from earlier presses was the need for precise, even pressure over a broad rectangular area, rather than the concentrated pressure required for squeezing liquids. The printing press needed to descend perfectly parallel to the type bed and to release cleanly after each impression.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The Wooden Press Design
Gutenberg’s press, and the “common press” that descended from it for centuries, was built entirely of wood (with some metal parts in the screw mechanism) and consisted of the following components:^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]
The framework: Two massive upright timbers (the cheeks) were connected by cross-beams at top and bottom, forming a sturdy, square frame. An intermediate cross-beam (the head) held the screw mechanism; another supported the bed.
The screw and spindle: A large wooden screw, threaded through a fixed nut in the upper cross-beam, extended downward. The thread pitch determined how much vertical travel the screw produced per revolution. The lower end of the spindle rested in a socket at the center of the platen.
The platen: A flat, rectangular block of wood (later faced with iron) suspended from the screw. When the screw was turned, the platen descended parallel to the bed and pressed the paper against the inked type. Because it was wooden, it was rarely perfectly flat, requiring compensating layers of woolen blanket to ensure even pressure.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The bar: A long wooden lever (the bar or rounce) was inserted through the spindle or attached to the screw. The pressman pulled the bar in a semicircular motion to turn the screw, bringing the platen down. After the impression, the bar was reversed to raise the platen. The labor involved was substantial — described as roughly equal to that of a plowman in the field.^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]
The bed and coffin: The type forme (the locked-up arrangement of movable type, furniture, and quoins) was placed on a flat bed, sometimes of stone but usually of wood, encased in a frame called the coffin. The bed was mounted on rails so it could be rolled in and out from under the platen.^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]
The Two-Pull System
The platen of Gutenberg’s press was smaller than the entire forme of type. A full-page forme could not be printed in a single impression. Instead, the pressman used the two-pull system: the forme was positioned so that only half of it sat under the platen; the bar was pulled to print that half; then the bed was rolled further in (or the carriage shifted) and the bar was pulled again to print the other half.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Lorck describes it precisely: “To print a forme, a double pull of the bar was necessary because the platen was not large enough to cover the full forme. The carriage was therefore first rolled only halfway in, and the first impression made, then rolled all the way in so that the other half could be printed.”^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
This meant that each sheet required two pulls for the first side, and two more for the reverse — four pulls in total to produce a single printed sheet. This halved the potential production rate but allowed the same press to handle large folio pages (used for the gutenberg-bible) without requiring an oversized platen.
The Frisket and Tympan (Paper Registration)
Two innovations were essential for producing clean, accurately registered prints on both sides of the sheet:
The tympan: A frame covered with parchment or cloth, hinged to the end of the bed. The sheet of paper was placed on the tympan, which was then folded down over the inked forme. The tympan included a soft blanket (the packing) that compensated for irregularities in the type height and the paper, ensuring an even impression.^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]
The frisket: A light frame covered with a sheet of paper, hinged to the tympan. This paper mask had rectangular windows cut out precisely where the type would print; the rest of the frisket protected the margins from accidental ink marks. The frisket was folded down over the sheet, then the tympan and frisket together were folded onto the forme. After the impression, the whole assembly was lifted, and the printed sheet was removed.^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]
Register points: To ensure that the reverse side of the sheet printed exactly in alignment with the first side, the pressman used pins or points fixed to the tympan. These pierced the paper at specific positions; on the second pass, the sheet was hung on the same points, guaranteeing that the printed area on both sides coincided precisely. De Vinne notes that four point-holes can be seen in early books from Caxton’s press.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Inking with Leather Balls
Before the introduction of rollers in the 19th century, ink was applied to the forme using ink balls (also called beating balls or Ballen). These were mushroom-shaped implements made of wood, stuffed with horsehair (or wool), and covered with tanned sheepskin or dog leather. The pressman (the Ballenmeister or “ball master”) dabbed the balls onto an ink slab to pick up ink, then worked it by rubbing the two balls together in a rhythmic motion to distribute the ink evenly. He then beat the forme by bouncing the balls across the type — first from top to bottom, then laterally — applying more pressure to areas requiring heavier color (such as large initials or woodcuts).^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
This was a skilled and physically demanding task. The balls had to be kept at the right consistency and humidity; over-inking caused smudging, under-inking produced gray, uneven sheets.
Pace of Work
The Gutenberg press was slow by any modern measure. The earliest documentary estimate comes from Philip de Lignamine, who wrote around 1472 that the printers of mainz produced about three hundred sheets per day.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] This was the output of a two-man crew working a single press:

The puller (pressman or Pressenmeister) operated the bar, sliding the carriage in and out, pulling the impression, and removing the printed sheets.
The beater (inkerman or Ballenmeister) handled the inking of the forme with the leather balls, rotating with the puller to share the labor.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md][raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]

The two-pull system meant that 300 sheets per day represented roughly 600 pulls of the bar (for one side) or 1,200 pulls for both sides. By the middle of the 18th century, improvements to the press (lighter construction, better screw design) allowed two pressmen to achieve 2,000—3,000 impressions per day on the common press — equivalent to 1,000—1,500 completed sheets, roughly five to ten times the output of Gutenberg’s original press.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] De Vinne notes that by 1840, a single hand-pressman in New York with an inking machine could produce 1,500 impressions, with each impression covering a surface area roughly eight times larger than those of the 15th century.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Evolution of the Press
The Blaeu Press (c. 1620)
The first significant recorded improvement to the wooden press was made by Willem Janszoon Blaeu, an Amsterdam printer, astronomer, and instrument-maker. Around 1620, Blaeu introduced several refinements:^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]

The spindle of the screw passed through a square block guided in the wooden frame, which prevented the platen from twisting and ensured a truer vertical motion.
The platen was suspended from the block by wires or cords, allowing it to settle flat against the forme regardless of minor variations in the screw alignment.
A mechanical device for rolling the bed in and out replaced the manual sliding of the heavy carriage.
An iron hand-lever replaced the wooden bar, giving the pressman better leverage.

Blaeu’s press became the standard across Europe and England. A press of this type was used by Benjamin Franklin as a journeyman printer in London in the early 18th century.^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md] Blaeu is said to have built nine presses, each named after one of the Muses.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Other improvements to the wooden press were made by Danner in Nuremberg, but the Blaeu design remained substantially unchanged for the next 180 years.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Common Press (c. 1500—1800)
The printing press in general use from Gutenberg’s time through the end of the 18th century is referred to as the common press. Lorck observes that “the press of 1750 was in principle and in all essential components the same as that from the year 1500.”^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] It was built from wood, though over time the spindle, the nut, and the platen were gradually made of brass or iron, and the foundation and rails were made of iron. But the fundamental mechanism — a screw-driven platen, a sliding bed, a two-pull operation — remained essentially unchanged for 350 years.^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]
The Stanhope (Iron) Press (1800)
The first major redesign of the printing press in three and a half centuries was the work of Charles Stanhope, 3rd Earl Stanhope, in England, around 1798—1800. The Stanhope press replaced the wooden frame with a single casting of iron, providing far greater rigidity and allowing much larger forms to be printed.^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]
Stanhope retained the screw but added a combination of levers that multiplied the pressman’s force, making it possible to apply the necessary pressure with less exertion. The press was extremely heavy and cumbersome, but it was the first iron printing press ever constructed. According to Hoe, the printers of the day were so eager to adopt the lever system that they retrofitted levers onto their wooden presses — which generally destroyed them, as the wooden frames could not withstand the strain.^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]
The Cylinder Press (Koenig, 1814)
The true revolution in press design came from Friedrich Koenig, a Saxon printer and engineer who moved to England. In 1812—1813, Koenig (assisted by mechanic Andrew Bauer) devised a press that replaced the flat platen with a revolving cylinder passing over a flat bed of type. This was the first practical cylinder press.^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]
Koenig’s press used a reciprocating bed: the forme moved back and forth under the cylinder; the cylinder made a partial revolution to print as the bed passed under it, then continued turning (with a reduced-diameter segment, so the returning bed cleared without touching). The press also incorporated automatic inking rollers, replacing the manual ink balls.
In 1814, Koenig installed two of his double-cylinder presses in the office of The Times in London, where they printed at the rate of 800 sheets per hour — roughly ten times faster than a hand press. The printers were kept in the dark about the new machinery until the moment of publication; the November 29, 1814 issue of The Times was the first newspaper ever printed on a steam-powered cylinder press.^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]
This marked the beginning of the end for the hand-press era. Within decades, cylinder presses — improved by Applegath, Cowper, Napier, and by Robert Hoe & Co. in America — became the standard for high-speed newspaper and book printing, while the hand press survived only for fine-press work and proofing.
Significance
The printing press as a physical machine is sometimes overshadowed by the intellectual achievement of movable-type, but without the press, the type would have been useless. The press provided the mechanical force that made rapid, consistent, large-scale printing possible. It was the first machine in history designed for the mass production of identical copies of text, and its basic principles — a reciprocating bed passing under an impression surface — remained the foundation of all printing technology until the late 20th century.
The press’s 350-year stability (c. 1450—1800) is itself remarkable: it demonstrates that Gutenberg’s design was so well-suited to its purpose that it took the combination of iron casting, steam power, and the demand for cheap newspapers to finally displace it.^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]
