entities/abraham-ortelius.title: Abraham Ortelius
entities/abraham-ortelius.content:
Abraham Ortelius
Abraham Ortelius (1527–1598), Flemish cartographer and publisher, creator of the Theatrum Orbis Terrarum (1570), the first modern atlas — a uniform-format collection of maps that established the atlas as a genre and set the standard for systematic cartography. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Early Life and Family
Born 4 April 1527 in Antwerp into an old Antwerp family. His father Leonard was a merchant and dealer in antiques who died in 1539 when Ortelius was twelve. His mother Anne Harrewayers continued the antique business. Ortelius was placed under the care of his uncle Jacob van Meteren, a noted printer and book dealer whose son Emanuel van Meteren became a lifelong friend and cousin. The family was sympathetic to the Reformation, which later influenced Ortelius’s circle. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
At age twelve, after his father’s death, Ortelius and his sisters began colouring maps to support the family — the entry point into the map trade. In 1547 he was admitted to the Guild of St. Luke as an “illuminator of maps.” Gerard de Jode was admitted the same year as a master merchant of prints, beginning a long commercial rivalry. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Career as Map Dealer and Publisher
Ortelius built his business as a dealer in antiques, coins, maps, and books. He travelled widely to European book fairs, especially the Frankfurt Fair, where he built an international network of correspondents and suppliers. His house in Antwerp became a gathering place for scholars, printers, and cartographers. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
He learned Latin, Greek, and mathematics, and his scholarly connections gave him access to the latest geographical discoveries. His business acumen and social skills were as important as his cartographic knowledge — he was described by contemporaries as a man who “knew how to make friends of scholars.” ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
First Map and Key Works
His first known map was the Nova totius terrarum orbis… (1564), a large wall map of the world (870 x 1507 mm printed on eight sheets), published by Gerard de Jode. This world map was inspired by Giacomo Gastaldi’s 1561 world map and showed Ortelius already working at the highest level of contemporary cartography. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
His map of Asia (1567) was widely copied, including by Donato Bertelli in Venice, testifying to its authority and commercial reach. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
The Theatrum Orbis Terrarum (1570)
Ortelius’s masterwork, the Theatrum Orbis Terrarum (“Theatre of the World”), published in Antwerp on 20 May 1570, was the first collection of maps designed to a uniform size and style — the first modern atlas. It contained fifty-three map sheets, each accompanied by descriptive text on the verso. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
The Theatrum was revolutionary in several respects:

Uniform format and scale: Earlier map collections were assembled from loose sheets of varying sizes and styles. Ortelius had all maps engraved to the same plate size and design language, creating a coherent book.
The Catalogus auctorum: The atlas included a printed list of the cartographers whose work Ortelius had consulted — the first systematic catalogue of map sources ever published. This catalogue, listing eighty-six cartographers, became a foundational document for the history of cartography and is the basis for Karrow’s Mapmakers of the Sixteenth Century. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Scholarly apparatus: Each map was credited to its original author, and Ortelius added historical and geographical notes, making the atlas a work of scholarship as well as a practical reference.
Commercial success: The Theatrum went through multiple editions and translations (Latin, Dutch, German, French, Spanish, Italian, English) during Ortelius’s lifetime, with regular updates and expansions called Additamenta. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]

The atlas was printed by Christophe Plantin, Antwerp’s leading printer-publisher, whose typographic standards matched Ortelius’s cartographic ambitions. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Relationship with Gerard Mercator
Ortelius and Gerard Mercator were intimate friends. They first met in 1554 when Ortelius visited Mercator, and maintained a close correspondence thereafter. Mercator allegedly delayed publishing his own atlas to allow Ortelius’s Theatrum to establish itself in the market — a gesture of remarkable collegiality in a competitive trade. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Ortelius included Mercator’s maps in the Theatrum and credited him in the Catalogus auctorum. Mercator, for his part, coined the term “atlas” for a collection of maps (from the legendary king of Mauretania, a philosopher-king and astronomer), though Ortelius’s Theatrum preceded Mercator’s Atlas by fifteen years. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Relationship with Giacomo Gastaldi
Ortelius drew heavily on Gastaldi’s maps, especially for Asia and the world map. His 1564 world map was explicitly inspired by Gastaldi’s 1561 world map. Ortelius’s note to the reader in the Theatrum discusses Gastaldi’s work and criticises Gastaldi’s reliance on Abulfeda (the 13th-century Arab geographer) for Asian geography. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Legacy
Ortelius died in 1598. The Theatrum continued to be published and expanded after his death, going through some thirty editions. It inspired imitators — notably Gerard de Jode’s Speculum Orbis Terrarum (1578), which tried and failed to compete — and successors, including Blaeu, Janssonius, and others who built the great Dutch atlas-publishing industry of the seventeenth century. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Ortelius is also significant for his role in the intellectual history of the late Renaissance. His correspondence network and his catalogue of mapmakers created a collaborative model for cartographic scholarship that anticipated the republic of letters of the seventeenth century. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]

entities/aldus-manutius.title: Aldus Manutius
entities/aldus-manutius.content:
Overview
Aldus Manutius (c. 1449 — February 6, 1515) was a Venetian printer, publisher, and scholar who revolutionised the book trade by making classical literature widely available in compact, portable editions. His Aldine Press, founded in the 1490s, was the first to specialise in printing Greek classics, developed the italic typeface, introduced the octavo format as a portable book, and created one of the first recognisable printer’s marks — the anchor and dolphin. He is the most influential publisher of the early modern period after johann-gutenberg. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Lowry’s study revised the traditional portrait of Aldus as a pure humanist patronised by like-minded princes, revealing instead a complicated figure who was a minority partner in a hard-nosed commercial syndicate, constantly struggling to balance scholarly ideals against the demands of investors and the brutal realities of the early printing trade. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Early Life
Aldus Manutius was born Teobaldo Manucci in Bassiano in the Romagna, around 1449 (Putnam gives 1450, the year Gutenberg completed his press). He studied in Rome and Ferrara, mastering Latin and then, under the tutorship of Guarini of Verona, devoting himself to Greek. Later he delivered lectures on both Latin and Greek classics. One of his fellow students in Ferrara was the precocious young scholar Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, whose friendship was afterwards of material service to Aldus’s career. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
In 1482, when Ferrara was besieged by the Venetians and scholarly pursuits were interrupted, Aldus was the guest of Pico at Mirandola. There he met Emanuel Adramyttenos, one of the many Greek scholars who, driven from Constantinople after the fall of 1453, had found refuge in the courts of Italian princes. Aldus spent two years at Mirandola, and under Adramyttenos’s guidance he deepened his knowledge of Greek language and literature. Adramyttenos had brought from the East a number of manuscripts, many of which entered Pico’s library. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Around 1482 Aldus took charge of the education of the young princes Alberto and Lionello Pio of Carpi, the nephews of Pico della Mirandola. The princess of Carpi (Pico’s sister) and her sons became lifelong friends and patrons. It was in Carpi that Aldus developed the scheme of using his scholarly connections to print Latin and Greek classics. The funds required for the undertaking were furnished by the Princess of Carpi and her sons, probably with some co-operation from Pico. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Through Pico, Aldus was introduced to Ermolao Barbaro of Venice, a distinguished Greek scholar, and to the broader circle of Venetian humanists. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Lowry emphasises that Aldus’s early life as a “wandering scholar” shaped his lifelong conviction that the printing press could serve as a vehicle for humanist education. His Greek studies under Guarini of Verona and later Adramyttenos gave him both the linguistic skills and the contacts among Greek refugee scholars that would define the Aldine project. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The Barbarigo-Torresani Partnership: Business Structure of the Aldine Press
Before 1495 Aldus was experimenting independently, possibly with capital from Alberto Pio, while Andrea Torresani remained an interested spectator. Some preliminary contract between Aldus and Torresani may have preceded the full partnership. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The formal business partnership was established in 1495 as “a company for the printing of books between the late lord Pierfrancesco Barbarigo, son of the most Serene Prince, on the one side, and the late lord Andrea Torresani, bookseller, with the late lord Aldus de Manutiis, a Roman, also taking a certain part.” This notarial act was discovered by Mario Brunetti in the records of the Procuratori di San Marco. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
To nineteenth-century scholars, even the partnership of Aldus and Andrea seemed to begin only in 1508. The association of doge Marco Barbarigo’s son with the company was known only from a rambling letter written more than forty years after the event by the antiquarian Zuane Bembo, who mentioned that Santo Barbarigo’s father “helped Aldus with several thousand ducats.” Brunetti’s archival discovery proved that Pierfrancesco Barbarigo was not merely a sympathiser but a shareholder who put the weight of his capital and the influence of his ducal family name behind the company from its very beginning. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Pierfrancesco Barbarigo’s father Marco had been doge for less than one year in 1485, succeeded by his uncle Agostino, who exercised power until 1501. Pierfrancesco himself rose to become a member of the Senate but died in 1499. After 1501 the Barbarigo family fell into disrepute due to corruption scandals involving the late doge. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The company was a powerful organisation underwritten by one of the most successful publishers of the age and the nephew of the titular head of the Venetian state. But the basic initiative was Aldus’s: Barbarigo and his family were interested only in dividends, and Torresani lacked the academic skills to direct the scholarly programme. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
However, Aldus’s control was limited. All payments recorded in the Barbarigo account book are divided squarely down the middle, one half going to the Barbarigo estate and the other to Torresani, to whose name Aldus’s is usually linked. The working capital and profits were divided into two equal shares: one controlled completely by the Barbarigo estate, the other held jointly by Torresani and Aldus. When Aldus and Andrea formally unified their property and assets in 1506, four-fifths of the total was Andrea’s. Aldus’s holding in the company was probably one-fifth of Andrea’s half-share, or one-tenth of the total — at most twenty-five per cent. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
This meant Aldus never had the decisive word on business policy. In 1499 he wrote apologising that books could not be offered at a reduced price “because they were a joint venture with certain others.” In 1505 John Cuno reported that Torresani was blocking further publication in Greek. Isabella d’Este wrote that she was returning vellum copies because they were worth barely half the sum asked and Aldus’s partners would accept no less. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Jenson-Torresani Connection
Andrea Torresani of Asola was active as a printer, bookseller and underwriter for more than a decade before forming a partnership with Aldus. He had purchased the matrices of Nicolas Jenson after Jenson’s death in 1480 and claimed to work with Jenson’s types. The colophon to his edition of Panormita’s commentaries on Decretals (1482) states: “Exactum est hoc opus inclytis instrumentis formosisque litterarum characteribus quondam in hac arte Magistri Nicolai Jenson Gallici.” The combined Aldine house thus brought together the typographical legacy of Jenson, the financial support of Torresani, and the scholarly direction of Aldus. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Lowry notes that a “Franciscus de Bononia quondam Caesaris aurifex” was directed by Jenson’s partner Johan Rauchfass in 1475 to copy two of Jenson’s Gothic types, raising the possibility that Griffo — the later Aldine punchcutter — had connections with Jenson’s workshop that linked the most celebrated Venetian printing houses. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Move to Venice and Founding of the Aldine Press
In 1490 Aldus settled in Venice, at that time the printing capital of Europe with some 150 presses in operation. Although the city was crowded with printers, Aldus spotted a gap: no one was publishing books in Greek. The Greek-speaking community of Venice, swelled by refugees from the fall of Constantinople in 1453, had the scholarship but lacked the means to print. Greek handwriting had never been standardised for type, and the technical difficulty was considerable.
Aldus found backers — his former pupils among the Pio family, the Venetian nobleman Pierfrancesco Barbarigo, and the established printer Andrea Torresani of Asola. In 1494, with their support, he founded the Aldine Press. He married Torresani’s daughter Maria, cementing the partnership and eventually gaining control of the printing office that had earlier belonged to Nicolas Jenson. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Aldus set up his workshop in the S. Polo area of Venice, near the church of Sant’ Agostin, some distance from the booksellers’ district of San Zulian and San Paternian but convenient for the Rialto business centre and Andrea Torresani’s shop “at the sign of the Tower” by the bridge. The building at No. 2311 is traditionally identified as Aldus’s house and workshop — an unpretentious fifteenth-century Gothic building on the square of Sant’ Agostin, beside the baker’s. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Writing of his visit in 1508, Erasmus described a household of some thirty people, including workmen, servants, the family, and eight or nine guests. This refers to the years after Aldus’s marriage to Maria Torresani, when the combined families lived together at the Torresani home in San Paternian. The conditions reflected an incredible mixture of sweatshop, boarding house, and research institute. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The Greek Classics and the Aldine Aristotle
Aldus’s great ambition was to preserve the entire corpus of Greek literature in print before the manuscripts decayed or were lost. In 1495 he obtained from the Venetian government a twenty-year monopoly on the printing of Greek texts — one of the earliest copyright privileges in history. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
His first publication, issued in 1495, was the Greek and Latin Grammar of Constantine Laskaris, a suitable forerunner for his great classical series. Laskaris was a refugee from the East and at the time of publication an instructor in Messina; his Grammar was probably the very first work by a living author printed in Italy. The second issue was the complete works of Aristotle, issued in five folio volumes between 1495 and 1498. This was the first printed edition of Aristotle’s complete works and a landmark in classical scholarship. It was followed in 1496 by the Greek Grammar of Theodore Gaza, himself a native of Greece who was for a time associated with the Aldine Press as a Greek editor, and in 1497 by a Greek-Latin Dictionary compiled by Aldus himself. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Before editors or proof-readers could prepare Greek texts for the press, these foundational dictionaries and grammars had to be created. Aldus’s own later grammars continued this work: in 1502 he published, in a handsome quarto volume, a comprehensive grammar titled Rudimenta Grammatices Linguae Latinae (with an introduction to Hebrew), the product of years of labour. He also wrote the Grammaticae Institutiones Graecae, which was not published until 1515, after his death. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Aldus demanded extraordinary rigour from his workforce: his Greek typesetters and proof-correctors were required to speak classical Greek on the premises or face dismissal. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Typographical Innovations
Francesco Griffo and the Development of Aldine Types
The type-fount was always the most expensive item in a printer’s capital equipment, and a Greek fount posed particular problems. Greek uses oxytone or perispomenon accents on all words except enclitics, and rough or smooth breathing-symbols over all initial vowels. These had either to be cast in every possible combination (requiring over 1,400 separate letter forms) or cast separately and set above the letter, slowing composition and increasing costs. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Aldus faced these difficulties with the aid of Francesco da Bologna (Francesco Griffo), arguably the most important single figure in the establishment of the Aldine company but now so utterly obscured by time that both his name and identity remain in doubt. He was once thought to have been the goldsmith Raibolini, but the goldsmith died in 1517 and the type-cutter was still active a year later. A more probable candidate is the “Franciscus Griffus de Bononia incisor Litterarum stampae” mentioned in a Perugian notarial act of 1512. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
There are only three fixed points for Griffo’s connection with Venetian printing: (1) the three-line tribute added by Aldus to the first text printed in italic cursive, the Virgil of 1501; (2) the claim by Gerolamo Soncino of Fano in 1503 that he had secured the services of the expert who had cut all Aldus’s types and deserved the real credit for their design; (3) the repetition of that claim by Francesco himself in an edition of Petrarch’s Canzonieri published on his own account in 1516. Shortly afterward Griffo brained his son-in-law with an iron bar — possibly an incomplete type punch — faced a murder charge in Bologna with unknown results, and vanished from history. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Soncino described Griffo as “a most excellent cutter of Latin, Greek and Hebrew letters, a man whose genius finds no equal in this craft.” If Griffo cut all Aldus’s types, he must have begun experimenting with Greek designs early in the 1490s, years before the publishing company existed. Aldus’s last distinct type was the small Greek cursive introduced for the Sophocles of August 1502; Griffo was in Soncino’s employ by July 1503, so he must have left Venice late in 1502, close to the date (14 November 1502) when Aldus was granted a comprehensive monopoly over all Greek publication and all Latin printing in italic within the Venetian dominions. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The connection between Aldus and Griffo lasted for ten or twelve years at most, and for only seven of these was the publishing company in production. During this period Aldus commissioned and used twelve type-founts in three languages: six rounded Roman Latin types plus the famous italic; four Greek cursives, similar in conception but different in detail; and one Hebrew fount, used sporadically throughout Aldus’s lifetime. After 1502 no new designs were introduced — experiment ended with Griffo’s departure. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Italic Type
In 1500, Aldus commissioned the punch-cutter Francesco Griffo of Bologna to cut a new typeface based on the cursive script used in the Vatican chancery. This became the first italic type — a slanted, compact letterform designed to fit more words per page. It was first used in 1501 for an edition of Virgil. In 1501 Aldus obtained a ten-year copyright for all works printed in this cursive or italic character. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
There was contemporary disagreement over who truly invented italic. Aldus’s petitions for privilege claimed he had “devised a new kind of letter called cursive,” but Soncino and Griffo himself countered that Griffo deserved the credit. By 1514 the Giunti of Florence were also claiming to have been first to print in italic. Aldus’s privilege, by outlawing imitation of his Greek and italic styles, effectively prevented Griffo from selling his most original designs to other printers, which likely caused their quarrel. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Lowry notes that Aldus’s Greek and Latin cursives followed sophisticated academic tastes so exactly that a lively argument has raged over the scribal models used. At least one critic attributes the pattern for the Greek cursive founts to Aldus himself. That Griffo both designed and cut the types as he claimed is most unlikely; the reality is that the credit for this complex operation — scribe, type-cutter, and intermediary — cannot be disentangled. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The Octavo Revolution
Before Aldus, scholarly books were printed almost exclusively in large folio or quarto formats — heavy, expensive volumes suited to libraries and lecterns. Aldus introduced the octavo format (roughly the size of a modern paperback), small enough to be carried in a pocket or saddlebag. These compact editions of the classics, printed in italic type to save space, dramatically reduced the cost of books and made them accessible to students, travellers, and the emerging middle class. They were the first true portable books and a direct forerunner of the modern paperback. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Lowry offers a significant revision: Aldus did not invent the portable book. Smaller formats already existed in manuscript and print, but for devotional works only. Jenson had printed minute Office books in the 1470s; Lazzaro di Soardis applied for copyright on octavo editions in 1497. Aldus’s originality lay in applying the small format to classical literature. His Latin octavos were all safe, established favourites: Horace, Valerius Maximus, Ovid, Catullus. By pruning away the commentaries that lumbered folio editions and combining the smaller format with the most acceptable titles, Aldus freed literature from the study and the lecture-room. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Lowry also challenges the assumption that Aldine octavos were cheap. No contemporary source describes them as inexpensive; Aldus himself emphasised that they were beautiful and convenient, not cheap. They were quickly undercut by pirated imitations. The notion that Aldus introduced both the octavo and the italic as a means of price-cutting is a modern inference unsupported by contemporary evidence. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The small volume, mass-produced in editions of up to three thousand copies, represented a social extension of the humanists’ conviction that literature could enlighten wherever it went. The shameless haste with which the model was copied by competitors is the clearest proof of its success. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The Anchor-and-Dolphin Device
Aldus adopted as his printer’s mark the image of a dolphin entwined around an anchor — a symbol of the classical adage festina lente (“make haste slowly”), meaning activity tempered by restraint. The device was taken from an illustration in the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili and is one of the first recognisable publisher’s logos in the history of printing. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (1499)
In 1499 Aldus printed one of the most beautiful books of the Renaissance: the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (“Poliphilo’s Struggle for Love in a Dream”), a mysterious and erotically charged allegorical romance written in a bizarre invented language mixing Italian, Latin, and Greek. The author was Francesco Colonna, a Venetian monk. The book was financed by a patron, Leonardo Grassi.
Commercially it was a disaster — an expensive, deliberately obscure work that sold very few copies. But typographically it was a masterpiece. Its 172 woodcut illustrations, its elegant Roman type (derived from Jenson’s), its decorated initials, and its harmonious integration of text and image have made it the most celebrated illustrated book of the fifteenth century. Some copies sell for over half a million dollars today. The typeface was later revived as Poliphilus. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Lowry notes that the Hypnerotomachia contains Hebrew characters used as early as 1498, predating Aldus’s formal Hebrew fount. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The Aldine Academy (Neacademia)
Aldus gathered around him a circle of Greek and Latin scholars known as the Aldine Academy (Neacademia, or New Academy). The academy’s rules were unusual: only Greek was to be spoken at meetings, with fines imposed on anyone caught speaking Latin or Italian. Members included Hieronymus Aleander (later a cardinal), Marcus Musurus (whose handwriting was used as the model for Aldus’s Greek type), and the great Dutch humanist Erasmus, who lived in Aldus’s household while preparing an edition of his Adagia and who was paid by Aldus for his editorial work. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Lowry provides a far richer account based on the Academy’s statute. The forty-nine line document, known as NEAKAAHMIAZ NOMOXZ (Statute of the New Academy), survives on a single sheet in the binding of a volume in the Vatican library. It lists seven names: Aldus as “leader”; Scipio Fortiguerra, who appears to have drafted it; a certain “John the Cretan” (possibly Rhosos or Gregoropoulos); Baptista Egnazio; Paolo da Canal; Hironimo Menochio; and Francesco Rosetto. The signatories bound themselves to speak only Greek when together, to pay a small fine for lapses, and to collect the fines until sufficient to finance an “Academicians’ banquet.” There were clauses on admitting other “philhellenes” or visitors who wished to learn Greek. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The statute appeared in print for the first time with the Sophocles of August 1502, which was published with the colophon “Venetiis in Aldi Romani Academia.” In November 1502 the ducal letter of Leonardo Loredan mentioned among Aldus’s services to literature that “he now even has a New Academy.” ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Lowry argues that the statute was designed to advertise as well as organise. Aldus’s editorial activity reached its zenith between 1502 and 1504, but the loss of Giorgio Valla and Brugnolo meant there was no longer a Hellenist among the public lecturers to provide discreet publicity. The Academy served to keep Greek scholarship in the public eye. Foreigners were taught Greek as promised: the German Dominican John Cuno lived and studied with Aldus at Sant’ Agostino, and his notes from John Gregoropoulos’s lectures on Aristophanes survive. The colophon “In Aldi Academia” vanished at the end of 1504, probably linked to the appointment of Leonico Tomeo to the vacant Greek lectureship. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The Academy also involved ambitious plans for an imperial academy under Maximilian. In June 1503 Aldus wrote to Conrad Celtis about making Germany “another Athens for the men of our time.” In August 1505 Aldus thanked the imperial secretary John Collauer for supporting his plan for founding an Academy at the court of Maximilian Caesar. John Cuno’s letter to Willibald Pirckheimer (21 December 1505) reported that Aldus was preparing to move to Germany to found a New Academy where scholars would instruct German youth in Greek, Hebrew, and even military exercises. The project collapsed due to Maximilian’s lack of funds. By the time of Erasmus’s visit in 1508, the word “academy” had become a household joke: Aldus would utter it in a squeaky, broken voice, hinting he would be senile if he ever lived to see such an institution. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Aldus never abandoned hope. Lucretia Borgia offered to establish the Academy at her own expense in Ferrara. The election of Leo X in 1513 inspired Aldus to write one of his most eloquent humanist addresses, dedicating the first edition of Plato’s complete works to the Pope and asking for funds to establish the Academy. The Pope founded a Greek College in Rome, but Lascaris and Callierges ran it, not Aldus. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Erasmus and the Aldine Press
Erasmus’s relationship with Aldus is one of the best-documented aspects of the Aldine Press. He arrived in Venice in 1507 and lived in the Torresani household while preparing the greatly expanded edition of his Adagia (proverbs), published by Aldus in 1508. Erasmus was paid twenty ducats for his various editorial services. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The conditions were memorable. Erasmus sat in one corner of the printing room, writing the Adagia from memory and handing his text sheet by sheet to the compositors, too busy, by his own account, to scratch his ears. In another corner sat Aldus, quietly reading proofs and countering all pleas that they had been checked already with the words “I’m studying.” Between them the types rattled in the compositors’ hands, and ink was daubed over everything in the way, far into the night, while the Dutchman’s stomach, unused to this pressure of work on short commons, rumbled in protest. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
In 1531, long after Aldus’s death, Erasmus was attacked by several Italians for alleged ingratitude to Aldus and gluttony during his stay. He replied with the dramatic dialogue Opulentia Sordida (“How to be Rich without Showing It”), in which he portrayed “Gilbert” (Erasmus) returning from “Synodium” (Venice) to a friend who comments on his wan appearance. Gilbert explains this by the rigorous life in the workshop of “Antronius” (Andrea Torresani) and his son-in-law “Orthrogonus” (Aldus). Erasmus maintained there had been nothing to eat in the Torresani household anyway. Lowry notes that this dialogue, once read as an attack on Aldus, becomes a compliment when Aldus’s true minority position in the partnership is understood. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Privileges and Business
The Venetian government granted Aldus exceptional privileges. In 1496 he secured a twenty-year monopoly on printing Greek texts. In 1501 he obtained a ten-year copyright covering all works printed in italic type. On 14 November 1502 he was granted a comprehensive monopoly over all Greek publication and all Latin printing in italic within the Venetian dominions. These privileges were among the earliest forms of intellectual property protection in the printing trade. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Despite these privileges, enforcement was weak. Papal privileges covered Catholic states in theory but lacked enforcement machinery. The privileges secured from Venice had effect only in Venetian territory. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Aldus has been compared to Atticus, the Roman publisher of the first century who earned that appellation for reproducing Greek classics for Italian readers. But Atticus was a man of large means derived from banking and tax-farming; Aldus began business without capital and died a poor man, reinvesting all receipts into fresh scholarly ventures. The payments Aldus made to editors and scholars were probably the first ever made in Italy for literary work connected with printing, and included compensation for the use of manuscripts that Greek refugees had saved from the Turks. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
In 1500, Aldus married Maria, the daughter of the printer Andrea Torresano of Asola, who had purchased Jenson’s matrices in 1479 and succeeded to his business. In 1507 the two printing concerns were united, and Torresano’s savings strengthened Aldus’s strained resources. The combined house thus brought together the typographical legacy of Jenson, the financial support of Torresano, and the scholarly direction of Aldus. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Lowry provides detailed cost estimates: wages for compositors (2.5-4.5 ducats/month), operators (2-3 ducats), and inkers (about 2 ducats), with a total wages bill of at least 40 ducats per month. Paper costs were roughly equivalent to labour costs. The monthly expenditure approached 100 ducats with only these two items. Erasmus is known to have earned 20 ducats for his services, Fra Giocondo 10 for his work on the Scriptores Rei Rusticae. In 1503 Aldus claimed to be producing 1,000 copies per month at a cost of around 234 ducats per edition. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Production Methods and Workforce
The Aldine workshop probably operated between four and six presses. Each press required three men: a compositor, an operator (torculator), and an inker. Fifteen or more workmen would have been employed. Erasmus said the workers never had more than half an hour throughout the day to spend on their meals. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Aldus had a turbulent relationship with his workforce. In 1501 he referred in a preface to “the conspiracies of my damned runaway slaves.” In 1503 he complained: “Four times now my hired men and workers have conspired against me in my own house, led on by that mother of all evils, Greed: but with the help of God I so smashed them that they all thoroughly regret their treachery.” Only two workers are known by name: Hilarius of Parma, a trusted servant, and Federigo da Ceresara, a distant relation who killed his brother and was seized by partisans in Mantua, provoking an international incident in which Aldus called on the imperial ambassador. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Distribution and Book Fairs
Aldus’s distribution network relied on international book fairs at Frankfurt and Lyons, which provided detailed information about production in different centres. The Barbarigo account book records block purchases by major customers such as Tadio Contarini. The Fugger family acted as intermediaries between Aldus and German scholars. In 1502 Reuchlin wrote to Aldus complaining about block-purchases that reduced his ability to sell individual copies. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Piratical Competition
Despite his privileges, Aldus faced constant competition from piratical editions. Piratical copies of his Rudimenta Grammatices (1502) promptly appeared in Florence, Lyons, and Paris. More broadly, pirated Aldine editions were issued in Cologne, Tubingen, and especially Lyons, where printers produced close imitations of the Aldine cursive type and issued volumes without imprint, date, or place of publication. The privileges secured from Venice had effect only in Venetian territory; papal privileges covered Catholic states in theory but lacked enforcement machinery. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Lowry identifies Lyons as the main centre for counterfeit Aldine editions. The pirated imitations quickly undercut Aldus’s prices, and his own former workers sometimes absconded with advance copies to sell to rivals. In his complaint about “the activities of the Lyon press-pirates,” Aldus revealed that his hired men had conspired against him four times. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Aldus also planned a polyglot Bible in several languages, but did not live to complete it. The project was eventually realised by Christophe Plantin in the 1560s. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Death and Legacy
Aldus Manutius died on February 6, 1515, in Venice. His press passed to his son Paulus Manutius (1512—1574), who maintained the family tradition and later established an Aldine branch in Rome under the patronage of Pope Pius IV. Paulus’s son, Aldus the Younger (1547—1597), was the last of the line. The firm operated under the name “Aldi Filii” (Sons of Aldus) and continued to produce distinguished editions for nearly a century after its founder’s death. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Aldus’s influence on the book trade was transformative. He created the first systematic program of classical publishing, invented the italic typeface, pioneered the portable book format, and established the principle that a printer-publisher could be both a businessman and a scholar. The Aldine Press set standards of textual accuracy, typographic elegance, and scholarly integrity that later printers such as the Estiennes of Paris, Froben of Basel, and the Elzevirs of Leyden sought to emulate. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Lowry offers a more complex assessment. Aldus’s company was not a club for literary dilettanti but a business organisation that had to make its way in a savage competitive world. Aldus may have been the mind that stirred the matter, but he had bills to pay and shareholders to satisfy. His achievement must be judged not only as the expression of an ideal but as an exercise in maintaining a delicate balance between tensions and pressures. The preponderance of intellectual evidence over economic evidence has made it tempting to speak of an “Aldine circle” as if Aldus were simply a humanist who turned printer; this does him much less than justice. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Key Achievements

Founded the Aldine Press in Venice (1494)
First printed edition of the complete works of Aristotle, 5 volumes (1495—1498) ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Commissioned the first italic type from Francesco Griffo (1500) ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Introduced the octavo format, creating the first portable books ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Printed the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (1499), the most beautiful Renaissance illustrated book ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Established the Aldine Academy for Greek scholarship ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Created the anchor-and-dolphin printer’s mark, the first modern publisher’s logo ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Secured early copyright privileges for Greek texts and italic type ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Commissioned twelve type-founts in three languages (Latin, Greek, Hebrew) from Francesco Griffo ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Published Erasmus’s Adagia (1508), one of the most influential scholarly works of the Renaissance ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]

entities/amsterdam.title: Amsterdam
entities/amsterdam.content:
Amsterdam
Amsterdam was the printing capital of the world in the seventeenth century. After the Spanish Fury devastated Antwerp in 1576, the centre of European printing shifted north to the Dutch Republic, and Amsterdam became the city where typographic excellence, press freedom, commercial wealth, and technical innovation converged. The Blaeu family’s atlases, the Elzevirs’ affordable classics, the first newspapers, and the most beautiful Hebrew types in Europe all belonged to Amsterdam. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Printing Landscape
Amsterdam’s printing industry was not as concentrated as Antwerp’s — Lorck notes that presses were “not as numerous” as in Leyden, but “very capable.” The city’s printers specialised in products that matched its commercial and maritime character: maps and atlases for the global trading network, navigation manuals for the East India Company, newspapers for the merchant class, Bibles for export, and clandestine Catholic liturgical works for the forbidden market. The city’s paper industry supplied both domestic needs and significant exports to England and Scandinavia. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Press freedom was Amsterdam’s decisive competitive advantage. During the seventeenth century, “the press of the Dutch Republic was more untrammeled than that of any state in Europe.” The Elzevirs “carried on their work under comparatively slight government restrictions, with few references to church censorship.” This freedom allowed Amsterdam publishers to print works that would have been impossible under Catholic censorship regimes, attracting authors and scholars from across Europe. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Blaeu Dynasty
The central figure in Amsterdam printing was Willem Jansz Blaeu (1571-1638), born in Alkmaar. Before becoming a printer, he studied astronomy under Tycho Brahe on the island of Hveen, a training that shaped his later specialisation in astronomical and cartographic works. He established his shop “In de Vergulde Zonwijser” (At the Gilded Sundial) on the Damrak. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
Blaeu was also a “tüchtiger Mechaniker” (capable mechanic) who improved the printing press. His workshop contained nine presses “of improved construction, named after the nine Muses,” with improvements to the elastic pull mechanism. Under his son Johann Blaeu (1596-1673), the firm reached its peak. In 1663, Johann published a magnificent atlas in twelve large folio volumes, followed by other equally grand works. The office was considered “the most significant and beautiful in Europe,” regularly employing over 40 workers, specialising in maps and illustrations. On 22 February 1672, the printing house burned completely. “Strict Protestants called it divine punishment because Blaeu printed many breviaries and missals for Catholics.” Johann died on 28 December 1673, succeeded by his sons Peter and Johann. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
For full details, see blaeu-family.
The Elzevirs in Amsterdam
While the Elzevir firm was founded in Leyden, an important branch was established in Amsterdam in 1638 by Louis Elzevir (grandson of the founder). In 1640, Louis added a printing office to the bookshop. The Amsterdam branch operated until 1680, when Daniel Elzevir died and his widow Anna issued the firm’s last publication. The Elzevir emblem in Amsterdam was an elm. The Amsterdam branch concentrated on the same small-format classics that made the Leyden house famous, and maintained its own network of international correspondents. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Joseph Athias and Hebrew Printing
Amsterdam became a centre for Hebrew printing in the seventeenth century. Joseph Athias, a Spanish Jew, owned a significant typographical establishment in Amsterdam and printed numerous Bibles in foreign languages. His Hebrew Bible, typeset in the fonts of Christoffel van Dyck, was famous and “still counted among the best.” The Athias press represented the continuation of the Hebrew printing tradition that had begun with Bomberg in Venice and the Soncino family in Italy. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Map and Atlas Printing
Beyond the Blaeu firm, Johann Jansson (not related to the Blaeu family) was active in Amsterdam from 1618 to 1664. He was particularly known as a printer of maps and atlases, competing with the Blaeu firm in the booming market for cartographic works driven by Dutch maritime expansion. The competition between Blaeu, Jansson, and Colom on the Damrak created a concentrated cluster of atlas-publishing expertise. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
International Reach
Amsterdam’s printers served markets far beyond the Dutch Republic. The Elzevirs’ correspondence reached France, Germany, and Italy. Blaeu’s atlases were sold across Europe. The city’s shipping connections meant that books could be exported to Scandinavia, the Baltic, England, and the Mediterranean more efficiently than from any inland printing centre. Peter the Great granted the Amsterdam printer Tessing a privilege to print books for Russia in 1698, and had Dutch types cut for Russia’s first newspaper (1705). ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The 1672 Watershed
The year 1672 — the “Year of Disaster” (Rampjaar) in Dutch history — was a turning point for Amsterdam printing. The Blaeu printing house burned in February. The French invasion and the Third Anglo-Dutch War disrupted trade. The Thirty Years’ War had already shifted the book fair centre from Frankfurt to Leipzig. Amsterdam printing did not cease, but its golden age was over. The Blaeu firm limped on for a few years under Peter and Johann; the Elzevir Amsterdam branch closed in 1680; Leyden’s concern ended in 1712. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Significance
Amsterdam was the printing capital of the seventeenth century because it combined four things no other city could offer at the same time: typographic excellence (the Van Dyck fonts, Blaeu’s maps, Athias’s Hebrew types), press freedom (attracting authors banned elsewhere), commercial wealth (the VOC, global trade networks), and technical skill (press improvements, paper quality, copperplate engraving). The succession was complete: Mainz (1450s) → Venice (1470s) → Antwerp (1550s) → Amsterdam (1600s).

entities/anton-koberger.title: Anton Koberger
entities/anton-koberger.content:
Overview
Anton Koberger (also spelled Anthoni Koburger; c. 1440 — 1513) was the most successful printer-publisher of 15th-century Germany and one of the largest printing entrepreneurs in all of Europe during the incunabula period. Operating from Nuremberg, he built a publishing empire that employed 24 presses and over 100 journeymen, produced more than 220 editions, and maintained an international distribution network stretching from Paris to Warsaw and from Rome to Antwerp. His most famous publication was the Nuremberg Chronicle (1493), a lavishly illustrated world history containing over 2,000 woodcuts. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Early Life and Family
Anton Koberger was born in Nuremberg around 1440, into an old patrician family of the city. One of his ancestors served as burgomaster of Nuremberg as far back as 1349 and took part in the successful effort to overthrow the rule of nobles over the city. For two centuries the Kobergers were among the leading citizens of Nuremberg. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
He was probably brought up as a goldsmith — an occupation he returned to in his later years. This metalworking background placed him in a tradition common among early printers: Gutenberg himself had been a goldsmith, and many of the first designers and engravers of typefaces came from the ranks of metalworkers. Albrecht Durer, whose original trade was also goldsmithing, served as godfather for one of Koberger’s children, and Koberger’s eldest son was apprenticed to Durer. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Koberger married twice and fathered more than twenty children. Several of his sons and nephews continued the business after his death, and some returned to the family’s original trade of working in gold and silver. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Printing Enterprise
The first printing office in Nuremberg had been established in 1470 by Heinrich Kefer of Mainz (who had been an assistant of Gutenberg) together with Johann Sensenschmid. Koberger devoted himself to the new art in 1472 and issued his first dated volume in 1473: Boethius’s De Consolatione Philosophiae with the commentary of Thomas Aquinas — a dignified work representative of the scholarly character of his subsequent output. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
By around 1509, according to the contemporary writer Johann Neudorffer, Koberger was employing approximately 24 presses with over 100 workmen, including compositors, pressmen, binders, correctors, illuminators, and designers. All were provided with meals by their employer in a building apart from the works, and they moved between the two buildings at regular hours with military discipline — a remarkably organized and industrial-scale operation for its time. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Known editions from his presses number 220 or more, almost all in folio format of considerable size, noted for their correctness and elegance. He printed at least 15 editions or impressions of the Bible, including a German Bible in 1483 (illustrated with woodcuts, using Gothic types) and multiple Latin editions with different commentaries. His catalogue included 33 editions of the Bible in total. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Typefaces and Printing Technique
Koberger followed Gutenberg in adopting Gothic (Fraktur) style types. For his 1475 edition of the Reformation der Stadt Nurnberg, he used a refined semi-Gothic script that closely approximated the later Fraktur style, and which was also used for the major work Leben der Heiligen (1488). In 1492, for his edition of Virgil, he employed a type based on Venetian models, similar to the types used by the father-in-law of Aldus Manutius. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
His printing office did not possess Greek type, leaving him at a disadvantage compared to Venetian and Parisian printers. In the edition of Boethius issued in 1576, lines of Greek quotations were left blank to be filled in by hand — a reminder of the technical limitations even at Europe’s largest printing operation. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Nuremberg Chronicle (1493)
Koberger’s most famous publication was the Liber Chronicarum (Book of Chronicles), commonly known as the Nuremberg Chronicle, compiled by the physician and scholar Dr. Hartmann Schedel. It appeared in 1493 in both Latin and German editions, and is one of the most remarkable printed works of the 15th century. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The book contained over 2,000 woodcut illustrations (many reused for multiple cities and figures), designed by Michael Wolgemut and Wilhelm Pleydenwurff — the workshop that included the young Albrecht Durer. A contract for the illustrations was made in 1491, demonstrating the considerable xylographic and typographic resources at Koberger’s disposal. The patrons were Sebald Schreyer and Sebastian Kammermaister, wealthy Nuremberg citizens who financed the illustrations. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The print run was estimated at 2,500 copies (1,500 in Latin, 1,000 in German). Koberger was paid four gulden for 500 pages of printing — approximately one pound sterling per page. The artists worked fourteen-hour days for an advance of 1,000 gulden (shared between them), and production took about two years. By 1509, 558 copies remained unsold, and the artists’ heirs were charged 1,200 gulden for unsold copies and debts. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The Nuremberg Chronicle included one of the first printed maps of Europe, reproduced from woodcuts. De Vinne describes it as a “large and thick folio … a summary of the history, geography and wonders of the world.” The reused woodcuts — the same portrait serving for Paris of Troy, Odofredus of Germany, and the poet Dante — reflected the immense production pressures of the period. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Publisher and Bookseller
Koberger’s activity as a publisher (Verleger) was so extensive that his own presses could not keep up with demand. He contracted work to other printers, notably Johannes Amerbach of Basel (who had begun his career as a corrector in Koberger’s shop) and Gruninger of Strasbourg. His surviving correspondence with Amerbach (the Koberger letter-book, covering 1493—1509) reveals him as a meticulous, orderly, and punctual businessman. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
He built an international distribution network with agents in Frankfurt, Leipzig, Vienna, Basel, Strasbourg, Cologne, Paris, Budapest, Warsaw, Venice, Florence, Rome, Antwerp, Bruges, and Leiden — a remarkable achievement given the risks and interruptions of travel and trade in the early 16th century. He was the first bookseller in Germany (and possibly in Europe) to issue a classified catalogue of current publications. Koberger’s bookshop was described by Kapp as the best-equipped repository for standard literature (Sortiments-Buchhandlung) in Germany. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Koberger’s network gave him a decisive advantage over his great contemporary Aldus Manutius of Venice, who struggled to maintain distribution north of the Alps. While Aldus relied on direct correspondence with individual scholars, Koberger worked through the organized book trade. For a number of years he was recognized as the natural leader of the German book trade. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Character and Reputation
Contemporaries spoke of Koberger in consistently glowing terms. Jodocus Badius (Badius Ascensius), the noted Paris printer, called him “that glorious Nuremberger … esteemed by honourable men everywhere as the prince of booksellers … the man who conducted his business with the most exact integrity, and with the highest ideals … with whom the production and distribution of good books was carried on as a sacred trust.” ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Conrad Leontorius and Jacob Wimpfeling described him as “a true Humanist,” despite his predominantly theological publishing list. He maintained close friendships with liberal thinkers such as Conrad Celtes, Albrecht Durer, and Willibald Pirckheimer. Emperor Maximilian addressed him as “our trusty Anthoni Koberger, whose great service entitles him to honour, alike from ourselves and from the realm.” ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
His associates emphasized his enormous capacity for persistent work, far-seeing enterprise, conscientious regard for the rights of others, large conceptions combined with careful attention to detail, keen sense of humour, and genial manner. He appears to have made many friends and no enemies, valued by Catholics as a serviceable ally and regarded by Reformers as a personal friend. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Decline and Death
Koberger died in 1513. His death came before the fiercest phase of the Reformation, which would transform the German book trade. The rise of Luther’s pamphlets and cheap vernacular literature (Flugschriften) undercut the market for the heavy theological folios on which Koberger’s business was built. His catalog was almost entirely devoted to Catholic theology in Latin — he printed only three German-language works in forty years. The new era demanded cheap books in the vernacular, not costly Latin folios. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The business continued under his nephew Johannes, and later under his sons Anthoni (the younger) and Melchior, but the energy and initiative of the founder had departed. In the 27 years after his death, only 53 works were added to the list. The last work bearing the Koberger imprint was the Bohemian Bible, issued by Melchior in 1540. A further factor in the decline was the impairment of capital from the withdrawal of shares due to the long series of heirs, few of whom wished to retain interest in the book trade. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Legacy
Koberger occupies a unique position in the history of printing. He was the first printer-publisher to organize book production on an industrial scale, anticipating the great publishing houses of later centuries. His operation — 24 presses, 100+ workers, international distribution, multiple typefaces, commissioning of external printers — was the largest and most sophisticated in 15th-century Europe. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
His imprint appeared on no fewer than 236 separate works between 1473 and 1513, nearly all substantial folios. In the words of Jacob Wimpfeling (1501): “We Germans practically control the intellectual world … It is for this work that we owe the largest acknowledgment for the service of a man like Koberger, who employs his publishing facilities only for the production of that which is best.” ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The typefaces and distribution networks he pioneered, the magnificent illustrated books of his press, and his model of the printer-publisher as a large-scale entrepreneur make Anton Koberger a defining figure of the incunabula age — the man who, more than any other, demonstrated that printing could be not merely a craft but a major industry. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Key Publications

1473 — Boethius, De Consolatione Philosophiae (first dated work)
1475 — Reformation der Stadt Nurnberg (with refined semi-Gothic type)
1478 — Biblia Latina (printed twice)
1483 — Die Deutsche Bibel, mit Bildern (German Bible, illustrated)
1488 — Leben der Heiligen (Lives of the Saints)
1491 — Schatzbehalter des Reichtums des ewigen Heils (woodcuts by Wolgemut)
1493 — Liber Chronicarum (Nuremberg Chronicle; Latin and German editions)
1494 — Gesta Romanorum (first printed edition)
1497-1504 — Biblia cum Postilla Hugonis (8-volume folio Bible, Koberger’s most costly work)
1511 — Biblia Latina

entities/antwerp.title: Antwerp
entities/antwerp.content:
Antwerp
Antwerp was the printing capital of the Low Countries in the sixteenth century and home to the largest and longest-lived publishing house of the early modern period, the Officina Plantiniana. Its position as a commercial depot between northern and southern Europe, its concentration of capital and skilled labour, and its role as the epicentre of the Reformation in the Netherlands made it the natural successor to Venice as Europe’s leading printing centre — until the Spanish Fury of 1576 shattered its dominance and shifted the centre of gravity north to Amsterdam and Leyden. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Rise as a Commercial and Printing Centre
Antwerp’s ascent as a printing centre was tied to the decline of Bruges. When Bruges lost its privileges due to its opposition to Emperor Maximilian I, those privileges were transferred to Antwerp. From the beginning of the sixteenth century, Antwerp “took a great upswing as a depot between north and south.” Under Charles V the city reached its highest bloom. By the end of the fifteenth century, out of sixty-five printers working in the Netherlands, thirteen were in Antwerp. By the time of Plantin’s arrival, an entire quarter of the city was devoted to the book trade. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Plantin-Moretus House (1555-1867)
The central figure in Antwerp’s printing history was Christophe Plantin (1514-1589), who established his press on the Friday Market (Vrijdagmarkt) in 1555. Plantin had learned his trade under Robert Macé in Caen and, after many travels, opened a small bookshop and bindery in Antwerp. His wife traded in linen goods to support the business. The court clerk Graphäus gave him advances by entrusting him with books to bind. He was admitted to the St. Luke’s Guild as a printer in 1550, but only in 1555 did he have a fully equipped workshop. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Under Plantin and his successors (the Moretus family), the house operated for 312 years, making it the longest-lived printing firm in history. In 1867 the city of Antwerp purchased the premises to create the Plantin-Moretus Museum, which preserves the complete workshop: presses, type, 15,000+ woodblocks, 7,000-8,000 copper plates, account books, and correspondence. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
For full details, see christopher-plantin.
Correctors and Scholars
Plantin gathered an exceptional team of correctors and editors. The foremost was Cornelius van Kiel (Kilianus), who worked in the Plantin house for fifty years, contributing greatly to its reputation. “Beyond all description unassuming, van Kiel never thought of promoting himself, content only that the house to which he had tied his existence prospered.” Theodore Pullmann, a fuller by trade but a passionate classical scholar, served as another pillar. Justus Lipsius, the greatest humanist of the Netherlands, maintained close business relations with Plantin. Franz Raphelingius, who had studied in Paris and Cambridge, served as corrector, married Plantin’s eldest daughter Margaretha, and later became professor of Hebrew at the University of Leyden. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Marriage Alliances and Succession
Plantin bound his key associates through marriage. His second daughter Martina married Johannes Moretus (Jan Moerentorff), a practical businessman who lacked Plantin’s scholarly ideals but excelled in management. The third daughter married Gilles Beys, who managed the Paris branch. Raphelingius took over the Leyden branch when Plantin returned to Antwerp in 1585. This system of marriage alliances ensured the firm’s continuity for three centuries. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Polyglot Bible
Plantin’s greatest undertaking was the Biblia Sacra Polyglotta (1568-1572), an eight-volume Bible in Hebrew, Chaldaic, Greek, and Latin. King Philip II of Spain approved costs of 24,000 gulden for printing and paper alone, advanced 6,000 ducats, and sent his chaplain Arias Montanus as supervisor of the literary production. The type was commissioned from the famous typefounder Guillaume le Bé of Paris. The Polyglot remains the most monumental achievement of Antwerp printing. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Censorship and the Proto-Typographer Office
In 1569, Philip II institutionalised control over printing in the Netherlands by creating the office of proto-typographer (supervisor of printing). Plantin was appointed to the post, which freed him from quartering soldiers and helped secure approvals for his publications. The first Index of Prohibited Books for the Low Countries had been printed in Louvain in 1546. The Antwerp Index commission, including the Bishop of Louvain and Arias Montanus, specified which portions of condemned books contained heretical material; booksellers were permitted to sell the expurgated remainder. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Spanish Fury and Decline
In 1576, the accumulating political and religious tensions culminated in the sack of Antwerp, known as the “Spanish Fury.” At this time Plantin had twenty-five presses and about 150 employees. The work of his printing office dwindled under the Spanish occupation and never fully recovered. The Catholic-Protestant division of the Netherlands was cemented: the southern provinces remained under Spanish Catholic rule, while the northern provinces (the Dutch Republic) became Protestant and independent. This political division reshaped the geography of European printing. Antwerp’s loss was Amsterdam’s and Leyden’s gain: Protestant printers and scholars fled north, carrying capital, skill, and connections. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Significance
Antwerp’s place in printing history is defined by a single firm, but that firm was the largest and most accomplished of the sixteenth century. The Plantin-Moretus house produced over 1,500 publications, pioneered the integration of copperplate engraving with typography, and survived for 312 years. Its physical survival as a museum makes it the most complete record of an early modern printing establishment anywhere in the world. Antwerp’s destruction in the Spanish Fury marked the end of one era and the beginning of another: the shift of European printing from the Catholic south to the Protestant north.

entities/blaeu-family.title: Blaeu Family
entities/blaeu-family.content:
Blaeu Family
The Blaeu family (Willem Jansz Blaeu, his sons Johan and Cornelis) was the leading Dutch printing and map-publishing dynasty of the seventeenth century, based in Amsterdam. Famous for their atlases (the Atlas Maior), they were also significant publishers of scholarly books in mathematics, navigation, astronomy, and the humanities. As press designers, they contributed important mechanical improvements to the printing press. ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Willem Jansz Blaeu (1571-1638)
Willem Jansz Blaeu was an Amsterdam mathematician, instrument maker, cartographer, and printer-publisher, described as possibly the most famous Dutch printer of the seventeenth century. ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
Around 1589, Blaeu spent an extended period on the island of Hveen in the Øresund (the Sound), working with the astronomer Tycho Brahe on scientific projects and gaining practical knowledge of astronomy and instrument-making. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
He established his printing and publishing shop “In de Vergulde Zonwijser” (At the Gilded Sundial) on the Damrak in Amsterdam, in direct proximity to his competitors Willem Janssonius and Jacob Aertsz Colom. His fame rests primarily on his atlases, but he also produced many books on mathematics, navigation, and astronomy. ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
Over the course of his career, he attracted eminent humanist authors including Caspar Barlaeus, Hugo Grotius, and Gerardus Joannes Vossius, and his list gradually expanded into the humanities. He distinguished himself through technical skill, content expertise, an impressive stock of books with good type and paper, a clear layout, capable correctors who also assisted with the compilation of indices, and an extensive distribution network. His seaman’s guides (zeemansgidsen) were a major part of his business alongside his scholarly and atlas publishing. ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
He also contributed to the mechanical improvement of the printing press. Alongside Danner of Nuremberg, Blaeu is named as one of the notable press improvers of the period. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Dilemma between Science and Commerce
Throughout his career, Blaeu was caught in a fundamental dilemma. He was driven by a scientific-mathematical preference that led him to interesting projects in mathematics, cartography, and technology. Yet he also had to keep the business running by publishing works that were less aligned with his scientific interests but generated profit. He specialized, for instance, in the semi-clandestine production of missals and other Roman Catholic literature, a niche that provided steady revenue. ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
Copernican Convictions
Blaeu published the third edition in history of Copernicus’ De revolutionibus. The 1617 Astronomia instaurata title page names Wilhelmus Iansonius at Amsterdam, under the Golden Sundial, and Mulerius’s dedication presents the edition as a correction of earlier typographical and numerical corruption. Although Blaeu disguised his cosmological views in his mariners’ guides, he was a convinced Copernican. ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md] ^[raw/articles/copernicus-astronomia-instaurata.md]
Competition with Janssonius and Colom
Competition among Blaeu, Janssonius, and Colom was fierce. Privileges only applied within the territory of the issuing authority — in the Dutch Republic, a privilege from the States-General gave a printer a monopoly (typically for seven years) on printing or reprinting a book. Once a privilege expired, the book became free game. Janssonius and Colom regularly reprinted Blaeu’s successful titles in a more economical typeface on cheaper paper to capture a share of the market. Janssonius followed this strategy relentlessly, and Blaeu responded in kind. ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
According to a 1638 letter from Vossius, the two arch-rivals Blaeu and Janssonius eventually reached a reconciliation. ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
Relationship with the Athenaeum Illustre
Blaeu served as printer to scholars associated with the Amsterdam Athenaeum Illustre, the city’s “Illustrious School” or pre-university academy. Many of his learned authors were connected to this institution. ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
Later Career and the Sons
In 1637, in partnership with his sons Johan and Cornelis, Blaeu opened a new and larger printing shop on the Bloemgracht. By this time Blaeu was nearing the end of his career, and it was primarily his son Johan who continued and expanded the business. ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
The Blaeu firm was known for producing some of the largest and most magnificent books of the seventeenth century, particularly the multi-volume Atlas Maior, one of the most expensive printed works of the era. The firm’s reputation, however, was also marked by a tortoise-like slowness that frustrated authors — Blaeu consistently took on more work than he could complete in a timely manner. ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
A notable posthumous publication was Grotius’s Annales et Historiae (1657), issued in folio by the Blaeu firm nine years after the founder’s death. ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
Financial Strain of the Atlas Projects
The atlas projects placed heavy strain on the firm’s finances. In a 1638 letter, Gerardus Joannes Vossius reported that Blaeu’s expenditure on his atlases weighed so heavily on the budget that it obstructed more specialized projects, such as the Greek-Latin edition of Grotius’s Anthologia Graeca. The printer had become depressed by the financial pressure and saw his life’s end approaching. ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
The Grotius-Blaeu Relationship
Although Van Netten characterizes the relationship between Grotius and Blaeu as not an equal friendship, Nellen’s review notes that Grotius himself repeatedly referred to “our Blaeu” and explicitly invoked the friendship that bound him to the printer. Blaeu, for his part, was a businessman focused on continuity, for whom dealings with high-placed star authors were primarily determined by the revenue they brought in. ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
The Blaeu Atlas as Inheritor of 16th-Century Cartography
The Blaeu firm’s atlases incorporated many map plates originally created by sixteenth-century cartographers. Maps by Johann Criginger (Saxony), Martin Helwig (Silesia), Tilemann Stella (Mansfeld), Johannes Mellinger (Luneburg), Bartholomaeus Scultetus, and Fernando Alvares Seco were all reprinted in Blaeu atlases from the 1630s onward. The Criginger map of Saxony, for example, was included in atlases by the successors and imitators of Ortelius — Hondius, Jansson, Blaeu, van den Keere, de Wit, Visscher, and many others. The Stella map of Mansfeld had an active life of about a century and a half, passing from the original Ortelius plate through the atlases of Hondius, Jansson, Blaeu, Moses Pitt, and finally Schenck and Valk. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
This demonstrates how the Blaeu firm functioned as a key inheritor and disseminator of the sixteenth-century Ortelian cartographic tradition well into the Baroque period.
The End of the Firm
The Blaeu printing dynasty came to an abrupt end in 1672, the rampjaar (disaster year) of the Dutch Republic, when a devastating fire destroyed the printing shop. The firm did not recover from this loss, although it continued in a diminished form before ultimately closing in the early eighteenth century. ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
Historical Record
No business archive of the Blaeu firm survives, and unlike the scholars he published, Blaeu himself rarely expressed himself in letters or other personal testimony. Scholars have had to rely primarily on his printed works and the often-impersonal addresses to the reader found in his books. ^[raw/articles/blaeu-review-nellen.md]
