entities/christopher-plantin.title: Plantin-Moretus Family
entities/christopher-plantin.content:
Plantin-Moretus Family
The Plantin-Moretus family operated the Officina Plantiniana (Plantin Press) in Antwerp from 1555 to 1867 — three centuries of continuous printing under a single family line, spanning twenty-seven generations of printers. Founded by Christophe Plantin (c. 1520-1589), the press passed to the Moretus family (Latinised from Moerentorff) through Plantin’s daughter Martina, who married Jan Moretus. The press produced over 1,500 publications in its first generation alone, and the surviving workshop — the oldest in the world — is preserved as the Plantin-Moretus Museum.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Christophe Plantin (c. 1520-1589)
Early Life and Training
Plantin was born in Mont-Louis, near Tours, France, around 1520. He received a good school education that included a working mastery of Latin, the universal literary language of the era. He learned bookbinding under Robert Mace in Caen, Normandy, a town whose university had made it a growing literary and publishing centre. After completing his apprenticeship and undertaking extensive travels, Plantin married Jeanne Riviere around 1546 and moved to Antwerp, where he secured citizenship and became a master-printer, admitted to the Guild of Saint Luke in 1550.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Antwerp and the Establishment of the Plantin Press
Antwerp in the mid-sixteenth century was at the height of its prosperity, arguably the leading commercial city of Europe. Before the close of the fifteenth century, thirteen of the sixty-five printers then active in the Netherlands worked in Antwerp; by Plantin’s arrival, an entire quarter of the city was devoted to bookmaking, a circumstance without parallel in Europe.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Plantin began as a bookbinder, soon adding a bookshop. In 1555, he entered upon his career as a printer and publisher with Institution d’une Fille de Noble Maison, followed in the same year by Flores de l’anneo Seneca in Spanish. He purchased a house on the Friday Market (Vrijdagmarkt) and installed a fully equipped printing workshop. His first printer’s mark (1555) showed a tree trunk with a vine winding around it; from 1558 he adopted the compass-and-hand device with the motto Labore et Constantia (By Labour and Constancy), which became one of the most famous printer’s marks in history.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Polyglot Bible (1568-1572)
Plantin’s masterpiece was the Biblia Polyglotta (Royal Bible), an eight-volume edition of the Scriptures in Hebrew, Greek, Latin, Aramaic, and Syriac. It was the most important work ever issued by the printers of the Low Countries and the most scholarly edition of the Scriptures yet put into print. King Philip II of Spain funded the project, promising 21,000 florins (later increased to 24,000 guilders), and appointed his chaplain Benito Arias Montanus as general editor. The typefounder Guillaume Le Be of Paris was commissioned to cut the typefaces.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Printing occupied forty workers continuously from 1568 to 1572. The edition comprised 1,213 copies: twelve on imperial vellum, thirty on fine vellum, two hundred on royal vellum from Lyon, and 960 on royal paper from Troyes. Pope Pius V initially refused to sanction publication, blocking the undertaking for years. His successor Gregory XIII proved more favourable, granting approval in 1572. Even then, Professor Leon de Castro of Salamanca denounced Plantin to the Inquisition; Montanus submitted a defence and received clearance only in 1580, narrowly sparing the Bible from the Index.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Financially the Polyglot Bible was a failure. Philip II never fully paid the promised subsidy, and five years after publication a considerable proportion of the edition remained unsold. Plantin remarked: “Now that the Bible is complete, I stand with surprise and astonishment before the work, which I would not do again even if someone gave me 12,000 crowns.”^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Political and Religious Navigation
Plantin operated in a city torn between Catholic Spanish rule and growing Reformed sentiment. In 1562 he was accused of heresy when an edition of Brieve instruction pour prier was printed in his absence. He was condemned in absentio, his goods seized and sold at auction, then acquitted after showing the book had been printed without his knowledge. Friends bought back his equipment, and a new company was organised in 1563 with Plantin as manager.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Plantin came under suspicion repeatedly but always presented evidence of Catholic orthodoxy. Only after his death were documents found showing that as early as 1550 he had been a member of the Family of Charity (La Famille de la Charite), a sect led by Niclaes of Munster, for whom he printed the Spiegel der Gherechtigkeit without his imprint. Throughout his career, he maintained Catholic standing with the theologians of Louvain, Philip II, and the Pope.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
In 1570, Philip II appointed Plantin Prototypographer of the Netherlands (proto-typographus), a post that made him the official supervisor of printing. He was to register all masters and apprentices, maintain lists of all works printed (the first and last sheets had to be delivered to him), and set book prices. No remuneration was attached, but the incumbent was freed from billeting soldiers and gained privileged access to approvals. Plantin thereafter styled himself “Printer to the King.” He sought to resign in 1576.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Spanish Fury and Leyden Interlude
In 1576, at the time of the Spanish Fury — the sack of Antwerp by mutinous Spanish troops — Plantin was operating twenty-five presses and employing about 150 workers. The war between Spain and the Dutch rebels devastated Antwerp’s trade. By 1585, when Spanish authority was restored, Plantin had only a single press at work.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
In 1583, pressed by creditors, Plantin left for Leyden at the invitation of Justus Lipsius. He purchased the printing establishment where Louis Elzevir had begun work and was appointed Printer to the University of Leyden in 1584. Plantin put Elzevir in charge of his Leyden presses, giving the founder of the Elzevir dynasty invaluable training. In November 1585, he transferred the Leyden office to his son-in-law Franciscus Raphelengius (who succeeded him as Printer to the University and later became Professor of Hebrew) and returned to Antwerp.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Typefaces and Typography
Plantin’s types bear comparison with those of Aldus Manutius and Henri Estienne. Lorck describes his italic as “especially elegant, not as cursive as the Aldine”; his roman as “somewhat bold and broad, pleasing to the eye, easily readable, fully the equal of Estienne’s fonts”; his Greek as “finer than Aldus’s.” The precision of casting and spacing was highly praised. He acquired punches and matrices from the best typefounders, including the celebrated Garamond types that became closely associated with his press and influenced type design for centuries.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
He was the first publisher to associate typography on a large scale with copperplate engraving. The series of copper plates produced under his direction represented an enormous advance in artistic publishing.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Publishing Output
Plantin’s press published over 1,500 works in Latin, Greek, Hebrew, French, German, Spanish, Italian, Dutch, and English. He printed the liturgical works of the Council of Trent, Breviaries, Missals, classical texts (Virgil, Horace, Ovid, Plautus, Juvenal, Terence, Catullus, Tibullus, Propertius), the works of Galen and other medical and scientific authors, the Corpus Juris Civilis in ten volumes, the Thesaurus Theutonicae Linguae dictionary, musical works requiring special fonts, maps by Ortelius and Mercator, and the writings of Church Fathers including Augustine (10 volumes), Jerome (5 volumes), and Tertullian (3 volumes).^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
His catalogue of 1566 included works in ten languages. The account books record payments to authors and editors — often in copies of the book rather than cash — and reveal the detailed economics of a sixteenth-century publishing house.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Death
Plantin died on 1 July 1589 at age seventy-five. His last work was the first volume of Baronio’s Annales Ecclesiastici. Having no sons, he left the Antwerp business to his son-in-law Jan Moretus, who had managed operations for two years. Raphelengius took the Leyden office; son-in-law Gilles Beys directed the Paris branch.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Jan Moretus (1543-1610)
Jan Moretus (Jean Moerentorff) was born in Antwerp on 22 May 1543. He began as a worker in Plantin’s shop and rose through practical competence. Lorck notes that Jan “did not possess deeper knowledge” (besass keine tiefergehenden Kenntnisse) but excelled at maintaining scholarly connections and running the business efficiently. He married Plantin’s daughter Martina.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
His greatest achievement was securing a ten-year papal monopoly on the printing and distribution of the revised Vulgate north of the Alps, granted by papal breve on 11 March 1597. The 1592 Sixto-Clementine Vulgate had been printed in Rome; Moretus obtained the exclusive right to reprint it for northern Europe, on condition of the greatest care in correction and printing, and that no changes whatsoever be introduced. This monopoly was enormously profitable and sustained the firm through a difficult period.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Jan also restored the facade of the Plantin house on the Vrijdagmarkt, preserving the ancient mark of the building while modernising its appearance.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Balthasar Moretus (d. 1641)
The son of Jan Moretus, Balthasar was “the learned” (der gelehrte), according to Lorck. Under his direction the press “maintained a highly respected position for a long time” (noch durch lange Zeit eine hochangesehene Stellung).^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Balthasar cultivated the scholarly and artistic networks that Jan had maintained. He corresponded with Justus Lipsius, the leading humanist of the Low Countries, and commissioned title pages and illustrations from Peter Paul Rubens, who designed some of the most famous title borders and frontispieces of the century. The Rubens-designed title pages for Plantin-Moretus editions are among the high points of baroque book design.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
A medallion portrait of Balthasar — an eagle holding a star (from the Moretus coat of arms) — still greets visitors entering the Plantin-Moretus Museum vestibule.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Long Decline (1641-1867)
After Balthasar’s death, the firm’s significance faded gradually. Lorck states: “Toward the middle of the 17th century its significance faded more and more, and with the beginning of the 18th century the commercial splendour of the house was extinguished” (Gegen die Mitte des xvii. Jahrhunderts jedoch schwand die Bedeutung mehr und mehr, und mit dem Beginn des xviii. Jahrh. war der geschäftliche Glanz des Hauses erloschen).^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The presses continued to run, but at greatly reduced volume. The firm remained in the Moretus family, with the 25th generation still active in the early 19th century. External operations continued until 1865-1867, when the city of Antwerp purchased the building and collections for 1,200,000 francs (the national government contributed 200,000, the city 1,000,000).^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
What made the firm’s survival significant, however, was not its commercial vitality in its later centuries but the remarkable preservation of its physical plant. The Moretus family kept everything in place — presses, type, matrices, woodblocks, copperplates, account books, correspondence — even after the business had ceased to be commercially significant. Lorck notes that “externally everything was preserved with great piety in its old state” (Ausserlich wurde jedoch alles mit grosser Pietat in dem alten Stand gelassen). This is why the museum is so complete today.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Plantin-Moretus Museum
The building on the Vrijdagmarkt, purchased by the city of Antwerp in 1867 and opened as a museum in 1877, preserves the oldest surviving printing presses in the world. Lorck provides a detailed description of the house as it stood in the late 19th century:
The courtyard is a large square, three of whose four sides retain their original appearance. Busts of Plantin, Johannes Moretus, Balthasar Moretus, Johann Jakob Moretus, and Justus Lipsius adorn the facades. The composing room still holds type cases filled with type, with composing sticks and galleys in place. Lorck writes: “It is as if work had only been interrupted by the usual midday break and would soon resume” (Es ist, als ware die Arbeit nur von der ublichen Mittagspause unterbrochen und als musste sie baldigst wieder begonnen werden).^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The museum’s holdings include:

The composing room with apparatus for 20-25 compositors, types still in cases
Seven wooden presses, two formes still ready for printing
The proof-readers’ chamber
The type foundry, with casting furnaces still containing remnants of metal
Approximately 15,000 woodblocks
7,000 to 8,000 copperplates
Portraits by Rubens, van Dyck, and others
The business archives from 1566 to 1865, including journals, ledgers, binders’ books, catalogue drafts, and correspondence drafts

The archives are of exceptional value: they include the journal and account books from three centuries, correspondence with scholars and authors across Europe, and — remarkable for the history of printing — correspondence between the Moretus family and the Elzevir family of Leiden regarding the purchase of type. Lorck notes that a typographical curiosity in the library is a volume compiled by Jan Moretus in 1576, dedicated to Plantin, containing a collection of the title pages of every book printed by Plantin up to that year — an early specimen book for printers.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Significance
The Plantin-Moretus firm is unique in the history of printing: no other press operated continuously for three centuries under a single family line, and no other press preserved its physical plant, equipment, and archives so completely. The firm’s business records from 1566 to 1865 are the most complete set of early printing house accounts in existence, and they have enabled scholars to reconstruct the detailed economics of early modern book production.
The firm’s typographic legacy is equally significant. Plantin’s types — especially the Garamond types he acquired and popularised — influenced European type design for centuries. The Plantin typeface, revived in the twentieth century for machine composition, is named after him. His pioneering use of copperplate illustration on a commercial scale set new standards for illustrated books. And the survival of his house as a museum provides an incomparable record of how a sixteenth-century printing shop actually worked.

entities/daniel-bomberg.title: Daniel Bomberg
entities/daniel-bomberg.content:
Daniel Bomberg
Daniel Bomberg (c. 1483 — 1549?) was a Christian printer from Antwerp who established the most important Hebrew printing press of the sixteenth century in Venice. Known as “the Aldus of Hebrew printing,” he published the first complete edition of the Babylonian Talmud and set the standard for Hebrew typography for centuries. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Early Life
Bomberg was born in Antwerp, in the Spanish Netherlands, around 1483. Unlike the Jewish printers who had pioneered Hebrew typography, Bomberg was a Christian — Lorck specifies “he was not a Jew” — but he dedicated his entire publishing career to Hebrew and rabbinical literature. The commercial and cultural connections between Antwerp and Venice, the two great commercial centres of the sixteenth century, likely facilitated his move to Italy. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Venice Hebrew Press
Bomberg founded a printing house in Venice devoted exclusively to Hebrew works. Lorck draws the direct parallel: “What the Aldi and the Giunta were for Greek, Latin, and Italian printing, Daniel Bomberg was for Hebrew.” Before Bomberg, Hebrew printing “had been practised only by Jewish printers at Soncino, Naples, Pesaro, and Constantinople” — small-scale operations with limited distribution. Bomberg brought the full resources of Venetian printing to Hebrew typography. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
His major publications included:

Three editions of the complete Hebrew Bible with the best rabbinical commentaries, in four folio volumes each
Five portable Bible editions in smaller formats for everyday use
The Babylonian Talmud in twelve folio volumes — the first complete printed edition, a landmark of both Hebrew typography and Jewish scholarship
Numerous rabbinical works by medieval and contemporary authors ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]

Editorial and Scholarly Standards
Bomberg employed the learned scholar Chaja Maier Ben David as chief corrector, who worked “together with many capable correctors” to ensure textual accuracy. This investment in scholarly editing was unusual for Hebrew printing at the time and reflected Bomberg’s commitment to producing authoritative texts — the same priority that Aldus Manutius had brought to Greek printing in the same city. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Typographic Legacy
Bomberg’s Hebrew types were cut to exceptional standards and are considered by Lorck “the most beautiful down to the present day.” A vellum impression of his 1525 Bible, preserved in the Wolfenbüttel library, is described as “a typographical jewel.” The elegance and readability of Bomberg’s Hebrew typefaces influenced all subsequent Hebrew printing and set the standard that later typefounders aspired to match. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Financial Difficulties
Like Aldus Manutius, Bomberg appears to have struggled with the economics of scholarly printing. Lorck records that he “is said to have spent between 3-4 million crowns on Hebrew printing, and not to have looked sufficiently to his own profit.” The vast investment — in type-cutting, paper, correctors, and edition sizes — suggests a publisher driven by scholarly and religious commitment rather than commercial calculation. The exact circumstances of his death (c. 1549) and the disposition of his press are not well documented in the available sources. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Significance
Bomberg transformed Hebrew printing from a small-scale enterprise run by Jewish printers for local communities into a professional, scholarly publishing operation on the Venetian model. His complete Talmud, his authoritative Bible editions with commentaries, and his beautiful types made Venice the centre of Hebrew printing for the sixteenth century. His work enabled the study of rabbinical literature by Christian Hebraists as well as Jewish scholars, contributing to the broader humanist project of recovering the original languages of the Bible. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]

entities/elzevir-family.title: Elzevir Family
entities/elzevir-family.content:
Overview
The Elzevir family (also spelled Elzevier) were the most celebrated Dutch printer-publishers of the seventeenth century, operating from Leyden and Amsterdam between c. 1580 and 1712. Their imprint became synonymous with compact, elegantly printed editions of the classics, and the name “Elzevir” passed into common usage as a generic term for small-format, well-printed books. Only Aldus Manutius among the early publishers achieved comparable prestige, and while the Aldine press preceded the Elzevirs by more than a century, the Elzevirs’ sustained output of typographically exquisite, affordable editions established a standard that endured for generations. The principal modern authority on the family is Alphonse Willems’s monograph Les Elzevir: Histoire et annales typographiques (Brussels, 1880). ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1880] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3543]
Louis Elzevir (c. 1540—1617): The Founder
Louis Elzevir, the founder of the dynasty, was born in Louvain (Leuven) in Brabant around 1540. He was raised as a bookbinder in the Flemish university town. Work records of Christopher Plantin indicate that a printer named Johann Helsevier from Louvain worked for Plantin from 1565 to 1588, possibly Louis’s father. Louis himself was employed by Plantin in Antwerp. Two of his children, Matthias (1564) and Louis (1566), were born in Antwerp to Mayke (Marie) Duverdyn. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3545]
Antwerp was the heart of the Reformation movement in the Netherlands, and Elzevir adopted the Protestant faith. When King Philip II sent the Duke of Alba in 1567 to stamp out heresy by fire and sword, thousands of families fled. Louis Elzevir’s family was among them, moving first to Wesel, where his third son Aegidius was born, and later to Douai, where sons Justus and Arnold were born. After a brief return following the Pacification of Ghent (1576), the renewed submission of the Walloon provinces to Spain in 1579 forced the Protestants to flee again. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1882] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3550]
Settlement in Leyden
In 1580, Elzevir crossed into Holland with his five sons and daughter Marie and settled in Leyden, then, after Amsterdam, the most populous city in the province. Leyden’s university had been founded by William of Orange in 1575 to commemorate the city’s heroic resistance during the Spanish siege, and it had quickly become a prestigious centre of European scholarship. Elzevir found support among the many Flemish Protestant exiles already established there, including Vulcanius, Drusius, Lipsius, Heinsius, and William Silvius, the first Printer to the University. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1882] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3552]
He began work as a bookbinder for the university community and soon added a bookshop. The venture proved unsuccessful — the student population was small and the practice of borrowing or sharing textbooks limited demand. Elzevir was forced to give up his first premises but applied to the university authorities for help. Recognising the value of a skilled bookseller, the University Council permitted him to construct a small shop within the university court and appointed him official bookseller and later publisher to the University. He was also made a beadle (pedell) in 1586 with a salary of 72 guilders. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1886] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3557]
Building the Business
With this fresh start, Louis Elzevir built an assured business foundation through persistent labour. He never mastered the art of printing himself — the typographical work bearing his name was done under contract with various printers and initially showed no special distinctiveness. His strength lay in his scholarly judgment and his extensive foreign connections. His correspondence throughout France, Germany, and Italy brought the name of Leyden University to literary circles across Europe and established commercial links with the major book-producing centres. For most of his lifetime, Louis was the only Dutch publisher and bookseller with such international reach. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1890]
The first work published as his own venture was an edition of Eutropius (1592), but regular publication began only after 1594, the year he became a citizen of Leyden. In 1595, he first used the trade-mark of an eagle grasping seven darts in its claw, the emblem of the Dutch Republic, with the motto Concordia res parvae crescunt (Small things grow through harmony). His name appeared for the first time that year in the list of publishers at the Frankfort Fair. From 1602 he made regular annual journeys to Paris, where foreign dealers were strictly regulated — they could visit only once a year, stay no longer than three weeks, and trade only with licensed members of the Booksellers’ Guild. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1894] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3571]
Death and Legacy
Louis Elzevir died in early February 1617, shortly after a fire in the university buildings (November 1616) had led to the suspension of his son Matthias as vice-beadle. The fire investigation blamed the beadles’ negligence, and the stress may have hastened Louis’s death. He was buried beside his wife, who had predeceased him by three years. During his thirty-four-year publishing career (1583—1617), he issued 101 separate works, nearly all in Latin, including editions of Scaliger, Aristotle, Horace, and Heinsius, as well as Grotius’s Mare Liberum (1609). ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#2031] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3584]
The Sons and the Second Generation
Louis left six sons. Two operated bookshops in Utrecht and The Hague in affiliation with the Leyden concern. One served the Dutch East India Company; another became a landscape painter. The eldest, Matthias (1564—?), and the youngest, Bonaventure (1583—1652), joined hands to carry on and greatly extend their father’s business. The famous imprint ex officina Elzeviriana dates from 1617, when the two young men assumed direction. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1898]
Louis II (c. 1566—1621) established a bookshop in The Hague in 1590, in a large hall of the Palace of the States-General. The Hague establishment was primarily a retail bookselling operation with limited publishing activity. After his death, the business passed to Bonaventure, then to Jacob Elzevir (third son of Matthias), who withdrew in 1636. The shop was finally closed in 1661, its stock transferred to Amsterdam or sold at auction. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1937] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3594]
Justus Elzevir (1575—?) became a bookseller in Utrecht. His eldest son, Louis III (1604—1670), would later found the Amsterdam branch.
Isaac Elzevir (1596—1651): The First Printer
Isaac Elzevir, second son of Matthias and grandson of Louis I, acquired a printing office in 1616, making him the first Elzevir to actually operate a press. He married Jaquemine Symons van Swieten in 1616, and her dowry likely enabled the purchase. From 1617 he printed primarily for his uncles Matthias and Bonaventure, and later for Bonaventure and Abraham. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3603]
On February 9, 1620, Isaac was appointed Printer to the University of Leyden, a post the family would hold until 1712. The arrangement required him to hold at least one and a half presses at the disposition of the faculty for printing theses and academic papers, to provide competent correctors for any language required, and to deposit one copy of every work in the university library. His annual stipend was fifty guilders. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1916] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3609]
After the death of the renowned Orientalist Thomas van Erpen (Erpenius) in 1624, Isaac purchased Erpenius’s entire collection of Oriental type punches and matrices, ensuring that this valuable typographic resource remained in Leyden. The university subsequently raised his stipend to one hundred guilders on condition that the Oriental material be kept available for academic use. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1922] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3618]
Isaac’s printer’s mark was an elm tree entwined with a grapevine bearing grapes, with a hermit standing beside it and the motto Non solus (Not alone). He also used a palm tree with the motto Assurgo pressa (Pressed down, I rise), inherited from Erpenius. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3622]
Despite the business’s favourable progress, Isaac retired in December 1625, ostensibly concerned about the long war in Germany. He transferred the office with five presses, one copperplate press, and ten thousand kilograms of type to his uncle Bonaventure and his nephew Abraham for 9,000 guilders, plus 2,000 for the premises. He resigned his university post in February 1626, entered naval service, and by 1648 was operating a brewery in Delft. He died in Cologne on October 8, 1651. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3627]
Bonaventure and Abraham (1625—1652): The Golden Age
Bonaventure (1583—1652), the youngest son of Louis I, and Abraham (1592—1652), son of Matthias, formed the partnership that brought the House of Elzevir to its greatest glory. Bonaventure, named after the scholar Bonaventura Vulcanius, had been sent on business travels by his father from an early age. Abraham had studied at Leyden and trained in typography with his brother Isaac. He married Catharina van Waesberghe in 1621, daughter of the Admiralty printer of Rotterdam, bringing independent means and connections. Bonaventure married Sarah van Keulen, daughter of the scholar Daniel Colonius, in the same year that the partnership acquired Isaac’s press (1625), gaining entry into a wide circle of learned contacts. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3634]
The following twenty-six years (1626—1652) were the most brilliant period of the House. From the outset, the partners aimed to elevate their work above the ordinary, and each year showed progress in type design, ornamentation, or presswork. Within ten years they were producing masterpieces such as their Caesar, Terence, and Pliny of 1635. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3643]
Major Initiatives
In 1625, they began the series of small “Republics” (Republiques), for which they obtained a privilege on May 15, 1626. In 1629, they inaugurated the celebrated series of Latin classics in duodecimo (16mo) with Horace and Ovid, a form modelled on the famous Aldine editions. In 1641, they began a collection of contemporary French drama with Corneille’s Le Cid, and in 1642 a series of French literary classics with the works of Regnier. Alongside these small formats, they continued to issue works in folio and quarto, including Oriental scholarship from the Erpenius types. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1910] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3643]
The Small-Format Revolution
The duodecimo classics were the Elzevirs’ most distinctive contribution to publishing. Well-edited by the finest critics and commentators of the age, carefully printed, and offered at remarkably low prices — typically one florin (about forty-three cents) for a volume of approximately five hundred pages — these handy editions won immediate and overwhelming popularity. A Virgil of 1636, a Pliny of 1640, a Cicero of 1642 — all sold at one florin. Quintus Curtius (1633) sold for sixteen sous, and Sallust, Terence, and Florus for fifteen sous. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1965]
Critics complained that such compact volumes diminished the dignity of great authors. The scholar De Put (Erycius Puteanus) wrote in 1629 that Horace deserved “a dignified form, with a certain majesty of appearance, not to have his thoughts buried in shabby little type.” Yet scholars and students across Europe welcomed the affordable format. Professor Matthew Berneggerus of Strasbourg, in the preface to his translation of Galileo’s System of the Universe (1635), called the Elzevirs “unquestionably the first typographers of the world.” The format became standard across Holland and Belgium and was adopted by several Parisian booksellers. Collectors soon became passionate about acquiring complete sets of Elzevir editions. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1967] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3650]
Typographical Excellence and Christophe Van Dyck
The beauty of the Elzevir editions owes much to Christophe Van Dyck, the punch-cutter who designed and engraved the fonts from which the exquisite Elzevir types were cast. Typographical experts consider these fonts to have surpassed, in the beauty of their proportion, the delicacy of their outline, and the distinctive grace of their general effect, anything previously produced in Europe. Van Dyck’s work was done between approximately 1630 and 1640. The discovery of his identity is due to Alphonse Willems’s research in the Plantin-Moretus archives, where a letter from Daniel Elzevir’s widow offering the type foundry for sale describes the types as “made by Christoffel van Dyck, the best master of his and our time, and consequently the most famous foundry that ever existed.” ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1957] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3754]
Printed Output
During their twenty-seven-year partnership (1625—1652), Bonaventure and Abraham published 461 separate works. These included a long series of Greek and Latin classics in the new duodecimo form (officially adopted for use in the schools of Holland and West Frisia), theological works (increasingly in Dutch, reflecting the expanding popular readership), legal codes and court decisions, the Oriental series of Erpenius, the sumptuous Academie de l’espee (1628, with 46 engraved plates), and the Latin translation of Galileo’s works (1635). ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#2097] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3643]
Bonaventure managed the commercial and bibliopolic side of the business, maintaining close relations with scholars and customers. Abraham devoted himself with equal care and dedication to the typographical department. The scholarly adviser Daniel Heinsius (1580—1655), professor at Leyden and a universal scholar, was the intellectual soul of the publishing enterprise, writing introductions, dedications, and advising on the selection of works. Heinsius was, however, a contentious figure whose personality alienated a number of scholars from the firm. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#2013] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3677]
Bonaventure died on September 17, 1652; Abraham had predeceased him by a month, on August 14, 1652. The university struck a gold medal in Abraham’s honour, an unusual mark of esteem. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3682]
John and Daniel (1652—1680): The Third Generation
Bonaventure’s son Daniel (1626—1680) and Abraham’s son John (1622—1661) inherited the business. Both had been trained through foreign travel — John to Paris (1638) and Denmark (1641), Daniel to Paris (1645—1648). Their early editions, including the Imitation of Christ and the Psalms (1653), were among the finest typographical achievements of the Elzevir press, described by Willems as “jewels of typography.” ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1912] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3693]
However, the partnership faced difficulties. Many of the learned friends and advisers who had sustained the previous generation had passed away, the university was in a period of decline, and the relationship with the university administration was strained. Daniel elected to leave the partnership after two and a half years and joined his cousin Louis III in Amsterdam in 1655. John continued alone in Leyden, engaging Karl Gerstekorn as a helper, but his publishing activity diminished. He died on June 8, 1661, aged only 39. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1912] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3701]
Eva van Alphen and the Widow’s Press
John’s widow, Eva van Alphen, assumed control of the Leyden printing office and successfully retained the university contract. She disposed of the publishing stock and the Hague inventory through auctions (1659—1661) and focused primarily on printing rather than publishing. The quality of the presswork remained high during her tenure. Under her management (1662—1681), 775 university theses were printed. After her death in 1681, the business passed to her son Abraham II. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1912] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3781]
The Amsterdam House: Louis III and Daniel (1638—1680)
Louis III (1604—1670), grandson of the founder (son of Justus of Utrecht), established the Amsterdam branch. He had studied in Leyden, living with his uncle Matthias, and had prepared himself through extensive travels across Europe. At age 33, seeing no prospect of an independent role in the Leyden business and unwilling to compete with it, he chose Amsterdam as his field of activity. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1939] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3711]
He opened a bookshop in 1638 and added a printing office in 1640. Louis III proved to be a publisher of bold independent judgment. He cultivated relations with Hugo Grotius in Paris, published all the works of René Descartes from 1642 onward (despite fierce opposition from Dutch Calvinist theologians who made it taboo even to mention Descartes’s name in Leyden), and issued the writings of the French Jansenists. He attracted scholars whom the contentious Daniel Heinsius had alienated from the Leyden firm. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#2019] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3716]
Between 1640 and 1645, the Amsterdam press issued 219 publications. The partnership with Daniel (from May 1, 1655) brought together the two ablest members of the family. During their nine years of collaboration, they produced about 150 works, including the magnificent Corpus Juris (1663, folio) and begun work on the great French Bible of Desmarets. Louis retired in 1664, leaving the business to Daniel, and died in 1670 from complications of a broken leg. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1939] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3720]
Their printer’s mark was Minerva with the aegis, an olive branch, and an owl, with the motto Ne extra oleas (Not beyond the olive trees), a reference to the ancient Greek custom of marking the finish line of a race with olive trees — meaning “keep within proper bounds; do not overshoot the mark.” The signboard of the Amsterdam premises, on the Water quay, was “In the Elm Tree.” ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3724]
Daniel Elzevir’s Later Years
After Louis’s retirement, Daniel ably managed the Amsterdam house alone through difficult times. The war with England (1665—1667) severely disrupted trade. Daniel engaged Jakob Zetter for the bookselling department and, in 1669, brought in Heinrich Wetstein (1649—?), who later became a noted Dutch typographer. Wetstein transformed the bookshop from a purely publishing and commission operation into a full retail and second-hand stock. In 1674, Daniel issued a comprehensive catalogue of over 20,000 works. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#2023] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3741]
The war with France (1672—1678) and the invasion of Holland brought almost all business to a halt. Daniel used the enforced idleness to prepare the great classified catalogue. Despite the difficult times, he published over 90 new works between 1675 and 1680. His correspondents included Nicholas Thoynard, who proposed an early form of stereotype printing to him in 1680 (Daniel dismissed it as “absolutely impossible”). ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#2023]
Daniel died on October 13, 1680, of a recurrent fever. John Locke wrote, “The death of Elzevir is a public misfortune.” With Daniel’s death, the history of the House of Elzevir as a major force in European publishing came to a close. The estate, after liquidation, realised about a quarter of a million marks in modern value. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#2027] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3749]
The End of the Leyden House (1681—1712)
Abraham II (1653—1712), son of John and Eva van Alphen, inherited the Leyden printing office in 1681. He had studied at Leyden, earned a doctorate (1679), and became a city magistrate (schepen) in 1695. Under his mismanagement, the press deteriorated completely. Complaints from faculty about the quality of thesis printing multiplied. His output was largely limited to university theses (1,899 between 1681 and 1712). Upon his death on July 30, 1712, the entire business was sold for less than 2,000 guilders — a fraction of its former value. The plant and material were auctioned in 1713 for the benefit of creditors and Abraham’s daughter. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1912] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3783]
The Leyden printing office had served the university for ninety-one years (1621—1712). The Elzevir type foundry eventually passed through Joseph Athias, Johann Roman, and Ploos van Amstel before being acquired by the Enschedé family of Haarlem, who preserved the matrices in their celebrated type specimen. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3762]
Foreign Connections and Unauthorised Publications
A distinctive feature of the Elzevir organisation was its extensive network of foreign agencies, initiated by the first Louis and maintained by two subsequent generations. The firm maintained depots in Frankfort (from 1595), Paris (from 1602), Copenhagen (a branch house established in 1632), and agencies in Italy and England. They were the primary suppliers of foreign literature to Germany for decades. In Copenhagen, a separate catalogue was printed in 1642. Daniel Elzevir visited Sweden in 1650 and received a flattering proposal from Queen Christina to establish a printing concern in Stockholm, which he declined. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1947] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md#3668]
With England, the Elzevirs had important relations both as booksellers and as printers of English authors who sought the superior quality of Elzevir typography, which could not then be equalled in England. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1945]
The Elzevirs were also known for issuing unauthorised editions (what would now be called pirated editions) under fictitious imprints. For sensitive political or religious works, they used bogus place names: Lugduni (Lyons) instead of Lugduni Batavorum (Leyden), and names such as Jouxte, Jean Sambix, and Nic Schouten (Cologne). Among the anonymously circulated works were Saumaise’s Defensio Regia, Milton’s Defensio Populi Anglicani, and Selden’s Mare Clausum. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1963]
Scholarly and Cultural Impact
The Elzevir publishing programme was distinguished by the range and quality of its authors. The Leyden house published the works of Scaliger, Grotius, Heinsius, Salmasius, and Galileo. The Amsterdam house published Descartes (the first complete edition of his works in 1643), Velthuysen, Vossius, Balzac, Corneille, and Moliere. Their editions of the Latin classics — Virgil, Horace, Cicero, Pliny, Caesar, Terence, Ovid, Livy, Sallust, and others in the compact duodecimo format — became the standard texts for scholars and students across Europe and remained benchmarks of typographical excellence for centuries. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1965]
The Elzevir achievement was to democratise access to classical and contemporary literature through a combination of editorial care, typographic artistry, and commercial shrewdness. As Balzac wrote to the firm in 1651: “For some architects reputation has come through the construction of pyramids and colossi, while others have gained no less fame through the art put into rings and seals… The excellence of work depends not upon its extent but upon its appropriateness and perfection.” ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md#1975]
Chronology

c. 1540 — Louis Elzevir born in Louvain
1580 — Louis flees to Leyden as a Protestant refugee
1592 — First work published under Louis’s imprint (Eutropius)
1595 — First appearance at Frankfort Fair; adoption of the eagle device
1602 — First documented Paris sojourn
1617 — Death of Louis Elzevir; Matthias and Bonaventure take over
1620 — Isaac Elzevir appointed Printer to Leyden University
1625 — Bonaventure and Abraham acquire Isaac’s press; begin the “Republiques” series
1629 — Initiation of the Latin classics duodecimo series (Horace, Ovid)
1632 — Copenhagen branch established
1638 — Louis III opens bookshop in Amsterdam
1640 — Louis III adds printing office in Amsterdam
1652 — Deaths of Bonaventure and Abraham
1655 — Daniel joins Louis III in Amsterdam
1661 — Death of John Elzevir in Leyden
1662—1681 — Eva van Alphen manages Leyden press
1670 — Death of Louis III
1680 — Death of Daniel Elzevir; Amsterdam house closes
1681—1712 — Abraham II manages declining Leyden press
1712 — Death of Abraham II; sale of the press
1713 — Auction of the Elzevir plant and material

entities/erasmus.title: Erasmus of Rotterdam
entities/erasmus.content:
Overview
Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam (1467 — July 1536) was a Dutch humanist scholar, theologian, and the most commercially successful author of the early sixteenth century. He was the first author after the invention of printing to secure large and continued returns from the sales of his writings. In popularity his books were excelled only by Luther’s, while the range of their distribution exceeded anything previously attained. His writings circulated in Latin among educated and ecclesiastical circles and in vernacular translations among all classes across Europe. He maintained close publishing relationships with Johann Froben of Basel, Aldus Manutius of Venice, and Jodocus Badius Ascensius of Paris. Although he refused to join the Protestant movement and held himself a dutiful son of the Catholic Church, his writings were a major factor in creating the conditions that made the Reformation possible. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Early Life and Education
Erasmus was born in Rotterdam in 1467, seventeen years after Gutenberg printed his first book. He was placed as a boy at the school run by the Brothers of Common Life in Deventer, a fraternity noted for its interest in the multiplication and circulation of literature. In 1485, at age eighteen, he took vows as a monk of the Order of St. Augustine (the same order to which Luther later belonged), vows from which he was released years afterward by Pope Leo X. In 1492, through the favour of the Bishop of Cambray, he was enabled to spend several years at the University of Paris, then still the leading university of Europe though somewhat degenerated. In 1506 he made his first visit to Italy and received the degree of Doctor of Divinity at Bologna. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Travels and Residences
First Visit to England (1498—1500): Erasmus spent nearly two years in England, chiefly at Oxford, where he formed lasting friendships with Thomas Linacre, William Grocyn, John Colet, and Sir Thomas More.
Venice with Aldus (1506—1509): After receiving his doctorate at Bologna, Erasmus took up residence in Venice in the house of the publisher Aldus Manutius, remaining there until 1509. During this period he published the enlarged edition of the Adagia through Aldus and drew extensively on Aldus’s library and scholarly associates, including Laskaris, Marcus Musurus, and Aleander.
Return to England (1509—1514): In late 1509 Erasmus was again in England, living with Sir Thomas More. It was at More’s house that he wrote The Praise of Folly.
First Sojourn in Basel (1514—1516): Erasmus made his first stay in Basel in 1514 and began his intimate association with Johann Froben. The reputation of Froben’s scholarly printing and the news that Froben was at work on an edition of St. Jerome drew Erasmus to Basel and away from England, where the press was still too far behind continental standards for the printing of important works.
Louvain (1517—1521): Erasmus took up residence at the University of Louvain and devoted much correspondence to the Lutheran controversies.
Basel with Froben (1521—1527): At the time of the Diet of Worms in 1521, Erasmus removed to Basel and took up residence with Froben, remaining with him until Froben’s death in 1527.
Freiburg (1529—1534): After the Reformation turmoil in Basel, Erasmus moved to Freiburg.
Return to Basel and Death (1534—1536): He returned to Basel in 1534 and died there in July 1536. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Erasmus at the Aldine Press
Erasmus’s stay in Venice from 1506 to 1509 was his most intense encounter with the printing world. He lived in the combined household-workshop of Aldus Manutius and Andrea Torresani in San Paternian, where some thirty people — workmen, servants, family, and up to eight or nine scholarly guests — lived and worked under one roof. The atmosphere was a fusion of sweatshop, boarding house, and research institute. Erasmus described himself sitting in one corner of the printing room writing the Adagia from memory, handing his text sheet by sheet to the compositors as it was written, too busy to scratch his ears. In another corner sat Aldus, quietly reading proofs, countering all pleas that they had been checked with the words “I’m studying.” Between them the types rattled in the compositors’ hands as ink was daubed over everything in reach, until far into the night, while Erasmus’s stomach — unused to this pressure of work on short commons — rumbled in protest. The household then dispersed according to social hierarchy: guests, family, and intellectuals upstairs to a Spartan meal and avid discussion; workmen to their separate dinner and the livelier pleasures of the city. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The press in 1508 operated four presses with fifteen or more workmen, sufficient to produce the flood of editions that made Aldus’s reputation. Erasmus’s insistence on speed and volume tested the limits of the household. He acidly remarked that becoming a baker’s apprentice was a great deal easier than living in the Torresani household. The remark reflects real tensions: the Aldine press was a business, not a scholarly retreat, and Erasmus’s stomach and patience both suffered under the regime. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Major Works
The Adagia
The Adagia was the first of Erasmus’s books to bring him fame. The first edition was printed in Paris in 1500, put together hurriedly according to Drummond, for the purpose of raising money via a publication that was “sure to sell.” Erasmus appears to have retained ownership of this Paris edition himself; in 1504 he wrote to Colet asking him to look into the matter of one hundred copies sent to London three years earlier for which he had received no returns.
When Erasmus took up residence with Aldus in Venice in 1507, he rewrote and greatly enlarged the book, changing its character entirely. The enlarged edition, published by Aldus in 1508, contained thirty-five hundred proverbs. Erasmus acknowledged his debt to Aldus’s suggestions and magnificent library, and to Aldus’s associates who placed valuable manuscripts at his disposal. Erasmus’s discussion of the proverb “Hasten slowly” (Festina lente) centred on a Roman coin showing a dolphin and anchor that Aldus had shown him — an image Aldus adopted as his printer’s mark. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The 1513 edition was reprinted by Froben from Aldus’s text in an edition rivalling Aldus’s in typographical beauty. The two publishers appear to have made a friendly arrangement to divide the market for Erasmus’s writings. In its final form the Adagia filled one of the eleven folio volumes of Erasmus’s collected works. Drummond described it as “a monument of vast learning … and a rich repository of anecdotes, quotations, and historical and biographical sketches.” ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Praise of Folly (Encomium Moriæ)
The Praise of Folly was written in 1509 while Erasmus was living in the household of Sir Thomas More. In the preface he mentions the plan took shape while he was riding across the Alps from Venice to London, noting the coincidence that “More” in Greek signified “fool.” In another letter he states the first suggestion came from More himself.
The first known edition was printed in Strasbourg in 1511 by a printer named Schurer. The Froben edition, printed in Basel in 1514, included a commentary by Gerard Listrius, a physician of Basel and a trusted friend of Erasmus. Later Froben editions contained the famous illustrations by Hans Holbein the Younger. Authorised editions were also published by Aldus in Venice and by Badius in Paris. Unauthorised editions appeared in Cologne, Lyons, Salamanca, and elsewhere. Translations appeared in many parts of Europe, most probably unauthorised. The book possibly secured a larger sale than any book except the Bible that had yet been printed. Kings, bishops, archbishops, and cardinals were delighted with it, and Leo X read it through from beginning to end. One result of its publication was the prohibition of Erasmus’s writings in the universities of Paris, Louvain, Oxford, and Cambridge, where ecclesiastical influence controlled. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Greek New Testament (1516)
Edited by Erasmus at the instance of Froben, the Greek New Testament was printed in Basel in 1516 and was the first time the complete Greek text had been put into type. Beatus Rhenanus wrote to Erasmus in April 1515: “Froben wants you to place in his hands your proposed edition of the New Testament, and promises that he will give for your work as much as anybody.” The work was based in part on the previous labours of Laurentius Valla, whose annotations Erasmus had earlier edited for Froben.
A second edition was required within three years, making a total printing of 3,300 folio copies up to 1519. In the second edition the text was largely altered and the volume was fortified with a papal brief, a copy of the Nicene Creed, and an engraving of the Trinity. The volume contained the first text approximating to correctness that Europe had yet known. It was utilised by Luther as the basis for his German version. Erasmus’s notes included a denial of the primacy of Peter in his commentary on Matthew 16:18, “Upon this rock will I build my church,” a comment made in a volume dedicated to the Pope. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Familiar Colloquies (1518)
Published by Froben in 1518, the Familiar Colloquies became, next to The Praise of Folly, the best known work of Erasmus. It is accepted by his biographers as expressing perhaps more directly than any other of his writings his personal opinions, prejudices, feelings, and preferences. The book was translated into nearly every European tongue. Authorised editions were many and profitable; unauthorised editions were still more numerous. One printer in Paris took advantage of a report that the University was about to condemn the work to print no fewer than 24,000 copies, from which the author derived no advantage. The work was finally condemned by the Sorbonne and later placed by the Inquisition in the first class of prohibited books. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The St. Jerome Edition
During his first year in Basel, Erasmus gave arduous labour to an edition of St. Jerome, the investment in which he shared with Froben. This was one of the major collaborative undertakings between author and publisher that cemented their relationship. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Publishing Relations
Aldus Manutius (Venice): Erasmus lived in Aldus’s combined household and workshop in Venice from 1506 to 1509. Aldus published the expanded 1508 edition of the Adagia with 3,500 proverbs. Erasmus drew heavily on Aldus’s library and scholarly circle. Aldus also published authorised editions of The Praise of Folly. The working conditions in the Aldine press were intense: Erasmus wrote the Adagia from memory, handing sheets directly to compositors while Aldus proofread beside him. The household of some thirty people included workmen, servants, family, and scholarly guests. Erasmus wrote in 1508 of Aldus: “If some deity friendly to literature will but favour the truly royal vows of Aldus, I can promise that within a few years the studious will possess, by his work alone, all the good authors there are in the four languages.” ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Johann Froben (Basel): Erasmus began his association with Froben in 1514 and remained with him, living in his house from 1521, until Froben’s death in 1527. Froben published the Greek New Testament (1516), the Familiar Colloquies (1518), the Froben edition of The Praise of Folly (1514, with later Holbein illustrations), the edition of St. Jerome, De Copia, the Institutio Principis Christiani (1516), the edition of Cyprian (1519), the Paraphrase of the New Testament (1524), and numerous other works including editions of Hilary, Irenaeus, Ambrose, Seneca, Augustine, Chrysostom, and Basil. Erasmus wrote after Froben’s death: “He was a true friend, so simple and sincere … To me his kindness was unbounded. What plots would he not lay, what occasions would he not seek, to force some present upon me!”
Jodocus Badius Ascensius (Paris): Badius published authorised editions of The Praise of Folly in Paris, alongside the Froben and Aldus editions.
After Froben’s death in 1527, Erasmus continued to work with the Froben press, successfully carried on by Jerome Froben, the eldest son of its founder. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Later Works
Erasmus’s later publications through Froben included: a treatise on the Confessional (1524); an exposition of the Lord’s Prayer; a treatise on Free Will (1524), defining his position against Luther; the Institution of Christian Matrimony (1526); the Christian Widow (1527); editions of Irenaeus (1526), Ambrose (1527, four volumes), Seneca (1529), Augustine (1529), Chrysostom (1530), Basil (1532); the Apopthegms of the Ancients (1531); and Ecclesiastes, a treatise on the preacher (1534), the last book he completed. His correspondence continued active until his death in July 1536. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Significance in Printing History
Erasmus is the most distinctive author for studying the publishing relations of the early sixteenth century. His commanding position as a scholar, his connections in both Protestant and Catholic circles, the unprecedented circulation of his writings, and his close association with Aldus, Froben, and Badius make his career of exceptional interest. He was the first author after Gutenberg to secure large and continued returns from the sales of his writings. Through the presses of Froben, Badius, and Aldus, his wit, learning, and intellectual force exerted a wider influence than was understood at the time and played a major part in the long contest against the rule of monkish superstition. His association with Froben also helped develop a spirit of independence on the part of the greatest author of the age, rescuing him from the demoralising influences of literary patronage. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]

entities/estienne-family.title: Estienne Family
entities/estienne-family.content:
Overview
The Estienne family (Latinised as Stephanus or Stephani) was the most distinguished dynasty of scholar-printers in sixteenth-century France and Geneva. Over three generations spanning more than a century and a half (c. 1502 – c. 1659), members of the family produced some of the most important scholarly editions of the Renaissance: the foundational Latin and Greek dictionaries of Europe, critical editions of the Bible that challenged the authority of the Sorbonne, and magnificent impressions of the Greek and Roman classics. Alongside the Aldine Press of Venice, the House of Estienne is the greatest name in sixteenth-century learned printing. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The family’s history was shaped by the University of Paris’s system of book trade regulation. The University claimed authority over all book production in Paris, exercised through four sworn booksellers (quatuor majores librarii) who governed the trade, set prices, and enforced an approval system for theological texts. This regulatory framework — designed to protect orthodoxy and established printers alike — became the battleground for the Estiennes’ most famous conflicts. ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Henri Estienne the Elder (d. 1520)
Henri Estienne (Henricus Stephanus the Elder) was the founder of the family printing business. His birth year is unknown. His name first appears as a printer in 1496, working in partnership with the German printer Wolfgang Hopyl. The first book bearing his sole imprint was an edition of Aristotle’s Ethics, Latinised by Aretinus, published in 1504 and considered the founding publication of the House. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Henri published roughly 130 editions, mostly in folio, almost exclusively in Latin and of a theological and philosophical character. Classical literature was still the domain of Italian printers. He associated with his press three learned doctors: Charles Boville, Jacques Lefevre d’Etaples, and Josse Clictou. Lefevre later became the instructor of Calvin and Farel and was targeted by the Sorbonne for his heretical opinions, escaping persecution only through the personal intervention of Francis I. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Henri was among the first Paris printers to assume personal responsibility for typographical accuracy, adding the names of his press correctors to title-pages and colophons as a guarantee of trustworthy work. He dismissed the celebrated scholar Beatus Rhenanus from the post of corrector for permitting errors to remain in a printed text. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Henri died in August or September 1520. He had three sons — Francois, Robert, and Charles — all of whom became printers or booksellers. His widow married Simon de Colines (Colinaeus) the following year, who took over the press and gave Robert his typographical education. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Robert Estienne (1503-1559)
Robert Estienne (Robertus Stephanus) was the most famous member of the family and is ranked among the great printer-publishers of the world. He was born in 1503 and trained under his step-father Simon de Colines. In 1524, at the age of twenty-one, he became proprietor of the family press. He married Perette (Petronilla), daughter of the publisher Jodocus Badius, a woman of such thorough classical education that she could read, write, and speak Latin fluently. In the Estienne household, Latin became the everyday language of conversation, spoken even by the servants and children. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Conflict with the Sorbonne
Robert’s first major undertaking was a revised Latin edition of the New Testament (1523), whose textual corrections immediately provoked the hostility of the Sorbonne. The divines objected to any critical analysis of the Vulgate and to the dissemination of Scripture in corrected editions. This conflict defined Robert’s entire career. Each new Bible edition brought him fresh denunciations tempered only by the personal protection of King Francis I. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Thesaurus Linguae Latinae (1531)
Robert’s greatest single work was the Thesaurus Linguae Latinae, published in 1531. Unable to find a scholar willing to undertake the enormous task, he compiled the dictionary himself over two years of day-and-night labour. It superseded all existing Latin dictionaries (including Aldus Manutius’s Cornucopia) and remained the standard authority for centuries. Revised editions appeared in 1536 and 1543. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Printer to the King
In 1539, King Francis I appointed Robert Imprimeur Royal for Hebrew and Latin, with an annual stipend. In 1540, following the death of Conrad Neobar, the distinction of Printer in Greek to the King was also conferred upon him. Robert produced the magnificent series of Greek ecclesiastical writers (Eusebius, Socrates, Theodoret, Sozomen, Evagrius) using the famous Greek types (Characteres Regii) designed by Claude Garamond from the calligraphy of Angelus Vergetius. These types, partly cut under the supervision of Robert’s fifteen-year-old son Henri, remain among the most beautiful Greek fonts ever created and were used into the nineteenth century. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Biblical Editions and Verse Division
Robert published numerous editions of the Bible in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. His Latin Bible of 1540 was the first to bear his title as Printer to the King. His 1551 Greek New Testament introduced the division of the biblical text into numbered verses (versiculi), a system that gained universal acceptance and is still in use today. According to tradition, Robert performed much of the work of subdividing chapters into verses while travelling on horseback between Paris and Lyons. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Flight to Geneva
The death of Francis I in 1547 removed Robert’s most powerful protector. His successor Henry II proved vacillating under pressure from the Sorbonne. After a series of escalating confrontations — including the compilation of 107 articles of heresy against his Bibles, and a formal prohibition of their sale — Robert fled Paris for Geneva in late 1551 or early 1552. There he joined the circle of Calvin and Beza, was granted citizenship, and continued his press. The divines of the Sorbonne reportedly burned him in effigy. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
In Geneva, Robert published Calvin’s definitive edition of the Institutes of the Christian Religion (1559) and a series of commentaries and theological works by the Reformers. One of his last and most significant publications was the final authorized edition of Calvin’s Institutio Christianae Religionis, the most important intellectual production of the Reformation. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Printer’s Mark and Legacy
Robert adopted as his printer’s mark an olive tree with broken branches, accompanied by an apostolic figure pointing to the fallen branches and the motto “Noli altum sapere, sed time” (“Be not high-minded, but fear,” from Romans 11:20). Thuanus praised Robert for excelling in judgment, technical skill, and typographic elegance even Aldus and Froben. Gesner called him “what the sun is among the stars” among printers and booksellers. Robert died in Geneva on September 7, 1559, aged 56. He printed over 600 works during his career. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Henri Estienne the Younger (1528-1598)
Henri Estienne (Henricus Stephanus the Younger), the second son of Robert, was the most finished scholar of the family. Born in 1528, he received a thorough humanist education, studying Greek under Petrus Danesius (tutor to the Dauphin) and mastering Latin in the family household where it was the daily language. He travelled extensively through Italy, England, and Flanders, collating manuscripts and learning Spanish, and was presented to King Edward VI of England. In Venice he became acquainted with the scholar Muretus; in Florence he impressed Petrus Victorius, one of the deepest Greek scholars in Italy, with a valuable codex of Anacreon. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Thesaurus Linguae Graecae (1572)
Henri’s crowning achievement was the Thesaurus Linguae Graecae, published in Geneva in 1572 in four folio volumes (with later supplementary volumes). The project had been conceived by his father Robert, who had collected preliminary material before his death, and Henri completed it — famously binding himself to produce a fixed quantity of copy each day for his compositors, often interrupted ten times an hour by business demands. The Thesaurus became the foundational lexicon of the Greek language and remained the standard for centuries. It impoverished its publisher: the monumental work brought Henri honour but serious financial loss. It was immediately plagiarized by Joannes Scapula, who produced a cheaper abridgement from Basel (1579) that Dr. Busby of Westminster School forbade his pupils to use on grounds of literary dishonesty. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Career and Publications
Henri began publishing in his own name in 1554 with an edition of Anacreon. For ten years (c. 1558-1568) he styled himself Fuggerorum Typographus, supported by a pension from the wealthy Augsburg patron Huldric Fugger. He divided his printing between Paris and Geneva, reserving the Geneva press for theologically sensitive works. His list of editions is enormous, including the works of Aeschylus, Aristotle, Xenophon, Diodorus Siculus, Herodotus, Plutarch in thirteen octavo volumes, Plato in a magnificent three-volume edition (1578) remarkable for its typographical accuracy, and many others. He also wrote extensively in his own name: the Apologia pro Herodoto (1566), a sharp attack on the Roman clergy that went through numerous editions; the Artis Typographicae Querimonia (a lament for the degraded state of printing); the Pseudo-Cicero Dialogus; and many volumes of poetry and commentary. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Henri received marks of favour from Henry III of France, who sent him to Switzerland to search for manuscripts. He was a regular attendee at the Frankfurt Book Fair. His last years were marked by financial difficulty. Henri Estienne died in March 1598 in a hospital in Lyons, aged nearly 70. His daughter Florence married the great scholar Isaac Casaubon, who had hoped to benefit from Henri’s manuscript collections but found his father-in-law jealously guarded his library. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Other Family Members
Francois Estienne (d. c. 1548)
Robert’s elder brother, a libraire jure of the University of Paris. His publications date from 1537 to 1547 and were mostly Latin classics. His device was a tripos standing on a closed book, with a vine shoot and the motto Plus olei quam vini (“More oil than wine”). He never came into open conflict with the Sorbonne. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Charles Estienne (c. 1504-1564)
The youngest brother of Robert, medically trained as a physician and naturalist, and a classical scholar of distinction. He produced works on dissection, horticulture (Praedium Rusticum), ornithology, ichthyology, and a Dictionarium Latino-Gallicum (1552) that was largely appropriated by later English lexicographers, including Cooper’s Thesaurus Linguae Romanae (1565). Forced against his will to take over the Paris printing business after Robert’s flight to Geneva, he operated only until 1561 but produced a series of fine editions. He died in prison in 1564, either for debts or for religious opinions. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Robert Estienne the Second (1530-1571)
The eldest son of Robert I, he remained in Paris as a Catholic, was appointed Typographus Regius in 1563, and rebuilt his father’s Paris establishment. His friends and clients included Joseph Scaliger, George Buchanan, and Sir Thomas Smith. He died in 1571; his widow married the printer Mamert Patisson. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Paul Estienne (16th-17th century)
Henri’s son, who carried on the press in Geneva. He lacked his father’s business energy. In 1619, the Greek matrices that Robert had brought from Paris were repurchased by the French government for 3,000 livres and returned to the Royal Printing House in Paris. Paul sold the Geneva business to the Chouet brothers in 1627. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Antoine and Henry Estienne (17th century)
The last generation of the House: Antoine, son of Paul, succeeded in 1620 and was appointed Imprimeur du Roi in 1623; his son Henry succeeded to the title in 1649 and continued printing until about 1659. Henry died childless, bringing the history of the House to an end after more than 150 years. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Printer’s Device
The Estienne printer’s mark was an olive tree, to which Henri Estienne the Younger added an apostolic figure pointing to the broken branches that had fallen from the tree. The motto was “Noli altum sapere, sed time” — from Romans 11:20, “Be not high-minded, but fear.” ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Key Achievements

Founded the Estienne printing dynasty in Paris, spanning three generations and over 150 years ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Thesaurus Linguae Latinae (1531) by Robert Estienne — foundational Latin dictionary for centuries ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Thesaurus Linguae Graecae (1572) by Henri Estienne the Younger — the foundational Greek lexicon ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Critical editions of the Bible in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew that provoked the Sorbonne’s censure ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Introduction of verse division in the New Testament (1551) ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Robert Estienne appointed Printer to the King for Hebrew, Latin, and Greek (1539-1540) ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Production of the royal Greek types (Characteres Regii) by Garamond, Vergetius, and the Estiennes ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Estiennes set standards of textual accuracy, typographical elegance, and scholarly integrity emulated across Europe ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
