entities/gerard-mercator.title: Gerard Mercator
entities/gerard-mercator.content:
Gerard Mercator
Gerard Mercator (1512–1594), born Gerard Kremer, was a Flemish cartographer, engraver, mathematician, and instrument-maker, best known for the Mercator projection (1569) — the map projection that allowed sailors to plot compass bearings as straight lines — and for coining the term “atlas” to describe a collection of maps. He is widely regarded as the greatest scientific cartographer of the sixteenth century. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Early Life and Education
Born 5 March 1512 in Rupelmonde, a few miles southwest of Antwerp, to Hubert and Emerentiana Kremer of Gangelt, a poor family. Hubert was a shoemaker. The family name Kremer (German for “shopkeeper”) was Latinised to Mercator (“merchant”). His uncle Gisbert, a priest in Rupelmonde, supported the children after Hubert’s death (1526/27) and Emerentiana’s death (1528). ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Mercator was educated at the Brethren of the Common Life school in ‘s-Hertogenbosch (from about age fifteen) and enrolled at the University of Louvain on 29 August 1530, at Castle College. He took his master’s degree in 1532. The Brethren’s emphasis on practical piety and learning shaped his intellectual temperament. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
At Louvain he studied under Gemma Frisius, the leading mathematical astronomer and instrument-maker of the Low Countries, whose lectures on astronomy, geography, and triangulation gave Mercator his technical foundation. He also studied engraving under Gaspar van der Heyden, acquiring the practical skills that let him engrave his own maps and globes — an unusual combination of theoretical and manual competence. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Early Career and Maps
Mercator’s first known maps were:

1537: Amplissima Terrae Sanctae descriptio — a map of the Holy Land, showing Palestine in detail.
1538: Orbis imago — a world map on a double cordiform (heart-shaped) projection. This map was the first to use the names “North America” and “South America,” anticipating widespread usage of the Amerigo Vespucci-derived nomenclature. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
ca. 1540: A map of Flanders, remarkable for its accuracy. It was based on triangulated surveys, using Gemma Frisius’s newly developed surveying technique — one of the earliest applications of triangulation to mapmaking. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]

In 1540 he also published Literarum latinarum…, the first manual of italic handwriting printed outside Italy, demonstrating his range as a scholar-craftsman. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Globes
Mercator constructed his first terrestrial globe in 1541 (twelve gores, approximately 420 mm diameter). It was innovative in several respects: it showed loxodromes (rhumb lines crossing meridians at constant angles), located the magnetic pole, and used a hollow wooden ball construction for durability. A celestial globe followed in 1551. These globes were commercially successful and established his reputation across Europe. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Religious Persecution and Move to Duisburg
In February 1544, Mercator was arrested on heresy charges (suspected of Lutheran sympathies, referred to in the documents as “lutherye”). He was imprisoned in the castle at Rupelmonde. Of the forty-two others accused with him, two were burned at the stake, one was beheaded, and a woman was buried alive. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
The University of Louvain argued for Mercator’s release, citing his scholarly value. He was freed after several months, but the experience left a deep mark. In March 1552 he moved to Duisburg in the Duchy of Cleves, a territory where he could practice his Reformed faith in relative safety. He became cosmographer to the Duke of Julich, Cleve, and Berg around 1564 and taught mathematics at the Duisburg gymnasium from 1559 to 1562. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Key Maps (1550s–1560s)

1554: Map of Europe on fifteen sheets — an enormously influential map that corrected many errors in earlier maps and became the standard for Europe for decades. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
1564: Map of the British Isles.
1569: Nova et aucta orbis terrae descriptio ad usum navigantium — the world map on the Mercator projection, his single greatest contribution to science. The projection preserved angles, allowing navigators to plot constant-compass-bearing (rhumb line) courses as straight lines. It remains the standard projection for nautical charts. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]

Chronologia and the Index of Prohibited Books
In 1569 Mercator published Chronologia, a chronological work that attempted to reconcile biblical and secular history. For mentioning Luther and Zwingli in its chronological scheme, it was placed on the Index of Prohibited Books — a rare distinction for a scientific work. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Ptolemy and the Atlas
In 1578 he published an edition of Ptolemy’s Geography with twenty-seven Ptolemaic maps, engraved to the highest standard. This was a scholarly work, reconstructing the ancient geography from Ptolemy’s coordinates, and it demonstrated Mercator’s deep humanist learning. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Between 1585 and 1595 he published his own atlas in three parts, the first work to use the term “atlas” for a systematic map collection. The name came from the legendary King Atlas of Mauretania, depicted in Mercator’s frontispiece as a philosopher-king and astronomer. The atlas contained 107 maps and was intended as a complete description of the known world. Mercator died before finishing it, and the final part was published posthumously in 1595 by his son Rumold. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Relationship with Ortelius
Mercator and Ortelius were close friends. They first met in 1554. Mercator allegedly held back his own atlas project so that Ortelius’s Theatrum (1570) could succeed commercially — an act of remarkable generosity. Ortelius included Mercator’s maps in the Theatrum and listed him prominently in the Catalogus auctorum. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Later Life and Death
Mercator suffered a stroke in May 1590 that left his left side paralysed and affected his speech. A cerebral haemorrhage in 1593 further weakened him. He died on 2 December 1594, “about mid-day, sitting in his chair before the hearth, as though dropping off to sleep.” ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Legacy
Mercator’s projection is his most enduring contribution — still in use on nautical charts, GPS displays, and web maps (in its Web Mercator variant). His atlas pioneered the modern concept of a systematic map collection. His globes, engravings, and scientific instruments represent the high-water mark of sixteenth-century practical mathematics. His move from the Catholic Spanish Netherlands to the Protestant Duchy of Cleves exemplifies the displacement of Northern European intellectual talent driven by religious persecution. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]

entities/giacomo-gastaldi.title: Giacomo Gastaldi
entities/giacomo-gastaldi.content:
Giacomo Gastaldi
Giacomo Gastaldi (c. 1500–1566), also known as Jacobus Gastaldus, was a Piedmontese cartographer active in Venice, called “cosmographer to the Republic of Venice.” He was the leading Italian cartographer of the mid-sixteenth century and the mapmaker whose work most influenced Abraham Ortelius and the first atlas. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Life and Career
Gastaldi was born in Villafranca Piemonte, in Piedmont, into a prominent local family. The exact date of his birth is unknown — it fell near the end of the fifteenth century or the first years of the sixteenth. He first appears in Venetian records in 1539. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
He was associated with Giovanni Battista Ramusio, secretary of the Venetian Senate and compiler of the great collection of travel narratives Navigationi et Viaggi (1550–1559). Ramusio inspired Gastaldi to devote himself to cartography. In 1546 Gastaldi was entrusted with the instruction of Ramusio’s son in cosmography. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
The Venetian Council of Ten referred to him as “Master Jacomo of Piedmont, our cosmographer” — a formal recognition of his role as the Republic’s official geographer. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Key Maps

1542 (published 1548): A map of Germany for a new edition of Ptolemy’s Geography — his first major cartographic work.
1544: Map of Spain, based on materials provided by the Spanish ambassador to Venice, Diego Hurtado de Mendoza. This was the first published map of the Iberian peninsula to incorporate modern survey data. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
1545: Map of Sicily.
1546: Universale — a world map that became widely influential through many editions, using a distinctive projection that became identified with Gastaldi. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
1559: Map of southeastern Europe.
1561: Large world map on an oval projection, printed on eight sheets with border decorations by Giulio Sanuto.
1561: Map of Asia in three parts.
1562: Large wall map of Africa. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]

Gastaldi’s maps were notable for their accuracy and for their incorporation of the latest geographical information from travellers and explorers. His Asia maps drew on Portuguese and Spanish sources, on reports from the Venetian embassy in Constantinople, and on the work of Arab geographers, especially Abulfeda (though Ortelius later criticised Gastaldi’s reliance on Abulfeda). ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Engineering Work
Alongside cartography, Gastaldi was an active public engineer in Venice, working on waterworks projects — the Brenta and Piave rivers, canals, and drainage schemes. Two proposals for his appointment as Engineer and Superintendant of Waterworks were voted down, requiring a two-thirds majority that was denied, according to Almagia, because he was not Venetian. His last known engineering map dates from 1565. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Technique and Innovation
Gastaldi worked primarily in copperplate engraving, which allowed the fine detail essential for maps. His maps were among the earliest cartographic works to consistently use copperplate rather than woodcut, following the precedent set by Sweynheym’s 1478 Rome Ptolemy. The shift from woodcut to copperplate for maps was a critical technical development: copper allowed finer lines, more detail in coastlines and mountains, and more readable lettering, though it required a separate intaglio press and could not be printed together with type. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Relationship with Ortelius
Ortelius’s 1564 world map was inspired by Gastaldi’s 1561 world map, and Ortelius used Gastaldi’s maps of Asia extensively in the Theatrum. Ortelius’s note to the reader in the Theatrum discusses Gastaldi’s Asia maps critically — noting Gastaldi’s reliance on Abulfeda — but the dependence of the Theatrum on Gastaldi’s work is clear. Many Gastaldi maps served as direct sources for Ortelius’s atlas. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Death
Gastaldi died on 19 October 1566, survived by his wife Anzola and daughter Isabetta (from an earlier marriage to Ieronima). Maps continued to appear under his name posthumously, indicating the commercial value of his cartographic brand. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Legacy
Gastaldi is a crucial figure in the chain connecting Ptolemaic cartography to the modern atlas. His maps, disseminated through Venetian publishing networks and as sources for Ortelius, established the cartographic foundations on which the Theatrum was built. His work as cosmographer to Venice — the most important centre of printing in sixteenth-century Italy — made him the most influential Italian cartographer of his generation. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]

entities/giunti-family.title: Giunti Family
entities/giunti-family.content:
Overview
The Giunti family (Latinised as Junta) was the most commercially successful dynasty of printer-publishers in Renaissance Italy, with operations spanning Florence, Venice, and later Lyon. Unlike the scholarly Aldus Manutius or the industrial-scale Koberger, the Giunti operated primarily as publishing financiers — professional underwriters who supplied capital, managed risk, and distributed books, while contracting the actual printing to other workshops. Their business model was the first pure publishing enterprise in the modern sense. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Family Origins
The Giunti family began in the manuscript trade in Florence. Niccolo di Giunta was active as a manuscript dealer towards the end of the fifteenth century, at a time when the manuscript trade was already beginning to decline under the pressure of printing. He is recorded as the founder of the Giunta (or Junta) family, which later took a significant role in printing and publishing across Italy. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Fillippo Giunta, active in Florence, called himself librarius et cartolajus — a bookseller and paper-maker/dealer. The combination was typical of early Italian publishers, many of whom began in the paper trade. Fillippo may have united a paper factory with his printing business, a vertical integration strategy that gave him cost advantages in the Florentine market. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Lucantonio Giunti: The Financier-Publisher
The most important member of the family was Lucantonio Giunti (1457-1538), who established the Venetian branch of the family. Under his leadership, the Giunti became one of the largest and most durable publishing operations in Italy, outlasting Aldus Manutius and continuing into the second half of the sixteenth century. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Lucantonio’s distinctive role was as a financial underwriter rather than a hands-on printer. Lowry explicitly describes him and his associate Amadeo Scotto as “professional underwriters” who “formed contracts with several different printers in various cities.” They provided capital, took calculated risks on editions, and managed distribution, while leaving the actual presswork to technical specialists. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The 1507 Syndicate
The clearest evidence of this business model comes from a surviving five-year syndicate contract from 1507. The partners were:






























PartnerRoleShareLucantonio GiuntiFinancial backing only, no printing1/4Amadeo ScottoFinancial backing only, no printing1/4Zorzi Arrivabene + de Tortis brothersFour presses + paper supply1/4(a fourth partner to be found)?1/4
Giunti and Scotto “in this instance provided only financial backing and were not involved in the actual printing.” The printed sheets were stored in a collectively-rented warehouse to which each partner had a key. Any decision affecting prices or edition sizes required a majority vote. This structure — pure financiers sitting alongside printer-publishers — marks the emergence of the modern publishing model. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Financial Growth
Lucantonio Giunti applied this capital efficiently. Lowry notes that between 1491 and 1499 Giunti “more than doubled his company’s capital base,” and “had almost doubled it again by 1511.” This 4x growth in twenty years demonstrates the profitability of the publisher-financier model compared to the precarious economics of the craftsman-printer. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Business Specialisation
The Giunti specialised in commercially reliable genres rather than speculative scholarly editions:

Liturgical books — missals, breviaries, and service books for the Church, which had guaranteed institutional demand
Legal texts — canon and civil law editions for the university and professional market
Vernacular literature — Italian-language works for the growing lay reading public
Classical texts — but in standard, affordable formats, not the premium scholarly editions Aldus produced

This commercial pragmatism contrasted sharply with Aldus’s scholarly idealism. Where Aldus died poor reinvesting everything into Greek type, the Giunti built a self-sustaining enterprise that grew its capital base across decades. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
The Venetian-Florentine Network
The Giunti operated as a family network across two cities. The Florentine branch (under Fillippo and later family members) handled distribution in Tuscany and maintained the paper-making connections. The Venetian branch (under Lucantonio) managed the larger-scale publishing operation, taking advantage of Venice’s superior paper supply, commercial networks, and access to international markets through the Adriatic. Lorck notes that the Giunti in Venice were one of the two dominant forces in Venetian printing alongside the Aldine Press. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Significance
The Giunti represent a crucial step in the evolution of publishing as a business. In the earliest phase (Koberger), the printer and publisher were the same person. The Giunti model — a pure publisher who financed editions without operating a press — separated the roles and created the template for the modern publishing industry. Lucantonio Giunti was the first major European publisher to treat book production as an investment portfolio rather than a craft. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]

entities/jodocus-badius-ascensius.title: Jodocus Badius Ascensius
entities/jodocus-badius-ascensius.content:
Overview
Jodocus Badius Ascensius (1462 — 1535), also known simply as Jodocus Badius or Ascensius, was a Flemish scholar-printer who established the most important learned press in Paris during the first third of the sixteenth century. Born in Ghent, Flanders, and educated at the University of Louvain with further studies in Italy, he settled in Paris and founded his printing house around 1498. Over the course of approximately twenty-five years, his press produced nearly four hundred separate works, almost all in folio or quarto format. Badius was a libraire jure (sworn bookseller) of the University of Paris, a scholar-publisher of the highest standing, and the first printer in Paris to use Greek characters in a printed text (1505). ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Early Life and Education
Badius was born in 1462 in Ghent, then part of the County of Flanders in the Burgundian Netherlands. He received a thorough humanist education at the University of Louvain and subsequently travelled to Italy to continue his studies, where he absorbed the classical scholarship then flourishing in the Italian academies. The epithet “Ascensius” derives from his birthplace — according to Lorck, he was named after the town of Asch near Brussels. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Move to Paris and Entry into Printing
Badius first came to prominence not as a printer but as a teacher, giving lectures on the Latin poets, first in Paris and later in Lyons. It was in Lyons that he first became directly involved in the book trade, having been engaged by the printer Johann Trechsel as a corrector of the press. He married Trechsel’s daughter, cementing his connection to the printing profession. After Trechsel’s death, Badius moved to Paris and established his own press around 1498. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Paris Press
Badius’s press quickly became the leading publisher of classical and humanist texts in Paris. According to the bibliographer Panzer, his output reached nearly four hundred separate editions over a twenty-five-year career, nearly all in the large folio and quarto formats suited to scholarly readers. He was a libraire jure of the University of Paris, a formal recognition of his standing in the academic book trade. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Paris Book Trade Context
The title of libraire jure was not merely honorary. The University of Paris exercised absolute authority over the book trade from the 13th century onward — confirmed by Charles VI in 1411, who declared that “it belongs and appertains to our said Daughter [the University], and to none other, to establish and institute all the booksellers.” From among the sworn booksellers, four were annually elected as the quatuor majores librarii or Grands Jurez, who governed the entire trade, set prices (the taxe), examined new shipments, and enforced the approval system for theological works. Badius, as a libraire jure, was both a beneficiary of this system — it protected established printers from unlicensed competition — and subject to its oversight, particularly where theological texts were concerned. ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Greek Type in Paris
Badius holds the distinction of being the first Paris printer to include Greek characters in a printed book. In 1505, he issued the Annotationes in Novum Testamentum of Lorenzo Valla, which necessarily included several passages of Greek. The Greek type used in this edition was designed by a certain Hermonymus, a Lacedaemonian then sojourning in Paris. In 1519, Badius also printed the Institutiones Imperiales, which included a few Greek passages. This was two years before the establishment of Giles Gourmont’s dedicated Greek press in 1507, giving Badius priority in the introduction of Greek typography to Paris. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Key Publications
Badius’s list reflects his close connections with the leading humanist scholars of his age:

Erasmus: He published editions of Erasmus’s Adagia and The Praise of Folly (Moriae Encomium), with Erasmus himself attesting to the thoroughness of Badius’s scholarship. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Budaeus (Guillaume Budé): Badius published the works of Budaeus, the greatest French humanist of the generation and a scholar comparable to Erasmus. This included Budaeus’s great Commentary on the Greek Language. The friendship and scholarship of Budaeus were of marked service to Badius throughout his career. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Ship of Fools: Badius published the first Paris edition of Sebastian Brandt’s Navis Stultifera (the “Ship of Fools”) and also printed a French translation, La Nef des Folz du Monde (the second French version), which he himself edited and to which he added his own variations. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Philobiblon: He produced an edition of Richard de Bury’s Philobiblon, the celebrated medieval treatise on the love of books. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Complete Works: His press issued the Opera Omnia of Politian and of Lorenzo Valla, among other substantial scholarly editions. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Censorial Works: As evidence of his accepted orthodoxy, Badius was employed by the University to publish certain censorial works against Martin Luther, including treatises on Luther’s doctrine (1521) and on “certain contentions of Dr. Luther” (1523). ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]

Printer’s Mark and Motto
Badius’s printer’s mark was a representation of a printing press of the time, one of the earliest pictorial depictions of a printing press used as a publisher’s device. Beneath it he occasionally used the motto:

Aere meret Badius laudem auctorum arte legentum.

According to Greswell’s interpretation, this is to be understood as meaning that Badius by his liberality elicits the praise of authors, and by his typographic skill and accuracy that of readers. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Scholarship and Character
Badius was unusual among early Parisian printers in uniting scholarly erudition with typographic skill. He was not merely a publisher but an editor and commentator: he provided many of his classical editions with his own annotations. Lorck describes his books as distinguished by beauty and correctness (Schonheit und Korrektheit), and notes that he was simultaneously a bookseller, printer, type cutter, and type founder — a complete master of every branch of the book trade. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Family and Succession
Badius’s three daughters married three of the most famous typographers of the sixteenth century:

Michael Vascosanus (Vascosan): Married one of Badius’s daughters and continued the business after Badius’s death, producing 297 works and eventually becoming Royal Printer in 1566. Vascosan’s books were noted for the beauty of their printing and paper, most printed in Roman type. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
John Roigny: Another son-in-law who became a notable Parisian printer. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Robert Estienne (Robertus Stephanus): Married Badius’s daughter Perette, who was herself a learned woman fluent in Latin. Robert Estienne became the greatest of the Estienne dynasty and one of the most important printer-publishers in European history. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]

Badius’s son, Conrad Badius, was also a learned scholar and printer. Persecuted as a Calvinist, he fled to Geneva in 1549, where he continued both his literary and typographical work. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Death and Legacy
Jodocus Badius Ascensius died in 1535. His press, carried on by Vascosanus and linked by marriage to the Estienne dynasty, left an enduring mark on French humanist printing. He was the leading figure in Parisian scholarly publishing in the generation before Robert Estienne came to prominence, and his press set the standard for classical text production in France. His introduction of Greek type to Parisian printing in 1505 was a milestone in the spread of humanist learning north of the Alps, and his editions of Erasmus, Budaeus, and the Latin classics made him the indispensable publisher of the early French Renaissance. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Key Achievements

First Paris printer to use Greek characters in a printed book (1505) ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Produced nearly 400 separate works over twenty-five years, mostly in folio and quarto ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Published Erasmus’s Adagia and The Praise of Folly ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Published the works of Guillaume Budaeus, the pre-eminent French humanist ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Published the first Paris edition of Sebastian Brandt’s Ship of Fools ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Libraine jure of the University of Paris ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
His printer’s mark depicted an actual printing press with a humanist motto ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
His three daughters married Vascosanus, Roigny, and Robert Estienne, linking the great printing dynasties of Paris ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
His son Conrad Badius continued the family tradition in Geneva ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]

entities/johann-froben.title: Johann Froben
entities/johann-froben.content:
Overview
Johann Froben (c. 1460 — October 1527) was a Basel printer, publisher, and scholar who ranks among the most enlightened and enterprising publishers of the sixteenth century. His press was celebrated for exceptional typographic quality — clear Roman typefaces, meticulous proofreading, and clean presswork — and for its close partnership with the great humanist scholar Erasmus of Rotterdam, who lived in Froben’s household for many years. Erasmus called Froben “the Aldus of Germany,” and his press was widely regarded as the northern equivalent of Aldus Manutius’s Aldine Press in Venice. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Early Life and Training
Froben was born in 1460 in Hammelburg, a village in Franconia (present-day Bavaria). He studied at the University of Basel, which had been founded the year before his birth in 1459, and achieved distinction as a scholar in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. He was trained as a type-setter and press-corrector by the renowned printer Johann Amerbach, one of the leading scholarly printers of the period. Thus equipped, he secured citizenship in Basel in 1490 and began business in his own name as a master printer and publisher in 1491. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Press in Basel
Froben’s first publication was a Latin Bible in the convenient octavo format — the earlier printed Bibles had all been issued in expensive folios, and this smaller, more affordable edition won immediate popularity. His undertakings were restricted to books in Latin and Greek aimed at scholars. He left the task of printing vernacular works for the common reader to later publishers, believing that the educational influence of the Reformation was needed before a genuine popular demand for reading matter would emerge. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
In 1500, at age forty, Froben married Gertrude, the daughter of the prosperous bookseller Wolfgang Lachner. Lachner supplied capital for the expansion of the printing office, which by 1504 had seven presses in operation. Over the thirty-six years of his business career, Froben printed no fewer than 257 separate works, many of them of considerable scope and importance. His more important publications included the complete works of Saint Jerome (1516, in nine folio volumes), Saint Augustine (completed posthumously in 1529, ten folio volumes), and the first printed edition of the Greek New Testament (1516), edited by Erasmus and later used by Martin Luther for his German translation. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Relationship with Erasmus
The defining relationship of Froben’s career was with Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam. Erasmus was the only contemporary author whose books Froben systematically undertook, and the partnership proved immensely profitable for both. Erasmus’s Encomium Moriæ (The Praise of Folly), first printed by Froben in 1515, sold 1,800 copies in its first six months and went through twenty-seven editions during the author’s lifetime, establishing Erasmus as the first European author to earn a significant income from his pen. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Erasmus lived in Froben’s house in Basel from 1521 until Froben’s death in 1527. Froben paid Erasmus two hundred guldens per year for his services as editor and reviser, and the scholar also received returns from the sale of his own works. The circle of intimates gathered around the two men during this period included the brothers Amerbach, Beatus Rhenanus, Henricus Glareanus, Johannes Oecolampadius, and other leading humanists. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Erasmus-Aldus-Froben Triangle
Erasmus’s publishing career connected the two greatest scholarly presses of the age. He worked first with Aldus Manutius in Venice (1506-1509), where he produced the expanded Adagia under the intense conditions of the Aldine household. When Erasmus moved north and began working with Froben in 1514, the relationship between the two publishers became a competitive and sometimes delicate triangle. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The two presses divided the market for Erasmus’s works: Aldus continued to produce authorised editions for the Italian and Mediterranean market, while Froben handled northern Europe. Erasmus appears to have encouraged this arrangement, maintaining good relations with both houses. The competition was not entirely amicable: Aldus’s heirs were reportedly unhappy when Froben reprinted the Adagia in 1513, and Erasmus had to mediate. But the arrangement benefited all parties — Erasmus secured maximum exposure and revenue, while both presses benefited from association with the most famous living author. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Lowry notes that the relationship between Aldus and Froben was shaped by the very different business environments of Venice and Basel. Aldus operated in a fiercely competitive capital-intensive market where speed was essential and pirates were always at the gates. Froben, with less immediate competition and a lower cost base, could afford the slower, more meticulous approach that produced the landmark nine-volume Jerome and the Augustine edition. The difference mirrored the broader contrast between Italian commercial printing and northern European humanist publishing. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
After Froben’s death, Erasmus wrote of him: “We have lost Froben, that most exceptional man. His life was devoted to earnest and conscientious labours and he died at his work… For the past eight years I have been his house guest and have had with him the most cordial friendship. A truer friend than Froben, I could not wish from the Gods.” ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Major Publications
Froben’s press produced some of the most important scholarly works of the early sixteenth century. Among them:

The Greek New Testament (1516) — The first printed edition of the Greek New Testament, edited by Erasmus. A second edition followed within three years, totalling 3,300 folio copies by 1519. The text served as the basis for Luther’s German translation and was a landmark both in biblical scholarship and in the Reformation. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Works of Saint Jerome (1516) — Nine folio volumes, a monumental undertaking that brought great prestige to the Basel publisher. A papal privilege was secured for five years through Erasmus’s influence. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Thomas More’s Utopia (1518) — Froben published the second edition (the first Basel edition) of More’s celebrated work. This edition was the occasion for Hans Holbein the Younger’s introduction to Erasmus and, subsequently, to More himself. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Works of Saint Augustine (1529) — Ten folio volumes, completed after Froben’s death by his son Hieronymus Froben with the cooperation of Erasmus and Beatus Rhenanus. Froben himself had been working on this edition in his final hours. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Erasmus’s Colloquia (1518) — The Familiar Colloquies, one of Erasmus’s most popular works, sold some 24,000 copies through authorised editions in ten years, with many more unauthorised editions. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
First Latin editions of the Greek Fathers — Including Cyprian (1519), Hilary (1523), Irenaeus (1526), and others, often prepared by Erasmus with enormous effort from corrupt manuscripts. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]

Typography and Book Design
Froben’s types, particularly the Froben Roman, were influenced by Venetian models — especially the work of Aldus Manutius and Nicolas Jenson. His Roman typefaces were clear, well-proportioned, and notably more readable than many of the gothic types then in use in German-speaking lands. He was one of the first northern printers to adopt the Aldine octavo format for scholarly works, making books more portable and affordable. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Froben’s title-page borders and decorative initials were designed by none other than Hans Holbein the Younger, whom Froben brought to Basel around 1517. Holbein produced over 300 woodcut drawings for Froben, including title-page borders, ornamental alphabets, and the printer’s own device. This collaboration between printer and artist set new standards for book design in northern Europe and contributed significantly to the development of early typefaces and book illustration. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Froben’s printer’s mark — a caduceus-like staff entwined by two serpents, with a dove perched on top — was famously interpreted by Erasmus as combining the wisdom of the serpent with the innocence of the dove. The device reflected Froben’s ideal of the scholarly publisher: learned, shrewd, and principled. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Scholarly Network and Business Methods
Froben gathered around him a remarkable circle of learned associates who served as editors, revisers, and press-correctors. The most important was Beatus Rhenanus, who acted as literary counsellor and to whose suggestions many of Froben’s scholarly undertakings were due. Others included Johannes Oecolampadius, Sigismund Gelenius, Wolfgang Musculus, and the Amerbach family. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Froben frequently collaborated with other publishers to share the financial risk of major projects. His principal associates included Johann Amerbach and Johann Petri of Basel, and Franz Birckmann of Cologne. Erasmus, writing in 1523, described three methods Froben used for bringing a book into print: Froben bearing the entire risk; publication on commission for an interested patron; and temporary partnerships of two or more firms. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Religious Position
Although Froben remained within the Catholic Church, his press occupied a complex position during the Reformation. His publications of the Scriptures, the Church Fathers, and Erasmus’s writings contributed materially to the intellectual conditions that made the Reformation possible. He printed one collection of Luther’s writings in 1518, which sold widely in France, Spain, Italy, Brabant, and England, but after 1520 he printed no further works for Luther, probably influenced by Erasmus’s counsel and his own relations with Pope Leo X. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Froben believed the Church was to be reformed not by being broken into fragments but by being brought back to the teachings of its founders and the Fathers. His editions of Jerome, Augustine, and other Fathers, together with his publications of Erasmus, represented his personal contribution to the great controversies of the age. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Business Realities and Financial Constraints
Despite his reputation as one of the greatest scholarly publishers of the age, Froben did not grow wealthy from his press. Lorck records that “Trotz aller Thätigkeit erwarb Froben kein Vermögen” (despite all his industry, Froben acquired no fortune), attributing this to “eine nicht gut geregelte Wirtschaft” (poorly managed household economy) and the enormous sums he spent on careful proofreading. His correctors — whom he called “Kastigatoren” — included Erasmus himself, his father-in-law Wolfgang Lachner, Marc Heiland, Wolfgang Musculus, and Johannes Oecolampadius. Such an editorial staff was expensive, but Froben considered textual accuracy the hallmark of his press. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Luther Challenge
Froben faced a peculiar commercial problem during the Reformation. His colleague Adam Petri became the Luther pirate of Basel: Petri’s reprints of Luther’s works followed the originals “blitzschnell” (lightning-fast) — Luther’s New Testament appeared in September 1522, and Petri’s reprint was out by December. Petri made far better business than Froben because Froben, remaining loyal to the Catholic Church, printed no Lutheran works after 1518. This was a deliberate choice: Froben believed the Church was to be reformed by returning to the Fathers, not by schism. But it cost him the most lucrative market of the age. Meanwhile, Erasmus noted with frustration that Luther’s writings “crowded out” everything else, including Froben’s scholarly editions. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Death and Succession
Johann Froben died in October 1527, collapsing after a fall from a ladder while at work. His death was a severe blow to Erasmus, who wrote: “I cannot endure the loss of Froben.” Erasmus ensured that Froben’s unfinished projects were completed for the benefit of his children: the landmark edition of Saint Augustine (ten folio volumes, 1529) was pushed through by Erasmus with the cooperation of Beatus Rhenanus. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The business was continued by Froben’s eldest son, Hieronymus Froben (1501-1563), who maintained the relationship with Erasmus. Erasmus continued to live in the Froben family house “Zur Luft” (At the Air) in Basel, where he died in 1536. Hieronymus printed in partnership with his brother-in-law Nikolaus Episcopius the Elder (Bischoff) and later with his own sons Ambrosius and Aurelius Froben. Together they produced a series of important scholarly works, maintaining the press’s reputation for typographic quality and textual accuracy into the later sixteenth century. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Legacy
Froben’s influence on the book trade was profound. Erasmus ranked him with Aldus Manutius, declaring that “the world has never seen a publisher who has striven so earnestly and so unselfishly in the cause of scholarship.” He set new standards of textual accuracy, typographic elegance, and scholarly integrity that influenced printers and publishers across Europe. His press was a key conduit through which Italian Renaissance book design — the Aldine octavo, Roman type, and humanist publishing — reached northern Europe and contributed to the spread of printing throughout the continent. Froben’s partnership with Erasmus established a model of author-publisher relations that was centuries ahead of its time. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Key Achievements

Founded one of the most important scholarly presses in northern Europe (Basel, 1491)
First printed edition of the Greek New Testament, edited by Erasmus (1516)
Published the complete works of Saint Jerome in nine folio volumes (1516)
Published Thomas More’s Utopia (1518)
Published Erasmus’s Praise of Folly, Colloquies, and numerous other works
Commissioned Hans Holbein the Younger for title-page borders, initials, and illustrations
Introduced the Aldine octavo format and clear Roman typefaces to northern Europe
Established the printer’s mark of the caduceus and dove, one of the most recognisable of the period
Created the model of the scholar-publisher, combining humanist learning with commercial enterprise

entities/johann-gutenberg.title: Johann Gutenberg
entities/johann-gutenberg.content:
Overview
Johann Gutenberg (c. 1397/1400 — February 3, 1468) was a German goldsmith, inventor, and printer who introduced mechanical movable-type printing to Europe. His invention of the printing press with an adjustable type-mould, oil-based ink, and the hand-held press transformed the production of books and laid the foundation for the modern knowledge economy. The Gutenberg Revolution is ranked alongside the invention of writing and the alphabet as one of the great turning points in human communication. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Gutenberg himself was a paradoxical figure: a conservative Catholic whose invention shattered Christendom, a businessman who died in debt, a genius who never put his name on any of his books. Yet contemporaries and near-contemporaries recognized his achievement. Ulrich Zell of Cologne recorded that “the art of printing was first invented in Mainz, by Johann Gutenberg.” Ivo Wittig erected a stone in 1507 that names Gutenberg as the first to make printing letters in brass. The historian Johannes Trithemius, writing in the early sixteenth century on the authority of Peter Schoeffer, confirmed Gutenberg’s role as the inventor of printing. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Birth and Family
Gutenberg was born in Mainz, a free city on the Rhine, probably around 1397 or 1400. The exact date is unknown; the conventional year of 1400 was adopted in the 1890s by Mainz city fathers for the convenience of a quincentenary celebration in 1900; Lorck gives the year as 1397. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
His father was Friele Gensfleisch zur Laden, a patrician of comfortable means who inherited a position as “Companion of the Mint” and a right to trade in cloth passing along the Rhine. His mother was Else Wirich, who brought into the family a country estate at Eltville, ten kilometres downriver. The family was among the hundred or so patrician families (Geschlechter) of Mainz. The marriage was a love match beneath Friele’s station — Else’s family had declined in status — and their children lacked the full patrician inheritance that would have given Gutenberg easy access to the mint business. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The name “Gutenberg” derives from the family house, originally called the Judenberg (Jewish Hill). The house had been seized by the archbishop’s treasurers after the pogrom of 1282 and was later acquired by Gutenberg’s great-great-grandfather Frilo. The practice of using house names as family identifiers was common in medieval Germany, and it was only after the death of Friele Gensfleisch in 1419 that his heirs formally adopted “zum Gutenberg” as part of the family name. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Education and Early Life
Little is known of Gutenberg’s formal education. He was baptised, according to unsubstantiated tradition, in St Christopher’s church, which stood next to the family home. He would have attended one of Mainz’s church or municipal schools, learned Latin, and probably studied at the University of Erfurt (founded 1379), which was popular with students from Mainz. A certain “Johannes de Altavilla” (the Latin name for Eltville) was registered there in 1418 and graduated in 1420. If this was Gutenberg, he would have been exposed to the Hussite debates, the Great Schism, and the German intellectual ferment that followed the founding of several new universities. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Through his father’s position as Companion of the Mint, Gutenberg would have been familiar with the craft of coin-making: the engraving of steel punches, the striking of dies, and the casting of metal in moulds. This practical knowledge of punch-cutting and metalwork was the mechanical foundation for his later invention of typography. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Gutenberg’s youth was shaped by the civil strife in Mainz between the patrician nobility and the burgher guilds. In 1420, violent clashes led to the destruction of noble houses and the exile of many patrician families, including the Gensfleisch clan. Though the Elector Conrad III granted an amnesty in 1430 and specifically named Johan Gutenberg in the proclamation, he did not return to Mainz. Instead, he settled in Strasbourg, about sixty miles up the Rhine. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The Strasbourg Period (1434—1444)
The first clear evidence of Gutenberg’s residence in Strasbourg dates from 1434, when he caused the arrest of a clerk from Mainz who happened to be in the city, as leverage to recover money the magistrates owed him. In Strasbourg, he took up the trade of a lapidary (polisher of precious stones and mirrors), a craft that gave him practical experience with engraving, metalwork, and presses. He lived at the St Arbogast monastery outside the Weissturm gate. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
In 1436, Gutenberg was sued for breach of promise by Anna von Isernen Thur (Anne of the Iron Gate), a woman of noble family from Strasbourg. The suit appears to have been settled by marriage, and the tax-roll of Strasbourg for 1443 records payment by “Ennel Gutenbergen,” widely understood to be his wife. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The Aachen Pilgrim Mirror Scheme
Around 1435, Gutenberg conceived an ambitious commercial venture tied to the seven-yearly pilgrimage to Aachen, where the holy relics of Charlemagne were displayed to tens of thousands of pilgrims. Convex metal mirrors, it was believed, could capture the healing radiance of the relics. Pilgrims bought them in enormous numbers — 130,000 badges were sold at one later pilgrimage. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Gutenberg planned to mass-produce 32,000 such mirrors, selling at half a gulden each, for a projected return of 16,000 gulden on an expenditure of 600 gulden — a profit of 2,500 per cent. It was an industrial-scale undertaking requiring a tonne of lead and tin for the metal mirrors, and the technical work involved pressing, stamping, and metal forming. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
To finance this, Gutenberg took on partners. The enterprise represents his first effort at mass production and the earliest documented use of a press in his workshop — possibly the same screw press later adapted for printing. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The 1438 Partnership and the Dritzehn Lawsuit
In 1438, Gutenberg formalised his partnerships. Hans Riffe, mayor of Lichtenau, joined him for the mirror scheme, with profits divided 2:1 in Gutenberg’s favour. Andreas Dritzehn and Andreas Heilmann, both of the furriers’ guild, talked their way in. The final profit split was: Gutenberg 50%, Riffe 25%, Dritzehn 12.5%, Heilmann 12.5%. Each partner paid 80 gulden for instruction in the new arts. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
In the summer of 1438, the plague struck Aachen, and the 1439 pilgrimage was postponed by a year, destroying the mirror scheme’s revenue. Dritzehn and Heilmann discovered that Gutenberg “knew of another secret art” — almost certainly printing — and pressed to expand the partnership to cover this as well. A new five-year agreement was made, with a crucial clause: if any partner died, his heirs would receive only 100 gulden at the end of the term, but not the secret itself, and the surviving partners would retain all equipment. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Andrew Dritzehen fell ill at Christmas 1438 and died shortly after. Immediately, Andreas Heilmann sent the carpenter Saspach, who had built the press for the partnership, to dismantle it — “so that no one would know what the pieces meant.” Gutenberg likewise sent his servant Lorenz Beildick on the same errand. But by the time either arrived, the press had already been removed. The “tool of four pieces” lying in the press that Gutenberg urgently ordered to be separated was almost certainly the adjustable type-mould. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Claus and George Dritzehen, the dead man’s brothers, sued Gutenberg and the surviving partners in December 1439, demanding to be admitted to the partnership. The court depositions provide the earliest documentary evidence of Gutenberg’s printing work. The goldsmith Hans Dunne testified that Gutenberg had paid him about 100 guilders exclusively for “work connected with printing” — the word drucken appears in the original German record. Witnesses described mysterious “forms” that were melted, a press, and the “tool of four pieces” held together by two screws. The entire record repeatedly refers to “the thing” and “the nice things,” in terms that made clear this was no ordinary craft. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The judge ruled in Gutenberg’s favour, accepting his sworn statement and ordering payment of 15 guilders to the Dritzehen heirs (the 100 guilders stipulated, minus 85 guilders Dritzehen still owed). But the partners abandoned the enterprise, and Gutenberg was left financially exhausted. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Return to Mainz and the Hidden Years (1444—1448)
Gutenberg disappears from the Strasbourg records after Easter 1444. His departure was likely hastened by the approach of the Armagnac mercenaries, who threatened the city. He spent the next four years — the so-called “hidden years” — in almost complete documentary silence. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
He reappears in Mainz on October 6, 1448, borrowing 150 guilders from Rynhard Bromser and John Rodenstein, with his kinsman Arnold Gelthus standing surety at 5% interest. His uncle, Henne Gensfleisch the elder, leased a house called the Hof zum Jungen and took Gutenberg in. Here he set up a printing office. The very fact that he could raise a loan of this size — equivalent to several years’ wages — indicates that his plans were already advanced. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Partnership with Johann Fust
By 1449 or 1450, Gutenberg had produced a small Donatus (a Latin grammar) in the large types later used for the 36-line Bible, and was ready for a major enterprise. He approached Johann Fust, a wealthy money-lender of Mainz, and formed a partnership. The contract of August 22, 1450 provided that Fust would lend Gutenberg 800 guilders at 6% interest to make tools and equipment (which would serve as security), and pay an annual sum of up to 300 guilders for wages, paper, vellum, and ink. The partnership was to last five years, during which Gutenberg was to complete “the work” — almost certainly the printing of the Bible. Fust was to receive half the profits but was exempted from any labour or liability. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The terms favoured Fust heavily. Gutenberg’s types and materials were mortgaged to Fust from the start. Fust delayed payment of the 800 guilders over two years, then proposed a modification: he commuted the remaining annual payments into an immediate lump sum of 800 guilders, in exchange for waiving interest. This second loan meant Gutenberg was now in debt for 1,600 guilders of principal plus accumulated interest. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Missal Project and Nicholas of Cusa
In December 1448, the cardinals Nicholas of Cusa and Juan de Carvajal arrived in Mainz to approve a new standardised missal being prepared by the Bursfeld Congregation, a reformist Benedictine union. Gutenberg almost certainly expected to print this missal — a guaranteed bestseller with a continent-wide Church market. But Mainz’s archbishop backed a competing liturgical text produced by the local monastery of St Jakob’s. With two conflicting texts, one backed by Rome and the other by the local prince-archbishop, Gutenberg found himself in an impossible position: to print either would be commercial suicide. The missal project collapsed. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
The Invention of Movable Type
Gutenberg’s genius lay not in any single component but in the integration of several innovations into a complete system for mass-producing books: ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]

The adjustable type-mould: The “tool of four pieces” from the Strasbourg trial was a hand-held mould that could be adjusted to cast type of any body size. The mould held a brass matrix (struck from a steel punch) and allowed the caster to produce uniform, reusable metal type in quantity. This was the key invention that made practical typography possible. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The punch and matrix system: A letter was engraved in relief on a steel punch, which was struck into copper or brass to create a matrix. The matrix was fitted into the mould and type was cast from a lead-antimony-tin alloy. The punch-cutting required extraordinary skill — steel cutting steel in minute flakes, with tolerances measured in fractions of a millimetre. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Oil-based ink: Gutenberg developed a varnish-based printing ink made from linseed oil varnish, soot, and amber that adhered to metal type and did not smudge on paper, unlike the water-based inks used by scribes and block-printers. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The press: Adapted from the screw presses used for wine-making and paper-making, Gutenberg’s press consisted of two upright timbers with a cross-beam, a wooden screw, and a platen. The type form was placed on a flat bed, inked with leather balls stuffed with wool, paper was laid over it with a blanket to soften the impression, and the screw brought the platen down to transfer the image. Output was approximately 300 sheets per day. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/hoe-history-of-printing-press.md]

Recent computer analysis by Paul Needham and Blaise Aguera y Arcas (2003) has suggested that Gutenberg’s type may not have been produced from single punches and matrices in the conventional way. Examination of hundreds of copies of each letter revealed dozens of distinct variants — the letter i, for instance, had ninety-four different dots and thirty-five different verticals. This has led to the hypothesis that Gutenberg used “elemental punches” to form temporary matrices from lead, sand, clay, or plaster, assembling each piece of type from multiple overlapping strokes rather than from a single matrix. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Early Printed Works
The D-K Type and the Donatus
Gutenberg’s first typeface was the Donatus-Kalender (D-K) type, a heavy Gothic textura designed to imitate contemporary manuscript hands. It contained 202 different characters: all the letters of the Latin alphabet (with no call for capital W, X, Y, or Z), ten variants of the letter a, twelve of p, and numerous ligatures and contractions to mimic scribal practice. The unjustified right-hand margin and multiple letter-forms were deliberate choices to make printed pages resemble manuscripts as closely as possible. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The first book printed with this type was the Ars Grammatica of Aelius Donatus, the standard Latin grammar used in every school in Europe — a short work of about 28 pages with a guaranteed market. Over the years, Gutenberg would print thousands of copies in twenty-four different editions. No complete copy survives; only odd pages used in the bindings of later books remain. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The Sibylline Prophecy
In 1892, a postcard-sized scrap of paper was found beneath the leather cover of an account book, bearing eleven-line extracts of a poem in the D-K type. It proved to be a fragment of a 750-line Thuringian version of the Sibylline Prophecies (Sibyllenbuch / Weltgericht), attributed to the flagellant leader Konrad Schmid, burned as a heretic in 1369. The poem foretells strife in the Holy Roman Empire, brutal Popes, and the resurrection of Emperor Frederick Barbarossa to usher in the Last Judgement. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The fragment’s type (D-K), the absence of a capital W (replaced by a small w), the poor vertical alignment, and the ink composition matching the 42-line Bible all point to Gutenberg’s workshop in Mainz, around 1450-1454. Some scholars have argued for Strasbourg and a date as early as 1440, but the majority view places it in Mainz. It may be the earliest surviving printed piece of Gutenberg’s press. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The Cyprus Indulgences (1451-1455)
In early May 1452, Nicholas of Cusa, newly made Bishop of Brixen, ordered the prior of St Jakob’s in Mainz to prepare 2,000 indulgences for sale in Frankfurt by the end of the month. Pope Nicholas V had granted King John II of Cyprus the right to sell plenary indulgences to fund mercenaries against the Turkish threat. Gutenberg printed these indulgences as single sheets — a simple, fast job that provided desperately needed cash flow while the Bible was in production. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Three editions survive: a 31-line form and two 28-line forms, dated 1454 and 1455. They are the earliest dated products of Gutenberg’s press, and twenty-three copies survive — precious evidence of his commercial printing alongside the grand Bible project. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The 42-Line Bible
Between 1452 and 1455, Gutenberg produced his masterpiece: the 42-line Bible (B42), so called because each column eventually contained 42 lines of text. It is a two-volume folio of 1,282 printed pages, each page with two columns. The type is a dense, black-letter Gothic (textura) — 290 different characters including 83 ligatures. Large initials and ornamental borders were left blank for hand-illumination by rubricators. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The production was an industrial operation on an unprecedented scale. Three punch-cutters — Hans Dunne, Gotz von Schlettstadt, and Hans von Speyer — worked for about four months cutting the steel punches. Six compositors worked simultaneously on three pages each, with approximately 46,000 pieces of type in use at any one time. Three presses operated at once, each with two pressmen. The paper was handmade in Italy (identifiable by its watermarks); the vellum required about 5,000 calfskins for the 30-45 vellum copies. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Gutenberg began printing at 40 lines per page. After the first nine folios (pages 1-9 and 257-263) were printed on all 180 copies, he stopped the presses, recalculated, and tried 41 lines on page ten. Satisfied that the reduction in spacing was unnoticeable, he settled on 42 lines — saving about 5% on vellum and paper costs. The golden-section proportions of the page, the justified right margins, the overhanging hyphens, and the careful letter-spacing all reflect extraordinary design attention. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The Bible was printed in an edition of approximately 180 copies, about 30-45 on vellum and the rest on paper. An illuminator’s colophon in one copy records that the work of illumination was completed on August 24, 1456. The ink is a lustrous carbon-black mixed with linseed oil; on well-preserved copies it retains its depth and sheen after more than five centuries. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The earliest external reference to the Bible comes from a letter by Enea Silvio Piccolomini (the future Pope Pius II), written in March 1455 to Cardinal Juan de Carvajal from Vienna. Piccolomini reports seeing quinternions (20-page sections) of the Bible at the Frankfurt fair, describes it as “extremely elegant and correct” and readable without glasses, and says 158-180 copies had been printed with buyers already ready. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The Lawsuit of 1455 and the Loss of the Printing Office
In November 1455, just as the Bible was being completed, Fust sued Gutenberg for repayment. The legal document, known as the Helmasperger Notarial Instrument (preserved at the University of Gottingen), records the proceedings held in the refectory of the Barefoot Friars’ convent in Mainz. Fust claimed 2,026 guilders: the two 800-guilder loans plus 250 guilders interest on the first, 140 guilders interest on the second, and 36 guilders compound interest. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Gutenberg did not appear in person but sent his workmen Heinrich Keffer and Bertolf von Hanau. His defence was that Fust had not paid the 800 guilders in full and on time, that the second loan was for “the work of the books” (das werck der bucher) and not a personal loan, and that the promised annual 300 guilders for operating expenses had not been paid. The court ruled against Gutenberg. He was forced to surrender his printing office and the types made with Fust’s money. Fust, assisted by Peter Schoeffer (Gutenberg’s former apprentice and later Fust’s son-in-law), took over the business and went on to print the celebrated Mainz Psalter of 1457. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Later Years and Death
Gutenberg was not broken by the loss. He established a new printing office at the Gutenberghof with financial backing from Conrad Humery, a physician and clerk of the town of Mainz. He retained the punches and matrices of the D-K types (the larger types used in the 36-line Bible). With these he printed calendars, a single-page prayer, the papal bull for a crusade against the Turks, and the Catholicon (1460), a Latin grammar and etymological dictionary by John of Genoa, a massive folio of 748 pages. The Catholicon was set in the smallest type devised to date — 5 million characters, almost twice the length of the Bible — and its anonymous colophon is the only known passage that can be securely attributed to Gutenberg’s own hand. It describes the book as printed “not by means of pen, or pencil, or stencil plate, but by the admirable proportion, harmony and connection of the punches and matrices.” ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The 36-Line Bible
Gutenberg also printed the 36-line Bible (B36), an earlier or concurrent edition in three volumes using a larger D-K type. The Cologne Chronicle of 1499, recording the testimony of Ulrich Zell, states that the first Bible was printed in 1450 “in a large letter, resembling the letter with which at present missals are printed” — a description that points to the 36-line Bible. The edition was about 80 copies (20 on vellum, 60 on paper). Most surviving copies were found in and around Bamberg, where the printer Albrecht Pfister acquired the types after Gutenberg’s death and used them for illustrated vernacular works (Boner’s Fabelbuch, 1461). Despite Pfister’s use of the types, the typographic quality of the 36-line Bible is far superior to anything Pfister himself produced, confirming Gutenberg as the printer. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Final Years
During the civil war between rival archbishops Diether of Isenburg and Adolph of Nassau, Mainz was sacked on October 28, 1462. Printing was disrupted throughout the city. Gutenberg appears to have moved his operations to Eltville, where Archbishop Adolph II granted him a court appointment in 1465, naming him a gentleman of his court with an annual allowance of twenty mout of corn, two voer of wine, and court dress. The document acknowledges “the agreeable and voluntary service which our dear and faithful Johan Gutenberg has rendered to us and our bishopric.” ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Johann Gutenberg died on February 3, 1468, in Mainz. He was buried in the Franciscan church, which was later destroyed. Conrad Humery received his printing materials from the archbishop, on condition that they remain in use only in the city of Mainz. No surviving portrait of Gutenberg is known to be authentic. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The Economics of the Bible
A hypothetical balance sheet for the 42-line Bible, reconstructed by the German book historian Leonard Hoffmann, reveals the venture’s financial reality. Costs included: six presses (240 gulden), type-cases and fittings (60 gulden), three years’ rent (30 gulden), heating (20 gulden), three hand-moulds (60 gulden), type-casting metals (100 gulden), ink (30 gulden), paper (400 gulden), vellum (300 gulden), wages (800 gulden), and a Bible exemplar (80 gulden) — totalling about 2,120 gulden for the Bible alone. Adding estimated costs for the second workshop (Donatus, indulgences, other jobs) brought total expenditure to approximately 4,500 gulden. Projected income: 30-45 vellum copies at 50 gulden each (1,500-2,250 gulden) plus 135-150 paper copies at 20 gulden each (2,700-3,000 gulden) = 4,200-5,250 gulden total. The venture was technically insolvent at completion in 1455, with profitability dependent entirely on future sales. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Significance
Gutenberg’s invention was the third great revolution in human communication, after writing and the alphabet. Within fifty years of the publication of the 42-line Bible, printing presses were operating in over 200 cities across Europe, producing an estimated 8 million books. The rapid dissemination of knowledge accelerated the Reformation, the rise of modern science, the standardization of vernacular languages, and the growth of literacy. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
The Gutenberg Revolution ultimately fulfilled a vision that transcended its inventor’s personal fortunes: making knowledge multipliable, affordable, and accessible to all. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
