entities/johannes-fust.title: Johannes Fust
entities/johannes-fust.content:
Overview
Johannes Fust (c. 1400 — 1466) was a Mainz goldsmith, businessman, and money-lender who financed Johann Gutenberg’s printing enterprise and, after a legal dispute that stripped Gutenberg of his workshop, became one of the first major printer-publishers in Europe. Working in partnership with Peter Schoeffer, Fust produced several of the most celebrated incunabula of the fifteenth century, including the 1457 Mainz Psalter, the first printed book to carry a colophon with the printer’s name, the date, and the place of printing. Fust’s role in the invention and commercialization of printing has been controversial for centuries: he is alternately painted as a predatory financier who robbed Gutenberg of his invention, or as a hard-nosed businessman who salvaged a viable enterprise from Gutenberg’s financial mismanagement. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Early Life and Background
Fust was born in Mainz around the year 1400 into a well-established family. His younger brother Jakob Fust served on the city council, as city treasurer, and eventually as burgomaster. Johannes himself was a member of the goldsmiths’ guild rather than the patrician class to which Gutenberg belonged; he represented the rising merchant class that was displacing the old nobility in Mainz’s commercial life. Contemporary records describe him as a wealthy money-lender, and a document discovered in 2001 (published by Reinhardt Schartl in the Gutenberg Jahrbuch) shows that he was taken to court in Frankfurt in 1446 over a failed business deal, confirming his active involvement in lending and commercial transactions before his association with Gutenberg. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Partnership with Gutenberg
In 1448 Gutenberg, newly returned from Strasbourg to Mainz, was working to perfect his printing system. By 1450 he had produced trial runs of a Donatus (Latin grammar) and was ready for a major project — almost certainly the 42-line Bible. To fund it, he needed capital beyond his own means, and turned to Fust. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The first contract, dated August 22, 1450, provided that Fust would lend Gutenberg 800 gold guilders (gulden) at 6 percent interest, secured against the printing equipment (das Gezuge). Fust also agreed to contribute up to 300 guilders annually for wages, house rent, parchment, paper, ink, and other running costs. The partnership was to last five years. If the partners fell into disagreement, Gutenberg was obliged to repay the 800 guilders. Crucially, the press, type, and all equipment remained Fust’s security from the start. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Fust appears to have delayed full payment of the initial 800 guilders, and by December 1452 Gutenberg was again in financial difficulty. A second contract was drawn up: Fust advanced another 800 guilders, this time with stricter terms. Not only the equipment but also “the work of the book” (the Bible itself) was pledged as security, and the profits were to be shared jointly. This second agreement effectively made Fust a full partner rather than merely a creditor. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The 1455 Lawsuit and the Helmasperger Notarial Instrument
By November 1455, just as the 42-line Bible was nearing completion, Fust sued Gutenberg for repayment. The proceedings were recorded by the notary Ulrich Helmasperger in a document now known as the Helmasperger Notarial Instrument, preserved at the University of Gottingen. The hearing was held in the refectory of the Convent of the Barefoot Friars (a Franciscan monastery) in Mainz. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Fust claimed a total of 2,026 gold guilders in principal and interest: the two 800-guilder loans plus accumulated interest. Gutenberg did not appear in person but sent his workmen Heinrich Keffer and Bechtolff von Hanau (Bertolf von Hanau) as witnesses. Through them, Gutenberg argued that Fust had not paid the first 800 guilders in full and on time; that the annual payments of 300 guilders were intended for the common profit of the enterprise, not as personal loans; and that Fust had promised not to charge interest on the first loan. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The court ruled in Fust’s favor, accepting his sworn oath. The precise settlement is not recorded, but the outcome is clear: Fust took possession of the Humbrechthof workshop, its presses, and the partially printed stock of Bibles. Gutenberg retained the Gutenberghof and the punches and matrices for the smaller type used in the 36-line Bible. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Partnership with Peter Schoeffer
Even before the lawsuit, Fust had secured the loyalty of Gutenberg’s most talented assistant, Peter Schoeffer. Schoeffer, born in Gernsheim around 1425, had studied at the University of Erfurt and worked as a scribe and illuminator in Paris, where he was a skilled calligrapher. Fust had taken him in as an adopted son, paid for his education, and brought him back to Mainz to work in Gutenberg’s shop. There Schoeffer proved himself an expert punch-cutter and type designer, making critical technical improvements to Gutenberg’s early typefaces. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
After the dissolution of the Gutenberg partnership, Schoeffer remained with Fust and soon married Fust’s daughter, Christine, solidifying the business and family alliance. The partnership of Fust and Schoeffer combined Fust’s capital and business acumen with Schoeffer’s technical mastery. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Mainz Psalter of 1457
The first major work to emerge from the Fust-Schoeffer workshop was the Mainz Psalter (Psalterium), completed on August 14, 1457. This 350-page book of psalms, canticles, and liturgical texts is one of the most magnificent achievements of fifteenth-century printing. It introduced three historic “firsts”: ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]

It was the first printed book to include a full colophon (imprint) giving the printer’s name, the date of completion, and the place of printing.
It was the first book to use color-printed initials — large two-color initial letters in red and blue, printed simultaneously with the black text using a sophisticated two-part printing technique.
It introduced two new typefaces, smaller and more refined than those used for the Bible.

The colophon reads (in translation): “The present copy of the Psalms, adorned with venerable capital letters and also distinguished by appropriate rubrications, was so fashioned thanks to the ingenious discovery of imprinting and forming letters without any use of a pen and completed with diligence to the glory of God by Johann Fust, citizen of Mainz, and Peter Schoeffer of Gernsheim, in the year of our Lord 1457, on the Vigil of the Assumption [14 August].” ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Psalter’s ornate two-color initials — particularly the large initial “B” (for Beatus vir), measuring 9 cm across its body and up to 31 cm including its decorative flourishes — were cut as whole metal blocks and inked in two colors separately. Only ten copies of the Psalter survive, all on vellum. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Continuation of the Printing Business
Encouraged by the Psalter’s success, Fust and Schoeffer produced a series of important works: ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]

1459: A second edition of the Psalter (slightly enlarged), and Durandus’ Rationale Divinorum Officiorum (Guillaume Durand’s guide to Christian liturgy), set in Schoeffer’s new type.
1460: The Constitutiones Clementis V, a collection of papal decrees.
1462: A political broadside — the first printed political pamphlet — issued in the form of an open letter from Archbishop Diether von Isenburg against his rival Adolf von Nassau, during the civil war that convulsed Mainz that same year. This imprudent publication likely contributed to the destruction of Fust and Schoeffer’s workshop when Adolf’s forces sacked the city on October 28, 1462.

Following the sack of Mainz, the partners rebuilt their operations. Around 1465 they printed Cicero’s De Officiis, the first book to include Greek type (cut in wood rather than metal). ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Death in Paris
In the summer of 1466, Fust traveled to Paris to sell his stock of printed books — his Bibles, Psalters, and other publications. Paris was a natural market: in 1462 Fust had already brought copies of his folio Bible to Paris, selling them for fifty crowns against the four to five hundred crowns typically charged for manuscript Bibles. The dramatic price difference gave rise to later legends that Fust was accused of sorcery for producing books too cheaply and too uniformly to have been written by hand. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Paris in 1466 was in the grip of a severe plague epidemic. Fust died there, probably in the autumn or winter of that year, a victim of the pestilence. He was about sixty-six years old. Peter Schoeffer, now bearing the title “sole heir and executor” in legal documents, continued the business alone, later expanding with a permanent agency in Paris that became the first continuous foreign outlet for German printing. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Historical Reputation
Fust’s historical reputation has oscillated widely. Contemporary and near-contemporary records often conflated his name with the legendary magician Faust of German folklore (the surname of both was Faust/Fust in Latinized form), and stories circulated that he had sold his soul to the devil to gain the secret of printing. The first historian of printing, Johannes Trithemius (writing on Schoeffer’s authority), credited Gutenberg with the invention but noted that Fust and Schoeffer carried it to perfection. Schoeffer himself, in later colophons, occasionally took credit for the invention, claiming that Fust had “first conceived and fathomed” the art. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Modern scholarship recognizes Fust as a pivotal figure — neither villain nor hero, but a shrewd businessman whose capital and legal action rescued printing from financial collapse and established it as a viable commercial enterprise. Without Fust’s investment, Gutenberg’s invention might have remained a neglected curiosity. Without Fust’s lawsuit, the printing shop that produced the Psalter and the 48-line Bible would never have existed. The Frankfurt monument to Gutenberg (by von der Launitz) places Gutenberg, Fust, and Schoeffer together in idealized harmony — an ironic tribute to three men whose real relationship was marked by conflict, ambition, and mutual dependence. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]

entities/mainz.title: Mainz
entities/mainz.content:
Overview

Caption: Mainz printer diaspora after the sack of 1462, showing routes from Mainz toward early printing centers.
Mainz (Mentz in contemporary English and French sources; Latin: Moguntia) is a city on the left bank of the Rhine, at the confluence of the Main. In the fifteenth century it was a free imperial city within the Holy Roman Empire and — more importantly — the seat of the Archbishopric of Mainz, the primatial see of Germany. The archbishop was one of the seven Prince-Electors who chose the Holy Roman Emperor, and the city’s political and ecclesiastical importance made it the natural birthplace for the most transformative invention of the age: mechanical movable-type printing.
Mainz was the cradle of European typography. Johann Gutenberg was born here around 1400, returned in 1448 to set up his printing workshop, and with his partners Johannes Fust and Peter Schoeffer produced within a single decade the 42-line Bible, the 1457 Mainz Psalter, and numerous other landmarks of incunabular printing. The sack of the city in 1462 by Archbishop Adolph of Nassau scattered Gutenberg’s workmen across Europe, directly precipitating the rapid diffusion of printing to Strasbourg, Cologne, Basel, Rome, Venice, and Paris.
Geography and Medieval Significance
Mainz occupies the left bank of the Rhine at the point where the river Main flows in from the east, creating a tongue of silt that forced ferry traffic to cross at this narrow. This strategic position — at the convergence of major river routes from the North Sea to the Alps, and from Frankfurt to the Rhineland — made Mainz a natural center of trade throughout the Middle Ages.
The city was enclosed by a wall and entered through fortified gates such as the Iron Tower (Eisenturm), named for the metalworkers whose stalls lined the foreshore. Inside, the streets bore the same names they carry today: Schusterstrasse (Cobblers’ Street), where the Gutenberg house stood, and the marketplace with its forty-eight licensed cloth-sellers’ booths. The cathedral, still under construction in Gutenberg’s youth, dominated the skyline alongside the spires of St. Christopher’s, St. Quentin’s, and other parish churches. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
At its peak in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, Mainz was the most powerful city of the empire — the city where emperors were crowned — and held first place in the league of free Rhenish cities. Its population may have reached 100,000 before a series of catastrophes reduced it. The Black Death of 1348–1349 killed perhaps 10,000 inhabitants — half the population. The plague returned twice in the following decades. By Gutenberg’s birth the city had shrunk to roughly 6,000 people, and the number of guilds had dropped from fifty to thirty-four. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The Archbishopric of Mainz
The Archbishop of Mainz was the premier ecclesiastical prince of Germany: Primate of the German church and Archchancellor of the Empire. The archbishopric controlled extensive territories along the Rhine and exercised both spiritual and temporal authority over the city, though Mainz had won the status of a free imperial city through centuries of struggle between patrician families and the archbishop’s administration.
This dual authority — the archbishop as prince-elector versus the city council dominated by guildsmen — generated chronic civil strife. In 1332, the guilds rose against the patricians and won representation on the town council. The patricians, including the Gensfleisch family to which Gutenberg belonged, retaliated by withdrawing to their country estates, leaving the city’s finances to collapse. The city’s debt reached catastrophic levels: 373,000 gulden by the 1440s, half of it consumed by annuity payments. A committee of guildsmen demanded transparency; the patricians resisted. This perpetual conflict drove Gutenberg’s own family into exile in the 1420s and shaped the inventor’s early life. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The Gensfleisch Family and the Gutenberg House
The house from which Gutenberg took his name stood at the corner of Schusterstrasse and Christophstrasse, a stone’s throw from the marketplace. Originally called the Judenberg (Jewish Hill), it had been a Jewish property seized by the archbishop’s treasurers after the pogrom of 1282. The treasurers, Philipp and Eberhard, named themselves de Gudenberg after their new acquisition, and the house later passed by purchase to Gutenberg’s great-great-grandfather Frilo. The family bore the name Gensfleisch (“Goose Flesh”) — a name whose origin is lost — and only gradually adopted “zum Gutenberg” as a surname after Frilo’s time. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The house itself was a solid upper-class residence of three storeys, built fortress-like with small ground-floor windows, two wings joined at an angle, and accommodation for multiple generations of the extended family. Next door stood St. Christopher’s Church, where Gutenberg is traditionally said to have been baptised.
Gutenberg’s father, Friele Gensfleisch zur Laden, was a patrician of comfortable means. He had inherited a “Companion of the Mint” position — a right to assay and trade in precious metals — along with an income from municipal loans. His mother, Else Wirich, brought the family a country estate at Eltville, ten kilometres downriver. Though neither rich nor aristocratic, the family was eminent enough to be counted among Mainz’s governing patrician class. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The Humbrechthof and Gutenberg’s Return (1448–1455)
After two decades in Strasbourg (c. 1434–1444), Gutenberg returned to Mainz in 1448. He borrowed 150 gulden from Rynhard Bromser and John Rodenstein, with his kinsman Arnold Gelthus standing surety, and took up residence in the house Zum Jungen (“The Youth”), leased from his uncle John Gensfleisch. Here he set up his first Mainz printing office.
The Zum Jungen became the birthplace of the European printed book. By 1450 Gutenberg had produced small trial works — a Donatus Latin grammar in large type — and was ready for a major enterprise. He approached Johann Fust, a wealthy Mainz money-lender, and formed the partnership that would produce the 42-line Bible. The contract of August 1450 provided 800 guilders for tools and equipment, with an annual 300 guilders for wages, paper, vellum, and ink. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The printing shop soon outgrew the Zum Jungen. Peter Schoeffer, a Mainz native who had been working as a manuscript copyist in Paris, joined the enterprise around 1452 as Gutenberg’s apprentice. The workshop was located in what is sometimes called the Humbrechthof — an area near the cathedral where multiple crafts were clustered. Here, between 1452 and 1455, Gutenberg, Fust, and Schoeffer produced the 42-line Bible in an edition of approximately 180 copies.
The Printing Boom of the 1450s
The 1450s saw an extraordinary concentration of printing activity in Mainz. After the 1455 lawsuit in which Fust seized Gutenberg’s shop, Fust and Schoeffer continued printing at the same premises. On August 14, 1457, they published the Mainz Psalter — the first dated printed book, the first book to carry a printer’s imprint and colophon, and the first to print in colors (red and blue initials). It was followed by Durandi’s Rationale divinorum officiorum (October 6, 1459), Clement V’s Constitutiones (June 25, 1460), and the 48-line Bible (1462).
Gutenberg himself, undeterred by the loss of his shop, established a new printing office with backing from Conrad Humery, a physician and town clerk of Mainz. He produced the Catholicon (1460), a massive Latin dictionary of 748 pages whose colophon — the only passage confidently attributed to Gutenberg — celebrates the invention as achieved “not by means of pen, or pencil, or stencil plate, but by the admirable proportion, harmony and connection of the punches and matrices.” The colophon proudly proclaims the work was printed in “the beloved city of Mentz, which belongs to the illustrious German nation, and which God has consented to prefer and to raise with such an exalted light of the mind and of free grace, above the other nations of the earth.” ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Sack of Mainz (October 28, 1462)
The single most pivotal event in the early diffusion of printing occurred on the night of October 27–28, 1462. Two rival archbishops contested the see of Mainz: Diether, Count of Isenburg, who had the support of the citizens, and Adolph II, Count of Nassau, who was backed by Pope Pius II. Adolph resolved to take the city by stratagem.
Traitors within the walls opened the gates under cover of darkness. Adolph’s followers stormed in, murdering the noblest citizens, plundering their possessions, and driving the survivors from the city. Half a thousand citizens were killed. The booty was sold publicly in the cattle-market. Fust’s house was burned with its printing materials. For three years after the sack, no books of value were printed in Mainz. The once-flourishing city was, in the words of the historian Schaab, “robbed in a few days of its privileges and utterly destroyed.” ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The sack of Mainz had an unintended consequence that transformed European intellectual history. The journeyman printers, suddenly thrown out of employment, “fled panic-stricken to other countries; and considering themselves freed from their oath, the great secret of thirty years was spread abroad.” ^[raw/articles/pearson-gutenberg-and-art-of-printing.md] The printing workers who had learned their craft in Gutenberg’s, Fust’s, and Schoeffer’s workshops carried the technology — and their practical knowledge of typefounding, presswork, and the punch-matrix system — to every corner of Europe.
The Dispersal of Printers
The diaspora from Mainz after 1462 seeded the first printing presses across Europe:

Cologne: Ulrich Zell, a priest and printer, established the first press in Cologne around 1465 and later provided crucial testimony in the Cologne Chronicle (1499) that “the art of printing was first invented in Mainz, by Johann Gutenberg.”
Strasbourg: Though Gutenberg himself had worked there earlier, Johann Mentelin and Heinrich Eggesteyn were printing in Strasbourg by the mid-1460s. Mentelin produced a Bible in 1466 and issued the first printer’s catalogue in 1471.
Basel: Berthold Ruppel (Berthold of Hanau), a Gutenberg workman, brought printing to Basel. By 1473, Michael Wenssler and Bernhard Richel were producing substantial editions. The city’s university, founded in 1460, made Basel a natural center for scholarly printing.
Rome: Sweynheym and Pannartz, two German printers, established the first press in Italy at the Benedictine monastery of Subiaco in 1464, and moved to Rome in 1467. Their colophons acknowledge Mainz as the birthplace of the art.
Venice: Johannes de Spira (John of Speyer) received a five-year monopoly on printing in Venice in 1469. His press was quickly followed by Nicolas Jenson’s roman type and Erhard Ratdolt’s decorated initials; Venice became the printing capital of Europe.
Paris: Fust himself had sold printed Bibles in Paris as early as 1462. After the sack, Ulrich Gering (a native of Constance who had probably learned printing in Mainz) established the first Paris press in the Sorbonne in 1469 with Fichet, Heynlin, Krantz, and Friburger.
Bamberg: Albert Pfister, who had worked with Gutenberg’s types, printed the first illustrated printed book (Edelstein, 1461) and the first printed German Bible.
Augsburg: Günther Zainer, probably a pupil of Fust or Schoeffer, began printing in 1468.

Lorck describes these wandering printers as “fearless apostles and predestined disseminators of a new faith,” who despite the dangers and hardships of fifteenth-century travel “carried the banner of the new art into foreign lands.” ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Printing in Mainz After 1462
Archbishop Adolph II, once in control, quickly recognized the value of printing. On the Saturday after St. Thomas’s Day 1462, he issued a proclamation promising protection to any who would return and resume trade. Peter Schoeffer, whose shop had survived the sack (though Fust’s was destroyed), rebuilt the business. After Fust’s death in Paris (probably of plague, around 1466), Schoeffer continued alone, producing the Institutiones of Justinian (1468), Breydenbach’s Peregrinatio in Terram Sanctam (1486), the Saxon Chronicle (1492), and a fourth edition of the Mainz Psalter (1502). He established the first book-trade network linking a printer’s own output with titles from other publishers, earning recognition as the first true “publisher” in the modern sense. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Gutenberg himself, after the sack, appears to have moved his operations to Eltville. In 1465, Archbishop Adolph appointed him a gentleman of his court, with an annual allowance of twenty mout of corn and two voer of wine. He continued printing — the Bechtermuntz brothers, his relatives by marriage, printed a Vocabularium ex quo with his types at Eltville in 1467. Gutenberg died in Mainz in early 1468 and was buried in the Franciscan church (destroyed in 1793). His printing materials, entrusted to Conrad Humery, were required by the archbishop to remain “only in the city of Mainz.” ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The types of Gutenberg had an afterlife of their own. They passed from Bechtermuntz to the Brothers of the Common Life at Marienthal, and were finally acquired in 1508 by Frederic Hauman of Nuremberg, who used them in a printing office in the Kirschgarten district of Mainz. The same types were still preserved in a house in Mainz at the end of the sixteenth century, where the historian Serarius reported seeing them. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Mainz as Jewish Center
Before the catastrophes of the fourteenth century, Mainz was the capital of European Jewry. It housed a Jewish academy for over 300 years and was revered as the home of Gershom ben Judah (c. 960–1040), the “Light of the Diaspora,” who first brought copies of the Talmud to Western Europe and whose takkanot (directives) helped Jews adapt to European practices. The Jewish community suffered pogroms in 1096 (1,300 killed) and repeatedly thereafter. In the plague year 1348, the Jews of Mainz fought back against the mob, killing 200 before being overwhelmed; on Bartholomew’s Day, 100 were burned outside St. Quentin’s Church. The Gutenberg house itself, originally called the Judenberg, stood on land that had been Jewish property seized after the 1282 pogrom — a somber reminder that the inventor’s very name derived from the expropriation of a persecuted community. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The Gutenberg Museum and Modern Legacy
Mainz’s commemoration of its greatest citizen was remarkably slow to develop. The first monument to Gutenberg was a stone tablet placed by Ivo Wittig in 1504 in the courtyard Zum Gutenberg, with the inscription: “To John Gutenberg of Mentz, who first of all invented printing letters in brass, and by this art has deserved honor from the whole world.” A century later, in 1740, other German cities (Dresden, Bamberg, Halle, Frankfurt) were celebrating Gutenberg centennials while Mainz remained indifferent.
It took the French — Napoleon’s army occupied Mainz in 1792 — to reawaken the city’s interest. The French prefect Jeanbon-Saint-André proposed a monument to Gutenberg in 1804. In 1837, the bronze Gutenberg statue was erected in the city square that now bears his name.
The decisive moment came in the 1890s. Mainz’s city fathers, seeking a grand celebration for the 1900 quincentenary, wrote to Gutenberg scholar Karl Dziatzko of Breslau, who confirmed that 1400 was as good a year as any for the inventor’s birth. The local paper, the Mainzer Anzeiger, proclaimed that “everyone agreed that Mainz was not only justified in opting for a festival — it had a duty to do so.” The Gutenberg Museum was established as a focal point for Gutenberg studies and tourism. The museum today houses two of the museum’s original 42-line Bibles (one on vellum, one on paper), a replica of Gutenberg’s workshop, and the world’s most comprehensive collection of printing equipment, from the fifteenth century to the present. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Significance
Mainz’s role in the history of civilization is unique. Within the span of a few decades in one mid-sized Rhenish city, the essential technologies of modern information — mass-produced identical text, the typefounder’s hand-mould, oil-based ink, the screw-press adapted to printing — were conceived, perfected, and commercialized. The sack of 1462, in scattering the printers who had mastered these techniques, paradoxically ensured their triumph. Every early press in Europe, from Subiaco to Seville, from Krakow to Westminster, can trace its lineage — through a printer or a type or a technique — back to the workshops of Mainz. The city that Gutenberg’s colophon called “preferred and raised above the other nations of the earth by the grace of God” had indeed given the world a gift that transformed it.

entities/martin-luther.title: Martin Luther
entities/martin-luther.content:
Martin Luther (1483–1546) — Publishing Phenomenon
This page documents Luther strictly as an author and publishing phenomenon: the economics, mechanics, and distribution of his printed works. No theological or biographical evaluation. All claims are traceable to Putnam, Books and Their Makers in the Middle Ages, Vol. II, Chapter X (“Luther as an Author”).

First Printers and Publishers
Luther’s first publisher was Johann Weissenburger (originally from Nuremberg, established in Landshut, Bavaria, 1513). In 1517 Weissenburger printed Luther’s tract Tractatus de his qui ad Ecclesias Confugiunt.
Later in 1517, Joh. Grunenberg in Wittenberg printed Luther’s Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms in Latin. This was immediately followed by a German version, which went through nine editions in five years.
In 1518, Luther brought Melchior Lotter from Leipzig to Wittenberg. Lotter was an experienced printer with good equipment, type, moulds, and a collection of collated texts. By 1519, Luther could report that Lotter had “completed the organisation here in Wittenberg of a well-appointed printing-office, fitted for work in three languages” (Latin, Greek, German; Hebrew fonts were added later). Lotter retained his Leipzig business and placed his two sons in charge of the Wittenberg operation.

The 95 Theses — Editions and Reach
The 95 Theses (1517, originally Disputatio pro Declaratione Virtutis Indulgentiarum) appeared in:

4 Latin editions from Wittenberg (3 more after the first, plus 1 in Nuremberg)
1 first German edition (1518, Wittenberg), followed by 22 other German editions within two years
Printed across Wittenberg, Leipzig, Nuremberg, Augsburg, Basel, and Breslau

It is not ascertainable from publishing records or biographies how many of these editions were authorised vs. piratical. Luther himself made no criticism of any printer who issued editions, except when they were printed in incorrect or incomplete form without his supervision. His only desire was the widest possible circulation.

Edition Sizes and Sales Velocity























WorkDateCopiesSales SpeedAddress to the Christian Nobility of GermanyAug 15205,000Sold out in 5 daysControversial address against Eck15181,400Sold in 2 days at the Frankfurt Fair
These figures illustrate the unprecedented popular demand for Luther’s writings. The Address to the Nobility was published without date or imprint on the title-page — only “Zu Wittenberg.”

The German New Testament (1522)
The complete German version of the New Testament, printed in Wittenberg, was Luther’s central literary achievement from a publishing standpoint.
Authorised Editions (Wittenberg)

First edition: September 1522 — 5,000 copies, folio, 1.5 guilders (~$6.25). Three presses were at work on it by end of July. Exhausted within three months.
Second edition: December 1522 — 5,000 copies.
Lifetime total from Wittenberg: Not less than 100,000 copies of the New Testament printed in Wittenberg alone during Luther’s life (Kapp record).

Pirated Editions
The piratical reprinters moved fast:

Adam Petri of Basel — first reprint before end of 1522; within three years printed 7 editions (4 octavo, 3 folio). During 1520–1530 Petri made a special business of Luther reprints and derived large profits from them. The Petri Press had good typographical reputation; Luther directed no specific complaints at Petri.
Wolf of Basel — 5 editions in the same period.
Hans Schönsperger of Augsburg — 3 editions (1523 edition with woodcuts by Schäuflein).
Evidence of Northern pirate editions: Petri’s Basel editions could hardly have reached Saxony, yet copies sold in Meissen in 1523 for as low as 15 groschens (vs. Wittenberg price of 30 groschens), proving pirate editions were produced in the North as well.


Pamphlet Production — Scale and Statistics
Tract: Die Deutsche Theologie (1518, Latin and German)

75–80 separate editions in four years (bibliographers disagree on exact number).

Sermon on Indulgences (1518 onward)

Kapp records 10 authorised editions in two years, plus 3 unauthorised editions from Leipzig, Nuremberg, and Augsburg.

Decem Precepta (same period)

Latin: 5 editions
German: 7 editions (including 3 unauthorised from Leipzig, Augsburg, Basel)
Plus a Bohemian edition from Prague (1520)

Overall Estimate (Köstlin)
By 1520, more than 100 editions of German versions of Luther’s sermons and tracts had been printed (including all unauthorised issues and the Wittenberg editions).
German Book Production Statistics (Panzer, Weller, Kuczynski, tabulated by Kapp)

























YearGerman-language works printed151390151814615205711523944
Ten-year aggregate (1513–1523): 3,113 separate works (mostly pamphlets/Flugschriften). Of these, 600 were printed in Wittenberg — a town that before 1517 had not possessed a printing press.

Distribution: Pedlars, Colporteurs, and Market-Place Reading
Distribution of Luther’s pamphlets was only partly effected through the regular book-trade. Three channels predominated:

Market-place sales: Thousands of copies sold by dealers of all kinds, many of whom had never before handled books.
Travelling pedlars and colporteurs: Carried supplies to readers out of reach of book-shops and market-places. Many colporteurs were travelling students working not for gain but for the Reform cause.
Oral reading: Pamphlets were read aloud in market-places, inns, and private homes, multiplying effective circulation enormously. In Nuremberg, reading Luther’s books aloud in the market-place became standard practice. Even after the writings were placed under interdict, public readings continued in places less liable to interruption.

Geographic Reach of Distribution

Froben of Basel wrote to Luther (Feb 14, 1519) that Basel editions were called for not only in Germany but in France, Spain, Italy, Brabant, and England.
Magdeburg (1520–1523): Became a centre for production and distribution of Protestant polemical literature. After Luther’s death, Magdeburg became the headquarters of the Reformers’ literary interests, especially Bibles, hymn books, and collected works, until the city’s destruction by Tilly in 1631.
Münster: Distributed large supplies of the New Testament and Lutheran writings throughout Westphalia and the northern provinces, until the Anabaptist upheaval (1535–36) destroyed the city’s printing business.
Out-of-the-way towns: Lutheran tracts were printed in Grimma, Zwickau, and Eilenburg, principally for sale through pedlars, often without imprint or date.
Austrian dominions: Church prohibition (1525) on Lutheran literature was evaded by pedlars for a time, but Jesuit persecution eventually crushed the business.
Speyer: Citizens had the books read to them at supper and made transcripts.


Form and Price Revolution
The Reformation brought a revolution in book form and price:

Costly folios and quartos were replaced by inexpensive twelvemos and sixteenmos.
The most influential writings were issued as pamphlets (Flugschriften), which functioned like modern magazines or weekly papers.
Typical tract price: 1 groschen (~2.5 cents; purchasing power equivalent to ~12 cents today).
Bible prices (1538): 18 groschens (Jena), 19 groschens (Leipzig Fair), 20 groschens (Frankfurt Fair).


Shift of German Publishing from South to North
Before Luther, the principal German publishing centres were Basel, Frankfurt, Augsburg, and Nuremberg — all in the South. The North had presses in Cologne and a beginning in Leipzig, but much less activity.
The Reformation and the superior intellectual activity of the Protestants transferred the literary and publishing preponderance from South to North Germany, a preponderance that continued and increased through subsequent centuries.

Economics: Author Compensation and Printing Costs
Luther’s Compensation
According to Kapp, Luther received no honorarium or compensation for his literary work beyond occasional copies of the printed volumes. This refers to the many unauthorised editions issued by printer-publishers as their own ventures. However, the Wittenberg editions (including the German Bible) were printed at Luther’s own risk and expense, and receipts from their sale (less commission) were paid to him.
In practice:

Every gulden received was at once expended on further printings and distribution machinery.
Luther did not treat his writings as property. His purposes were accomplished when his teachings, correctly printed in authorised editions at the lowest prices compatible with accurate typography, had secured the widest possible circulation.
Putnam’s judgment: Luther’s experience as an author did not help advance recognition of authorial rights. To Luther, his writings were “not property, to be controlled for the benefit of the author, but great truths and sound doctrine essential for the saving of souls, and to be scattered widely for the benefit of the reader.”

Printing Costs
Each new impression required resetting the type entirely — the process of taking casts or clichés was an invention of a much later period.

Luther’s Publishers and Printers in Wittenberg








































NamePeriodRoleJoh. Grunenberg1517–1518Printed early Latin and German worksMelchior Lotter (brought from Leipzig 1518)1519–1530sOrganised Wittenberg’s first 3-language printing office; brought equipment, type, and textsGeorge Rhaw (established Wittenberg 1521)1521–Printed Small and Large Catechisms (1529), Augsburg Confession (1531, accepted as standard), many Melanchthon worksLucas Cranach & Döring (partnership formed 1524)1524–1534Established new printing office; also operated a paper-warehouse and book-shop. Cranach’s portraits are the chief authority for Luther’s appearanceCranach-Döring successors: Goltz, Schramm, Vogel (1534)1534–Acquired privilege for the complete Bible from Elector Johann Friedrich, plus Cranach’s Apocalypse woodcuts; continued with Melchior Lotter the youngerHans Lufft1523–1584Printed many Luther publications after 1524; special achievement was the German Bible in parts and completed volume

The Bull of Leo X (1520) and the Censorship Paradox
The 1520 papal bull excommunicated Luther, condemned his works, ordered existing copies burnt, and prohibited printing, sale, distribution, or possession of his writings under severe penalties.
Immediate effect: Largely increased sales throughout nearly all parts of Germany, and considerable demand from other countries.
The Edict of Worms (1521) committed Emperor Charles V against Luther and announced the beginning of imperial censorship (confirmed and extended by the Nuremberg Edict of 1524). In Protestant regions, the only effect was increased circulation. In Catholic regions, ecclesiastics stopped distribution by taking harsh measures against colporteurs.

Luther’s Stance on Piratical Reprinting
Luther’s principal complaints about reprints were inaccuracy and incompleteness, not the fact of reprinting itself.
In a letter (September 1525) to the magistrates of Nuremberg:

Proof-sheets of a volume of his sermons had been stolen from his Wittenberg printing office and used in Nuremberg for a piracy edition, published before the complete work — causing “merklichen Schaden” (serious injury) to his printers.
Luther requested not a ban on reprints but a delay of 7–8 weeks before reprinting, out of “Christian feeling.”
He also asked that reprints be printed with “decent regard for correctness and completeness.”

The Nuremberg magistracy promised an edict. In 1532, an edict was finally issued — not forbidding reprints, but forbidding the use of the false Wittenberg imprint on Nuremberg publications (a reiteration of imperial law) and requiring greater textual accuracy.
In another letter (1525) to Spengler, Syndic of Nuremberg, Luther referred to an association of leading Rhine-city printers formed to repress piracy, and asked that Koberger be induced to join. Koberger apparently did not participate; his firm published scholarly Latin works that did not attract German reprinters.
Putnam’s assessment: The widespread piratical reprinting, while aggravating to Luther and his authorised publishers, furthered the rapid spread of Reformation doctrines and built up the publishing and bookselling business, developing the habit among common people of buying and reading books.

Legacy for the Book Trade
Luther’s publishing phenomenon had lasting effects on the German book trade:

Laid the foundation of the book-trade of Germany and of Europe.
Created the habit among masses of buying and reading printed matter.
Gave incentive to printers and booksellers.
Established the practice of distributing books by pedlars and colporteurs in areas far beyond book-shops.
The form of the book shifted from expensive folios to cheap pamphlets and small formats.
German replaced Latin as the language of popular publication, creating modern German high literature.
Wittenberg, which had no press before 1517, became a major publishing centre with 600 works in a decade.

Cochläus (Catholic opponent): “Luther’s New Testament was multiplied by the printers in a most wonderful degree, so that even shoemakers and women and every lay person acquainted with the German type, read it greedily as the fountain of all truth.”
Erasmus (1523): Since the publication of the New Testament, the whole book-trade seemed absorbed with Luther’s writings; it was very difficult to find publishers willing to place their imprint on works in behalf of the papacy.
Matthäus Zell (Strasburg, 1523): “The Lutheran books are for sale here in the market-place immediately beneath the edicts of the Emperor and of the Pope declaring them to be prohibited.”

References
All content derived from Putnam, George Haven. Books and Their Makers in the Middle Ages. Vol. II. New York: G.P. Putnam’s Sons, 1897. entities/nicholas-of-cusa.title: Nicholas of Cusa
entities/nicholas-of-cusa.content:
Overview
Nicholas of Cusa (1401 — 1464), known in Latin as Cusanus, was a German cardinal, canon lawyer, philosopher, church reformer, and cartographer. Born in Kues (Cusa) on the Mosel River eighty kilometres west of Mainz, he was a contemporary of Johann Gutenberg and is suspected by several historians of having been the hidden force behind Gutenberg’s invention. His life overlapped with Gutenberg’s in ways that Man describes as “intriguing” and that “act as a lens through which to observe his world.” His career spanned the Council of Basel, the Ferrara-Florence Council, the Bursfeld monastic reforms, and the literary revolution that followed the rediscovery of Plautus. Karrow’s Mapmakers of the Sixteenth Century documents him as “theologian, philosopher, diplomat, church reformer, cardinal, maker of a single map, and, possibly, a globe.” ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Early Life and Education
Nicholas was born in 1401 to a father who was no aristocrat but well off, with a boat business and several houses. According to tradition, he was educated at a school set up in the late fourteenth century by the Brethren of the Common Life in Deventer in the Netherlands. The Brethren were mystics who devoted themselves to a simple, communal life and the care of the poor, and who also promoted scholarship by producing books — hand-copied and then block-printed ones. Known widely as the “Brothers of the Quill,” they were proud to spread the Word “not by word but by script.” Mysticism, scholarship, writing, and the idea of reproducing information were passions built into Nicholas in his youth. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
He studied at Heidelberg and Padua, where he learned law, mathematics, and astronomy. At Padua he formed a lasting friendship with the physician, mathematician, and astronomer Paolo Toscanelli, with whom he studied astrology. He returned to the Rhineland as a newly qualified canon lawyer — a specialist in Church law — and in 1427 became secretary to the archbishop of Trier, and then, as word of his legal skills spread, secretary to the papal legate in Germany, Cardinal Giordano Orsini. This was the beginning of his career as an ecclesiastical lawyer and statesman. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Career at the Council of Basel
In February 1432, Nicholas arrived in Basel to put the case for a new claimant to the archbishopric of Trier. Though he lost that case, he settled into the anti-papal camp and made himself the council’s chief legal adviser. In November 1433 he presented De Concordantia Catholica (Of Catholic Harmony), arguing that society should be based on an order in which the parts submit to the whole, the whole being the combination of Church and Empire, of Pope and emperor, united by the council. The work drew on recent history: the Council of Constance had ended the Great Schism by deposing three Popes and imposing a fourth. If that was valid, Nicholas reasoned, then the council — not the Pope — represented the true spirit of the Church and could advise, reprimand, and in extreme cases depose him. Authority, he wrote, should arise from the consent of those governed, summing up the principle as: “Quod omnes tangit debet ab omnibus approbari” (“What touches all should be approved by all”). ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Nicholas also helped negotiate with the Hussites in 1433, suggesting a compromise by which they could receive Communion “in two kinds” while agreeing not to use that as an argument to break the unity of the Church. The agreement was signed in Prague the following year, effectively resolving the Bohemian-Hussite crisis. He also turned his attention to calendar reform, presenting De Reparatione Calendarii (On Revising the Calendar) to the council in 1437, proposing a new lunar cycle and the omission of a week. The proposals were not adopted but were later echoed in the Gregorian calendar of 1582. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Switch to the Papal Side
Around 1436-37, Nicholas abruptly abandoned his conciliarist position and joined the pro-papal minority. Man identifies several factors: the council’s growing dysfunction; the prospect of reunification of the Eastern and Western Churches; proposed reforms that would have abolished the Pope’s power to grant benefices, on which Nicholas depended; and the glass ceiling of his non-noble birth, which blocked him from becoming a bishop through the German Church’s aristocratic leadership. He helped create a document bearing the council’s stamp that supported the Pope’s order to transfer the council to Ferrara — a document widely seen by scholars as a forgery. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
From that moment he became one of the Pope’s ablest champions, called the “Hercules of the Eugenians” by his friend the scholar and future Pope Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini. He carried the invitation to the Byzantine emperor and patriarch in Constantinople and escorted the Greek delegation of 700 bishops, monks, and scholars back to Italy. Nicholas argued the papal cause in town after town across Italy and Germany, eventually helping Frederick III turn against the rump council. Just before his death in 1447, Pope Eugenius IV made Nicholas a cardinal, a confirmation that was ratified by his successor Nicholas V. Shortly afterwards, the new Pope appointed him bishop of Brixen (now Bressanone) in the Tyrol. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The Bursfeld Missal Project
The idea of a standardised missal came from Johann Dederoth, the Benedictine abbot of Bursfeld. Presented at the Council of Basel, his aim was to cleanse the Church of abuses and centralise authority through a new missal, the Ordinarius. The task was inherited by Dederoth’s successor, Johann Hagen, who in 1446 formed a union of six monasteries, the Bursfeld Congregation, which later linked eighty-eight abbeys and monasteries in northern and western Germany, including St Jakob’s in Mainz. In December 1448, Pope Nicholas V sent the Spanish cardinal Juan de Carvajal to Mainz to approve Hagen’s new Ordinarius. Accompanying Carvajal was his friend and co-cardinal, Nicholas of Cusa. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Conflict arose when Mainz’s archbishop backed an alternative liturgy produced by St Jakob’s monastery. The dispute came to a head in 1451-52 during Nicholas’s tour of Germany, when his aide, the Scottish prelate Thomas, favoured Hagen’s text and declared the St Jakob version deviant “both from Benedictine rites and from those of the established Church.” Nicholas obtained a papal bull allowing him to raise an army if necessary. He called a synod in Mainz and then in Cologne in March 1452, at which seventy Benedictine abbots promised to reform their monasteries, including stocking their libraries with good editions of the Bible. Hagen’s text was approved, and St Jakob’s prior was replaced by a Bursfeld nominee. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The 1451 Cyprus Indulgences
In 1450, King John of Lusignan of Cyprus, fearful of the Turkish advance, appealed to the Pope for help. In August 1451, Pope Nicholas V granted the king the right to produce plenary indulgences for the next three years, raising cash to pay mercenaries to protect Cyprus from the Turks. In early May 1452, Nicholas of Cusa — newly made Bishop of Brixen and still on his grand legation of Germany — ordered his new appointee, the prior of St Jakob’s in Mainz, to prepare two thousand indulgences for sale in Frankfurt by the end of the month. Man writes that “Nicholas’s order must have come as music to Gutenberg’s ears,” providing a cash-flow solution just when the planned missal had “hit the buffers.” ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Possible Connection to Gutenberg
Man presents the connection between Nicholas and Gutenberg as circumstantial but significant. Both were born to well-off, non-noble families in the same region (Kues is eighty kilometres west of Mainz). Nicholas was in Mainz for a court case in 1424, when both were twenty-four-year-olds. A later meeting between 1428 and 1432, after Gutenberg had left Mainz and before Nicholas arrived in Basel, could have planted the germ of an idea: Nicholas wanted Christian unity, and unity required uniform texts across all Christendom. “What if Nicholas of Cusa and Johann Gutenberg shared this vision of somehow, no one knew how, duplicating texts to perfection?” ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
When Carvajal and Nicholas arrived in Mainz in December 1448 to approve the Bursfeld missal, Gutenberg had just returned to the city that same year. Man suggests Nicholas would have been gratified to discover the means of printing the new missal was to hand. During Nicholas’s 1451-52 visit to Mainz to settle the liturgical dispute, Gutenberg was already hard at work. At the synod of seventy Benedictine abbots, Nicholas emphasised the need for monastic libraries to possess a well-translated and edited Bible. Man notes that “as he should have known by then — because Gutenberg had been at work in the city for the last three years — there was only one way to achieve this: by printing from a single source, fixed in metal.” Nicholas ordered a copy of Gutenberg’s Bible for his own church in Brixen, now in Vienna. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Giovanni Andrea de Bussi, who had been Nicholas’s secretary and became chief librarian of the Vatican, wrote in the preface to the 1470 Sweynheym-Pannartz edition of St Jerome: “It is that which the soul (rich in honours and meriting heaven) of Nicholas of Cusa … so fervently desired: that this holy art, whose shoots became visible at that time in Germany, should be transplanted to Roman soil.” ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The Plautus Rediscovery
In 1429, Nicholas brought to Rome manuscripts containing twelve plays by the Latin comedy writer Plautus. When published — they went through thirteen editions by 1500 — they influenced European comedy from that point onward. Man traces the debt through Nicholas Udall, author of the first English comedy Ralph Roister Doister (1552), to Shakespeare (The Taming of the Shrew), Moliere (The Miser), and the modern French playwright Jean Giraudoux (Amphitryon 38, 1929). ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Philosophy and Character
Nicholas’s philosophy was built on the concept of the coincidentia oppositorum — the coincidence of opposites — in which God, as the infinite maximum, coincides with the minimum. His notion of docta ignorantia (“learned ignorance”) held that the purpose of knowledge is to learn how inadequate all learning is when seeking God. His whole life was defined by the “obsession to make opposites coincide, to establish the unity foreshadowed by ancient Rome and Charlemagne.” In practical terms, this meant incessant travel, persuasion, and writing as tools to stitch together a fragmented Christian commonwealth. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Cartography
Karrow’s Mapmakers of the Sixteenth Century (entry no. 23) documents Cusanus as a significant figure in cartographic history: “theologian, philosopher, diplomat, church reformer, cardinal, maker of a single map, and, possibly, a globe.” His map of central Europe is one of the earliest printed maps of the region and “one of the most remarkable maps of the fifteenth century.” ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
The 1491 Map of Central Europe (Eichstatt Map)
The only surviving evidence of Cusanus’s map comes from a printed copper engraving called the Eichstatt map, an impression apparently made between 1514 and 1518. The map proper (copper engraving, ca. 397 x 570 mm plate mark) consists of two distinct parts: a main section (section D) showing all of central Europe from Sweden in the north to the Italian Alps in the south, from Brussels in the west to the Black Sea in the east, and a later extension (section E) carrying coverage as far south as the fortieth parallel in central Italy. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Three inscriptions in the top margin provide the historical record:


Inscription A (added last, engraved rather than punched): “For the shared use of learned people, Conrad Peutinger, a legal scholar from Augsburg, has entrusted the printing of this copper-plate (which he bought with his own money) to his fellow-citizen, the painter Hans Burgkmair, who has rendered him great service.” Only one copy with this full inscription existed (in GyMW, destroyed in World War II); all seven surviving copies were pulled after the inscription had been cut from the plate. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]


Inscription B: Twelve hexameter verses crediting Cusanus with the map: “because the whole of Germany has been depicted on a small map, and also the side of Italy which faces the icy Alps, and the wild tribes of the Sarmatians… let thanks be given to Nicolaus of Cusa who was formerly clad in Tyrian purple [i.e., a cardinal], and was a great splendour of the Roman senate, and who ordered places, unexplored by any predecessors, to be engraved on a copper-plate of modest size” (trans. O. A. W. Dilke). ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]


Inscription C: “Completed at Eichstatt the 12th day before the Calends of August [21 July] 1491.” This date has been much debated since Cusanus died in 1464. Hildebrand (1892) theorised the engraver misread a handwritten “5” for a “9,” implying 1451, the year Cusanus was in Eichstatt — but his visit occurred in April, not July. The inscription likely marks completion of the engraving, not the manuscript. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]


Seven extant copies survive: FPBn, GyBS, GyDiS, GyNGm, GySwftS, GyWZ, UkLBI. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Manuscript Origins and Surveying Methods
Cusanus probably completed a manuscript of his map sometime in the 1450s. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md] As papal legate for Germany (1450), he traveled extensively through Germany and the Low Countries in 1451-1452, collecting geographical data. He established many locations himself using an astrolabe and a torquetum (“Turkish instrument,” a device rather like a theodolite) that he acquired in 1444. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
His inspiration for mapping likely came from Ptolemy’s Geography (in one of its early Latin editions) and from his Padua friend Paolo Toscanelli, who was a close friend of Leon Battista Alberti, whose treatises on surveying and the mapping of Rome (Descriptio urbis Romae, ca. 1445) and on “mathematical games” (Ludi matematici, ca. 1450) were precocious for the period. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
No manuscript map that can be unequivocally attributed to Cusanus survives, although Sebastian Munster apparently had such a map in his possession when he wrote his account of it in 1530. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Connection to the Rome Ptolemy and Conrad Sweynheim
The Eichstatt map is lettered with the same set of letter-punches that Conrad Sweynheim perfected in Rome between about 1474 and 1477 for the 1478 Rome edition of Ptolemy’s Geography. In this technique, individual capital letters were punched into the copperplate instead of being cut with a graver. No other fifteenth-century engravings are known to have used these punches, except the Eichstatt map and an engraved coat of arms of the bishop of Eichstatt. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
This suggests that Sweynheim may have carried out the engraving of the Cusanus map separately from the Ptolemy project — perhaps because of a personal pledge to Cusanus. Cusanus almost certainly knew the German clerics Sweynheim and Pannartz and may even have been responsible for their setting up the first printing establishment in Italy, at Subiaco, the year after his death. Cusanus may have come to know Sweynheim in Mainz, where the latter probably apprenticed with the printers Fust and Schoffer. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
The map is drawn on the trapezoidal projection attributed to Nicolaus Germanus, giving it a superficial resemblance to the regional maps in the 1478 Rome Ptolemy. However, the Eichstatt map was not included in any Ptolemy edition. The punches might have continued in use for some time: the Rome Ptolemy was reissued in 1490 (still without modern maps), and in 1507 a new edition included seven modern maps lettered with the 1478 punches plus one additional small font that appears in section E of the Eichstatt map. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Printing History
The plate had a long, complex printing history:

The engraving was completed at Eichstatt in 1491, perhaps only a few proof copies pulled on that occasion.
Conrad Peutinger (1465-1547) acquired the plate, probably after 1491. Hans Burgkmair (1473-1531), who became a master printer in 1498, printed it around 1514. A letter by Peutinger from January or February 1514 mentions a map: “I have not sent the map to your abbot… I had just a few printed.” ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
In 1518, the editor Johannes Eck wrote in his forward to Maciej z Miechowa’s Tractatus de duabus Sarmatiis that “the excellent prince and lord, Lord Nicolaus Cusa, showed the learned German kingdom in a little map.” ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
The last known printing was by Sebastian Munster in 1530, published by Andreas Cratander of Basel. Cratander apparently removed the Peutinger/Burgkmair inscription (A) by cutting it from the plate. All seven extant copies were printed from this state. The plate remained in Peutinger’s possession; his brother-in-law Christoph Welser noted in 1535 that Peutinger still had the “bronze archetype.” Based on watermark evidence, sporadic printings may have been made as late as the 1560s or 1570s. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]

Related Maps and Influence
The Cusanus map had some influence on the later mapping of Germany but “was not decisive” and “probably not widely circulated” until 1530, by which time better maps were becoming available. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md] Related maps include:

23/1.1 — Henricus Martellus Germanus (ca. 1485): Manuscript of central Europe (460 x 575 mm) in Florence, thought by Ptolemy scholar Joseph Fischer to be a copy of the Cusanus manuscript. It shows Cusanus’s tiny birthplace, Cues. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
23/1.3 — Francesco Rosselli (ca. 1492): Copper engraving (ca. 330 x 470 mm), possibly engraved in Florence, showing affinities with the Leiden manuscript. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
23/1.4 — Germania in the Nuremberg Chronicle (1493): Woodcut map (392 x 579 mm) drawn by Hieronymus Munzer and cut by Michael Wolgemut (teacher of Durer), showing traces of the Cusanus map in its depiction of rivers. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
23/1.5 — Marcus Beneventano (1507): Map titled “Tabvla moderna Polonie, Vngarie, Boemie, Germanie, Russie, Lithvanie” in the 1507 Rome Ptolemy, strikingly similar to the Rosselli version. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
23/1.6 — Martin Waldseemuller (1513): Woodcut map of Sarmatia, Hungary, Poland, Russia, Prussia, and Wallachia in the 1513 Strasbourg Ptolemy. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
23/1.7 — Giovanni Andrea Vavassore (ca. 1530): The only later map showing clear evidence of copying directly from the Eichstatt map (as opposed to a manuscript prototype). Letterpress in rectangular cartouche quotes the hexameters from inscription B. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
23/1.9 — Ferando Bertelli (1562): Copper engraving (373 x 503 mm) published in Venice, referencing a “new and exact description” of Germany and surrounding regions. Listed in the table of contents as “Central and Eastern Europe, by Paolo Forlani and Ferando Bertelli, after Nicolaus Cusanus (Venice, 1562).” ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]

Celestial Globe
The library in Bernkastel-Kues holds two fifteenth-century celestial globes: a large wooden globe (272 mm diameter) that Cusanus acquired in 1444 (at the same time as the torquetum), and a smaller, incompletely engraved copper globe (166 mm diameter) that Cusanus almost certainly commissioned and may even have made himself. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Significance in Cartographic History
Despite being the maker of only a single known map, Cusanus holds an important place in cartographic history. His map of central Europe was among the first printed maps of the region; it used systematic latitude determinations via astrolabe and torquetum; it was one of the earliest maps engraved on copper using Sweynheim’s punched-letter technology; its 1491 completion date makes it a landmark in early German copper engraving. The map has generated “a vast literature and much speculation,” with Tony Campbell (1987, 35-55) providing “an informed and judicious guide, while adding important findings of his own” on its physical manufacture. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Death
Nicholas of Cusa died at Todi, in Umbria, on 11 August 1464 and was buried in Rome. His later years after being made bishop of Brixen were a continual political struggle with the German prelates whose aristocratic ranks he had been thrust into by papal favour. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Legacy
Nicholas of Cusa was famous in his lifetime but mostly forgotten until a Cusanus renaissance in Germany in the mid-nineteenth century. The University of Trier maintains a major research institute devoted to him, based on the library of books and manuscripts he left on his death. Cusanus societies exist in both America and Japan, where he is regarded as an honorary Buddhist. His role in bringing the Plautus manuscripts to Rome, his push for liturgical uniformity through the Bursfeld missal, his orchestration of the Cyprus indulgence campaign in Mainz, and his possible influence on Gutenberg’s invention combine to make him a pivotal figure in the story of the printing revolution. His 1491 map of central Europe ranks as one of the most remarkable maps of the fifteenth century and a landmark in the history of European cartography. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Key Achievements

Brought twelve Plautus manuscripts to Rome (1429), influencing European comedy through Shakespeare, Moliere, and others
Wrote De Concordantia Catholica (1433), a landmark of conciliarist political theory
Helped negotiate the 1434 agreement with the Hussite moderates at Prague
Proposed calendar reform (1437), later echoed by the Gregorian calendar
Played a central role in the Ferrara-Florence Council and the failed reunification of Eastern and Western Churches
Became the only German cardinal of his era, “Cardinal Teutonicus”
Championed the Bursfeld missal, standardising the liturgy across eighty-eight monasteries
Ordered the preparation of two thousand Cyprus indulgences (1452), providing a potential commission for Gutenberg
Ordered a copy of Gutenberg’s Bible for his see in Brixen
His secretary, Giovanni Andrea de Bussi, recorded his desire to transplant printing to Italy
Created a manuscript map of central Europe (ca. 1450s), later engraved and printed as the Eichstatt map (1491/1514), one of the earliest printed maps of the region and “one of the most remarkable maps of the fifteenth century”
Used astrolabe and torquetum for latitude determinations during his travels as papal legate
Commissioned a copper celestial globe (ca. 1444-1464), possibly made by his own hand
His map influenced later cartographers including Henricus Martellus, Francesco Rosselli, Marcus Beneventano, and Giovanni Andrea Vavassore
The map’s lettering connects it directly to Conrad Sweynheim’s Rome Ptolemy (1478), one of the earliest uses of punched-letter engraving
