entities/nicolas-jenson.title: Nicolas Jenson
entities/nicolas-jenson.content:
Overview
Nicolas Jenson (c. 1420—1480) was a French-born master engraver, typefounder, and printer who, after being dispatched by King Charles VII to learn the new art of printing in Mainz, established himself in Venice where he created the most admired Roman typeface of the fifteenth century. His types set the standard for Latin typography across Europe and directly influenced the work of Claude Garamond, William Morris, and Bruce Rogers. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Early Life and Background
Jenson was born in France around 1420. He served as master of the mint in Tours, where his skill as an engraver of coins and medals earned him a reputation as one of France’s most accomplished craftsmen. The precision required for die-cutting coinage translated directly into the punchcutting skills that would later define his typographic work. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Mission to Mainz (1458)
Following the appearance of Gutenberg’s Bible, the French court took notice of the revolutionary new art. On October 3, 1458, King Charles VII issued an order to the royal mint-masters to select an experienced man and send him to Mainz to learn the art of printing. The choice fell on Nicolas Jenson, described in the Arsenal document as a man “dexterous in the engraving of stamps and of letters.” ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Jenson was instructed to inform himself of the invention and report back to France. He succeeded in acquiring the art as ordered, but by the time he was ready to return, Charles VII had died (1461). His successor, Louis XI, showed little interest in the undertaking. Jenson, understanding that the new monarch would not support his mission, never returned to Paris. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Move to Venice (c. 1468)
Rather than return to a France indifferent to printing, Jenson carried his knowledge to Venice, the most powerful commercial republic in Europe. He arrived around 1468 and by 1470 had established his own press. Venice at the time was already home to German printers — Johannes de Spira (John of Speyer) had begun printing there in 1469 — but Jenson brought something they lacked: the eye of a master engraver and an intimate understanding of humanist letterforms. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Jenson Roman Type (1470)
Jenson’s crowning achievement was the Roman typeface he cut for his edition of Eusebius’s De Praeparatione Evangelica, printed in 1470. This typeface is widely regarded as one of the most beautiful ever created. It combined:

Evenness of colour: Perfectly balanced stroke weights across all characters, giving the printed page a uniform grey texture far more legible than dense blackletter.
Clean serifs: Sharp, horizontal serifs derived from Roman monumental inscription capitals, providing a clear baseline.
Generous proportions: Open counters and generous spacing that made each letter distinct without sacrificing page colour.
Harmonious letterfit: Adjacent letters sitting together without awkward gaps or collisions.

De Vinne records that Jenson’s Roman “supplanted” the Black letter throughout Italy, France, Spain, and eventually England. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] The type was so perfectly proportioned that it remains a benchmark of type design to this day. Jenson’s letterforms reconciled the best traditions of humanist handwriting with the precision of metal punchcutting, achieving a synthesis that manuscript scribes could never match and that later printers have rarely surpassed. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The type became known in Italy as lettera antiqua tonda (round antique letter), while northern Europe called it Antiqua, France and the Netherlands called it Romain or Romeyn, and England called it Roman. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Printing Office and Major Publications
Jenson’s printing office became one of the largest in Venice, producing a steady stream of high-quality editions. He also cut Gothic types and a Greek type (without capitals) to suit the diverse demands of the market. His major publications include:

Eusebius, De Praeparatione Evangelica (1470): His masterpiece, printed in the celebrated Roman type.
Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (1472): A landmark edition of the great natural history encyclopedia, printed with his finest Roman face.
Works of St. Jerome: A substantial folio edition of the Church Father’s writings.
Nosce Te (1480): A book of devotion by Giovanni di Dio, notable as the earliest example in Venice of an ecclesiastical testamur (imprimatur) printed in a book. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]

The quality of Jenson’s presswork was exceptional in every respect. Lorck notes that the ink in Jenson’s Venetian editions was “intensely black, velvet-soft and glossy” — superior even to the ink used in the Gutenberg Bible. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Business Enterprise
Jenson’s printing operation was one of the most heavily capitalised in fifteenth-century Venice. He was backed from an unknown date by two Frankfurt merchants: Johan “Big John” Rauchfass, a merchant whose diverse activities made his shares in Jenson’s company “little more than an exotic item in his portfolio,” and Peter Uglheimer, who became a considerable book-collector in his own right. This triangular partnership was ultimately liquidated by the payment of 1,000 ducats in gold to Uglheimer’s heirs. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Jenson’s will disposed of approximately 4,000 ducats, placing him among the wealthiest printers of his generation. His focus shifted increasingly from production to sales as his career progressed. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The Company (1480)
By the late 1470s, Jenson and his rival John of Cologne — who had inherited the press of Wendelin of Speyer after the overproduction crisis of 1473 — were the two dominant forces in Venetian printing. Together they produced 260 of the approximately 600 editions printed in Venice up to 1481 (43% of the total). Their nearest rivals averaged only seven editions each. As Victor Scholderer observed, there was “a sharp contrast between the few successful men at the top and the crowd of transient and financially embarrassed phantoms down below.” ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Fearing plague and market saturation, the two rivals joined forces. On May 29, 1480, a protocol created the five-year syndicate of Nicholas Jenson, John of Cologne, and Company — a partnership to which John contributed an initial 5,000 ducats worth of books. The syndicate was able to turn out some twenty folio editions in its first twelve months and exercised such absolute domination over the Venetian industry that it became known simply as “The Company.” Both main partners died almost immediately afterwards, and evidence of “The Company’s” overt activity vanishes from the end of 1481. But its influence persisted: shares in the partnership passed through the Torresani family and into the Aldine circle, and the model of “The Company” served as “a golden image of success, beckoning the next generation to imitate, and prosper.” ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The partnership structure involved Andrea Torresani as a printer, bookseller, and underwriter active for more than a decade before he formed his own partnership with Aldus. Jenson’s matrices ultimately passed to Torresani, who claimed to have worked with Jenson’s types — connecting Jenson’s Roman letterforms directly to the Aldine Press. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Rivalry and Competition
Jenson worked alongside and competed with the German printers who had preceded him to Venice. Johannes de Spira (John of Speyer) had received a five-year monopoly on printing in Venice in 1469, but died the following year. His brother Wendelin continued the press and eventually formed a partnership with Johann of Cologne, who in turn later united with Jenson himself. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] The Venetian printing scene was crowded and competitive; by the end of the century some 150 presses were operating in the city.
Recognition by the Pope
Jenson’s reputation extended beyond the printing trade. Pope Sixtus IV recognised his mastery and honoured him with the title of Count Palatine (Pfalzgraf), a rare distinction for a printer. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Death and Succession
Nicolas Jenson died in 1480, a wealthy and respected figure. His printing office was purchased in 1479 (or shortly before his death) by Andrea Torresani of Asola, who continued the business. Torresani’s daughter Maria married Aldus Manutius around 1500, and Aldus thus gained control of Jenson’s former press, inheriting both its physical plant and its typographic tradition. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] This direct line of succession connects Jenson’s workshop to the Aldine Press, the most famous publishing enterprise of the Renaissance.
Typographic Legacy
Jenson’s Roman type exercised an influence on typeface design that extends to the present day. It became the prototype for the Roman types used by:

Claude Garamond (sixteenth century): The great French typefounder whose Roman faces were themselves inspired by Jenson’s proportions.
William Morris (nineteenth century): Revived Jenson’s Roman for the Kelmscott Press, using it as the model for his Golden Type.
Bruce Rogers (twentieth century): Designed the Centaur typeface (1914) directly inspired by Jenson’s original.

The Jenson Roman established the convention that Latin and vernacular texts would be printed in Roman letters, while German-language works continued in blackletter — a typographic divide that persisted well into the twentieth century. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
One of the most beautiful books of the Renaissance, the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (1499) printed by Aldus Manutius, used a Roman type directly derived from Jenson’s, and the type was later revived commercially as Poliphilus. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Key Achievements

Master of the mint at Tours, royal engraver to Charles VII
Dispatched to Mainz (1458) to learn Gutenberg’s printing art
Created the Jenson Roman type, arguably the most beautiful Roman typeface ever cut (1470)
Printed the Eusebius De Praeparatione Evangelica (1470), one of the masterpieces of incunable printing
Printed Pliny’s Natural History (1472), a landmark of classical publishing
Established one of the largest and most productive printing offices in Venice
Honoured by Pope Sixtus IV with the title of Count Palatine
His types passed to the Torresani/Aldus circle, directly influencing the Aldine Press
Posthumously inspired type revivals by Garamond, Morris, and Rogers ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]

entities/peter-schoeffer.title: Peter Schöffer
entities/peter-schoeffer.content:
Overview
Peter Schöffer (c. 1425 — 1503), also spelled Schoeffer, was a German scribe, type designer, punchcutter, printer, and publisher who served as Gutenberg’s most skilled assistant, later became Johann Fust’s partner and son-in-law, and eventually sole proprietor of the most important printing house in Mainz in the late fifteenth century. He designed the type for the 1457 Mainz Psalter (the first dated printed book), introduced the first printer’s mark, and made significant technical innovations in punchcutting, multi-color printing, and typographic spacing. Though he and Fust systematically downplayed Gutenberg’s role in the invention of printing, Schöffer was a master craftsman and shrewd businessman who kept the Fust-Schöffer press productive for nearly fifty years.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Early Life and Paris Years
Schöffer was born in Gernsheim, a village on the Rhine south of Mainz. The exact year is uncertain; some authorities place it around 1425, others closer to 1430. His father died when he was young, and he was taken under the protection of Johann Fust, a wealthy Mainz moneylender and goldsmith who effectively adopted him. Fust paid for Schöffer’s education at the University of Erfurt (probably Gutenberg’s alma mater as well) and then sent him to the University of Paris.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
In Paris, Schöffer worked as a manuscript copyist. A colophon in an old manuscript book records: “This book was completed by me, Peter, of Gernszheym, or of Mentz, during the year 1449, in the most glorious University of Paris.”^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] This training in calligraphy and manuscript production gave him the eye for letterforms that would later distinguish his printed work. It is uncertain whether he was also trained as an illuminator, but he was certainly qualified to read and correct proofs of Latin texts.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Work with Gutenberg
Around 1452, Fust brought Schöffer back to Mainz and placed him in Gutenberg’s workshop. Schöffer was perfectly suited for the role: his calligraphic training, engraving skills, and Latin literacy made him valuable both as a type designer and as a proofreader. He may have assisted in punchcutting — engraving steel punches used to strike matrices for typefounding — and in designing the textura types used in the 42-line Bible. Some traditions, preserved in later claims by Schöffer and his descendants, assert that he was the first to perfect the method of cutting steel punches and striking matrices, but this is almost certainly an exaggeration: Gutenberg’s types, cast well before Schöffer’s known arrival, already show the use of the punch-matrix system. Nevertheless, Schöffer did refine and systematize the technique.^[raw/articles/pearson-gutenberg-and-art-of-printing.md]^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
One account says Schöffer privately cut matrices for the entire alphabet and cast letters from them, presenting the result to Gutenberg and Fust as a demonstration of his skill — a story preserved in fictionalized form by Pearson but reflecting a genuine tradition of his technical competence.^[raw/articles/pearson-gutenberg-and-art-of-printing.md]
The Lawsuit of 1455 and Switch to Fust
The Helmasperger Notarial Instrument of November 1455 records the lawsuit in which Fust demanded repayment of 2,020 guilders from Gutenberg. Schöffer was present at the hearing in the refectory of the Barefoot Friars’ convent — not as one of Gutenberg’s designated witnesses, but as an independent observer. During the months the case took to conclude, Fust had quietly recruited Schöffer, promising him control of the workshop if the judgment went against Gutenberg.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Schöffer would not have needed much persuasion: he was closer to Fust than to Gutenberg, having been raised and educated by Fust. Talented, ambitious, and with a streak of pragmatism, he neatly bridged the gap between Gutenberg’s artistic obsessions and Fust’s business opportunism. After the judgment stripped Gutenberg of his printing office and types, Schöffer and Fust took over the Humbrechthof workshop.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The Mainz Psalter of 1457
The first major work of the new partnership was the Mainz Psalter, completed on 14 August 1457. It is a landmark in printing history on multiple counts:

First dated printed book — it carries the first printed colophon with a specific date.
First printer’s imprint — the colophon announces the book was “made by the masterly invention of printing and also of type-making, without the writing of a pen, through the industry of Johan Fust, citizen of Mentz, and Peter Schoeffer of Gernszheim.”
First printer’s mark — surviving copies (notably the Vienna copy) have the Fust-Schöffer device, two shields hanging from a twig, the earliest known printer’s emblem in the history of typography.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Multi-color printing — the Psalter’s 175 leaves contain two-color printed initials in red and blue, achieved through careful separate inking of text and ornament blocks, with remarkably accurate register.
Elaborate decorative initials — the large initial B of Beatus vir features intricate filigree work in metal as fine as mesh, with images incised within the letterform itself (a dog hunting a bird in the vertical stroke).^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]

Though the Psalter was almost certainly designed under Gutenberg’s direction before his expulsion, the execution and completion were the work of Fust and Schöffer. The colophon pointedly omits Gutenberg’s name — the first move in a deliberate campaign to rewrite the history of the invention.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
De Vinne notes that the presswork of the Psalter is not superior to the 42-line Bible and is sometimes rougher, with uneven inking and typographical errors. The multi-color initials, he argues, were likely painted onto separate blocks with brushes rather than printed in the modern sense.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The Fust-Schöffer Partnership (1457—1466)
After the Psalter, the firm produced a series of notable works:

Rationale Durandi (1459) — a guide to liturgy by Guillaume Durand, the first book in which Schöffer identifies himself as “clerk of the diocese of Mentz.” It became an astonishing success, with over forty editions following.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Constitutions of Pope Clement V (1460) — with commentaries by Bishop John Andrew, a complex layout of nested text and notes.
Bible of 1462 — a two-volume folio in the same tradition as Gutenberg’s Bible.
Papal bulls and proclamations during the Mainz civil war (1461—1462), printed for both sides — Fust and Schöffer took contracts from Archbishop Adolf von Nassau, while Gutenberg (backed by Konrad Humery) printed for Diether von Isenburg.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]

The sack of Mainz on 28 October 1462 interrupted printing throughout the city. Fust’s house and materials were reportedly burned, though the punches and matrices survived. No books bearing the Fust-Schöffer imprint appeared between 1462 and 1464. The dispersal of their workmen during this period carried the knowledge of printing to Cologne, Basel, Augsburg, Nuremberg, and beyond.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Technical Innovations
Schöffer introduced several genuine improvements to the printer’s craft:

Leading — in the 1465 edition of Cicero’s De Officiis, he inserted perceptible leads (about one-tenth of an inch thick) between lines of type, the first known use of leading to improve readability.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Greek type — the same Cicero edition printed Greek characters (crudely engraved on wood) for the first time in a printed book.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Punchcutting refinement — Schöffer systematized the method of cutting steel punches and striking brass matrices, giving typefaces a finish and uniformity that earlier hand-cut or soft-metal methods could not achieve.^[raw/articles/pearson-gutenberg-and-art-of-printing.md]
Multi-color registration — the Psalter initials, however achieved, demonstrated a method of registering two colors on the same printed sheet that was not surpassed for decades.

De Vinne, however, is skeptical of Schöffer’s reputation as a typefounder: his types were fewer in number and of inferior design compared to Gutenberg’s, and he never again matched the quality of the Psalter initials after Gutenberg’s departure.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Sole Proprietorship (1466—1503)
Johann Fust died of plague during a sales trip to Paris in 1466, and was buried at the Church of Saint Victor. Schöffer inherited the business and married Fust’s daughter, Christina, consolidating his control. He continued at the head of the firm for nearly forty more years, becoming the first truly international bookseller-printer.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
He established sales agencies in Frankfurt (where he became a freeman of the city) and Paris, supplying missals and liturgical works across Central Europe. He also acted as a bookseller for other printers’ output. In 1474, Louis XI of France intervened personally to protect Schöffer’s Paris stock from seizure by the licensed book-dealers’ guild, a sign of Schöffer’s high standing at court.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Schöffer bound his workmen by oath to secrecy about the technical processes — an attempt to preserve a monopoly that was ultimately broken by the dispersal of printers after the 1462 sack of Mainz. His later output declined in quantity: only six books appeared from his press between 1490 and 1502. His last publication was a fourth edition of the Psalter (1502), the book with which his typographical career began.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
In his later years, Schöffer served as a judge in Mainz, a civic honor that reflects his status as one of the city’s leading citizens. He died in 1503, rich, respected, and eminent. His sons Johann Schöffer and Peter Schöffer the Younger carried on the family printing business into the Reformation era.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Legacy and Controversy
Schöffer’s reputation is entangled with the long-running controversy over who invented printing. Beginning with the colophon of the 1457 Psalter, and amplified by the statements of his son Johann and of the historian Johannes Trithemius (who claimed to have heard the story from Schöffer himself), the Fust-Schöffer family propagated the claim that Fust was the true inventor and Schöffer the man who perfected the art. Trithemius wrote:

“They discovered a method of founding the forms of all the letters of the Latin alphabet, which they called matrices, from which they again founded types, either in tin or in brass… Before Schoeffer’s name is mentioned, it is said that ‘they’ [Fust and Gutenberg] discovered a method of making matrices.”^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]

De Vinne dismisses these claims as self-serving: Schöffer’s types show no evidence of the inventive genius he claimed, and his boasts were not published until after Gutenberg and Fust were both dead and could not contradict him. Nevertheless, Schöffer’s genuine contributions — the Psalter design, the refinement of punchcutting, the introduction of leading, the first printer’s mark — constitute a real, if secondary, chapter in the invention of printing.^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Significance
Schöffer occupies a unique position in early printing history: he was Gutenberg’s apprentice and successor, the bridge between the inventor’s genius and the commercial viability of the press. Where Gutenberg was a visionary who died in debt, Schöffer was a pragmatist who built a lasting business. He ensured that the books the Church needed — missals, psalters, liturgical guides — were produced in quantity and quality. His introduction of the printer’s mark and colophon established conventions that printers still follow today. His sons and their descendants carried the Schöffer name in printing for another century, though Mainz itself never regained its primacy as a center of the new art.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]

entities/sebastian-munster.title: Sebastian Munster
entities/sebastian-munster.content:
Sebastian Munster
Sebastian Munster (1488–1552), German cosmographer, Hebrew scholar, and cartographer, author of the Cosmographia universalis (1544) — the most widely read geographical work of the sixteenth century, which went through dozens of editions and translations and shaped the European understanding of the world for generations. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Early Life and Education
Born 20 January 1488 in Nieder-Ingelheim, near Mainz. His father Andreas was a master of a hospital; his grandfather and uncle were priests. At age seventeen (1505) he entered the Franciscan order in Heidelberg, beginning a clerical career that he would later abandon for the Reformation. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
He studied at Louvain in 1507 (mathematics, geography, astronomy), then moved to Freiburg, where he fell under the influence of Gregor Reisch, author of the Margarita philosophica, a widely used encyclopaedia. In 1509 he was sent to the monastery of St. Katharina in Rufach to study Hebrew and Greek with Konrad Pelikan, the leading Hebrew scholar of the German-speaking world. By 1510, at age twenty-two, he had produced a Hebrew grammar and a five-thousand-word Hebrew-Latin dictionary — precocious scholarly work that established his reputation. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
He was ordained a priest in 1512 in Pforzheim. He followed Pelikan to Tubingen in 1514 and attended lectures of Johann Stoffler, mathematician and astronomer, deepening his geographical and astronomical learning. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Move to Basel and the Reformation
In 1518 Munster moved to Basel, drawn by the circle of Reformation scholars gathering there. He worked initially as a proofreader in Adam Petri’s printing shop — the same shop that printed Luther’s early works — which gave him firsthand experience of the printing trade. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
He published his Hebrew grammar in 1520 and took a lectureship in Hebrew at Heidelberg. In 1524 he was appointed professor of Hebrew at Heidelberg University, where he also established lectures in mathematics and cosmography — an unusual combination of subjects that reflected his conviction that the languages of scripture and the geography of the world were complementary fields of knowledge. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
He left the Franciscan order and became a committed supporter of the Reformation, a move that severed him from the Catholic scholarly networks of his youth but connected him to the broader Protestant humanist community. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Cartographic Career
Munster’s first map, published in 1525, was the “Instrument of the Suns” — a broadsheet that combined a circular map of Germany with a calendar, astrological almanac, sundial, and nocturnal (a navigation instrument for telling time from the stars). This multi-purpose format demonstrated the popular appetite for accessible geographical knowledge. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
In 1528 he published a booklet containing a famous appeal: he asked German scholars, city councils, and travellers to send him local maps and geographical descriptions, promising credit in the final publication. This crowd-sourced approach, using the printing press itself as a recruiting tool, was unprecedented in scale and created the network of over one hundred and twenty collaborators who would contribute to the Cosmographia. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Key Works

1538: Edition of Solinus’s Polyhistor and Pomponius Mela’s De situ orbis, with twenty woodcut maps — a warm-up for the larger project. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
1540: Geographia — a new edition of Ptolemy’s Geography with forty-eight maps, based on the most recent scholarship. This cemented his reputation as the leading cartographic editor in the German-speaking world. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
1544: Cosmographia universalis — his magnum opus, published by his stepson-in-law Heinrich Petri in Basel. The Cosmographia was a comprehensive description of the world, covering ancient and modern geography, ethnography, natural history, and local history. It included city views, regional maps, descriptions of customs, and historical narratives drawn from over one hundred and twenty collaborators across Europe. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]

The Cosmographia was an instant success. It went through dozens of editions and was translated into German, French, Italian, and other vernacular languages. It played a role comparable to that of the Nuremberg Chronicle a half-century earlier — a printed compendium that organised and popularised knowledge for a broad readership. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Map Sources
Munster relied heavily on earlier maps. His maps of Germany drew significantly on Waldseemuller’s maps and the Ulm Ptolemy of 1486 (Leonhard Holl’s edition with Johann Schnitzer’s woodcut maps). His circular map of 1525 owed much to Nicholas of Cusa’s earlier map of central Europe. Munster had apparently possessed a manuscript copy of Cusanus’s map, which he mentioned in his 1530 account. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Hebraic Scholarship
Alongside his cartographic work, Munster was one of the most important Christian Hebraists of the sixteenth century. He published approximately eighty works on theology and Hebrew, translated the entire Hebrew Bible into Latin, and produced the first translation into Hebrew of any part of the New Testament (the Gospel of Matthew). He mastered Hebrew, Arabic, Aramaic, and Coptic. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
His dual career as Hebraist and cosmographer is less eccentric than it appears: for Munster, biblical geography was the link between the two fields. Understanding the physical setting of scripture was essential to its correct interpretation — a distinctly Reformation concern. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Relationship with Printing
Munster’s career was inseparable from the printing press. He worked at Petri’s shop in Basel, published with Heinrich Petri, Jacob Kobel in Oppenheim, and others. The Cosmographia was designed as a printed book from the start: its woodcut illustrations and maps were integrated with the text, and its layout took advantage of the press’s ability to combine image and typography on the same page. It could not have existed in manuscript form — the quantity and precision of its illustrations demanded print. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Relationship with Ortelius
Munster died before Ortelius published the Theatrum (1570), but his maps and cosmography were foundational sources. Ortelius listed him in the Catalogus auctorum and his work stands as a direct precursor to the atlas concept. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]
Death and Legacy
Munster died in Basel in 1552 during a plague outbreak. The Cosmographia continued to be published and expanded after his death, with new editions appearing well into the seventeenth century. His combination of Hebrew scholarship, geographical synthesis, and popular publishing made him a unique figure — a scholar who used the press to reach audiences far beyond the university. ^[raw/articles/karrow-mapmakers-16th-century.md]

entities/strasbourg.title: Strasbourg
entities/strasbourg.content:
Strasbourg
Strasbourg was one of the crucial bridge cities in the early history of European printing: it was the place where johann-gutenberg lived during the 1430s and early 1440s, where the documentary record first hints at his secret technical work, and one of the earliest cities to develop a stable printing trade after mainz. Its position on the Upper Rhine connected German, Swiss, French, and Italian trade routes, making it a natural relay point in the spread-of-printing. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Gutenberg’s Strasbourg Period
Gutenberg appears in Strasbourg records by 1434. The city gave him room to work outside the political conflicts of Mainz, and his activities there combined metalwork, mirror-making, gem-polishing, partnership finance, and secret technical experimentation. The 1439 Dritzehen lawsuit is especially important because witnesses refer to a press, forms that were to be separated or melted, and a mysterious tool of four pieces that later historians identify with the adjustable hand mold used in movable-type. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Strasbourg evidence does not prove that Gutenberg had a complete printing shop there. It does show that several essential elements of the later Mainz system were already being explored: metalworking, presses, secrecy, investment partnerships, and repeatable production. For that reason Strasbourg belongs in the invention story, even though Mainz remains the place where the system became a working book-production technology. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Printing After Gutenberg
Strasbourg became an early printing center in its own right. Johann Mentelin is usually treated as the city’s first established printer, active by the late 1450s or early 1460s. Strasbourg’s printers helped spread German blackletter traditions while also serving markets that reached toward Switzerland, France, and the Rhine cities. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Significance
Strasbourg matters because it shows that printing was not born in a single heroic instant. The invention emerged from a Rhine-world network of metalworkers, merchants, lenders, guilds, religious markets, and mobile craftsmen. The city links the experimental prehistory of johann-gutenberg to the later commercial geography of incunabula. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Open Questions

How far had Gutenberg’s printing experiments progressed in Strasbourg before his return to Mainz?
Was the “tool of four pieces” definitely an adjustable type mold, or only plausibly so?
How much did Strasbourg’s craft economy shape Gutenberg’s later technical system?

entities/sweynheym-and-pannartz.title: Sweynheym and Pannartz
entities/sweynheym-and-pannartz.content:
Overview
Konrad Sweynheym (also Conrad Sweynheym, Schweinheim; from Schwanheim near Mainz) and Johann (Arnold) Pannartz (from Prague) were two German printers who introduced the art of printing to Italy. They established the first press in the Italian peninsula at the Benedictine monastery of Santa Scholastica in Subiaco in 1464 and printed Italy’s first book, the works of Lactantius, in 1465. Sweynheym and Pannartz were probably students of Gutenberg and were among the many German printers who, after the Mainz civil wars, carried the new technology across Europe. Their types were transitional — a semi-Gothic blending German and Italian scribal traditions that evolved into one of the earliest Roman typefaces. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Background and Origins
Sweynheym came from Schwanheim (also spelled Schweinheim), a village between Mainz and Frankfurt. He may have been a protégé of Gutenberg himself. Pannartz was from Prague, and like Sweynheym, likely learned printing in the Mainz workshops that had been scattered after the 1462 sack of the city. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Lorck handbook calls them “wahrscheinlich zwei der überall hin verstreuten Schüler Gutenbergs” — probably two of Gutenberg’s students scattered everywhere. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The German monks at Subiaco and their abbot, Cardinal Juan de Torquemada (Johannes a Turrecremata), played a key role in summoning the printers south. Torquemada, who became a cardinal and was an admirer of the new art, arranged through German monks at the monastery to bring Sweynheym and Pannartz from Germany in 1464. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Subiaco: The First Press in Italy (1464—1467)
Sweynheym and Pannartz arrived at Santa Scholastica in Subiaco, some seventy kilometres east of Rome, in 1464. The Benedictine monastery, founded by Saint Benedict himself in a cave in the hills, was remote and difficult to reach — the Lorck handbook describes it as “in unwirtlichster Berggegend 14 Stunden von Rom” (in a most inhospitable mountain region, 14 hours from Rome), a monastery perched on naked rock that could only be climbed with great difficulty. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Connection to Nicholas of Cusa
There is good reason to believe the choice of Subiaco was not coincidental. Nicholas of Cusa (Nikolaus von Kues), a cardinal, philosopher, and reformer who had close ties to the Benedictine order, had been invited to Rome by his friend Pope Pius II. He had known Gutenberg and may have suggested Subiaco as a suitable location. The 1470 preface to the Sweynheym—Pannartz edition of Saint Jerome, written by Giovanni Andrea de Bussi (who had been Nicholas of Cusa’s secretary and was now Vatican librarian), states explicitly that it was Nicholas’s ardent desire “that this holy art, whose shoots became visible at that time in Germany, should be transplanted to Roman soil.” ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
First Printed Books
In 1465 they printed Italy’s first book from movable type: the works of Firmianus Lactantius (Divinae Institutiones), an early Christian apologist. This was followed later in 1465 by Cicero’s De Oratore (though some sources dispute order), and in 1467 by Augustine’s De Civitate Dei and a Donatus grammar. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
The Subiaco Type
The type used at Subiaco was a semi-Gothic transitional form — neither purely Gothic Textura nor fully Roman. It blended the rounded humanist letter with certain Gothic features and is known as the Subiaco type. The Lactantius was the first book printed in a type inspired by Roman handwriting. According to Lorck, a manuscript of Augustine’s De Civitate Dei written in Italy in 1459, preserved in Paris, shows the same script that was used for the Lactantius type. On the first sheets of the work, space was left for Greek quotations to be written in by hand; in later sheets the first Greek types were used. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
De Vinne judged the Subiaco Roman type imperfect: “It was not a successful effort, for the traces of Gothic mannerisms are noticeable in almost every letter.” ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Rome (1467—1472)
The isolation of Subiaco made business difficult. In 1467, Sweynheym and Pannartz accepted an invitation from the brothers Pietro and Francesco, the Marchesi Massimi (Massimi), to move to Rome. They set up their press in the Massimi palace, printing Cicero’s Epistolae Familiares as their first Roman work. This edition introduced what Lorck calls the “pure Antiqua” — a cleaner Roman face closer to the humanist handwriting of the papal chancery. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
In Rome, they were encouraged and supported by Giovanni Andrea de Bussi (also Andrea Bussi, Bishop of Aleria), Vatican librarian and a noted humanist scholar, who served as their editor and corrector. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
The Roman Press
Over five years in Rome (1467—1472), Sweynheym and Pannartz produced twenty-eight titles — a stately series of editions including:

Classical authors: Cicero, Apuleius, Aulus Gellius, Caesar, Virgil, Livy (1469, a celebrated edition of which one copy sold in 1815 for nearly 20,000 marks), Strabo, Lucan, Pliny, Suetonius, Quintilian, Ovid
Church Fathers: Augustine, Jerome, Cyprian
Biblical works: A Latin Bible and the Bible commentaries of Nicholas de Lyra in five volumes ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]

They made new fonts of Roman, Greek and Round Gothic types for the Roman press. In their Roman editions they abandoned the Subiaco type for a purer Roman face, establishing a market for books printed in the new style. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Overproduction and Financial Ruin
Despite the quality and importance of their output, Sweynheym and Pannartz overestimated the market. Their editions ranged from 275 to 550 copies per work (the smaller number for specialized classical texts, the larger for popular works). By 1472 their house was filled with unsold, unbound books. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Their friend and patron Giovanni Andrea de Bussi petitioned Pope Sixtus IV on their behalf, setting forth that they had printed 11,475 copies of twenty-eight works, a very large portion of which remained unsold — and that they were in great distress. The petition is historically important because it records that the standard edition size of the period was 275 copies, and 550 for popular works. But Sixtus IV, who had just succeeded to the papacy and was more concerned with providing for his relatives than supporting a publishing business, declined to help. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
The partnership dissolved in 1472. As Lorck puts it: “In dem Verhältnis, wie sich das Bücherlager von Sweynheim und Pannartz füllte, leerte sich ihre Kasse” — as the book warehouse of Sweynheim and Pannartz filled, their cashbox emptied. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Later Years
Pannartz
Johann (Arnold) Pannartz continued printing on his own until about 1475 or 1476, around which time he died. The record of his activities after the dissolution is sparse. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Sweynheym: Map Engraving and Ptolemy
After the partnership ended, Sweynheym turned to engraving maps on copper. He undertook to produce a landmark edition of Ptolemy’s Geography — one of the earliest attempts to illustrate a printed book with engraved copper plates. Sweynheym did not live to see its publication; he died around 1475 or shortly after (some sources suggest 1473 is the last date we hear of him). The Ptolemy was eventually completed with plates finished by Arnold Bucking and was published in 1478. ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
The Lorck handbook notes that Sweynheym “machte auch die ersten Versuche, Landkarten für die Buchdruckerpresse in Kupfer hoch geschnitten herzustellen” — he also made the first attempts to produce maps for the printing press in high-cut copper. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Typographic Significance
Sweynheym and Pannartz are pivotal figures in the history of typography. Their Subiaco type represents the first deliberate break with the Gothic tradition and the first attempt to create a printed letterform inspired by Italian rather than German manuscript models. The De Vinne account notes that “to please the tastes of their Roman readers they made a new font of Roman types,” though it was still imperfect. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Their typographic evolution followed a clear trajectory:

Subiaco type (1465): Semi-Gothic, transitional — blending humanist rounded forms with Gothic angular features
Roman type (1467 onward): A cleaner Antiqua, closer to Carolingian minuscule and humanist handwriting, first appearing in the Cicero Epistolae Familiares printed at Rome

This transition from Gothic to Roman was not merely aesthetic. It reflected a deeper cultural shift: German printers adapting their craft to Italian scribal traditions and reader expectations. As the spread-of-printing concept notes: “The German printers did not merely transplant a technique; they adapted it.” ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Historical Significance and Legacy
Sweynheym and Pannartz were the pioneers who established printing in Italy, a country that would surpass Germany itself in total book production before 1500. Within five years of their arrival at Subiaco, printing had spread to nearly every city in Italy, almost exclusively through German printers. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Their commercial failure demonstrated the economic risks of overproduction that would haunt the early book trade. Rome, despite being a centre of learning, lay outside the major European trade routes, and their unsold stock consumed their capital. Yet by their ambitious programme of classical and patristic publishing — twenty-eight titles in Rome alone — they established the market for printed books in Italy and proved that the press could serve humanist scholarship as well as religious devotion.
Their petition to the Pope survives as a unique document of early printing economics, recording edition sizes and the scale of overstock in a way no other source from the period does. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
The maps Sweynheym engraved for Ptolemy’s Geography were among the earliest copperplate illustrations used in a printed book, pioneering a technique that would become central to Renaissance cartography and scientific illustration.

entities/ulrich-gering.title: Ulrich Gering
entities/ulrich-gering.content:
Overview
Ulrich Gering (d. 23 August 1510) was a German printer from Constance (Konstanz) who, together with Michael Friburger and Martin Crantz, established the first printing press in France at the Sorbonne in Paris in 1470. Invited by the Sorbonne professors Guillaume Fichet and Johann Heynlin (also known as Johann von Stein), Gering and his partners printed the first book produced on French soil — the Letters of Gasparino of Bergamo — in a Roman type modelled on the Venetian work of Nicolas Jenson. Gering continued printing in Paris for four decades, eventually adopting Gothic type for a wider commercial market and amassing a fortune that he bequeathed to the university at his death. His press laid the foundation for the Paris book trade, which by 1500 had grown to sixty-six printing offices. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Origins and the Sorbonne Invitation
Gering was born in Constance, a city on Lake Constance in the German-speaking lands. According to the Lorck handbook, he learned the art of printing in Mainz itself. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The impetus for bringing printing to Paris came from the Sorbonne. In the late 1460s, two distinguished scholars of the university — Guillaume Fichet, a doctor of the theological faculty, and Johann Heynlin (Johann von Stein, after his birthplace Stein bei Konstanz), known in the records of the Sorbonne as Jean de Lapierre — saw printed books being produced in Germany and resolved to introduce the art to France. ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md] Chevillier, writing in 1694 as Doctor and Librarian of the Sorbonne, calls them “les deux Theologiens de la Societe de Sorbonne Guillaume Fichet & Jean de Lapierre, qui prirent soin de faire venir les Allemands a Paris, pour pratiquer dans l’Universite l’Art de l’Imprimerie.” ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Fichet wrote to the historian Robert Gaguin describing “a wonderful new method for the production of books” that had been discovered in Germany. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Heynlin, a native of the Constance region, summoned his countryman Ulrich Gering to Paris. Gering brought with him Michael Friburger (from Colmar) and Martin Crantz (from Basel), and the three Germans set up the first printing office in France within the buildings of the Sorbonne itself, around 1469—1470. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Chevillier’s Sorbonne Archive Account
Chevillier, drawing directly on the Sorbonne’s own records, provides the most detailed account of how the invitation was made. He writes that Jean de Lapierre (Heynlin) wrote to Germany to summon the printers, having the contacts and knowledge of his native country to do so. The epigram on the first book confirms this with the words: A tuis Germanis Impressoribus, quos tua Germania in hanc Urbem librarios ascivisti (“From your German printers, whom your Germany brought to this city”). ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Chevillier speculates that Lapierre may have been from the same town or diocese as Gering, and that this common origin was a powerful motive for the printers to come to Paris: “je ne doute point que ce ne fut un puissant motif a ces premiers Imprimeurs pour se resoudre a venir a Paris, s’y voyant invitez & attendus par un habile homme de leur Nation, qui parloit le meme langage, qui leur offroit le College de Sorbonne pour y exercer leur Art, ses soins pour leur preparer des Copies, voir les Epreuves, & les aider dans leurs Editions; outre le gain & le profit qui paroissoit leur dans une grande riche Ville comme Paris.” ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
The press was set up in a hall of the Sorbonne at the beginning of 1470, the year in which Jean de Lapierre was Prior of the Sorbonne for the second time (his first priorate was in 1467). Chevillier establishes this from the registers of the Faculty of Theology. ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
The exact year is further confirmed by eight verses the printers placed at the end of their Sallust edition, which refer to the war that Louis XI declared against Charles Duke of Burgundy in 1470. ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Fichet’s letters to Pope Sixtus IV, Cardinal Bessarion, Cardinal Rolin, and Rene King of Sicily are all dated from the Sorbonne. The letter to Cardinal Rolin is dated “Ex aedibus Sorbonae Idibus Julii” 1470, proving the press was active by mid-1470 at the latest. ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
The First Books and Roman Type
The first book printed in Paris was a collection of the Letters of Gasparino of Bergamo (Gasparini Pergamensis Orthographiae Liber), issued in 1470. It was printed in Latin, using a Roman-form type despite the German origin of the printers. Putnam records the opinion of bibliographer Humphreys that specimens of the beautiful volumes printed in Venice by Nicolas Jenson had been sent to Paris and served as models for the earliest Paris press. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Chevillier’s First List (Sorbonne Editions, 1470-1471)
Chevillier, cataloguing books still preserved in the Sorbonne library in his own time (1694), provides the following list of early Sorbonne imprints, all printed in the same round Roman type from the same matrices ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]:

Gasparini Pergamensis Epistolarum Liber — one volume in 4to (two copies in Sorbonne)
Lucii Annaei Flori de Tota Historia Titi Livii Epitome (Florus’ epitome of Livy)
Caii Crispi Sallustii de Lucii Catilinae Conjuratione Liber and De Bello Jugurthae — one volume in 4to on vellum
Guillelmi Ficheti Alnetani Rhetoricorum Libri Tres (Fichet’s own Rhetoric) — one volume in 4to on vellum
Gasparini Pergamensis Orthographiae pars prima & secunda with Guarini Veronensis Libellus de Diphthongis — one volume in 4to
Epistolae Cynicae (Letters of Phalaris translated by Francesco Aretino, Letters of Brutus with Mithridates’ reply, Letters of Crates the Cynic) — one volume in 4to
Roderici Zamorensis Episcopi Speculum Humanae Vitae — one volume in folio
Bessarionis Cardinalis Epistolae (three letters and two orations, including a translation of Demosthenes’ First Olynthiac) — one volume in 4to
Guillelmi Ficheti Epistolae (to Cardinal Bessarion, Pope Sixtus IV, Rene King of Sicily, Cardinal Rolin, and Guillaume Chartier Bishop of Paris) — one volume in 4to
Laurentii Vallae Elegantiarum Linguae Latinae Libri Sex with preface by Petrus Paulus Senilis and a letter from Jean de Lapierre — one volume in folio
Jacobi Magni Sophologium — one volume in folio

Chevillier notes that this list is not complete — some books have been lost, and there are reasons to believe not everything was preserved. He mentions, for instance, that Johann Saubert catalogued a Quintilian “de l’impression de Paris 1471” at Nuremberg, which would have been printed by Gering if genuine. ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Typographic Description of the First Editions
Chevillier gives a precise physical description of these first Paris editions:
“Tous ces Livres sont imprimez de memes Lettres, fondues dans les memes Matrices. C’est un Caractere rond, de gros Romain. Comme l’Impreffion ne faisoit que de naistre, & que ces premiers Livres sont comme des essais de l’Art, il se trouve en quelques-unes des Lettres a demi formees, & des mots a moitie imprimez, qu’on a achevez avec la main. Il y a meme quelques Epitres imprimees, dont l’inscription n’est que manuscripte. Il n’y a point de Lettres capitales. Les premieres Lettres des Livres & des Chapitres sont omises, on y a laisse de la place pour y peindre une premiere lettre en or ou en azur. Il y a plusieurs mots abregez. … Le papier n’est pas bien blanc, mais il est fort, & bien colle. L’Encre est d’un beau noir. Ils imprimerent aussi quelques lignes en lettres rouges sur velin.” ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
The books have no titles, no foliation (page numbers), and no signatures (collation marks). Signatures — alphabetical letters at the bottom of pages — were not introduced in Paris until 1476. Titles first appeared in 1477. Catchwords (reclames) were adopted late, around 1520. ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Fichet’s Preface Letter
Fichet placed at the head of the Gasparino volume a letter addressed to Jean de Lapierre, serving as a preface. In it he thanks Lapierre for “the great advantage he has procured for the study of the Sciences, by means of the Germans he has brought.” The letter includes the key phrase: A tuis Germanis Impressoribus, quos tua Germania in hanc Urbem librarios ascivisti (“From your German printers, whom your Germany brought as librarians/booksellers to this city”). ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
The printers added an eight-verse epigram to Paris itself, including the lines:
Primos ecce Libros, quos haec industria finxit / Francorum in terris, aedibus atque tuis. / Michael, Udalricus, Martinusque Magistri / Hos impresserunt, ac facient alios.
(“Behold the first books, which this industry produced in the lands of the Franks, and in your buildings. Michael, Ulrich, and Martin, the masters, printed these, and will make others.“) ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Chevillier uses this evidence to refute the claim that Nicolas Jenson was the first to bring printing to France — noting that Jenson’s books were all printed in Venice, not in Paris. ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Move to Rue Saint-Jacques and the Second Press
Around 1473, after Fichet had left for Rome (called by Pope Sixtus IV at the end of October 1471) and Lapierre was preparing his return to Germany, Gering and his partners moved their press from the Sorbonne to a house on the rue Saint-Jacques at the sign of the Soleil d’or (Sun of Gold). ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Chevillier’s Second List (Rue Saint-Jacques Editions)
Chevillier provides a second list of books printed at the Soleil d’or, including ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]:

Guido de Monte Rocherii, Manipulus Curatorum (folio, completed 1473 — names all three printers)
Bartholomaei Pisani, Summa de Casibus Conscientiae (folio — with verses naming Martin, Michael, and Ulrich as “quos genuit Germania, nunc Lutetia pascit”)
Guillelmi Durandi, Rationale Divinorum Officiorum (folio, 1475)
Roderici Zamorensis, Speculum Vitae Humanae (folio, 1475, reprinted from the Sorbonne edition)
Biblia Sacra (folio — the first Bible printed in France, with verses naming the three printers)
Gregorii Magni Homiliae (folio, 1475)
Leonardi de Utino, Sermones de Sanctis (folio, 1476)
Angeli de Aretio, Tractatus de Criminibus (folio, 1476)
Legenda Aurea Jacobi Januensis (folio)
Francisci de Platea, Tractatus de Usuris (folio, 1476)
Jacobi Magni, Sophologium (folio, 1477)
Leonardi de Utino, Sermones Quadragesimales (folio, 1477, near Saint-Benoit)
Aristotelis Opera quaedam Logica (folio, printed by Gering alone)
Guidonis de Monte-Rocherii, Manipulus Curatorum (4to, 1478, Gering alone)
Alberti Eyb, Margarita Poetica (folio, 1478, Gering alone)
Joannis Nider, Consolatorium Timoratae Conscientiae (4to, 1478, Gering alone)
And many others through the 1480s, including works by Nicolas de Lyra, Gregory the Great, and Hugues Cardinal

New Types for the Second Press
Chevillier notes that the books of this second list are not in the same type as the first. “Ces Editions de la rue S. Jacques, sont toutes nouvelles Lettres, fondues dans de nouvelles Matrices. On ne voit plus dans leurs autres Impressions ces Caracteres de Sorbonne, qui ont este les premiers essais de l’imprimerie de Paris: & il semble qu’en retirant leurs Presses de cette Maison, ils rompirent tous les instruments qui n’avoient servi qu’a faire voir le nouvel Art dans son enfance.” ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
He identifies three or four kinds of characters in these editions. Some books (the 1473 Manipulus Curatorum, Bartholomew of Pisa, Durand) use a type resembling common handwriting of the time, “comme une escriture a la main” — not Gothic, similar to the Mainz impressions of Peter Schoeffer. Others (the Bible, the Zamora, the Sophologium, the 1475 Gregory) use a larger version of the same type. Still others (the Eyb, the 1478 Guido, the Aristotle, the Nider) use a large, clear, well-formed Roman letter. Chevillier judges these later Roman types to be as beautiful as the best Venetian work of John and Wendelin of Speyer, Nicolas Jenson, John of Cologne, and others. ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
“De sorte que c’est une louange due avec justice a Ulric Gering, qu’il est non-seulement le premier Imprimeur de Paris & de France, mais qu’il est celui qui a porte cet Art dans un haut degre de perfection en ce Royaume, & qui a imprime de la plus belle Lettre qui ait paru en son temps.” ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
The first Bible printed in France was Gering’s edition (c. 1476), as Chevillier notes: “Ulric imprima la sainte Bible l’annee 1475. C’est la premiere Bible imprimee en France.” ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Naturalisation and the Partners’ Departure
In 1474, following the example of Peter Schoeffer’s agent (whose stock had been seized by the Paris guild on the grounds of alien ownership), Gering applied for and received letters of naturalisation from King Louis XI, securing legal protection for his business. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
In 1477, after the printing of Leonard of Udine’s Sermones Quadragesimales, Crantz and Friburger abandoned printing and returned to Germany. Chevillier confirms this: “depuis cette annee-la il n’est plus parle d’eux nulle part, au lieu qu’on voit Gering passer le reste de ses jours a Paris, y faire de nouveaux Associez, avec qui il fait beaucoup d’Editions.” ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md] ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Move to Gothic Type and Later Career
When Gering moved his printing office from the Sorbonne to the rue Saint-Jacques, he adopted the Gothic (Textura) type that was more popular with the general reading public — the so-called lettres de forme or Allemand (German) letter. This shift from Roman to Gothic marked a strategic turn: the Sorbonne scholars preferred Roman type for humanist and classical texts, but the larger commercial market favoured the familiar Gothic script. Smaller type used for schoolbooks was called lettres de somme, decorative initial capitals were lettres cadeaux, and the rounded chapter initials were lettres tourneurs. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Chevillier on Gering’s Gothic Period (Part II)
Chevillier devotes the entire second part of his dissertation to the question of Gothic printing. He states that Gering “commenca l’Imprimerie a Paris, il ne donna que de bons Caracteres, & tint ferme long-tems contre le torrent des autres Imprimeries, qui introduisoient la Lettre Gothique. Mais enfin il se laissa entrainer lui-meme.” ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Gering was not the first to use Gothic in Paris — Chevillier notes that a Gregory of Rimini on the Sentences was printed in Gothic as early as 1482, and Louis Martineau printed in Gothic in 1484. The third list of Gering’s books shows a mixture: the Holkot, the Alberc, Guy Juvenal, St. Gregory on the Canticles, and Nicolas Perot are in Roman letters; the rest — except Virgil — are in Gothic letters, which Gering employed for books used in Church service and others. ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Chevillier’s Third List includes Gering’s works with his partner Berthold Rembolt at the Soleil d’or, rue de Sorbonne (after 1489), including ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]:

Rob. Holcot, Librum Sapientiae (4to, 1489)
Albertus Magnus, De arte vivendi (4to, 1491)
Guidonis Juvenalis, Interpretatio in Elegantias Vallae (4to, 1494)
Psalterium ad usum Parisiensem (4to, 1494, vellum)
S. Gregorii, Moralia in Job (folio, 1495)
Diurnale Ecclesiae Parisiensis (8vo, 1495)
Breviarium Ecclesiae Cameracensis (8vo, 1497)
Missale ad usum Ecclesiae Parisiensis (folio, 1497, vellum)
P. Virgilii Maronis Opera (folio, 1498, corrected by Paulus Malleolus)
S. Gregorii, Expositio super Cantica (4to, 1498)
Horae B. Mariae Virginis (8vo, 1498)
S. Augustini Sermones (folio, no date)
Guillelmi Peraldi, Sermones (8vo, 1498)
Venerabilis Bedae, Expositio in Epistolas Pauli (folio, 1499)

Chevillier describes the Corpus Juris Canonici with gloss — the largest work Gering printed — as having been printed in red and black, and notes that a later edition of it perished because it was Gothic (“a peri parce qu’il etoit Gothique”). ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
De Vinne remarks that Gering, like Jenson, found it expedient to cut and cast types in the Round Gothic fashion, because “the Roman character was most admired by scholars” but the market demanded Gothic. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Later in his career, Gering took on Berthold Remboldt as a partner. Remboldt’s edition of Virgil was so carefully corrected by scholars that it was considered error-free. Gering’s masterpiece was the Corpus juris canonici, a monumental work printed in five columns, using multiple typefaces in red and black. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Competition and Rival Presses
As early as 1473, two of Gering’s former employees — Peter Keyser (Caesaris) and John Stol — set up a rival printing office in Paris, having served a three-year apprenticeship with Gering. This competition drove down book prices. Gering responded by reprinting their titles as soon as he could procure copies, and each house boasted of the superior accuracy of its editions. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]
Chevillier’s Account of Caesaris and Stol
Chevillier provides a much more detailed account of these rival printers. They were “deux Allemands qui etudioient dans l’Universite” — two Germans studying at the University. Caesaris had taken the degree of Master of Arts. They were instructed by Gering and established the second printing press in Paris in 1473. ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Their first work was the Manipulus Curatorum of Guy de Montrocher (1473), which the University later cited as evidence that the earliest printers were Masters of Arts. Their other works included:

Speculum Vitae Humanae of Zamora (folio, identified by colophon: Presserunt Petrus Caesaris, simulgue Johannes)
A collection of opuscules (includes Tractatus de Origine Nobilium, Poggio’s letter on the infelicity of princes, Aeneas Silvius on the miseries of courtiers, Seneca on remedies of fortune)
Seneca’s Epistles (4to, 1473)
Valerius Maximus (folio, 1475)
The beautiful Dialogue of Ockham (2 vols. folio, 1474) — which Naude had attributed to Gering but Chevillier, comparing the types, convincingly assigns to Caesaris and Stol

Chevillier notes that all these books are in Roman letters, “mais beaucoup moins belles que celles des premieres Editions d’Ulric Gering rapportees cy-dessus dans la premiere Liste.” ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Caesaris lodged on the rue Saint-Jacques at the sign of the Swan (le Cygne), in a house belonging to the Sorbonne doctors who granted him a life lease in 1473. He held it until 1505. ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Despite this rivalry, the number of presses in Paris grew rapidly. By the end of the fifteenth century, there were sixty-six master printers in Paris. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Death and Legacy
Ulrich Gering died on 23 August 1510 in the house of the Sun of Gold, rue de Sorbonne, after working at printing in Paris for forty years. ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
Chevillier records that he was assisted in his final illness by the doctors of the Sorbonne, with whom he had lived for more than thirteen years “en qualite d’Hote & de Bienfaicteur.” ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
His burial place was disputed: du Boulay and Mentel claimed he was buried in the Chapel of the College of Montaigu, pointing to a painting of Gering among the benefactors there. But Chevillier argues this painting — showing Gering among more than twenty benefactors, dated 1546 — proves only that he was a benefactor, not that he was buried there. Chevillier suggests he was more likely buried at Saint-Cosme, his parish church. The testamentary executor asked for three brass tablets recording Gering’s legacy: one in the Sorbonne chapel (still there in Chevillier’s time), one in the Church of the Mathurins (where the University assembled), and one in Saint-Cosme (where he was probably buried). ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
The Society of the Sorbonne kept his memory annually with an Office of the Dead: Vespers, Matins with nine psalms and nine lessons, Lauds, a High Mass, and two low Masses. The Necrologe read: “Obiitus Ulrici Gering, Civis ac Incolae Parisiensis, insignis Benefactoris hujus Domus.” ^[raw/articles/chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris.md]
By his death he had amassed a considerable fortune, the bulk of which he willed to the Sorbonne — a final gesture of loyalty to the institution that had first brought him to Paris four decades earlier. ^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Gering’s historical significance rests on three foundations:

Pioneer of French printing: He established the first press in France, a full generation before printing was widely adopted in the country.
University press model: His press operated under the direct auspices of the Sorbonne, producing scholarly texts selected by university authorities — an early model of the academic press.
Typographic transition: His career traced the arc from Roman to Gothic and back, reflecting the tension between humanist scholarly taste and commercial market reality that would define European printing for centuries.

Though the first book printed in the French language (Les Grandes Chroniques de France, 1476) was issued by Pasquier Bonhomme rather than Gering, the foundation that Gering laid in the rue Saint-Jacques and the Sorbonne enabled Paris to become, within a generation, one of the largest book-trade centres in Europe. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
