entities/venice.title: Venice
entities/venice.content:
Venice
Venice became the leading printing city of fifteenth-century Europe. If mainz was the birthplace of European movable-type printing, Venice was the first great international capital of the printed book. By 1500 it had produced thousands of editions and had become a center for humanism, classical scholarship, commercial publishing, and the development of Roman and italic type. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Why Venice Was Ideal for Printing
Venice combined several advantages: long-distance trade networks, capital, paper supply from northern Italy, skilled artisans, a large literate elite, and access to Greek and Latin scholars. Its maritime commerce made books easier to distribute, while its republican institutions could grant privileges and monopolies to printers. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The first rag paper was made around 1300, and paper-making soon became important in Italy. In 1373 the Venetian Senate forbade the exportation of rags from the dominions of the Republic — an act that recalls the edict of Ptolemy Philadelphus in 290 BC forbidding the export of papyrus from Alexandria. This ensured a domestic supply of raw materials for paper production. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Venice’s watery defences made it nearly impossible to blockade or besiege, so its commercial undertakings went on practically undisturbed even during wars that devastated other Italian states. The Venetian government was also prompt to recognise the value of the new industry, giving more care to furthering printing by privileges, concessions, and recognition of the printers’ guild than any other Italian state. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Venetian Connections with Constantinople and the Greek Manuscript Trade
Venice possessed valuable relations with the Greek world through its old commercial ties with Constantinople and Asia Minor. Through these connections Venetian printers secured first pick of the manuscripts of many Greek texts that became known to Europe between 1490 and 1540. These texts were brought partly from monasteries spared by the Turkish conquerors and partly by scholars who fled Constantinople after the fall of 1453. As word spread that Venice offered compensation for editing Greek texts for the press, impoverished refugee scholars found their way to the city, bringing their manuscripts with them. This gave Venice a commanding lead in Greek publishing. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Opposition from Scribes: The Genoa Card-Makers Petition (1474)
The scribes and manuscript copyists recognised that their art was endangered by the new technology. In 1474, the copyists of Genoa went so far as to petition the Senate for the expulsion of the printers. The petition was disregarded, but the incident demonstrates the resistance the new art faced. The Genoese scribes had earlier petitioned (1471) to be protected from printer competition in producing breviaries, Donati, and psalters, claiming these were their livelihood. The Genoese printers were eventually driven out by a cabal of scribes, making Genoa the only Italian city where the old scriptores succeeded, even temporarily, in expelling the printers. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
The Cost and Scale of Early Venetian Printing
As an example of printing costs in Venice, an agreement from 1478 shows that 930 copies of the complete Bible were printed for 430 ducats (paper furnished separately). The selling price of Bibles in 1492 varied from 6 to 12 ducats (approximately 30 to 60 in late-19th-century valuation, depending on binding). ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
By the 1490s a demand had arisen for cheap popular books. Venetian printers increasingly used Gothic type because it saved space, enabling lower prices. The last decade of the fifteenth century was the peak of Venetian printing: it witnessed the founding of the Greek press by Aldus, Vlastos, and Caliergi, the first printing in Arabic and other Eastern languages, and the beginning of romance and novel publishing. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
The Venetian Printing Industry Structure
An Unregulated and Hazardous Trade
The printing industry grew up too quickly for the regulations that normally controlled medieval crafts. As Erasmus wrote acidly, becoming a printer was a great deal easier than becoming a baker. This freedom of access explains the bewildering variety of people involved in printing — from noblemen like Andrea Badoer and Francesco Viaro (whose names stand on copyrights of the 1490s) to debt-ridden former teachers and choir-masters like Gerard of Lisa. The “boom” of the fifteenth-century press in Venice was a mad scramble in which numerous competitors trampled one another underfoot for a vision of prosperity that few attained. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Survival Rates of Printing Companies
Rather more than 100 printing companies have been identified in Venice up to 1490: twenty-three were still active during the following decade; only ten survived the century. Some were so small and short-lived that the only surviving traces of their existence are two or three unattributed and often undated editions. As Lowry captures the contrast: “the printer, better informed, complained of the ‘treacherous rage and rivalry which are usual in this miserable trade.’ He knew that he was operating in a transient, hazardous and ruthless world.” ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Capital Investment and Labour Costs
The first obstacle for any printer was capital equipment. Jenson’s workshop contents were valued at 500 ducats — a very high figure for the time. The press itself was the least problematic item: a wooden printing press could be bought for as little as 16 ducats (as recorded in a 1474 sale in Padua). Far more costly was type — the punches, matrices, and type-metal required specialised skills. Goldsmiths figure largely in early printing because the filing of letter-forms onto steel punches was familiar from their work with hallmarks, coins, and seals. Subcontracting began very early: Gutenberg paid 100 gulden to the goldsmith Dunne. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Labour was also expensive. A compositor in Padua earned 3 ducats per month in 1475 — precisely the sum the Venetian government offered in 1492 to a skilled hydraulic engineer. The master printer was normally responsible for housing and feeding his workmen, costing between 5 and 50 ducats per year in rent, facing constant problems of fluctuating food prices. Disputes were frequent and domestic: a group of compositors in Padua once staged a walk-out because their beds had not been made. They were sacked. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The Rise of the Publisher-Underwriter
The need for capital investment soon created a special kind of entrepreneur — the publisher or underwriter. The Frankfurt merchant Johan Rauchfass (“Big John”) regarded even his shares in Jenson’s company as little more than an exotic item in his portfolio. Lucantonio Giunti and the Scotto family operated as professional underwriters, forming contracts with several different printers. Giunti more than doubled his company’s capital base between 1491 and 1499, and had almost doubled it again by 1509. Andrea Torresani was active as a printer, bookseller, and underwriter for more than a decade before forming a partnership with Aldus. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
From the first decade of its existence, the Venetian printing industry was acquiring a thoroughly capitalistic structure, with control passing into the hands of merchants and printer-booksellers. By the end of his life, Jenson was concerned almost entirely with sales. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Syndicate Structures
Printers banded together to spread risk. In 1507, the de Tortis brothers, Zorzi Arrivabene, Lucantonio Giunti, and Amadeo Scotto set out a joint plan for five years. Expenses and profits were divided into four equal shares: Giunti and Scotto provided only financial backing (one share each); Arrivabene and the de Tortis offered four presses and paper (third share). Printed sheets were stored in a warehouse to which each partner had a key, and decisions on prices and print runs were taken by majority vote. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Other contracts reveal the harsh realities of the financier-craftsman relationship. In 1478, Leonardus of Ratisbon and Nicholas of Frankfurt agreed to produce 930 copies of the Bible over nine months. Nicholas provided paper and 243 ducats expenses; Leonardus handled press-work but could draw the money only in instalments as each batch of sheets was delivered, and was barred from taking other work. As Lowry summarises: “the craftsman, in fact, was bound hand and foot to the financier.” In Padua, the printer Peter Maufer ended with debts of 225 ducats to his sponsor Bartolomeo Valdezocco, who took possession of the entire workshop. The new contract made him “the servant” of the financier. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The 1472-3 Overproduction Crisis
An uncontrolled enthusiasm for the classical revival, inspired by the scholars who advised printers, deluged the Italian market with more Latin classics than it could absorb. The Venetian industry reeled, its output declining by 65 per cent in 1473. In Rome, Sweynheim and Pannartz claimed to have printed 20,475 copies but were left with unsold stock, their workshop “full of printed sheets, empty of necessities.” This crisis taught printers caution: both Jenson and John of Cologne followed much more conservative policies after 1475. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The Academic Market and Legal Publishing
Law made the fortunes of the leading printers. Legal texts accounted for 29 per cent of Jenson’s output and 48 per cent of John of Cologne’s; later, 51 per cent of Arrivabene’s and 53 per cent of Torresani’s editions were legal. The Venetian industry was perfectly placed to supply the nearby universities of Padua, Bologna, Pavia, and Ferrara. A legal text represented a large investment in paper, time, and labour, but for established men who could sound out the market, profits could be sure and large. The printer Bonetus Locatellus avoided law entirely and concentrated on philosophy — which accounted for over half his total production — while Torresani brought out Aristotelian commentaries in the early sixteenth century. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The printers’ caution and conservatism extended beyond legal texts. They favoured established circles of readers and did little to encourage a popular market, playing follow-my-leader with academic trends. By the early 1490s they were operating in predictable grooves. Classical authors remained popular — Virgil, Horace, the elegiac poets, satirists, Livy, and above all Cicero — with Philippus Pincius reprinting Virgil four times during the 1490s alone. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
German Immigrant Printers and the Venetian Industry
For the first decade of its existence, the Venetian printing industry was dominated largely by German immigrants. John of Speyer came from Speyer; his brother Windelin continued after him; John of Cologne was from Cologne; Nicholas of Frankfurt and Leonardus of Ratisbon both operated in Venice. Even the humanist Giorgio Merula, while working enthusiastically for John of Cologne, could not forget that the invention had come from “that once rugged and brutish land of Germany.” ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
When Italian printers began to push themselves forward after 1480, they still came from outlying towns and kept their local origins before the public — Philippus Pincius of Mantua, Bernardinus Benalius of Bergamo, and Andrea Torresani of Asola. Differences of dialect and local prejudice were strong: it was perilously easy for sophisticated, metropolitan Venetians to treat the newcomers as boorish, grasping, and provincial. Until the age of Aldus, there was little sign of anything more than a business relationship between printers and scholars. The printer, with his grubby ground-floor workshop and drunken assistants, was regarded as a small artisan — a world apart from the humanists he served. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The Jenson-Torresani-Barbarigo Office and the Aldine Partnership
Andrea Torresani and the Jenson Inheritance
Andrea Torresani of Asola was active as a printer, bookseller, and underwriter for more than a decade before he formed a partnership with Aldus Manutius. His claim to have worked with Jenson’s types and the fact that some thirty founts similar to Jenson’s design can be traced across Italian centres suggest that Jenson’s technical legacy flowed directly into the Aldine Press. The tradition that Jenson sold matrices to other printers is strongly supported by this evidence. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The Barbarigo Partnership
The Aldine Press was not a small scholarly venture but a powerful organisation underwritten by one of the most successful publishers of the age (Torresani) and the nephew of the titular head of the Venetian state. A notarial act discovered by Mario Brunetti in the records of the Procuratori di San Marco reveals that Pierfrancesco Barbarigo — son of Doge Marco Barbarigo and nephew of Doge Agostino Barbarigo — was a formal shareholder in the company founded in 1495. The act speaks of “a company for the printing of books between the late lord Pierfrancesco Barbarigo…on the one side, and the late lord Andrea Torresani, bookseller, with the late lord Aldus de Manutiis…also taking a certain part.” ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Pierfrancesco Barbarigo was not merely a sympathiser who helped Aldus on one occasion, but a shareholder who put the weight of his capital and the influence of his ducal family name behind the company from its very beginning. Zuane Bembo, writing admiringly of Pierfrancesco’s son Santo, noted that Santo’s father had “helped Aldus with several thousand ducats.” The documents show payments divided squarely down the middle: one half going to the Barbarigo estate, the other to Torresani (whose share is linked with Aldus’s name). The working capital and profits were divided into two equal shares, with the Barbarigos controlling one and Torresani and Aldus jointly holding the other. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The Physical Book Trade and the Printers’ Quarter
The printers rapidly took over the parishes of San Zulian and San Paternian as their particular quarter. By the early 1490s, rank upon rank of bookstalls tempted the passer-by walking from the Rialto down the Merceria towards San Marco. Two of the largest and fastest-growing private libraries of the age belonged to Venetian citizens: the diarist Marin Sanudo and Cardinal Domenico Grimani. The look of the city itself was affected by the burgeoning trade in printed books. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
First Venetian Printers
The Decor Puellarum and the Earliest Books
The first book printed in Venice was the Decor Puellarum (A Treatise of Instruction for Young Girls), but its date is disputed. Venetians claimed it was printed in 1461, but the weight of authority places it at 1471. The printer was Nicolas Jenson, a Frenchman, and the contest for priority in Italian publishing rests between Jenson and the two Germans of Subiaco. Another early volume, Epistolae Familiares, appeared in 1470 from John of Speyer (Johannes de Spira), a German who received a monopoly from the Venetian government in 1469. A fourth early book, Miracoli della Gloriosa Verzine, was printed by an Italian, Lavagna of Milan, and was the only early printed Venetian book in the Italian language. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
The 1469 Monopoly Grant to John of Speyer
The earliest official document relating to the printing-press in Venice was published in 1493 by the Abbate Jacopo Morelli, prefect of the Marcian Library. This document is an order of the Collegio (cabinet) of Venice, dated September 18, 1469, proposed by the Doge’s councillors, granting John of Speyer (Johannes de Spira), a German resident, a five-year monopoly on printing in Venice and its territories. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Lowry notes that petitions of this sort were very common in Venice — they covered everything from improved windmills to experiments with poison-gas — and were normally treated with the same polite encouragement John received; few came to anything. The thirty or so members of the College who voted on the privilege had much else on their minds: war with the Ottoman power in the Aegean, the manoeuvring of Italian neighbours suspicious of Venice’s rapid mainland expansion, and above all the preservation of the lucrative Eastern trade Venice had monopolised since her defeat of Genoa in 1381. John’s petition was a small item of extra business, and there was little to show that printing would transform the city more radically than the Sultan would ever do. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
John died within months of gaining the monopoly in 1470. His work was continued by his brother Windelin, but the privilege died with the original holder and competitors were soon thrusting themselves forward. A disgruntled scribe complained in 1473 or 1474 that the city was “stuffed with books” — and he was perfectly right: 176 editions had been published since the beginning of the decade; by the end of the same decade the figure would be 593; by the end of the century roughly 150 Venetian presses had turned out over 4,000 editions. This represented nearly twice the known production of Paris (Venice’s nearest rival), between a seventh and an eighth of total European output, and, roughly, twenty books per individual member of the Venetian population. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
John of Speyer was one of the few early printers to record his edition sizes. His first edition of the Epistolae Familiares comprised just 100 copies, but demand was so great that a second edition of 600 copies was begun four months later and completed (in two impressions) within three months. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Madonna Paola, Widow of John of Speyer
The widow of John of Speyer, Madonna Paola — daughter of the painter Antonello da Messina — played a remarkable role in the early Venetian printing industry. After John’s death, she brought her personal talents to bear on cementing and diversifying the interests of John of Cologne’s company, which had salvaged the remains of Windelin of Speyer’s operation after the overproduction crisis of 1473. She first moved in with the printer Manthen (though apparently without marrying him), then at an unknown date married another printer, Rinaldus of Nijmegen, who was promptly drawn into the syndicate. Finally, in 1477, she married off her daughter Hironima to the prosperous bookseller Gaspar of Dinslaken, who gained a dowry of 3,000 ducats — well above the limits permitted in Venice — and was immediately made a partner. Hironima, long after, still held stocks valued at 660 ducats in 1511 and was owed a further 207 ducats in gold by Lucantonio Giunti. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Nicolas Jenson and the Growth of Venetian Printing
Nicolas Jenson, born in Champagne c. 1420, was sent by Charles VII to Mainz in 1458 to learn the secrets of printing. He returned to France in 1461 but found no opportunity there; by 1465 he was in Venice, and in 1470 he began a printing and publishing business that became the most important in Italy. He perfected one of the most admired Roman types of the fifteenth century, giving printed pages a clarity and proportion that contrasted sharply with the dense Textura of the gutenberg-bible. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Lowry provides crucial new detail on Jenson’s career and business. If the tradition that Jenson was trained in the French royal mint is correct, this would explain much about his success, his influence, and the size of his investment. To the trained metallurgist, filing letter-forms onto steel punches was a familiar task from experience with hallmarks, coins, and seals — the punch, matrix, and mould processes were readily derived from existing mint techniques. He valued the contents of his workshop at the very high figure of 500 ducats, specifically excluding the steel punches which he bequeathed separately to one of his partners. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Marin Sanudo called Jenson “richissimo,” the most celebrated publisher in Venice during the 1470s. Jenson died in 1480 as a papal Count Palatine and the head of an international company, but his actual fortune — approximately 4,000 ducats as revealed by his will — was modest by Venetian standards: a mere tenth of the sum one spice-dealer made from a single year’s shortage, and nothing alongside the hundreds of thousands left by Venice’s merchant-noblemen. Sanudo’s epithet captured the reputation of printers’ wealth in a city where “the glitter of gold was more inviting than anywhere in fifteenth-century Europe.” ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Jenson’s Business Partnerships and “The Company”
Jenson was backed from an unknown date by two Frankfurt merchants, “Big John” Rauchfass and Peter Uglheimer (a considerable book-collector in his own right). Uglheimer’s shares in this triangular partnership were ultimately liquidated by the payment of 1,000 ducats in gold to his heirs. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
During the central and later 1470s, Jenson and the rival company of John of Cologne fenced cautiously — Jenson concentrating on legal texts, John of Cologne on commentaries — both anxious to avoid the overproduction that had choked the market in 1472-3. But in 1478 plague convulsed the Venetian industry: exactly half of the twenty-two active companies either suspended business or left the city. The two main rivals, among the few strong enough to survive, decided that there was more to be gained by joining forces. On 29 May 1480 a protocol brought into being the five-year syndicate of Nicholas Jenson, John of Cologne, and Company — a partnership to which John made an initial contribution of nearly 5,000 ducats worth of books. This syndicate was able to turn out some twenty folio editions in the next twelve months and exercised such absolute domination of the Venetian industry that it became known simply as “The Company.” Both main partners died almost immediately afterwards. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
By the end of his life Jenson was concerned almost entirely with sales rather than production, a sign of the capitalistic structure overtaking Venetian printing. Law made the fortunes of both Jenson and John of Cologne, accounting for 29 per cent of the Frenchman’s output and 48 per cent of the German’s. According to Victor Scholderer’s calculations, rather more than fifty presses turned out some 600 editions up to the end of 1481: of those, 260 (43 per cent) were the work of Jenson and John of Cologne’s companies alone; their numerous rivals averaged only seven editions each. As Scholderer commented, there was “a sharp contrast between the few successful men at the top and the crowd of transient and financially embarrassed phantoms down below.” ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Jenson’s Types and the Torresani Connection
In 1479, Jenson sold to Andrea Torresano of Asola (later Aldus Manutius’s father-in-law) a set of his punched matrices, which probably became the foundation of the Aldine Press plant. That same year Pope Sixtus IV made Jenson a Count Palatine. Jenson died in 1480. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Lowry adds that Andrea Torresani claimed to have worked with Jenson’s types, and some thirty founts similar to Jenson’s design can be traced in various Italian centres — the strongest suggestion that Jenson also sold matrices to other printers. In 1475 one of Jenson’s partners, Johan Rauchfass, directed Francesco da Bologna (possibly the later Francesco Griffo) to copy two of Jenson’s Gothic founts, probably by striking matrices from his punches. This provides a direct technical connection between Jenson, through Torresani, to Aldus, linking the most celebrated Venetian printing houses. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The three earliest Venetian printers — John of Windelin, John of Speyer, and Nicolas Jenson — employed Roman, Gothic, and Greek characters. Before Greek fonts existed, blanks were left in texts for Greek passages to be filled in by hand. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1.md]
Aldus Manutius and the Portable Book
Aldus Manutius, active from the 1490s, made Venice central to the history of compact scholarly books. His Aldine Press issued Greek and Latin classics, popularized the small octavo format, and used italic type cut by Francesco Griffo. In this form, the printed book became not only a library object but a portable intellectual tool. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Lowry emphasises that the company of Barbarigo, Torresani, and Manutius represented a fusion of economic and intellectual power that could not easily have been copied. Aldus was the most active member of the most active printing industry in Europe, at least between 1499 and 1504, then again after 1512. He produced editions of up to 3,000 copies — and must be regarded on purely numerical grounds as the most important focus for the distribution of literature to contemporary Europe. He produced first editions of 94 classical and post-classical Greek writers, including Plato, Aristotle, Herodotus, Thucydides, Xenophon, Demosthenes, and all the Greek dramatists except Aeschylus. This amounted to an almost complete cross-section of the Greek literary heritage as reconstituted by the fifteenth-century humanists. Erasmus wrote that Aldus was producing a library not limited by place or time, and Thomas More sent his fictional traveler Raphael Hythlodaye beyond the known world with Aldine editions in his luggage. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
The partnership operated with Aldus as the academic force — selecting material, hiring compositors who could work with Greek type, and preparing editions — while Barbarigo provided capital and political connections, and Torresani contributed commercial expertise. The Annulment of 1542 spoke of the company as the foundation of Torresani and Barbarigo, with Aldus only “taking a certain part.” Aldus’ share was never stated but cannot have been large: all payments were divided squarely down the middle between the Barbarigo estate and Torresani. ^[raw/articles/lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius.md]
Significance
Venice shows the second stage of the printing revolution. Gutenberg’s system solved production; Venice solved scale, design, distribution, and cultural prestige. The city linked movable-type to commercial publishing, classical learning, and durable typographic standards. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]

entities/william-caxton.title: William Caxton
entities/william-caxton.content:
Overview
William Caxton (c. 1422 — 1491) was the first English printer and the man who introduced the printing press to England. Born in Kent, he spent most of his adult life in Bruges as a successful cloth merchant and Governor of the English Nation, before taking up printing late in life. He learned the art in Cologne (1471—1472), set up a press in Bruges with Colard Mansion (1473—1474) where he printed the first books in the English language, and in 1476 moved his press to Westminster, England, where he established it at the Sign of the Red Pale in the Almonry of Westminster Abbey. Over the following fifteen years he printed about 100 titles, many of them translations he made himself, and played a crucial role in the development and standardisation of English as a literary language. He died in 1491, and his business was taken over by his successor, Wynkyn de Worde.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Early Life and Apprenticeship
Caxton was born in the Weald of Kent, probably around 1422. The exact year is uncertain; the conventional range of 1421—1424 is inferred from the fact that he was apprenticed in 1438 to Robert Large, a wealthy mercer of London and a future Lord Mayor. Apprenticeships typically lasted seven years and ended at age 24, which suggests a birth year of about 1421—1422.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Robert Large was one of the most eminent merchants of the City of London, and admission to his household was, under the conditions of the time, evidence that Caxton came from a family of good standing. William Blades, the great Caxton bibliographer, believed Caxton to be a descendant of the Caunstons, who held the manor of Caunston in Kent. The young Caxton received the education of a merchant’s apprentice — practical training in accounting, correspondence, and the cloth trade, rather than the university learning he would later acquire on his own.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Bruges and the English Nation
In 1441, after Robert Large’s death, Caxton was sent to Bruges, then the commercial capital of northern Europe and the seat of the Burgundian court. There he became a member of the “English Nation” — the term used for the association of English merchants residing in Bruges, who controlled the wool and cloth trade between England and the Continent. He rose steadily in this mercantile community and was eventually elected Governor of the English Nation in Bruges, a position roughly equivalent to a consul, responsible for representing and regulating English commercial interests in the city.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
A colony of Flemish wool-manufacturers had long been established in the Weald of Kent, so Caxton’s early environment had given him some familiarity with Flemish language and customs before his departure — an advantage that would serve him well throughout his long residence abroad. He lived in Bruges for about thirty-three years, during which time the city rivalled Paris as the literary capital of northern Europe. The Burgundian court under Philip the Good and later Charles the Bold was a great patron of the arts, and the ducal library contained nearly three thousand magnificent illuminated manuscripts.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The Burgundian Court and the Turn to Literature
After the marriage of Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, to Margaret of York (sister of King Edward IV of England) in 1468, Caxton’s position brought him into close contact with the Burgundian court. Margaret took a keen personal interest in Caxton and induced him to give up his mercantile career and enter her service as a kind of literary adviser and secretary. He received a yearly salary and devoted himself to literary pursuits.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
It was in 1469, in this new role, that Caxton began the translation of Le Recueil des Histoires de Troye (The Collection of the Histories of Troy), a popular romance compiled by Raoul Lefevre, chaplain to Philip the Good. The translation was a labour of love that he undertook in his spare time, writing by candlelight after his official duties. When the completed translation found favour at court — Margaret herself is said to have encouraged and corrected it — Caxton conceived the idea of multiplying copies by the new mechanical art of printing.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Learning to Print in Cologne (1471—1472)
The critical question of where Caxton learned the art of printing was long debated. Earlier German historians maintained that he was trained in Cologne, and the evidence now strongly supports this view. In 1471, Caxton was in Cologne, where Ulrich Zell (one of Peter Schoeffer’s proteges) had set up a press in 1466. Caxton contracted with one of Zell’s assistants, Johann Veldener, “at his great charge and dispense” either as a teacher, a printer for his book, or both. The expense was considerable, but Caxton, now in his early fifties, was determined to bring the art to England.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
It is possible that a book known as the Cologne Chronicle (1499), which records that “the art of printing was first invented in Mainz, by Johann Gutenberg,” also notes that Caxton was in Cologne learning the trade. At any rate, the types Caxton later used show clear affinities with those of the Cologne school.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Printing in Bruges with Colard Mansion (1473—1474)
Returning to Bruges from Cologne, Caxton set up a press in collaboration with Colard Mansion, a skilled scribe and illuminator who had been active in Bruges since at least 1450. Mansion had received commissions from Duke Philip for illuminated manuscripts and was a member of the Guild of St. John the Evangelist, the book-makers’ guild. Together, they produced the first six books from Caxton’s press, which are conventionally listed as:^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]

The Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (Caxton’s own English translation, c. 1473—1474) — the first book ever printed in the English language, 351 folio pages.
Le Recueil des Histoires de Troye (the French original, printed shortly after).
The Game and Playe of Chesse — a moral treatise on chess, translated by Caxton, with a prologue.
Les Meditacions sur les Sept Pseaulmes Penitenceaux.
Les Fais et Processus du Chevalier Jason.
Les Quatre Dernieres Choses Advenir.

The Recuyell in particular was a landmark: it established that a market existed for printed books in English, and the copies sent across the Channel sold well enough to encourage Caxton to make the move to England. Mr. Blades was of the opinion that these Bruges books, while nominally Caxton’s productions, were actually printed by Mansion with Caxton acting as publisher and translator — but in learning to supervise the work, Caxton gained sufficient technical knowledge to carry on a printing office of his own.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Move to Westminster (1476)
In 1476, after an absence of about thirty-five years, Caxton returned to England, bringing with him a printing press, type, and equipment. He established his workshop in the precincts of Westminster Abbey — not within the church itself, but in the Almonry, a space within the abbey enclosure where alms were distributed to the poor. The tenement he occupied was called the “Sign of the Red Pale” (the Rood Pale, a reference to a red-painted post or paling). In the same enclosure stood the almshouses built by Lady Margaret Beaufort, mother of the future Henry VII. Caxton described his address as “in thabbey of Westmynstre” or “at the reed pale,” and his proximity to the court gave him access to the nobility and clergy who became his patrons and customers.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
The First Printed Book in England (1477)
The first book printed by Caxton in England that carries a complete imprint is The Dictes or Sayengis of the Philosophres (November 1477), a translation by Anthony Woodville, Earl Rivers (the brother-in-law of Edward IV), of a French compilation of sayings from the philosophers. This is generally regarded as the first book printed on English soil. It is a folio volume, printed in Caxton’s Type 2, and its colophon reads: “Emprynted by me William Caxton at Westmestre the xviii day of Novembre the yere of our lord M.CCCC.lxxvii.”^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
By comparison, the first printed book in Italy appeared in 1464 (a Donatus), the first in France in 1469 (the Letters of Kaspar von Bergamo), and the first in Germany proper (after Gutenberg’s Bible) in various cities from the 1450s onward. England was a latecomer, but Caxton’s press quickly became productive.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Caxton’s Output and Major Works
Over the fifteen years of his Westminster press (1476—1491), Caxton produced approximately 94 to 100 separate editions. Blades listed 98 identified works, plus 8—10 doubtful ones, including 6 or 7 printed in Bruges and 3 that appeared after Caxton’s death, probably completed by his successor Wynkyn de Worde. Of these, at least 33 survive as unique copies, often in imperfect condition, suggesting that the actual number of editions was substantially larger.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The most notable of Caxton’s publications include:


Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales (1477, first edition) — This was the first printed edition of Chaucer’s masterpiece, a folio of 742 pages. Caxton printed it in two editions; the second, of 622 pages, corrected from a superior manuscript. Chaucer’s works dominate Caxton’s list: he also printed The Parliament of Fowls, Anelida and Arcite, Boethius de Consolacione Philosophiae (translated by Chaucer), The Complaint of Chaucer to His Purse, and others. Caxton’s Chaucer editions were instrumental in establishing Chaucer’s canonical status.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]


Malory’s Le Morte d’Arthur (1485) — Caxton printed Sir Thomas Malory’s great prose romance of King Arthur, the only manuscript source for the work that survives. Caxton divided Malory’s narrative into twenty-one books and added his own preface, explaining that he had printed the book “to the entente that noble men may see and lerne the noble actes of chyvalrye.” Without Caxton’s edition, Malory’s work might have been lost entirely.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]


The Golden Legend (1483) — At 892 pages, this was Caxton’s largest and most ambitious work, a translation of Jacobus de Voragine’s Legenda Aurea with additional lives of English saints. It is profusely illustrated with woodcuts, and although no complete copy survives intact, it is considered Caxton’s masterpiece. The illustrations, however, are crude by continental standards: wood-engraving in England was still in its infancy.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]


Polychronicon (1482) — Ranulf Higden’s universal history, translated by John of Trevisa, continued by Caxton to the year 1461. A folio of 890 pages.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]


The Chronicles of England (1480) — Often called “Caxton’s Chronicle,” based on the old Brute chronicle, brought down to the Battle of Towton (1461).^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]


The Mirrour of the World (1481) — Caxton’s own translation of a French encyclopaedic work, with woodcut illustrations.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]


Reynard the Fox (1481) — Caxton’s translation from a Flemish version of the popular beast-epic.^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]


Other publications included editions of Lydgate, Gower, Cicero’s De Senectute and De Amicitia (translated by Worcester and Tiptoft), Cato (the first English book with woodcuts — two crude cuts that Blades believed to be the earliest specimens of wood-engraving in England), and numerous service-books (breviaries, missals, and psalters following the Use of Salisbury).^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Caxton as Translator
Caxton was not merely a printer but a prolific translator. He translated many of the works he printed, often adding prologues and epilogues in which he speaks in his own voice — a novelty in the history of the book. These personal remarks are one of the chief sources of information about his life and working methods, and they give the reader a vivid impression of a modest, earnest, and self-deprecating man. He frequently apologises for his “symple” and “rude” English, and laments the rapid change of the language:

“Certaynly our langage now used varyeth ferre from that which was used and spoken when I was borne.”^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]

In the prologue to the Recuyell, he describes the labour of translation in affecting terms:

“I have practysed and lerned at my grete charge and dispense to ordeyne this said book in prynte after the maner and forme as ye may here see, and is not wreton with penne and ynke as other bokes ben.”^[raw/articles/pearson-gutenberg-and-art-of-printing.md]

Caxton’s English is, for modern readers, much more accessible than Chaucer’s. His printing fixed a version of the London-Midlands dialect that became the foundation of modern standard English. The choices he made in spelling, vocabulary, and idiom — sometimes conscious, sometimes accidental — were propagated through his hundreds of copies and influenced generations of writers and readers.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
Caxton’s Advertisement
Around 1480, Caxton issued what is generally regarded as the first printed advertisement in English. It reads:

“If it plese any man spirituel or temporel to bye ony pyes of two and thre comemoracios of Salisburi ose emprynted after the forme of this present lettre whiche ben and truly correct, late hym come to Westmenester in to the almonesrye at the reed pale and he shall have them good chepe.”^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]

This handbill — a single printed sheet — advertises service-books (breviaries or ‘pie’ books) for the Salisbury (Sarum) Use, printed in the typeface shown on the sheet itself.
Typefaces
Caxton used a series of eight distinct typefaces during his career (often catalogued as Type 1 through Type 8), all of them Gothic or Blackletter in design. The earliest — used in the Bruges books — was a Burgundian or Bastard script, a form of cursive Gothic popular in the Burgundian court circle. Over the course of his career in London, his types evolved toward a heavier, more angular textura better suited to the English market. His types were mostly cut by himself or by his assistants, rather than imported from the Continent. They are generally considered crude in comparison to the sophisticated types of Gutenberg, Schoeffer, or the Venetian printers, but they were serviceable and legible.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]^[raw/articles/de-vinne-invention-of-printing.md]^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Lorck’s assessment is blunt: “Die Technik sowohl als die Korrektur seiner Bücher waren hochst mangelhaft und die Holzschnitte sehr untergeordneter Natur” (The technique as well as the proofreading of his books were extremely deficient, and the woodcuts of a very subordinate quality). This was typical of English printing at the time: there was no tradition of fine book-production in England comparable to that of Italy, Germany, or the Low Countries.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Character and Business Methods
Caxton was not, like many continental printers, an enthusiast who loved the art for its own sake. He was a practical English businessman who printed books that he hoped would sell. He did not seek scholarly editions of the classics or impose exacting standards of typographical correctness. His selection of titles — chivalric romances, moral treatises, edifying histories, popular saints’ lives, and devotional works — reflects the taste of the middle-class and courtly audience he served. If the survival rate of his books (only 5—600 copies of his editions survive, most in British collections) is any guide to the rate of consumption, his business judgment was sound: copies were read to pieces.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]
At the same time, he was conscious of his historical role. He describes himself with characteristic modesty as “the symple person William Caxton,” and marvels that “the most excellent and renowned art of printing has come into my hands.” His prologues and epilogues reveal a man of genuine piety, loyalty to the crown, and gratitude for the opportunity to serve the commonwealth by disseminating useful knowledge.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]^[raw/articles/pearson-gutenberg-and-art-of-printing.md]
Death and Succession
William Caxton died late in 1491, honoured and respected. The exact date is not recorded, but the evidence from documents and from the dates of his last publications suggests the end of that year. He was buried in the churchyard of St. Margaret’s, Westminster, within the shadow of the Abbey where he had plied his craft. The site is now lost.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
His business was taken over by his successor, Wynkyn de Worde (originally a native of Wortheim in Alsace, who had come to England as Caxton’s assistant). De Worde continued the Westminster press at the Sign of the Sun in Fleet Street, publishing well into the sixteenth century and expanding Caxton’s legacy. Some authorities list three books that appeared after Caxton’s death but were evidently in preparation while he lived, and these are attributed to de Worde’s completion of Caxton’s work.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
The 400th anniversary of Caxton’s introduction of printing into England was celebrated in 1877 with great splendour; a Caxton Celebration Exhibition was held in London, and bibliographers like William Blades produced definitive studies of his life and work.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Significance
Caxton’s significance lies not in technical innovation — by continental standards his presswork was mediocre — but in three profound contributions:


The introduction of printing to England — He brought the art across the Channel fifteen years after the first presses were set up in Paris, and within a generation England was part of the European print network.


The printing of English literature — Without Caxton’s editions, many major works of Middle English literature, including Malory’s Morte d’Arthur and multiple works by Chaucer, might have survived in only a handful of manuscripts or been lost entirely. He fixed the canon of English literature at a critical moment.


The standardisation of the English language — Caxton’s choice of the London-Midlands dialect as the medium for his printing had incalculable consequences. English was changing so rapidly that Caxton himself noted how “the language now used varies far from that which was used and spoken when I was born.” His press both fixed the language on the page and accelerated the process of standardisation, laying the foundation for modern written English.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]


In the broader narrative of the spread-of-printing across Europe, Caxton represents the penetration of the new art into the Atlantic archipelago. Like the printers who carried the invention from Mainz to Cologne, Basel, Rome, Venice, and Paris, Caxton was a crucial node in the network of knowledge: a businessman who, in his fifties, mastered a new technology and used it to serve the needs of his country. The fact that he was not a German, not a scholar, and not a trained artisan made him an unlikely apostle of the press; but he succeeded precisely because he understood the English market and supplied it with what it wanted.^[raw/articles/john-man-gutenberg-revolution.md]^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]

entities/wynkyn-de-worde.title: Wynkyn de Worde
entities/wynkyn-de-worde.content:
Overview
Wynkyn de Worde (d. 1534), also spelled Wynken de Worde, was the dominant English printer of the early sixteenth century and the successor to william-caxton. Born in Wortheim (Worth) in Alsace (then part of Lorraine), he came to England around 1476 as Caxton’s assistant and foreman, inherited the business after Caxton’s death in 1491, and over the following four decades transformed English printing by moving it out of Westminster into the City of London, vastly expanding its output, and shifting the market from expensive folios to smaller, cheaper books for a broader readership. He printed over 800 editions during his career — far more than Caxton’s approximately 100 — and was the first to introduce Roman type to England. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Early Life and Move to England
De Worde was born in Worth or Wortheim, a town in Alsace (the German-speaking region of Lorraine), from which his adopted surname derives. The precise year of his birth is not recorded, but he was already active as a skilled craftsman by the time Caxton returned from Bruges to establish his press at Westminster in 1476. He appears to have accompanied Caxton to England, serving as his assistant and foreman through the fifteen productive years of the Westminster press. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Lorck records that he was born in Lorraine and came to England together with Caxton, becoming his collaborator and successor, and that as a printer he significantly surpassed his master. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Succession to Caxton (1491)
When Caxton died late in 1491, de Worde inherited the printing business — the presses, type, stock, and the lease of the Westminster premises at the Sign of the Red Pale in the Almonry of Westminster Abbey. He completed several works that Caxton had left unfinished at his death, including the Vita Patrum (the Lyves of Holy Faders) and the second edition of Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales. In the colophon to the Vita Patrum, de Worde paid tribute to his master, recording that Caxton had died while translating the work. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
For the first nine years of his independent career (1491—1500), de Worde continued to operate from Caxton’s old premises in Westminster, styling himself “Printer to Margaret, etc., the King’s Grandame” — referring to Lady Margaret Beaufort, the mother of King Henry VII, who became his patron. During this period he printed the Acts of Parliament with the Royal Arms, and a steady stream of books in the Caxton tradition. ^[raw/articles/pearson-gutenberg-and-art-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Move to Fleet Street (c. 1500)
Around 1500 (the exact year is debated; Lorck gives “probably 1499”), de Worde moved the press from Westminster to Fleet Street in the City of London, to a shop at the Sign of the Sun in the parish of St. Bride. This was the first printing press established within the City of London proper — a crucial step that brought the printing trade into the heart of the commercial and legal district. Fleet Street would remain the centre of English printing and publishing for the next four centuries. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Sign of the Sun became one of the best-known addresses in the English book trade. From this location de Worde produced the vast majority of his editions, building a printing and publishing operation that dwarfed anything Caxton had attempted. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Output and Publishing Strategy
De Worde’s output was prodigious. Modern scholarship attributes more than 800 separate editions to his press, compared to Caxton’s roughly 100. Pearson and Putnam both give the contemporary estimate of “over four hundred volumes” in forty years, but more recent bibliographic research has substantially raised that number. ^[raw/articles/pearson-gutenberg-and-art-of-printing.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Where Caxton had concentrated on large folio volumes — richly decorated chivalric romances, substantial histories, and the works of Chaucer — de Worde shifted the business strategy decisively toward smaller, more affordable formats. He printed predominantly in quarto and octavo, producing:

Grammars and schoolbooks: Latin grammars by Donatus and Alexander de Villa Dei, and English instructional works. Lorck specifically notes that grammatical works formed a significant part of his output. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
Popular romances: Bevis of Hampton, Guy of Warwick, The Four Sons of Aymon, and other chivalric tales that appealed to middle-class readers.
Religious works: Primers, books of hours, devotional tracts, and new editions of The Golden Legend.
Practical manuals: Books on husbandry, medicine, and conduct.
Poetry and literature: New editions of Chaucer, Gower, Lydgate, and Skelton.

This strategy of publishing smaller, cheaper books for a wider audience was de Worde’s most important commercial innovation. He identified and exploited a growing market among merchants, lawyers, students, and literate laypeople — readers who could not afford Caxton’s expensive folios but could buy a quarto or octavo pamphlet for a few pence. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Typographical Innovations and Illustration
De Worde significantly improved the technical quality of English printing. Where Caxton’s types had been crude by continental standards, de Worde cut new punches and cast superior type. Lorck describes his types as “completely different from those used before, distinguished by the beauty of their casting and excellent preparation,” and notes that de Worde was probably his own type founder, since his types are frequently found in the works of other printers. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
He was the first English printer to introduce Roman type into England, using it to mark striking passages in his texts, though he continued to use blackletter for most of his work. ^[raw/articles/pearson-gutenberg-and-art-of-printing.md]
De Worde made extensive use of woodcut illustrations and decorative borders. He was the first English printer to regularly use title-page borders, often repeating the same popular blocks across many editions. Many of his woodcuts were imported from the Continent, purchased at second hand from Flemish and German printers, and were often used indiscriminately — the same block might appear in a romance, a saint’s life, and a grammar, with little regard to its appropriateness to the text. The practice was widespread among early English printers and reflected the scarcity and expense of original illustration. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Major Publications
Among de Worde’s most notable publications were:

The Golden Legend (new editions, 1493 and later) — Jacobus de Voragine’s collection of saints’ lives, which Caxton had translated and first printed in 1483. De Worde issued several new editions, keeping this popular work in print.
Le Morte D’Arthur (1498) — Sir Thomas Malory’s Arthurian romance, following Caxton’s first edition of 1485.
The Canterbury Tales (1498, 1502) — Chaucer’s masterpiece, in editions that built on Caxton’s.
Polychronicon (1495) — Ranulf Higden’s universal history, in folio. Lorck singles this out as one of de Worde’s most beautiful books. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
The Ship of Fools (1509) — Alexander Barclay’s English adaptation of Sebastian Brant’s Narrenschiff, with woodcut illustrations.
The Book of Hawking and Hunting (reprints of the St. Albans Press’s famous treatise).
Numerous editions of Alexander de Villa Dei’s Doctrinale and other Latin grammars that were standard school texts.

De Worde appears not to have undertaken any translating or significant editorial work himself, distinguishing him from Caxton, who had been his own translator for many of his publications. No English printer of the sixteenth century, Putnam notes, is to be placed among the scholar-printers of the calibre of Aldus Manutius, Froben, or the Estiennes. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Printer’s Mark and Relations with Rivals
De Worde’s printer’s mark combined Caxton’s monogram (the letter W with a cross) with his own name, consciously linking his press to that of his predecessor. In this he may have been asserting continuity and legitimacy in a trade where reputation was everything. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
His chief rival was Richard Pynson, another of Caxton’s former assistants, who became King’s Printer. Pynson was a more refined printer who introduced better types from France and produced some of the finest English books of the period. Despite being competitors, Lorck records that de Worde and Pynson maintained good relations. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md] ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Copyright and Privileges
In the early 1530s, de Worde became involved in what is considered the first recorded copyright dispute in English printing. A printer named Trevers reprinted, without authorisation, a work for which a privilege had been granted to de Worde. The preface to de Worde’s second edition (1533) contains a vigorous complaint against this “piratical interference with his rights,” though it does not record what action was taken. The work in question was probably Thomas Lupset’s Treatise of Charitie, though the identification is not certain. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Death and Succession
Wynkyn de Worde died in 1534 at an advanced age (Lorck says he died “hochbetagt” — very old). An edition of Aesop’s Fables bearing the date 1535 still carries his name, suggesting that some work may have been completed posthumously or that his name was used by his successor. ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
His printing business was taken over by his apprentice and former assistant, John Byddell, who continued the press at the Sign of the Sun. Byddell had been working with de Worde since at least the 1520s and maintained the character of the press, though the output declined in volume. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md]
Significance
Wynkyn de Worde was arguably more influential on the shape of English printing than Caxton himself, for three reasons:


Scale: He multiplied the output of the English press by a factor of eight, producing over 800 editions and making printed books far more common and accessible than they had been in Caxton’s day.


Format innovation: By shifting from folios to quartos and octavos, he created a market for cheap books that reached far beyond the aristocratic and clerical readers who had been Caxton’s primary audience. This was the beginning of popular publishing in England.


Location: His move from Westminster to Fleet Street established the geography of the English book trade for centuries. Fleet Street became synonymous with printing and publishing, a connection that endured until the late twentieth century.


In the broader narrative of the spread-of-printing across Europe, de Worde represents the consolidation and commercialisation of the press in England. Where william-caxton brought the technology and established its viability, de Worde built the business model that made it sustainable. He was not a scholar-printer like the great continental figures, but a practical businessman who understood his market and supplied it efficiently. His early-typefaces and woodcut practices, while crude by continental standards, were appropriate to the English market of the time, and his output laid the foundation for the flourishing of English printing in the later sixteenth century. ^[raw/articles/putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol2.md] ^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
