Wiki Index

Content catalog. Every wiki page listed under its type with a one-line summary.
Read this first to find relevant pages for any query.
Last updated: 2026-08-25 | Total pages: 89

Entities

abraham-ortelius — Abraham Ortelius (1527-1598), Flemish cartographer; creator of the Theatrum Orbis Terrarum (1570), the first modern atlas.
aldus-manutius — Aldus Manutius (c. 1449-1515), Venetian printer and scholar; Aldine Press, italic type, octavo format, Greek classics, Hypnerotomachia Poliphili, the Aldine Academy.
amsterdam — Amsterdam, the seventeenth-century world printing capital; Blaeu atlases, Elzevir and Athias presses, map and newspaper printing, press freedom, the 1672 watershed.
antwerp — Antwerp, the sixteenth-century printing capital of the Low Countries; the Plantin-Moretus Officina (312-year firm), the Polyglot Bible, the Spanish Fury of 1576 and the shift of printing to the north.
anton-koberger — Anton Koberger (c. 1440-1513), Nuremberg printer-publisher; 24 presses, 100+ workers, 220+ editions, the Nuremberg Chronicle (1493).
blaeu-family — The Blaeu family of Amsterdam; Willem Jansz Blaeu (1571-1638), atlas publisher, press improver, scholar-printer; Johan and Cornelis Blaeu; the firm’s end in the 1672 fire.
christopher-plantin — Christophe Plantin (c. 1520-1589) and the Plantin-Moretus family; Antwerp’s Officina Plantiniana, the Polyglot Bible, 1,500+ publications, Jan Moretus and the Vulgate monopoly, Balthasar Moretus and the Rubens connection, the three-century firm history, and the Plantin-Moretus Museum.
daniel-bomberg — Daniel Bomberg (c. 1483-1549), Christian printer of Hebrew in Venice; first complete Babylonian Talmud, finest Hebrew types, three Bible editions with rabbinical commentaries.
elzevir-family — The Elzevir publishing dynasty (c. 1580-1712), Leyden and Amsterdam; affordable duodecimo classics, elegant typography.
erasmus — Erasmus of Rotterdam (1466-1536), scholar and humanist; publishing relations with Aldus, Froben, Badius; the Adagia, Greek New Testament (1516), Praise of Folly, Colloquies.
estienne-family — The Estienne (Stephanus) family of scholar-printers in Paris and Geneva; Robert Estienne’s Thesaurus Linguae Latinae (1531), flight to Geneva, Henri Estienne’s Thesaurus Linguae Graecae (1572).
giacomo-gastaldi — Giacomo Gastaldi (c. 1500-1566), Piedmontese cartographer; cosmographer to the Republic of Venice, leading Italian mapmaker of the mid-1500s.
gerard-mercator — Gerard Mercator (1512-1594), Flemish cartographer; Mercator projection, coined “atlas,” globes, maps, and instruments.
giunti-family — The Giunti family of printer-publishers in Venice and Florence; Niccolo di Giunta and Fillippo Giunta, commercial publishing in Renaissance Italy.
jodocus-badius-ascensius — Jodocus Badius Ascensius (1462-1535), Flemish scholar-printer of Paris; nearly 400 works over 25 years, published Erasmus and Budaeus.
johann-froben — Johann Froben (c. 1460-1527), Basel printer and publisher of Erasmus; first printed Greek New Testament (1516), Holbein title borders.
johann-gutenberg — Johann Gutenberg (c. 1400-1468), inventor of movable-type printing; life from Mainz to Strasbourg, partnership with Fust, the 42-line Bible, lawsuit, later years.
johannes-fust — Johannes Fust (c. 1400-1466), Mainz goldsmith and financier; loans to Gutenberg, the 1455 lawsuit, partnership with Peter Schoeffer, the 1457 Mainz Psalter.
mainz — Mainz, birthplace of European typography; Gutenberg’s family and workshop, the 1462 sack and Printer’s Dispersal, the Gutenberg Museum.
martin-luther — Martin Luther (1483-1546) as a publishing phenomenon; the Flugschriften explosion, German New Testament distribution, Wittenberg printers, the shift of German publishing from South to North.
nicholas-of-cusa — Nicholas of Cusa (1401-1464), cardinal, philosopher, and church reformer; the Bursfeld missal project, the 1451 Cyprus indulgences, possible connection to Gutenberg.
nicolas-jenson — Nicolas Jenson (c. 1420-1480), master type designer in Venice; the Jenson Roman type, sent to Mainz by Charles VII in 1458 to learn printing.
peter-schoeffer — Peter Schoeffer (c. 1425-1503), Gutenberg’s apprentice and Fust’s partner; type designer, printer of the 1457 Mainz Psalter, punchcutting refinements.
sebastian-munster — Sebastian Munster (1488-1552), German cosmographer and Hebrew scholar; the Cosmographia universalis (1544), the most popular geography of the 16th century.
strasbourg — Strasbourg, Gutenberg’s experimental city in the 1430s/1440s and an early Rhine printing center.
sweynheym-and-pannartz — Konrad Sweynheym and Johann Pannartz, first printers in Italy (Subiaco 1464, Rome 1467); produced Italy’s first printed book, the Lactantius of 1465.
ulrich-gering — Ulrich Gering (d. 1510), first printer in Paris; Sorbonne press (1470), invited by Fichet and Heynlin.
venice — Venice, the leading fifteenth-century printing capital; Jenson’s Roman type, Aldus Manutius, italic, humanist publishing, and commercial scale.
william-caxton — William Caxton (c. 1422-1491), first English printer; Bruges, Cologne, Westminster, Chaucer, Malory, and English vernacular printing.
wynkyn-de-worde — Wynkyn de Worde (d. 1534), Caxton’s successor; 800+ editions, moved printing to Fleet Street, expanded the English book trade.

Concepts

block-printing — Xylography, the pre-Gutenberg technique of carving entire pages from wooden blocks; Chinese and European history, block-books, playing cards, woodcuts, and limits.
book-trade — The commercial networks, markets, fairs, routes, and institutional buyers that turned printing into a Europe-wide industry.
censorship-of-the-press — How Church and state authorities tried to control printing; Berthold of Mainz’s 1486 edict, the Index, the Venetian privilege system, the Reformation’s explosion of uncensorable pamphlets.
early-printers-tools-and-techniques — Typefounding, punchcutting, the adjustable hand mold, inking, compositing, presswork, and the division of labor in early printing shops.
early-typefaces — The evolution of typefaces in the first 50 years of printing: Textura, Roman, Italic, Fraktur, Greek and Hebrew types, punchcutting economics, and type design.
authors-and-the-printing-press — The slow emergence of the author in the first 250 years of print: from irrelevance and patronage through Erasmus (the first to earn from writing), Luther (who refused payment), the dedication system, Shakespeare (stage-right not book-right), Milton (£5 for Paradise Lost), and Dryden (£1,300 for Virgil).
gutenberg-bible — The 42-Line Bible, the first major book printed in Europe with movable type (c. 1450-1455), physical description, edition size, and significance.
hebrew-and-oriental-printing — Hebrew printing from the Soncino family through Daniel Bomberg (Venice) to Eastern Europe; Christian Hebrew scholarship (Reuchlin, Estienne); oriental presses and polyglot Bibles; unique typographic challenges.
incunabula — Books printed before 1501; definition, physical characteristics, formats, typeface evolution, statistics, and the transition from manuscript to print.
spectrum-of-printed-output — The full range of what came off early presses, organised by market tier: luxury vellum folios, standard editions, school texts, indulgences, broadsides, almanacs, maps, and other ephemera; survival bias and the economics of each tier.
literary-property-and-copyright — The development of copyright in Europe from Venetian privilege systems through the Copyright Act of 1709.
manuscript-culture — The world of scribes, scriptoria, illuminated manuscripts, and book production before Gutenberg’s invention; the cost of books, the pecia system, incunable consciousness.
manuscript-to-printed-book-trade — How the book trade re-invented itself in the first century of printing (1450-1550): from the manuscript pecia system through Koberger’s network, the Frankfurt Fair, guild formation, and the Reformation’s transformation of distribution.
maritime-publications — Printed works for mariners and navigators: pilot books, navigation manuals (Medina’s Arte de Navegar), island books (Bordone’s Isolario), sea atlases (Waghenaer’s Spieghel der Zeevaerdt), and the business of maritime publishing.
map-making-and-the-printing-press — How cartography and printing developed together: Ptolemy’s Geography, the atlas as a new book genre, woodcut vs. copperplate maps, Ulm and Rome Ptolemies, and the atlas-publishing industry.
medieval-libraries — Medieval libraries from the manuscript period: monastic collections, the armarius system, chained libraries, the great collections.
movable-type — Definition, history, and technical details of reusable metal letters; Gutenberg’s hand mold, alloy, punch-matrix process, Korean precedent, and success conditions.
pamphlets-and-ephemeral-printing — Short-format printed matter: indulgences, broadsides, school texts, political pamphlets, Flugschriften, and chap-books; pre-Gutenberg block-prints through the Reformation explosion; survival bias.
paper-in-europe — Paper from Cai Lun’s Chinese invention through the Arab world, Spanish and Italian mills (Fabriano), cost advantage over vellum, 16th-17th century developments, and its essential role in making printing viable.
patronage-and-finance — How capital, credit, patrons, privileges, and lawsuits shaped early printing from Gutenberg and Fust onward.
print-runs-and-pricing — Edition sizes, material costs, pricing factors, and why early printed books multiplied access without yet becoming cheap mass goods.
printers-publishers-and-booksellers — The overlapping roles of printer, publisher, bookseller, editor, financier, and typefounder; the evolution from combined to separate roles; the rise of the pure publisher.
printing-economics — Printing as a high-fixed-cost business: tools, type, paper, labor, risk, scale, and market demand.
printing-revolution — Comprehensive synthesis of the printing revolution: pre-print culture, Gutenberg’s system, Mainz finance, spread across Europe, design and reading, consequences including the Reformation and censorship, and the limits of print in the Islamic world.
publishing-houses-compared — Side-by-side comparison of six major publishing houses (Koberger, Aldus, Plantin, Estienne, Elzevir, Blaeu) by capital, scale, distribution, market position, and longevity.
reformation — The Reformation as a print-amplified religious and political movement; cautious account of print’s role in vernacular controversy and diffusion.
seventeenth-century-printing — How printing transformed in the 1600s: the Blaeu press, Dutch typefounding industry, the birth of the newspaper, the atlas peak (Blaeu Atlas Maior), the novel (Don Quixote, First Folio), Bible printing (KJV, “Wicked Bible”), the English press control struggle, the Statute of Anne (first copyright law), the Frankfurt-Leipzig shift, stereotyping experiments, copperplate replacing woodcut, and Moxon’s Mechanick Exercises.
sixteenth-century-printing — How printing transformed after 1500: the Reformation and vernacular explosion, smaller and cheaper books, the professionalisation of typography, music printing, new genres (atlases, science, travel, the novel), systematic illustration, systematic censorship, the northern shift of the trade, and the maturation of the book trade into an industry.
spread-of-printing — The rapid diffusion of printing across Europe, 1450-1500; Mainz dispersal, regional timelines, German immigrant printers, Venice, Paris, England, and Spain.
the-coster-legend — The Haarlem claim that Laurens Janszoon Coster invented movable type before Gutenberg; Junius’s Batavia account, Van der Linde’s demolition, modern consensus.
the-indulgence-trade — How the Church’s system of indulgences became the first big commercial market for printing; Gutenberg’s 1454-1455 indulgences, the blank-form business model, and the road to the Reformation.
the-printing-press — The physical printing machine from Gutenberg’s wooden screw press through the Blaeu/common press, Stanhope iron press, and Koenig cylinder press.

Comparisons

block-printing-vs-movable-type — Side-by-side comparison of fixed page blocks versus reusable alphabetic type; explains why modularity mattered.
gutenberg-fust-schoeffer — Comparison of the inventor, financier, and technical successor whose conflict and collaboration shaped early Mainz printing.

Primary Sources

angerhofer-in-aedibus-aldi — Angerhofer, Maxwell & Maxwell, “In aedibus Aldi” (1995): BYU Harold B. Lee Library exhibit catalog of Aldine holdings; thematic entries on Greek/Latin classics, humanists, Counter-Reformation print, Manutii as authors, New World books, bindings, and a full library checklist.
chevillier-origine-imprimerie-paris — Chevillier, “L’Origine de l’Imprimerie de Paris” (1694): clean French text; four parts on the Sorbonne press, Gering, Greek/Hebrew types, and the University’s book trade rights.
de-vinne-invention-of-printing — De Vinne, “The Invention of Printing” (1876): comprehensive history of printing from ancient methods through Gutenberg, strong on technical detail and the Coster legend.
draper-intellectual-development-europe — Draper, “A History of the Intellectual Development of Europe” (2nd ed., 1864): full 26-chapter Victorian scientific historiography (Greece → Faith → Reason); wiki mines Ch. XX–XXI on printing, 1470–1500 edition geography, pulpit vs press, newspapers, and liberty of the press.
foxe-acts-monuments — John Foxe, “The Acts and Monuments” (Pratt ed., 1877): the Book of Martyrs; 3 volumes (II, IV, V) from the 8-volume set — a landmark of Elizabethan printing by John Day, foundational for Reformation history.
eisenstein-printing-press-agent-of-change — Elizabeth Eisenstein, “The Printing Press as an Agent of Change” (1979): landmark argument that print constituted a communications revolution — fixity, standardization, the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution, and the permanent Renaissance.
falkenstein-geschichte-buchdruckerkunst — Falkenstein, “Geschichte der Buchdruckerkunst” (1840): Fraktur OCR, ~50% readable; German printing history from origins to 1840.
hoe-history-of-printing-press — Hoe, “A Short History of the Printing Press” (1902): mechanical evolution of the press from Gutenberg’s screw press to power presses.
john-man-gutenberg-revolution — John Man, “The Gutenberg Revolution” (2002): modern narrative biography of Gutenberg, accessible and strong on business and human drama.
karrow-mapmakers-16th-century — Robert W. Karrow, “Mapmakers of the Sixteenth Century and Their Maps” (1993): bio-bibliographies of the cartographers of Abraham Ortelius; 75 entries including Mercator, Munster, Gastaldi, and Cusanus.
lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst — Lorck, “Handbuch der Geschichte der Buchdruckerkunst” (1882): German encyclopedic handbook, strong on block-books and regional printing history.
lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius — Martin Lowry, “The World of Aldus Manutius” (1979): business and scholarship in Renaissance Venice; the Aldine Press, its structure, authors, and distribution.
nature-of-the-book-johns — Adrian Johns, “The Nature of the Book” (1998): revisionist cultural history of English print c. 1580–1720; challenges Eisenstein on fixity; Stationers’ Company, piracy, licensing, and the social construction of print credibility.
copernicus-astronomia-instaurata — Copernicus / Mulerius, Astronomia instaurata (Amsterdam: Wilhelmus Iansonius / Willem Jansz Blaeu, 1617): restored and annotated Latin edition of De revolutionibus with dedication, Osiander preface, six-book index, tables, errata, and computational apparatus.
pearson-gutenberg-and-art-of-printing — Pearson, “Gutenberg and the Art of Printing” (1871): Victorian-era biography combining historical narrative with dramatic dialogue.
putnam-books-and-their-makers — Putnam, “Books and their Makers during the Middle Ages, Vol. II” (1896): book trade and publishing history, strong on censorship, Plantin, Aldus, and Koberger.
putnam-books-and-their-makers-vol1 — Putnam, “Books and their Makers during the Middle Ages, Vol. I” (1896): manuscript book production, monastic scriptoria, libraries, university book trade, and the first printer-publishers of Italy.
stationers-registers-arber-vol1 — Edward Arber (ed.), “Transcript of the Registers of the Stationers’ Company,” Vol. I (1875): Register A (1554–1571), Company ordinances, Barker’s 1582 Report on printing patents.
stationers-registers-arber-vol2 — Arber, Stationers’ Registers Vol. II (1875): Register B (1576–c.1605); Star Chamber decree 1586; freemen, apprentices, book entries of the high Elizabethan trade.
stationers-registers-arber-vol3 — Arber, Stationers’ Registers Vol. III (1876): Register C (1595–1620); late Elizabethan and early Jacobean entries.
stationers-registers-arber-vol4 — Arber, Stationers’ Registers Vol. IV (1877): Register D (1620–1640); late Jacobean and Caroline trade through the Long Parliament edge.
stationers-registers-arber-vol5 — Arber, Stationers’ Registers Vol. V Index (1894): publishers list 1553–1640, bibliographical summary to 1603, general index; Rivington on Company records.
typographical-antiquities-ames — Joseph Ames / William Herbert, “Typographical Antiquities” Vol. II (1786): printer-by-printer bibliography of British and Irish printing to 1600 (Elizabethan masters, patents, imprint catalogues).
van-netten-blaeu-review — Review by Henk Nellen of Djoeke van Netten’s “Koopman in kennis” (2014): Willem Jansz Blaeu (1571-1638), Amsterdam atlas printer and publisher.
winship-gutenberg-to-plantin — George Parker Winship, “Gutenberg to Plantin” (1926): narrative survey of early printing from Gutenberg through the master printers to Plantin; 15 chapters covering Germany, Venice, France, the Low Countries, and the New World.

Queries

primary-sources/angerhofer-in-aedibus-al.title: In aedibus Aldi: The Legacy of Aldus Manutius and His Press (Angerhofer et al.)
primary-sources/angerhofer-in-aedibus-al.content:
In aedibus Aldi: The Legacy of Aldus Manutius and His Press
Paul J. Angerhofer, Mary Ann Addy Maxwell, and Robert L. Maxwell, with binding descriptions by Pamela Barrios. In aedibus Aldi: The Legacy of Aldus Manutius and His Press. Provo, Utah: Friends of the Harold B. Lee Library, Brigham Young University, 1995. xii + ~180 pages (196 PDF pages including plates). ISBN 0-8425-2329-4. LC 95-12312. Internet Archive: inaedibusaldileg0000ange.
Exhibition catalog accompanying a display in the Harold B. Lee Library Special Collections Department, 1 March–15 July 1995, marking the quincentenary of the Aldine Press’s first publications (1495). Thematic, not chronological: selected Aldines and related books from one of the stronger North American Aldine holdings, with full title-page reproductions, colophon transcriptions, collations, binding notes, and bibliographical references keyed to a terminal checklist and bibliography.
Authors and collection context

Paul J. Angerhofer, Mary Ann Addy Maxwell, Robert L. Maxwell — catalog authors; translations by the authors unless noted.
Pamela Barrios — binding descriptions (basic structure and visible decorative tooling).
Collecting foundation: the Marco Heidner collection of c. 500 incunabula and sixteenth-century books, acquired 1966 to support Reformation/Renaissance teaching; curators named in the prefatory matter include Scott Duvall and Chad Flake, with long-term building of the Aldine collection also credited to A. Dean Larsen.
Stated holdings (preface): of the 142 books issued by the Aldine Press before Aldus the Elder’s death in 1515 (Rostenberg & Stern 1977), BYU then held nearly eighty—more than half—including sixteen incunabula; plus 423 titles produced under successors (first partner and father-in-law Andrea Torresani, then son Paulus Manutius, then grandson Aldus the Younger). Total: just over 500 of the 1,120 separate Aldine editions printed 1495–1597 listed by Renouard. Also: books of the press’s Paris agents, a selection of the “Lyon forgeries” (unauthorized Lyonnese reproductions of Aldines issued in Aldus the Elder’s lifetime), and other sixteenth-century imitations.

Arrangement of the catalog
Rather than a straight chronological shelf-list, the exhibit and catalog are grouped thematically around the development of the press’s program:

Noteworthy individual books (highlights)
Greek and Latin classics (Aldus the Elder’s core program)
Contemporary humanist authors
The press under Paulus as printer connected with the Roman Catholic Church / Counter-Reformation print
Writings of the three Manutii as published by their own press
Books tied to Aldine interest in New World exploration
Bindings essay; bibliography; checklist of Aldine editions in the HBLL; index

Each catalogued article typically includes: reproduction of the printed portion of the title page; colophon transcription; collation; binding description; short discussion; and references to standard bibliographies and further literature. Initials and decorative material throughout are taken from the 1499 Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (no. 3); tailpieces from the 1592 Vulgate (no. 53). Title pages missing from the BYU copies of nos. 5, 10, and 12 are transcribed from UCLA copies.
Summary of contents
Preface (p. ix): Funding (HBLL professional development funds; Friends of the Library); acknowledgments to readers and exhibit staff; note that the former Friends of the Brigham Young University Library Newsletter series of exhibit catalogs has been discontinued; cover design uses an initial and the dolphin-and-anchor motif from the 1499 Hypnerotomachia.
Introduction (pp. 1–3 and following): Frames movable type and the press as a communications change comparable to the late-twentieth-century “information revolution.” Humanism predated print and had no intrinsic link to the craft, but created sustained demand for classical texts, Greek/Latin instructional books, and contemporary scholarly and popular works. Aldus trained as a humanist and private tutor; printing was still widely seen as a rough, competitive craft rather than a career for a man of letters. His program: flood Europe with classical Greek and Latin texts and with the grammars and tools students needed—hence the catalog’s opening with Theodoros Gazes and Constantine Lascaris (nos. 1–2).
Key typographic and format claims stressed in the introduction and early entries:

1501 Virgil (no. 5) as the vehicle for two linked innovations: italic type (Francesco Griffo of Bologna; earlier Griffo romans in Bembo’s De Aetna, 1495, nos. 6–7) and the portable octavo format (sheet folded to eight leaves), aimed at gentlemen, schoolmasters, lawyers, and students who wanted books for travel and leisure reading—not only “stately” folios of liturgy or collected fathers.
Immediate counterfeiting of italic, especially elsewhere in Italy and at Lyon; Aldus’s pursuit of early privilege/copyright protections, of limited practical effect against Lyonnese rivals.
Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (Francesco Colonna, 1499, no. 3) as typographic masterpiece—often ranked among the most influential books in printing history for layout, woodcut design, and ornament rather than for continuous reading.
Scriptores astronomici veteres (1499, no. 10) as another illustrated high point (zodiac and astronomical woodcuts).
From 1502, the anchor-and-dolphin device (speed and steadiness; festina lente), first used on Poetae Christiani veteres (no. 8)—treated here as an early and influential model of the printer’s mark among sixteenth-century shops.
Religious and vernacular strands alongside the classics (e.g. Catherine of Siena’s letters, no. 4).
Overall assessment: lasting fame more typographic than purely scholarly; printer–scholar alliance that showed fine scholarly books could be produced profitably and that convinced scholars of print’s value; diffusion of Italian Renaissance scholarship across Europe.

Greek classics and early program (catalog nos. ~1–11, printed pp. ~4–21+): Specimen entries begin with:

No. 1 — Theodoros Gazes, Grammatikes introductivae libri quattuor; De mensibus; with Apollonius Dyscolus, De constructione, and Aelius Herodianus, De numeris — Aldine Greek grammar program and early Greek fonts.
No. 2 — Constantine Lascaris (and related Greek instructional material); bilingual/interleaved pedagogical practice; connection to the first dated Greek book tradition and to Bessarion’s circle.
No. 3 — Francesco Colonna, Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (1499) — physical description, woodcuts, design influence.
No. 4 — Catherine of Siena, Epistole devotissime.
No. 5 — Virgil (1501) — italic + octavo.
Nos. 6–7 — Bembo / early roman and type comparisons (De Aetna line).
No. 8 — Poetae Christiani veteres — first anchor-and-dolphin.
Further Greek poets and school texts (Theognis, Pythagoras Carmen aureum, Oracula Sibyllina, Hesiod, Theocritus, etc.).
No. 10 — Scriptores astronomici veteres (Firmicus Maternus, Manilius, Aratus, Proclus, etc.).
Aristotle multi-volume Greek program (entry cluster around printed p. 21).

Latin classics (section from printed p. ~25; nos. through the 30s): Portable and scholarly Latin: Book of Hours / Horae; Philostratus Vita Apollonii; Lucian; Aesopic and mythographic miscellanies (Babrius, Cornutus, Palaephatus, Heraclides, Horapollo, Aphthonius, Hermogenes, etc.); Plutarch Moralia; Pindar with Callimachus, Dionysius Periegetes, Lycophron; Musaeus Hero and Leander; Aeschylus; Horace; Catullus–Tibullus–Propertius; Pliny the Younger with De viris illustribus, Suetonius De grammaticis, Julius Obsequens; Livy; Ovid; Cicero Epistolae familiares and rhetorical works; Scriptores rei rusticae (Cato, Varro, Columella, Palladius) in successive issues (e.g. 1514 cluster); Tertullian Apologeticum with Lactantius, etc.
Contemporary authors (from printed p. ~65; nos. ~33–47): Humanist and vernacular production beyond pure classics—e.g. Cardinal Bessarion In calumniatorem Platonis; Angelo Poliziano Opera; Giovanni Gioviano Pontano (verse and prose Opera); Jacopo Sannazaro (Arcadia; Italian Opera); Judah Abrabanel (Leone Ebreo) Dialoghi d’amore; Pietro Bembo Gli Asolani; Baldassare Castiglione Il libro del cortegiano; Isabella Sforza Della vera tranquillità dell’animo; Erasmus’s Latin Euripides (Hecuba & Iphigenia in Aulis); Guillaume Budé De asse; Christophe de Longueil; Matthaeus Fortunatus’s Seneca Naturales quaestiones; Vinko Pribojević Della origine et successi de gli Slavi.
Church, censorship, and Counter-Reformation print (from printed p. ~89; nos. ~48–53): Entries including conciliar/canonic material, Tridentine Index librorum prohibitorum, and related official or confessional productions—documenting the later Aldine firm’s entanglement with Catholic reform print and control of reading.
The Manutii as authors (from printed p. ~99; nos. ~54–60): Works written by family members and issued at the press—e.g. Paulus Manutius on Cicero’s orations; Aldus the Younger on Tuscan and Latin elegance, Latin orthography, and the Vita di Cosimo de’ Medici; other grammatical and historical titles under Paulus and the younger Aldus.
New World / geography cluster (from printed p. ~113; nos. ~61–67): Aldine or Aldine-related books tied to exploration, geography, and Venetian historical writing—e.g. Dionysius Periegetes Orbis terrae descriptio; Galeazzo Flavio Capella; Bordone; Pietro Bembo Historiae Venetae libri XII; Paulus Manutius Epistolae, etc.
Bindings (from printed p. ~125): Separate discussion by Pamela Barrios of bindings on the exhibited copies (structure and visible decoration rather than full tool-by-tool monographs).
Bibliography (from printed p. ~129): Works cited; keys the short-title references used in individual articles.
Checklist of Aldine editions in the Harold B. Lee Library (from printed p. ~137): Library-wide checklist beyond the exhibited subset—principal finding aid for the BYU Aldine corpus as of 1995.
Index (from printed p. ~167).
Relevance to the wiki
Complements lowry-world-of-aldus-manutius with a bibliographical, copy-specific, and typographic lens rather than a full business-and-scholarship monograph. Useful for:

Concrete census of what a major teaching collection held of Aldine output (Elder vs Torresani/Paulus/Younger; Renouard 1,120 baseline)
Entry-level narratives of italic, octavo, Griffo, anchor-and-dolphin, festina lente, and the Hypnerotomachia as design object
Lyon counterfeits and early privilege/copyright practice
Later firm history: Paulus, Roman/Catholic commissions, Tridentine Index, Aldus the Younger as author-printer
Binding evidence on surviving copies; path into standard Aldine bibliographies (Renouard and later lists cited in the catalog)

Does not replace Lowry for partnership structure (Barbarigo/Torresani), shop economics, or deep archival reconstruction of the Neacademia.

primary-sources/chevillier-origine-impri.title: L'Origine de l'Imprimerie de Paris (Chevillier)
primary-sources/chevillier-origine-impri.content:
L’Origine de l’Imprimerie de Paris (Chevillier)
André Chevillier, L’Origine de l’Imprimerie de Paris. Dissertation historique et critique, en quatre parties (Paris: Jean de Laulne, 1694). PDF scan, 36,179 lines of clean text. The long ‘s’ (ſ) appears as ‘f’ in the text, which is standard for 17th-century French typography.
Author
André Chevillier (d. 1720) was a doctor of the Sorbonne and librarian of the Maison et Société de Sorbonne. He had direct access to the Sorbonne’s archives, making his account of the introduction of printing to Paris particularly valuable. His position gave him firsthand knowledge of the documents and records that later historians had to reconstruct from secondary sources.
Summary of Contents
Part I — The Establishment of Printing in Paris
Chapter I: Three men share the honor of the invention — Gutenberg, Fust, and Schöffer. A re-examination of Trithemius’s account. The engraving of letters is not a new invention. The first printed book. Early printed books with false dates. The five oldest dated printed books that survive today. Whether printed books only received dates from 1466 onward. A claim of a print earlier than 1459 is dismissed as too hasty. Johann Fust brings his Bible to Paris (1461) where it is mistaken for a manuscript; he is prosecuted and forced to flee.
Chapter II: The University of Paris hears about the new art. The professors Guillaume Fichet and Johann Heynlin invite German printers to Paris. The three printers — Ulrich Gering from Constance, Michael Friburger, and Martin Crantz — arrive and set up the first press within the Sorbonne itself. The first book printed in Paris: the Letters of Gasparino of Bergamo (1470). Fichet’s role and his letters about the new art.
Chapter III: Further evidence for the origin of printing in Paris, partly drawn from the Sorbonne’s own archives. Details of the first Parisian editions.
Chapter IV: Two other Germans invited by Gering — Pierre Keyser (Peter Keyser) and Jean Stol (John Stol) — who set up a rival press. The early competition in Parisian printing.
Chapter V: Continuation of the early Parisian printing trade.
Chapter VI: Where Gering came from and his background.
Part II — Reflections on the Books Printed by Gering
Chapter I: Ulrich Gering prints some books in Gothic type. Other printers using Gothic in Paris, Tours, and Lyon. The strongest impressions were in Gothic type. Gering’s Gothic is praised by some booksellers. Badius (Jodocus Badius Ascensius) persisted with Gothic. Too-frequent abbreviations in early printing. Early printers mixed red and black ink; Gering did this. Gering was the first printer of Breviaries and Books of Hours in Paris. The origin of italic type in Paris.
Chapter II: Gering’s types and their succession.
Chapter III: Particularities of several other printers. An abridged account of the printing houses of Paris.
Chapter IV: Even learned men made errors in their editions — a catalogue of notable printing errors.
Chapter V: Continuation of printing errors.
Chapter VI: Names of some early correctors. Marcus Musurus and his work.
Chapter VII: Complaint made in Gering’s Virgil against certain printers.
Chapter VIII: Further observations on the Parisian printing trade.
Part III — The Origin of Greek and Hebrew Printing
Chapter I: The beginning of Greek printing in Italy. The first books printed in Greek. Praise of the learned Greek printer Aldus Manutius. What he wrote over the door of his study. A singular artifice he used in some impressions. The origin of the two columns (Greek and Latin). The sacred books gave the idea of two columns. They oblige authors to produce more polished translations and reveal printing errors. Examples. They displeased Muret and Scaliger. Books in folio in a single language should be printed in two columns. Why they are preferable to long-line editions.
Chapter II: Hebrew printing in Italy and its establishment in Paris through the efforts of the University professors. The first Hebrew books printed in Europe.
Chapter III: Printing outside Europe. The question of whether printing was practiced in China before Europe, and whether block-printing (with engraved tables) began in Haarlem — the Coster controversy. An examination of the Dutch claims and the evidence.
Chapter IV: Greek printing in Paris. The first Greek books printed by the Sorbonne press.
Part IV — The Rights of the University over the Book Trade
Chapters I-VII: A detailed account of the rights the University of Paris held over the book trade, both before and after the invention of printing. Topics covered include:

The pricing of books (la taxe) — the University’s authority to set book prices
The approval system for theological works — which books required ecclesiastical approval before publication
The establishment of the four censors and their role
The privileges of the libraires jurés (sworn booksellers)
The University’s authority over book importation
The relationship between the University and the Crown in matters of censorship
The decline of the University’s authority over the book trade in the 16th-17th centuries

Appendices
Four alphabetical tables (indices) covering the contents of each part.
OCR Quality
The text is clean and very readable — 17th-century French Roman typeface, approximately 95%+ accuracy.

primary-sources/copernicus-astronomia-in.title: Astronomia instaurata (Copernicus / Mulerius, 1617)
primary-sources/copernicus-astronomia-in.content:
Astronomia instaurata (Copernicus / Mulerius, 1617)
Nicolai Copernici Torinensis Astronomia instaurata, libris sex comprehensa, qui de revolutionibus orbium coelestium inscribuntur is the 1617 Amsterdam edition of Copernicus’s De revolutionibus, restored and annotated by Nicolaus Mulerius, professor of medicine and mathematics at the new Academy of Groningen. The title page names Wilhelmus Iansonius at Amsterdam, “sub Solari aureo” (at the Golden Sundial), the imprint associated with Willem Jansz Blaeu before the Blaeu name stabilized. The source is therefore useful both as a scientific classic and as evidence for Amsterdam’s early-seventeenth-century learned and astronomical publishing.
Author: Nicolaus Copernicus (1473-1543)
Editor / annotator: Nicolaus Mulerius (Nicolaas Mulerius, 1564-1630)
Printer / publisher: Wilhelmus Iansonius / Willem Jansz Blaeu, Amsterdam, at the Golden Sundial
Year: 1617
Language: Latin
Raw file: wiki/raw/articles/copernicus-astronomia-instaurata.md
Original source file: Nicolai Copernici Torinensis_ Astronomia instaurata _ libris -- Copernicus, Nicolaus, 1473-1543 -- Netherlands, 1617 -- Excudebat VVilhelmus Iansonius -- oclc 222934765 -- b7706ff6c392a5595035312ce2600cd0 -- Anna’s Archive.zip
OCR unit: 516 page-level text files joined in natural page order with visible page markers.
Completeness Assessment
The raw extraction appears to cover the full scanned 1617 edition: blank or ownership-mark pages at the beginning, title page, Mulerius’s dedication, Osiander’s anonymous Ad lectorem on the hypotheses of the work, Copernicus’s preface to Pope Paul III, the six books of De revolutionibus, Mulerius’s notes, tables/canons, errata, and a closing Thesaurus astronomicus section. OCR quality is usable for source-page mining but visibly early-modern: long-s/f confusion, broken spacing, damaged Latin words, and table-heavy numerical pages. Read the raw file with page markers when exact wording or numerical tables matter.
Why This Belongs in the Printing-Press Wiki
This is not just a scientific text. It is a concrete example of how the press carried a difficult mathematical astronomy book across editions, corrections, tables, and scholarly apparatus. Mulerius explicitly frames his work as a repair of texts damaged by earlier printers and by corrupt numerical transmission. The edition also sits inside the commercial-scientific world of Blaeu: a printer trained in astronomy, selling maps, globes, nautical works, and learned books from Amsterdam.
For the wiki’s existing synthesis pages, this source strengthens sixteenth-century-printing and printing-revolution on scientific books in print; map-making-and-the-printing-press on astronomy/cartography overlap; and amsterdam / blaeu-family on learned Dutch publishing before the Atlas Maior era.
Narrative Source Flow
Front Matter and Publishing Frame
The title page presents the work as Copernicus’s astronomy “restored” after injuries by earlier authors and “illustrated with notes” by Mulerius. The printer line reads Amsterdam, Wilhelmus Iansonius, under the Golden Sundial, 1617. This front matter is valuable for the book-trade side of the source: it shows Blaeu/Iansonius marketing an improved, portable, annotated edition rather than merely reproducing the Nuremberg or Basel folios.
A short printer/editor note says Copernicus had already appeared in two folio editions, Nuremberg and Basel, but this form was preferred because the available types suited it and because it could be joined with the Frisian tables printed five years earlier. That is a direct statement about format, type, companion tables, and the packaging of scientific works for students of astronomy.
Mulerius’s Dedication to Groningen and Ommelanden
Mulerius dedicates the edition to the authorities of Groningen and the Ommelanden, praising their support of arms and letters and the newly established academy. He explains that, as one of the first professors called to teach there, he wanted to contribute to public use by restoring important astronomical authors. His complaint is typographical as much as scholarly: the best astronomical authors had been so foully handled by printers that readers either struggled through them or were led into errors in chronological calculation.
This dedication is one of the source’s richest printing-history passages. Mulerius presents editing as a medical repair of corrupted books: authors are “repurged,” corrected, and restored to their former health. He says Copernicus’s astronomy had been orphaned at birth, published in the same year its author died, and exposed to injuries because it lacked a guardian. Tycho Brahe and others had complained of those injuries; Mulerius therefore retells his edition as a scholarly rescue through printing.
Osiander’s Ad lectorem
The edition reprints the famous Ad lectorem de hypothesibus huius operis, the anonymous preface attached to the original De revolutionibus. It warns readers not to treat astronomical hypotheses too literally and presents them as calculating devices. In a printing-history context, its presence matters because the printed object carried not only Copernicus’s argument but an interpretive frame around it.
Copernicus’s Preface to Pope Paul III
Copernicus’s own preface explains his hesitation to publish a system assigning motions to the Earth, anticipating that many readers would reject the novelty and absurdity of the opinion. He describes the pressure from learned men to publish and presents mathematical astronomy as a search for truth as far as reason permits. This section is central for future mining into the scientific revolution and print: a controversial theory became durable and discussable because it could circulate in a stable printed form.
Index of the Six Books
The index maps the six books of De revolutionibus. Book I covers the spherical world, the spherical Earth, circular celestial motion, objections to terrestrial motion, the order of the celestial orbs, and the triple motion of the Earth. Book II treats circles, declinations, ascensions, horizons, oblique sphere tables, and fixed stars. Book III treats precession, solar motion, equinoxes, obliquity, and the year. Book IV covers lunar theory, parallax, eclipses, and distances. Book V covers planetary motions in longitude for Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury. Book VI covers planetary latitude.
The printed index is itself useful: it makes a mathematically dense work navigable and shows the mature apparatus of post-incunable scholarly books — numbered chapters, page references, tables, errata, and canons.
The Six Books of De revolutionibus
The main body begins with Book I, Chapter I, on the spherical form of the world, followed by the spherical Earth and the arguments around motion. The OCR preserves extensive diagrams and mathematical exposition only imperfectly, but the structure is clear. Many body pages interleave Copernicus’s text with Mulerius’s notes, making the source a commentary edition rather than a bare reprint.
Books II-VI are heavy with trigonometry, astronomical tables, fixed-star descriptions, planetary observations, and computational canons. These sections are less immediately useful for general narrative history, but they are excellent evidence for the kind of numerical and diagrammatic material early modern printers had to set accurately. The tables also explain why Mulerius stresses correction: a single wrong number or misplaced heading could damage the utility of the whole book.
Errata and Thesaurus astronomicus
Near the end, the edition prints a list of remaining errors, partly inherited from earlier editions and partly introduced in this one. Several entries concern numerical tables and astronomical calculations. The errata page is a high-value printing-history artifact because it makes correction visible: even an edition devoted to repairing earlier typographical and numerical corruption had to publish its own residual mistakes.
The final pages continue with an observational and computational Thesaurus astronomicus. They include planetary observations, references to Ptolemy, Copernicus, Bernard Walther, and Johannes Schoner, and roots of mean motions for chronological calculation. This material connects Copernican theory to the tabular and observational tradition that printed astronomy preserved and standardized.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Title page: restored and annotated Copernicus, Amsterdam 1617, Wilhelmus Iansonius under the Golden Sundial.
Printer/editor note: Nuremberg and Basel folio editions existed; the new format was chosen because the printer’s types suited it and because it could be bound with Frisian tables.
Mulerius dedication: printers had mishandled astronomical authors so badly that readers were misled in time-reckoning; his edition aims to restore the author’s health.
Osiander preface: printed paratext framing heliocentric hypotheses as computational tools.
Copernicus preface: publication anxiety over Earth’s motion and the decision to bring the work into public light.
Six-book index: compact map of the work’s structure and topics.
Errata: residual inherited and new errors in a mathematically demanding printed book.
Thesaurus astronomicus ending: observations and mean-motion roots showing how printed astronomy functioned as computational infrastructure.

Suggested Future Pages or Enrichments

Add a short Copernicus subsection to printing-revolution or a future scientific-printing page, focused on diagrams, tables, and correction rather than biography.
Enrich sixteenth-century-printing with the 1617 Blaeu/Mulerius edition as a post-1543 afterlife of scientific printing.
Enrich blaeu-family with a more precise note on Blaeu’s Copernican/scientific publishing and the Golden Sundial imprint.
If the wiki later adds a dedicated entity page for Copernicus, use this source mainly for publication history, paratext, and edition transmission rather than for a full astronomy explanation.

primary-sources/de-vinne-invention-of-pr.title: The Invention of Printing (De Vinne)
primary-sources/de-vinne-invention-of-pr.content:
The Invention of Printing (De Vinne)
Theodore Low De Vinne, The Invention of Printing: A Collection of Facts and Opinions Descriptive of the Origins and Development of Typography (New York, 1876). 26 chapters, ~550 pages, with over 200 illustrations.
Summary of Contents
The book covers the history of printing from its earliest antecedents to the establishment of typography in Germany around 1500. It is organized in six parts:
Part I — Methods and Antecedents (Chapters I-VI): Definitions of the four printing methods (copper-plate, lithography, typography, xylography). Ancient impression techniques — Babylonian brick stamps, Assyrian cylinders, Roman stamps — and why they did not develop into printing. The mechanical key to the invention: the adjustable hand mold, the punch, and the matrix. The earliest European woodcut prints: St. Christopher (1423), the Annunciation, St. Bridget. The introduction and mass-production of playing cards. Chinese woodblock printing and the limited Chinese use of movable type in clay and wood.
Part II — Materials and Context (Chapters VII-X): The introduction of printing into Italy (Subiaco 1465, Rome, Venice). The history of paper from China through the Arab world to Europe — the Fabriano mills, rag-gathering, watermarks, the cost advantage over vellum. The world of manuscript production: scriptoria, scribes, illuminators, binders, the university book trade, the cost of books before print. The social conditions that created demand for printing: commerce, vernacular literacy, devotional markets, clerical corruption, the inadequacy of the manuscript system.
Part III — Block-Books and Early Typography (Chapters XI-XV): A survey of European block-books: image-only prints (the Eight Rogueries, the Dance of Death), image-and-text block-books (the Biblia Pauperum, Ars Memorandi, Ars Moriendi, the Antichrist, the Life of St. Meinrat). The Donatus grammar fragments — the most frequently printed text of the 15th century and the testing-ground for early typefaces. The Speculum Humanae Salvationis in its four editions, with analysis of its types, paper, and presswork. The anonymous Dutch printers of the third quarter of the 15th century.
Part IV — The Coster Legend (Chapters XVI-XIX): The dating of the Speculum editions by paper-marks and type comparison. The full Coster story as told by Hadrianus Junius (1588): the walk in the wood, carved beech letters, the Speculum as Coster’s first book, the theft by the treacherous servant. The elaboration of the legend by Scriverius, Boxhorn, Meerman, Koning, and De Vries. Van der Linde’s archival demolition — Coster was a tallow-chandler and innkeeper, the Coster pedigree was forged, no mention of printing in Haarlem archives. De Vinne’s own typographic critique.
Part V — Gutenberg and the Mainz Inventors (Chapters XX-XXIII): Gutenberg’s Strasbourg period (c. 1434-1444), the 1439 Dritzehn lawsuit, the mirror partnership, secret arts. Return to Mainz, partnership with Fust (1450), the 42-line Bible, the 1454-1455 indulgence forms. The break with Fust (1455, Helmasperger Notarial Instrument), Gutenberg’s later work with Conrad Humery, the Catholicon (1460), his death in 1468. Fust and Schoeffer’s 1457 Mainz Psalter — first dated printed book, first colophon, first printed music. Schoeffer’s technical improvements in punchcutting and presswork.
Part VI — Synthesis and Tools (Chapters XXIV-XXVI): Review and dismissal of other alleged inventors (Castaldi, Mentel, Jenson, Regiomontanus). The spread of printing after the 1462 sack of Mainz — a timeline of first presses in each major European city. The physical equipment of the early printing house: the wooden hand press, the frisket, the tympan, ink-balls, the composing stick, the type case, the two-pull system.
Chapter-by-Chapter Detail
Part I: Methods and Antecedents (Chapters I-VI)
Chapter I — The Different Methods of Printing (pp. 17-28): Definitions of the four printing methods — copper-plate (intaglio), lithography (planographic), typography (relief from movable type), and xylography (relief from wood blocks). The mechanical differences between each method. The argument that typography’s superiority lies in the mobility of its types and their capacity for infinite re-combination.
Chapter II — Antique Methods of Impression and their Failure (pp. 29-48): A survey of ancient impression techniques: Babylonian brick stamps, Assyrian clay cylinders, Egyptian wood stamps, Roman stamps for pottery and bread, medieval branding irons. De Vinne’s argument that these are stamping, not printing — they lack ink, paper, and the concept of transferring multiple copies of verbal text. The failure traced to the lack of suitable ink, the absence of cheap writing material, and the limited number of readers.
Chapter III — The Key to the Invention of Typography (pp. 49-68): The mechanics of typefounding. The punch (steel letter engraved in relief), the matrix (copper impression struck from the punch), and the mold (adjustable instrument for casting type bodies of uniform width and height). The adjustable hand mold as the essential key to the invention.
Chapter IV — The Image Prints of the Fifteenth Century (pp. 69-87): The earliest European single-leaf woodcut prints — the St. Christopher (1423), the Annunciation, St. Bridget, the Brussels Print, the Berlin Print. Their date, style, and technique.
Chapter V — Printed and Stenciled Playing Cards (pp. 88-108): The introduction of playing cards into Europe from the East. Methods of production: stenciling, woodcut, and combinations. Playing cards as the first mass-produced printed artifacts, creating the technical and commercial foundation for block-book production.
Chapter VI — The Chinese Method of Printing (pp. 109-121): Chinese woodblock printing — paper, ink, book formats, and block-carving technique. The Chinese use of movable type (clay and wood). De Vinne’s conclusion that the Chinese system never developed the punch-matrix-mold mechanism.
Part II: Materials and Context (Chapters VII-X)
Chapter VII — The Early Printing of Italy (pp. 122-132): The introduction of printing to Subiaco (1465), Rome, and Venice. The work of Sweynheym and Pannartz.
Chapter VIII — The Introduction of Paper in Europe (pp. 133-145): Paper from its Chinese invention through the Arab transmission to Spain and Italy. The Fabriano mills. Rag-gathering and paper-making. The cost advantages of paper over vellum. Paper-marks (watermarks) as tools for dating early printed books.
Chapter IX — The Book-Makers of the Middle Ages (pp. 146-170): Manuscript production — the scriptorium, the scribe, the illuminator, the binder. The cost of books. The university book trade (the pecia system). The social conditions that created demand for a cheaper alternative.
Chapter X — The Preparations for Printing (pp. 171-192): The state of education, literacy, and religious devotion in the early fifteenth century. The growth of commerce, the spread of vernacular literacy, the demand for devotional images and books, the corruption of the clergy, the inadequacy of the manuscript system.
Part III: Block-Books and Early Typography (Chapters XI-XV)
Chapter XI — Block-Books of Images without Text (pp. 193-229): Early block-books consisting only of images: the Eight Rogueries, the Dance of Death, other xylographic prints. The technique of cutting the block and the printing process (frotton or screw press).
Chapter XII — Block-Books of Images with Text (pp. 230-253): Major block-books with text and images cut on the same block: the Biblia Pauperum, the Ars Memorandi, the Ars Moriendi, the Antichrist, the Wonders of Rome, the Pomerium Spirituale, the Life of St. Meinrat. Analysis of each for its typographic features.
Chapter XIII — The Donatus, or Boy’s Latin Grammar (pp. 254-263): The Donatus fragments — the Latin grammar by Aelius Donatus, one of the most frequently printed texts of the fifteenth century. The typographic Donatus fragments attributed to Gutenberg (36-line and 42-line types). The Donatus as the testing-ground for early typefaces.
Chapter XIV — The Speculum Salutis, or Mirror of Salvation (pp. 264-281): The Speculum Humanae Salvationis — the block-book/typography hybrid at the center of the Coster controversy. All four editions (two Latin, two Dutch). Analysis of types, illustrations, paper, and presswork. Conclusion that they belong to the 1460s or 1470s.
Chapter XV — The Works and Workmanship of an Unknown Printer (pp. 282-307): Types used in the Speculum editions compared with other Dutch incunabula — the Fables of Lorenzo Valla, the Epitaphs of Pope Pius II, the Enschede Abecedarium. An anonymous school of Dutch printers in the third quarter of the fifteenth century.
Part IV: The Coster Legend (Chapters XVI-XIX)
Chapter XVI — The Period in which the Speculum was Printed (pp. 308-325): Dating the Speculum editions using paper-marks and type comparisons. The paper bears watermarks found in other books of known date from the 1460s-1480s. The types are stylistically later than Gutenberg’s 42-line Bible.
Chapter XVII — The Legend of Lourens Janszoon Coster (pp. 326-346): The Coster story as told by Hadrianus Junius (1588): the walk in the wood, the carved beech letters, the development of ink, the Speculum as Coster’s first book, the theft of the types by the treacherous servant identified as Johann Fust. Junius says wooden types but the Speculum has cast metal. Coster is said to have died in 1439/1440, but records show a Lourens Janszoon Coster alive until 1483.
Chapter XVIII — The Growth of the Legend (pp. 347-359): The elaboration of the Coster story: Scriverius (1628, moving the date to 1428), Boxhorn (1640, moving it to 1420), Meerman (1765, the Origines Typographicae), Koning (1816, confabulating two different Laurens Janszoons), De Vries (c. 1830, claiming 1423).
Chapter XIX — The Downfall of the Legend (pp. 360-374): Van der Linde’s archival evidence from Haarlem records: Lourens Janszoon Coster was a tallow-chandler and tavern-keeper, not a printer. The Coster pedigree was a forged or falsified document from c. 1550. No mention of printing in any Haarlem archive. De Vinne’s typographic critique: no dated Coster print exists, the types are cast metal, and Haarlem produced no printing for forty years after the alleged invention.
Part V: Gutenberg and the Mainz Inventors (Chapters XX-XXIII)
Chapter XX — John Gutenberg at Strasburg (pp. 375-402): Gutenberg’s Strasbourg period (c. 1434-1444). The 1439 Dritzehn lawsuit records. The mirror-manufacturing partnership and secret arts. References to “forms” and “presses” suggesting printing experiments.
Chapter XXI — Gutenberg and his Earlier Work at Mentz (pp. 403-430): Gutenberg’s return to Mainz. The partnership with Johannes Fust (c. 1450). The 800-guilder loan. The 36-line Bible (considered earlier than the 42-line). The 1454-1455 indulgence forms — the first dated products of Gutenberg’s press.
Chapter XXII — The Later Work of Gutenberg (pp. 431-448): The break with Fust (1455, the Helmasperger Notarial Instrument). Gutenberg’s later work with Conrad Humery. The Catholicon of 1460. Gutenberg’s death in 1468.
Chapter XXIII — The Work of Peter Schoeffer and John Fust (pp. 449-479): Fust’s partnership with Peter Schoeffer after the lawsuit. The 1457 Mainz Psalter — first book with a printed date, first with a printer’s colophon, first with printed music. Schoeffer’s technical improvements in punchcutting and presswork.
Part VI: Synthesis and Tools (Chapters XXIV-XXVI)
Chapter XXIV — Alleged Inventors of Printing (pp. 480-491): Review and dismissal of other claimants: Panfilo Castaldi of Feltre, Johann Mentel of Strasbourg, Nicolas Jenson, Regiomontanus, and others.
Chapter XXV — The Spread of Printing (pp. 492-513): The diffusion of typography from Mainz after the 1462 sack of the city. Timeline of first presses in Strasbourg, Cologne, Basel, Rome, Venice, Paris, London, and the Low Countries.
Chapter XXVI — The Tools and Usages of the First Printers (pp. 514-542): The physical equipment of the early printing house: the wooden hand press (screw or lever mechanism), the frisket (paper holder), the tympan (packing), ink-balls (inking pads), the composing stick, the type case, the practice of printing in two pulls.
