primary-sources/eisenstein-printing-pres.title: The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (Eisenstein)
primary-sources/eisenstein-printing-pres.content:
The Printing Press as an Agent of Change: Communications and Cultural Transformations in Early Modern Europe (1979) is Elizabeth Eisenstein’s landmark — and explicitly provisional — argument that the invention of movable type in the mid-15th century constituted a “communications revolution” that fundamentally transformed early modern European society.
Author: Elizabeth L. Eisenstein
Edition: 1st paperback edition
Publisher: Cambridge University Press, 1980 (original hardcover 1979)
Pages: xxi + 794
Raw text: eisenstein_printing_press_raw.txt
Scope and Method
Eisenstein’s argument is about Western Europe’s literate elites — primarily Latin-reading professionals (clergy, lawyers, physicians, humanist scholars). She explicitly sets aside Eastern Europe, the Near East, and the New World, as well as mass literacy and popular culture. Her concern is what printing did to the circulation of knowledge among those who could already read Latin.
She is not a technological determinist: print enabled certain transformations, but did not cause them mechanically. Typographical choices were contingent and practical.
Summary of Contents
Part I: Introduction to an Elusive Transformation (Chapters 1–3)
Chapter 1 — The Unacknowledged Revolution. Printing’s consequences have been systematically underestimated precisely because they are so foundational. Historians, who work through printed texts, cannot easily observe what print transformed. While Francis Bacon recognised printing (alongside gunpowder and the compass) as one of the three most consequential inventions, academic historians have never given it sustained analytical treatment.
Chapter 2 — Defining the Initial Shift. The core contrast between scribal and print cultures. A person born in 1453 would, by age fifty, have witnessed approximately 8 million printed books — more than all European scribes had produced in the preceding millennium. Six features distinguish print culture: dissemination (multiplication of identical copies); standardization (enabling comparison and correction across distance); reorganization (title pages, indexes, running headers, footnotes); data collection (tables, charts, illustrated material); preservation (texts fixed against corruptions of copying); and amplification (cumulative cross-referencing). Master printers emerged as cultural impresarios bridging university and commerce.
Chapter 3 — Some Features of Print Culture. The shift from oral-mnemonic to reading-based learning was a genuine cognitive transformation. Print created “fixity” — the same text simultaneously present in identical form across Europe — that manuscript culture structurally could not achieve. This fixity made the Reformation irreversible: once Luther’s ideas were in print, no bishop could confiscate every copy.
Part II: Classical and Christian Traditions Reoriented (Chapters 4–5)
Chapter 4 — The Renaissance Recapitulated. Two distinct phases: the early quattrocento revival was fragile and geographically limited, dependent on scarce manuscripts and personal networks. The second phase (post-1470, north of the Alps) was a permanent international transformation enabled by print. Greek studies flourished after Constantinople’s fall because printed grammars liberated Northern scholars from dependence on émigré teachers.
Chapter 5 — The Permanent Renaissance. Print “permanently secured” classical texts that medieval scribes had preserved but could not stabilize. Humanists did not “discover” classical texts but made them permanently available. Print also enabled the shift from copying to editing — critical collation, comparison, and emendation had no scribal equivalent.
Part III: The Book of Nature Transformed (Chapters 6–9)
Chapter 6–7 — Technical Literature Goes to Press. Printing transformed natural philosophy by making technical literature (mathematical tables, anatomical illustrations, surveying manuals, engineering drawings) widely available and systematically comparable. Vesalius’s De Fabrica (1543) was a collaboration between anatomist, artist, and printer producing exactly repeatable pictorial statements — structurally impossible in manuscript culture. Artisan-authors (Agricola, Paré, Palissy) used print to cross the gap between workshop knowledge and university learning.
Chapter 8 — Expanding the Community of Science. Print created a “community of science” — scholars comparing observations against identical reference texts. Two astronomers in different cities could now work from identical editions of Ptolemy and identify divergences precisely. This cumulative comparability was the structural precondition for the Copernican revolution.
Chapter 9 — The Book of Nature Transformed. Exact repeatability of pictorial and numerical data enabled experimental procedures. Print also created a problem of authority: when dozens of printed editions of Galen or Ptolemy existed, which was correct? The pressure to collate drove critical editing, undermining the authority of the ancients.
Part IV: The Scripture Revised (Chapters 10–12)
Chapter 10–11 — The Eucharistic Controversy. Printing created the Reformation in two ways: distributing biblical texts widely in vernacular translations, and standardizing the text of scripture such that disagreements about its meaning became public controversies. Printed indulgences preceded the crisis; printed polemics defined and spread it. “Book religion” developed on both sides of the confessional divide.
Chapter 12 — Conclusion. Print enabled the Reformation and Scientific Revolution, but also Catholic Counter-Reformation propaganda, alchemical literature, and astrological almanacs. The press amplified whatever movements were already in motion. Printing is the necessary but not sufficient cause — it created infrastructure within which human choices and conflicts unfolded.
Key Themes





































ThemeSummaryThe “Unacknowledged Revolution”Printing is arguably the most significant transformation in Western history, yet historians treat it as a footnoteFixity and StandardizationPrint fixed texts in a way manuscript could not — identical diagrams, maps, and biblical texts across distances”Securing” vs. “Discovering” antiquityHumanists did not discover classical texts — print permanently secured them against the corruption of manuscript transmissionReformation and PrintThe first movement to fully exploit print for mass communication; Luther’s pamphlets spread at manuscript-unprecedented speedScientific RevolutionPrint enabled standardized illustrations, maps, data-tables, and a cumulative “community of science” across EuropeMapmaking RevolutionPrinting made accurate, repeatable maps possible — the same diagram in every copyMethodological cautionThe work stops roughly at Newton/Locke; learned journals and editorial offices replace the master-printer as knowledge-gatekeeper
Relationship to Other Sources

























SourceRelationshipThe Gutenberg Revolution (John Man)A popular narrative history of Gutenberg that treats Eisenstein’s framework as received wisdom, though Man’s focus is biographical rather than analyticalThe World of Aldus Manutius (Martin Lowry)Lowry’s detailed study of the Aldine Press provides granular business and scholarly evidence that tests Eisenstein’s claims about humanist printing against a specific casePutnam, Books and their MakersOlder institutional history that provides some of the evidence-base Eisenstein synthesises into her broader argumentDe Vinne, The Invention of PrintingNineteenth-century technical history that Eisenstein draws on for her arguments about standardization and fixity
Sources
Eisenstein, Elizabeth L. The Printing Press as an Agent of Change: Communications and Cultural Transformations in Early-Modern Europe. 1st paperback ed. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1980.

primary-sources/falkenstein-geschichte-b.title: Geschichte der Buchdruckerkunst (Falkenstein)
primary-sources/falkenstein-geschichte-b.content:
Geschichte der Buchdruckerkunst (Falkenstein)
Dr. Karl Falkenstein, Geschichte der Buchdruckerkunst in ihrer Entstehung und Ausbildung (Leipzig, 1840). Google Books scan, Fraktur OCR. 49,136 lines.
A comprehensive German-language history of printing, published as a Jubelschrift (celebration volume) for the 400th anniversary of the invention. Karl Falkenstein was Oberbibliothekar (chief librarian) of the Royal Library in Dresden. Lorck describes it as “the only work which attempts to carry the history up to the most recent time, 1840.”^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
OCR Quality
The text is the output of automated OCR on a Fraktur-type original. Readability varies by section:

Body text (narrative passages): approximately 50-60% readable — the subject and some details can be extracted, though many individual words are corrupted
Lists, names, headers: more garbled, often less than 30% readable
Overall: roughly 40-50% of the content is intelligible

Contents
As described by Lorck, the book covers the prehistory and invention of printing, Gutenberg’s life, the Coster controversy, the spread of printing, and the later development of the art through 1840, with many illustrations. It was written from a bibliographic/librarian’s perspective and was a strong defender of Gutenberg’s priority against the Haarlem claim.^[raw/articles/lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst.md]
See Also

lorck-handbuch-buchdruckerkunst — cites and discusses Falkenstein; clean text
de-vinne-invention-of-printing — covers the same ground in English, clean text

primary-sources/foxe-acts-monuments.title: The Acts and Monuments of John Foxe (Pratt Edition, 1877)
primary-sources/foxe-acts-monuments.content:
The Acts and Monuments of John Foxe — commonly known as Foxe’s Book of Martyrs — is the great martyrological work of the English Reformation, a massive chronicle of Protestant persecution from the early Church through the Marian persecutions under Mary I. This is the fourth edition, revised and corrected by the Rev. Josiah Pratt (with an introduction by the Rev. John Stoughton), published by the Religious Tract Society, London, 1877.
This was the definitive Victorian edition of Foxe, an 8-volume set. Four volumes from this set are present in this wiki.
Also present are Vol. III from the earlier 1841 Seeley & Burnside edition and Vol. VI from the Townsend 3rd edition (Seeley, also revised by Pratt).




































































VolumeEditionCoverageRaw textSizeVol. ITownsend 3rd ed.Early church through Wycliffefoxe-acts-monuments-vol1-townsend.txt49,687 linesVol. II1877 PrattLollards, early Reformation through Henry VIIIfoxe-acts-monuments-vol2.txt69,989 lines, 3.6 MBVol. III1841 Seeley & BurnsideHenry VIII reign, mid-Reformationfoxe-acts-monuments-vol3-1841.txt60,010 linesVol. IV1877 PrattMarian Persecutions — Latimer, Ridley, Cranmerfoxe-acts-monuments-vol3.txt58,000 lines, 3.0 MBVol. V1877 PrattLater Marian martyrs, Elizabethan Settlementfoxe-acts-monuments-vol5-pratt.txt67,546 linesVol. VITownsend 3rd ed.Appendices and documentary evidencefoxe-acts-monuments-vol6.txt61,422 linesVol. VIISeeley & BurnsideGlossary and indicesfoxe-acts-monuments-vol7.txt60,306 linesVol. VIII1877 PrattSupplementary material, appendicesfoxe-acts-monuments-vol4.txt85,295 lines, 4.0 MB
Author: John Foxe (1516–1587)
Editor: Rev. Josiah Pratt, M.A. (Trinity College, Cambridge)
Publisher: The Religious Tract Society, London (56 Paternoster Row, 65 St. Paul’s Churchyard, and 161 Piccadilly)
Year: 1877
Edition: Fourth edition, revised and corrected
Historical Significance
Foxe’s Acts and Monuments is the single most important printed source for the history of the English Reformation from a Protestant perspective. First published in English in 1563 (the Latin edition appeared in 1559), it went through four editions in Foxe’s lifetime. The work was ordered to be placed in every cathedral church in England alongside the Bible, and it shaped English Protestant identity for centuries.
The work covers:

Early Church persecutions under the Roman emperors
Medieval martyrdom — the Lollards, Wycliffe, Hus
The Marian Persecutions (1553–1558) — the heart of the work, documenting over 280 burnings at the stake under Mary I, including Latimer, Ridley, and Cranmer
The Elizabethan Settlement and the triumph of Protestantism

Significance for the Printing Press Wiki
Foxe’s Acts and Monuments was a landmark of Elizabethan printing:

Printing by John Day — the original 1563 edition was printed by John Day, the leading English printer of the Elizabethan era, in a massive folio of over 1,800 pages
Scale of production — the first edition was one of the most ambitious printing projects undertaken in 16th-century England, requiring enormous capital, paper, and labor
Illustrations — the 1563 edition contained over 60 woodcut illustrations (many of burnings at the stake), making it one of the most heavily illustrated books printed in England up to that time
Censorship and licensing — the work was both a product of and a contributor to the Tudor system of press control; it was officially authorised and promoted by the Elizabethan regime
Reception and reprinting — the work went through numerous editions (1563, 1570, 1576, 1583, 1596, 1610, 1641, 1684, and this 1877 Pratt edition), making it a continuous presence in English print culture for over 300 years

Relationship to Other Sources

























SourceRelationshipTudor Censorship and the Press (England 16th c. wiki)Foxe exemplifies the Elizabethan regime’s use of the press to shape public opinion — the book was both a product of and a contributor to state-controlled printingThe English Reformation (England 16th c. wiki)Foxe’s work is the foundational narrative of the English Reformation from the Protestant side, framing the persecution narrative that shaped English Protestant identityEisenstein, The Printing Press as an Agent of ChangeFoxe’s Acts and Monuments is a textbook case of Eisenstein’s “fixity” and “amplification” theses — a printed work that fixed a particular historical narrative and amplified it across generationsWinship, Gutenberg to PlantinFoxe’s printer John Day represents the Elizabethan master-printer, a contemporary of Plantin operating within a very different (state-controlled) English market
Sources
Foxe, John. The Acts and Monuments of John Foxe: A New and Complete Edition. Ed. Rev. Josiah Pratt. 8 vols. London: The Religious Tract Society, 1877.

primary-sources/hoe-history-of-printing-.title: A Short History of the Printing Press (Hoe)
primary-sources/hoe-history-of-printing-.content:
A Short History of the Printing Press (Hoe)
A Short History of the Printing Press and of the Improvements in Printing Machinery from the Time of Gutenberg up to the Present Day by Robert Hoe (New York, 1902) traces the mechanical evolution of the printing press from Gutenberg’s wooden screw press through the rotary web perfecting presses of 1900. The book is organized as a continuous chronological narrative covering roughly 20 distinct eras of press development.
Summary of Contents
The book describes the mechanical design, operation, and performance of printing presses across four and a half centuries. It covers wooden hand presses (c. 1450-1800), the first iron hand presses (1800-1827), bed-and-platen power presses (1822-1858), flat-bed cylinder presses (1814-1850s), rotary type-revolving presses (1846-1870s), web perfecting presses (1865-1902), and folding mechanisms. Throughout, the text gives specific press speeds (sheets or impressions per hour), mechanical principles (screw, toggle joint, lever, crank, cam), and descriptions of how each machine handles inking, impression, sheet feeding, and delivery.
Detailed Breakdown of Contents
1. Gutenberg’s Wooden Press (c. 1450)
Opening description of the original printing press: two upright timbers with wooden cross pieces, a wooden screw passing through a cross-beam, its lower point resting on the center of a wooden platen which was screwed down onto the type. The form was inked with a ball of leather stuffed with wool, paper spread over it, and a blanket laid on the paper to soften the impression. The mechanical principle is traced to the cheese and linen presses of medieval times. Hoe estimates Gutenberg’s output at approximately 300 sheets per day.
2. The Wooden Common Press (1450-1620)
The screw press worked with a movable bar continued in use for about 150 years without material change. Forms of type were placed on wooden (sometimes stone) beds enclosed in frames called “coffins,” moved in and out by hand. After each impression the platen had to be screwed up with the bar so the printed paper could be removed and hung to dry.
3. The Blaeu Press (c. 1620, Amsterdam)
First recorded improvements by Willem Janszoon Blaeu. The spindle of the screw passed through a square block guided in the wooden frame, from which the platen was suspended by wires or cords — the block preventing any twist in the platen and ensuring more equal motion to the screw. A device was added for rolling the bed in and out, and a new form of iron hand lever for turning the screw. This press was introduced into England and used on the continent; substantially the same press Benjamin Franklin worked on as a journeyman in London.
4. The Common Press in the 18th Century
Little further improvement before 1798. The labor in working one of the old screw presses was described as about equal to that of a plowman. The iron platen had been used on wooden presses before the all-iron press appeared.
5. The Stanhope Iron Press (1800, Earl of Stanhope)
The first major redesign in 350 years. The frame was cast in one piece of iron instead of wood. The screw was retained but a combination of levers was added to give greater power with less exertion. These were the first all-iron printing presses ever constructed. Printers added lever combinations to their wooden presses, which generally destroyed them as the wood could not withstand the strain.
6. Clymer’s Columbian Press (c. 1816, George Clymer)
An iron machine entirely dispensing with the screw. A long cast-iron lever was placed over the platen, one end attached to the upright of the cast-iron frame and the other raised and lowered by a combination of smaller levers worked by the pressman. The impression was given and the platen raised and lowered by a spindle or pin attached to the center of the large cross lever at the top, balanced to facilitate raising. Clymer took his invention to England, where it was known as the “Columbian” press.
7. Smith Press (1822, Peter Smith)
Peter Smith, connected with R. Hoe & Co. in New York, devised a machine with a cast-iron frame that substituted a toggle joint for the screw-and-lever combination.
8. Washington Hand Press (1827, Samuel Rust)
Samuel Rust of New York perfected a press that was a great improvement on the Smith press. The frame had hollowed cast-iron uprights admitting wrought-iron bars riveted at top and bottom, giving additional strength while reducing the amount of metal. The patent was purchased by R. Hoe & Co., who improved on it and manufactured the press as the “Washington” press. Over 6,000 were made and sold by Hoe & Co. alone. Made in seven sizes.
Mechanical description: the bed slides on a track and is run in and out from under the platen by turning a crank with belts attached to a pulley on its shaft. The impression is given by a curved lever acting on a toggle joint; the platen is lifted by springs on either side. Attached to the bed is a “tympan” frame covered with cloth, standing inclined to receive the sheet. Another frame called the “frisket” is attached to the tympan, covered with paper with parts cut away to prevent the chase and furniture from soiling the sheet. The frisket is turned down over the sheet and tympan, and all are folded down when the impression is taken. Automatic inking rollers were attached, operated by a weight raised by the pressman’s pull; the descent of the weight drew the rollers over the type and returned them to the inking cylinder while the pressman placed another sheet. Further improvements in inking apparatus were patented by Hoe & Co., in which ink distribution was effected by an apparatus driven by steam power.
9. Bed and Platen Power Presses (1822-1858)
Daniel Treadwell (1822, Boston): the first steam-powered bed-and-platen press, with wooden frames. Only three or four were constructed.
Isaac Adams (1830, 1836): the best machines of this description. First made with wooden frames, afterward with iron frames. In 1858 Adams’s business became the property of Hoe & Co., who continued manufacture with added improvements. Over 1,000 sold in 57 sizes.
Mechanical description: type placed on an iron bed, which is raised and lowered by straightening and bending a toggle joint by means of a cam, giving the impression against an iron platen fixed above and held in position by upright iron rods secured to the bottom bar. The ink fountain is at one end of the press; inking rollers travel twice over the form in a movable frisket frame while the bed is down; paper is taken in by grippers on the frisket and carried over the form; the bed rises and the impression is given; sheets pass forward from the frisket by tapes to a sheet flier which delivers them on the fly board. Maximum speed: 1,000 sheets per hour for the larger sizes.
Otis Tufts (1834, Boston): also described.
10. Koenig’s Cylinder Press (1814)
Friedrich Koenig (a Saxon who visited England in 1806) devised the first practical flat-bed cylinder press, assisted by mechanic Andrew Bauer. The form of type was placed on a flat bed, the cylinder above having a three-fold motion: the first third of the turn received the sheet upon one of the tympans and secured it by the frisket; the second gave the impression and allowed the sheet to be removed; the third returned the tympan empty to receive another sheet.
Koenig devised the reciprocating motion of the type bed: a pinion carried on the inner end of a long shaft turned by gearing from outside the press frame, with a universal joint in its length allowing an up-and-down motion of the pinion as it revolves. Underneath the bed and fastened to it is a “rack” with a crescent-shaped segment of hard metal at each end. The wheel at the outer end of the shaft revolves the pinion and moves the bed by the teeth in this rack. At reversal, the pinion turns around over a pin or stud, against the segment on the rack, and re-engages its teeth in the opposite side, carrying the bed back.
In 1814 Koenig patented a continuously revolving cylinder press, with the part of the periphery not used for impression slightly reduced in diameter to allow the form to return under it freely. He showed designs for single-cylinder, two-cylinder (printing one side), and two-cylinder perfecting presses (printing both sides). The perfecting press had two forms placed at each end of a long bed; paper printed on one side was carried by tapes over a registering roller to the other cylinder for the reverse side.
Koenig installed two two-cylinder presses at the London Times in 1814, printing on one side only at 800 sheets per hour.
11. Improvements to the Cylinder Press (1814-1840)
Napier (1828, 1830): introduced grippers or fingers for conveying sheets around the cylinder during impression and for delivering them after printing (tapes had previously been used). First to manufacture presses with small impression cylinders making two or more revolutions per sheet. Devised toggles for bringing cylinders down to print on the form and raising them to let the form run back without touching.
Applegath & Cowper: various improvements, mostly simplifying Koenig’s presses. Also improved Koenig’s perfecting press into an efficient machine.
Bacon & Donkin (1813), Cowper (1816, 1818), Applegath (1818): various patents.
12. Hoe & Co.’s Flat-Bed Cylinder Presses (1832 onward)
In 1832, Sereno Newton was sent to England to investigate cylinder press improvements. Resulted in the “Single Small Cylinder,” “Double Small Cylinder,” and Large Cylinder “Perfecting” Press.
Single Large Cylinder: the first flat-bed cylinder press ever used in the United States. The whole circumference of the cylinder was equivalent to the entire travel of the bed forwards and backwards; the cylinder made one revolution for each impression without stopping. A portion of the cylinder took the impression; the remainder was turned down small enough to allow the type on the bed to pass back under it without touching. Hundreds were made. Output: up to 2,000 impressions per hour.
Double Small Cylinder: the travel of the bed was long enough that the form passed backward and forward under both cylinders. Two feeders put in sheets; maximum speed about 4,000 per hour from the two cylinders (2,000 each), printed on one side.
Hoe & Co. patented bed-driving mechanism (1847): two racks facing each other but not in the same vertical plane, separated by the diameter of the driving wheel on a horizontal shaft movable sideways to engage either rack. Bed reversal accomplished by a roller at either end of the bed entering a recess in a disc on the driving shaft, which in a half-revolution brought the bed to a stop and started it in the opposite direction. A crank action operating directly upon the bed from a shaft having a fixed centre.
13. Stop Cylinder Press (Dutartre, 1852)
Devised and patented by a Frenchman named Dutartre in 1852, introduced into the United States about 1853 by Hoe & Co., who patented many improvements. Mechanical description: type secured on a traveling iron bed moving back and forth on steel friction rollers, driven by a simple crank motion, stopping and starting without noise or jar. All running portions made of fine steel. The cylinder is stopped by a cam motion pending the backward travel of the bed; during the interval of rest the sheet is fed down against guides and grippers close before the cylinder starts, ensuring accuracy of register. After impression, the sheet is transferred to a skeleton cylinder with grippers which delivers it over fine cords onto a sheet flier. Ink distribution by a vibrating polished steel cylinder and a flat table at the end of the traveling bed; form-inking rollers vary from four to six. Various sizes. Average output of a press with bed 36x54 inches: 1,000 to 1,500 impressions per hour. A larger version with bed 45x62 inches ran at 1,700 impressions per hour.
14. Hoe Type Revolving Machine (1846)
The landmark rotary press, with patents by Richard M. Hoe. The first was placed in the Philadelphia Ledger in 1846. Type was securely fastened on a central horizontal cylinder by means of cast-iron beds (one for each page of the newspaper) with V-shaped column rules tapering toward the feet of the type, allowing the type to be held firmly in position with the surface forming a true circle. Around the central cylinder, four to ten impression cylinders were grouped.
Sheets were fed in by boys, taken from the feed board by automatic grippers or fingers operated by cams in the impression cylinders, and conveyed around against the revolving form. A patented sheet flier consisted of a row of long wooden fingers fastened to a shaft, operated by a cam and springs; the printed sheet was conducted out underneath each feed board by tapes to the sheet fliers, which laid them in piles on tables.
Inking: composition rollers placed between each impression cylinder; the fountain below underneath the main type cylinder. The portion of the type cylinder surface not occupied by type was used as a distributing table (its surface lower than the type), with inking rollers rising and falling alternately to place ink on the type and receive a new supply from the distributing surface.
Four-cylinder machines achieved about 8,000 papers per hour printed on one side (2,000 per feeder). Ten-cylinder machines achieved about 20,000 papers per hour printed on one side. Adopted throughout the United States and Great Britain; the London Times eventually ordered two Ten-Cylinder presses to replace its Applegath machine. 175 were made in total.
15. Curved Stereotype Plates
The perfection of casting stereotype plates on a curve using flexible paper matrices cast in curved moulds to any desired circle. These plates were placed on the Hoe Type Revolving Machine on beds adapted to receive them. Newspaper publishers could duplicate forms and run several machines simultaneously. In some large offices (New York Herald, London Daily Telegraph, London Standard), as many as five machines ran at once.
16. Applegath’s Vertical Type-Revolving Press (1848)
Constructed for the London Times. All cylinders were vertical instead of horizontal. Type was placed on a large upright central cylinder whose circumference represented flat surfaces for each column (polygonal, not circular). Around this central cylinder were eight smaller vertical impression cylinders; inking rollers inked the type as it passed between impression cylinders. Sheets fed down by hand from eight flat horizontal feed-boards through tapes, grasped by another set of tapes and passed sideways between impression cylinder and type cylinder. Maximum output: 8,000 impressions per hour on one side. Only one was ever made; it was removed to make way for Hoe Type Revolving Presses.
17. Bullock’s Web Press (1865)
William Bullock of Philadelphia constructed the first printing machine to print from a continuous web or roll of paper (1865). Two pairs of cylinders: two form/plate cylinders and two impression cylinders. The second impression cylinder was made large to provide additional tympan surface and lessen offset from the first printed side. Sheets were cut before printing; cutting done by knives in cylinders. Delivery by a series of automatic metal nippers placed on endless leather belts at distances apart to grasp each sheet successively. The machine was put up in several offices but rejected for unreliability, especially in delivery; it was later improved enough to see considerable use.
London Times rotary perfecting press (c. 1868): similar to Bullock’s in printing apparatus, but cylinders all of one size and placed one above the other. Sheets severed after printing, brought up by tapes, and carried down to a sheet flier that moved back and forth. Marinoni (Paris) devised a similar machine with the impression and form cylinder of one size placed one above the other, with separate fly boards for delivery.
18. Hoe Web Perfecting Press (1871)
R. Hoe & Co.’s rotary perfecting press printing from a continuous web. Major difficulties addressed: set-off of the first side (rapid-drying inks were developed), paper strength in rolls (paper-makers improved manufacture), rapid severing of sheets after printing, and reliable delivery.
Stephen D. Tucker’s patented gathering cylinder solved the problem of rapid flat delivery: sheets were not entirely severed by cutters but simply perforated after printing, then drawn by accelerating tapes (which completely separated them) onto a gathering cylinder constructed so that six perfect papers could be gathered one over the other. By means of a switch, these were turned off onto one sheet flier at the proper moment. The gathering and delivery cylinder solved the problem of rapid flat delivery.
First machine placed at Lloyd’s Weekly Newspaper in London; first in the United States at the New York Tribune. When run at full speed: 18,000 perfect papers per hour (printed both sides, cut, and delivered accurately on one feed-board). Average speed in printing offices: 12,000; some at about 14,000 per hour.
19. Folding Mechanisms (1875 onward)
Early folding machines used hand-fed folding mechanisms: sheets carried by tapes running on pulleys under striking blades which forced them between pairs of folding rollers. After the first fold, sheets were carried under striking blades at right angles to the first for a second fold. None could work above 8,000 per hour.
Stephen D. Tucker’s rotating folding cylinder (1875): folded papers as fast as they came from the press, at 15,000 per hour. The first Hoe folding machines were exhibited at the Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia in 1876. They combined a gathering cylinder with a rotary folding cylinder and tapes conveying printed sheets under horizontal folding blades that thrust them between folding rollers at alternate angles, finally delivering them on traveling belts by a small flier.
20. Double Supplement Press (c. 1876)
Produced four, six, eight, ten, or twelve-page papers at 24,000 per hour, and sixteen-page papers at 12,000 per hour, with odd pages inserted and pasted, papers cut at top and delivered folded. Constructed in two parts: cylinders in one portion twice the length of those in the other; short cylinders used for supplements. Paper entered from two rolls through two portions of the machine, carried between two pairs of type and impression cylinders, printed on both sides. The two webs passed over turning bars laid evenly one over the other and pasted together. Webs passed down upon a triangular “former” which folded them along the center margin, then over a cylinder for the final fold — a revolving blade within the cylinder projecting and thrusting the paper between folding rollers, while a knife in the same cylinder severed the sheet. Several hundred were made and operated in the United States, Great Britain, and other countries.
21. Quadruple Press (1887)
Constructed in 1887; first placed in the New York World. Supplement portion increased in width. Produced eight-page papers at 48,000 per hour; ten-to-sixteen-page papers at 24,000 per hour; all delivered cut, pasted, and folded. A “straight-line” form of the Double Supplement and Quadruple machines arranged cylinders in horizontal rows or tiers, one above the other, with two pairs of cylinders in each tier and folding and delivery apparatus at the end of the machine.
22. Sextuple Press (1891, New York Herald)
Constructed for James Gordon Bennett of the New York Herald; occupied about 18 months to build; composed of about 16,000 pieces. Form and impression cylinders all placed parallel. Fed from three rolls, each more than five feet wide. Six plate cylinders, each carrying eight stereotype plates (representing eight pages of the Herald), and six impression cylinders. At full speed, cylinders made 200 revolutions per minute. Consumed 25.75 miles of 63-inch-wide paper per hour (equivalent to 51.5 miles of Herald-width paper). A double folding mechanism and two delivery outlets automatically counted papers in piles of fifty.
Capacities: 90,000 four-page papers per hour; 72,000 eight-page papers per hour; 48,000 ten or twelve-page papers per hour; 36,000 sixteen-page papers per hour; 24,000 fourteen-to-twenty-four-page papers per hour. All printed, cut, pasted, folded, counted, and delivered.
23. Rotary Type-Revolving Web Perfecting Press (1881)
Designed to print from one form of type at greater speed. Forms of type for both sides placed on a central cylinder surrounded by impression cylinders and inking rollers. No feeders and no grippers — the roll of paper passed around impression cylinders at one side of the form cylinder, turned upside down at the lower part, carried upwards, and the opposite side presented in turn between each impression cylinder and the forms. Four impression cylinders: 12,000 per hour; eight impression cylinders: 24,000 per hour. One or two rolls of paper used depending on configuration.
24. Three-Page-Wide Press (1888)
Capacity: two-page papers with one fold at 60,000 per hour; four-page papers with two folds at 24,000 per hour; eight-page papers folded twice at 12,000 per hour; twelve-page papers similarly folded at 12,000 per hour. Outside pages could receive first or last impression at will, enabling large cuts to print without offset. Grippers, horizontal folding knives, and all tapes except short leaders eliminated — movements all rotary. Dimensions: 6 ft 1 in high, 8 ft wide, 15 ft 5 in long.
25. Newspaper and Pamphlet Press (1889)
Plates or forms for both sides placed on one cylinder (one side on each half). One impression cylinder only, extended inking apparatus. Produced sheets of 8 to 128 pages, folded in 12mo, 8vo, 4to, or folio sizes, ready for the binder. Paper supplied from roll, passed over a “former” into the folding machine. Curved electrotypes used. The first press to bring average book and catalogue work within the range of web press work. Speed on a 32-page form: about 16,000 copies per hour. Plates admit of underlays and overlays as on a flat-bed press. No tapes; folding on rollers and small cylinders without smutting. Knives cut the sheet to the right size for folding; papers automatically delivered counted in lots of fifty.
26. Rotary Art Press (1890, De Vinne Press)
Built for Theodore L. De Vinne (Century Magazine). Sixty-four plates bent to the proper curve fastened on one cylinder (60 inches long, about 30 inches in diameter). Sixteen inking rollers supplied with ink from two fountains. Shafts of the impression cylinder and plate cylinders (4.5 inches in diameter) — described as not giving or springing under the strongest impression. Fed by four feeders from single sheets. The first rotary press capable of fine illustration work, combining the quality of stop-cylinder work with rotary speed.
27. Octuple Perfecting Press with Folders
Prints from four rolls, each four pages wide. From four deliveries: 96,000 four-to-eight-page papers per hour; 72,000 ten-page; 60,000 twelve-page; 48,000 fourteen or sixteen-page; 42,000 eighteen-page; 36,000 twenty-page; 24,000 twenty-four-page papers per hour. Further developed into the Improved Combination Octuple (Double Quadruple) and Color Machine, also producing papers in colors.
28. Double Sextuple Press (c. 1898-1902)
Two separate complete printing mechanisms, each fed from three four-page-wide rolls of paper, with gathering and folding apparatus in the center between the two sections. Twelve plate cylinders total, each carrying eight plates the size of a newspaper page. Ink applied by four form rollers after distribution by vibrating rollers and cylinders. Angle bars for transferring half-width webs.
Full capacity (all black, six rolls): 96,000 twelve-page papers per hour. Fourteen and sixteen-page papers at 72,000 per hour; eighteen to twenty-four-page papers at 48,000 per hour. As a color press: 48,000 sixteen-page papers per hour with outside pages in four colors and black. Dimensions: length 35 ft, height 17 ft, width 9 ft; weight about 225,000 pounds; approximately 50,000 parts.
29. Color Printing Developments (late 1890s)
With properly prepared inks and suitable plates, colors could be printed almost simultaneously without mingling. Accurate register maintained when printing from a roll. The largest color press (built for the New York Journal): eleven separate impressions or colors on a single copy (six on one side, five on the other). Speed of about 16,000 eight-page papers per hour. Four to thirty-two-page papers from one, two, or three double-width rolls. Magazine forms (half the page size) at 16,000 to 24,000 per hour, delivered folded, cut, and automatically wire-stitched.
Press Speeds Given in the Text

Gutenberg’s wooden press: approximately 300 sheets per day
Washington hand press: 250 impressions per hour (stated in the Herald quotation comparing 1829 to 1891)
Koenig’s cylinder press (1814): 800 sheets per hour
Adams bed-and-platen press: maximum 1,000 sheets per hour
Single Large Cylinder: up to 2,000 impressions per hour
Double Small Cylinder: about 4,000 per hour (2,000 from each of two cylinders)
Stop Cylinder (36x54 in bed): 1,000-1,500 impressions per hour
Stop Cylinder (45x62 in bed): 1,700 impressions per hour
Flat-bed with new crank motion (48x65 in): 1,800 impressions per hour
Lithographic/Zincographic press (30x44 in): up to 2,000 impressions per hour
Lithographic/Zincographic press (44x64 in): up to 1,700 impressions per hour
Hoe Type Revolving Machine, four-cylinder: ~8,000 papers per hour (one side)
Hoe Type Revolving Machine, ten-cylinder: ~20,000 papers per hour (one side)
Hoe web perfecting press: 18,000 perfect papers per hour (maximum); 12,000-14,000 average
Tucker folding cylinder: 15,000 per hour
Double Supplement press: 24,000 per hour (four-to-twelve-page); 12,000 (sixteen-page)
Quadruple press: 48,000 eight-page per hour; 24,000 ten-to-sixteen-page per hour
Sextuple press: 90,000 four-page per hour; 72,000 eight-page; 48,000 ten-to-twelve-page; 36,000 sixteen-page; 24,000 fourteen-to-twenty-four-page
Three-page-wide press: 60,000 two-page per hour; 24,000 four-to-six-page; 12,000 eight-to-twelve-page
Octuple press: 96,000 four-to-eight-page per hour; 72,000 ten-page; 60,000 twelve-page; 48,000 fourteen-to-sixteen-page; 24,000 twenty-four-page
Double Sextuple press: 96,000 twelve-page per hour (all black); 48,000 sixteen-page per hour (color)
Rotary Art press: described as equal to four stop cylinders
Book/web press (32-page form): ~16,000 copies per hour
New York Journal color press: ~16,000 eight-page papers per hour

primary-sources/john-man-gutenberg-revol.title: The Gutenberg Revolution (John Man)
primary-sources/john-man-gutenberg-revol.content:
The Gutenberg Revolution: The Story of a Genius and an Invention that Changed the World (2002) is a narrative history of Johann Gutenberg and the invention of movable-type printing, covering the period from c. 1400 to the Reformation.
Summary of Contents
The book traces Gutenberg’s life from his birth in Mainz around 1400 through his exile in Strasbourg, his return to Mainz, the invention of printing with movable type, the production of the 42-line Bible, his financial ruin, and the subsequent spread of printing across Europe. It also covers the political and religious context of 15th-century Europe — the Holy Roman Empire, the Great Schism, the Council of Constance, Nicholas of Cusa, and the role of print in the Reformation. Two appendices provide a hypothetical balance sheet for the Bible project and a list of German printers abroad.
Chapter-by-Chapter Detail
Introduction: The Third Revolution
Positions printing with movable type as the third great revolution in human communication, after the invention of writing and the alphabet, and before the internet. Uses the Frankfurt Book Fair as a contemporary symbol of what printing has become, and sets up the central irony of the book: Gutenberg was a businessman who aimed to profit from the Catholic Church’s continent-wide market, but his invention ultimately shattered Christian unity through the Reformation.
Chapter 1: A Golden City, Tarnished
Describes Mainz around 1400 — its streets, guilds, architecture, the Rhine foreshore, and the Gutenberg family house (the Gutenberghof, originally called Judenberg / Jewish Hill). Covers the Black Death and its impact on Mainz (population halved, anti-Jewish pogroms of 1348-49, the burning of Jews outside St Quentin’s Church). Explains the patrician-guild conflict that dominated city politics, the annuity system that bankrupted the city, and the Gutenberg family’s exile to Eltville in 1411 and 1413. Details Gutenberg’s father Friele Gensfleisch zur Laden and his mother Else Wirich, Gutenberg’s probable education (possibly at Erfurt University), his familiarity with coin-making and punch-cutting, and the creation of the 1400 birth-year as a public-relations decision by Mainz city fathers in the 1890s.
Chapter 2: The Strasbourg Adventure
Covers Gutenberg’s move to Strasbourg by 1434. Describes his arrest of Mainz burgomaster Niklaus von Wörrstadt to recover 310 gulden in unpaid annuities. Details his relationship with Ennelin zur Yserin Thure (Little Annie Iron Door) and the breach-of-promise lawsuit brought by her mother Ellewibel. Explains the Aachen pilgrim mirror scheme: Gutenberg planned to mass-produce 32,000 convex metal mirrors for the 1439 pilgrimage, selling at half a gulden each, for a projected 2,500% profit. Describes the partnership formed in 1438 with Hans Riffe, Andreas Dritzehn, and Andreas Heilmann (Gutenberg: 50%, Riffe: 25%, Dritzehn: 12.5%, Heilmann: 12.5%). Covers the postponement of the 1439 Aachen pilgrimage due to plague, Dritzehn’s death in December 1438, the panic to dismantle press and formes to preserve secrecy, and the 1439 Dritzehn lawsuit. Presents the witness depositions including goldsmith Hans Dunne’s testimony about earning 100 gulden “just for that which pertains to the pressing,” the references to “formes,” a press, and the “tool of four pieces” held by two screws that Gutenberg ordered dismantled.
Chapter 3: A Hercules Labouring for Unity
Covers the political and religious context of Gutenberg’s Europe. Introduces Nicholas of Cusa (Nikolaus von Kues, 1401-1464), born near Mainz, roughly contemporary with Gutenberg. Describes Nicholas’s education with the Brethren of the Common Life in Deventer, his studies at Heidelberg and Padua, his career as canon lawyer and statesman, his book De Concordantia Catholica arguing that authority arises from consent, his role at the Council of Basel (1431-1449), the Hussite negotiations (Communion in both kinds), the calendar reform proposal, and his switch from conciliarist to papal champion. Covers the Ferrara-Florence Council (1438-1439) and the failed reunion with the Greek Orthodox Church. Describes Nicholas’s rise to cardinal and bishop of Brixen, the Bursfeld Congregation’s reform of Benedictine monasteries, the push for a standardized missal, and the possibility that Nicholas and Gutenberg met and shared the vision of duplicating texts to achieve Christian unity.
Chapter 4: Something in the Air
Surveys the precursors to Gutenberg’s invention. Covers the Phaistos Disc (1700 BC), Chinese invention of paper (AD 105), block-printing in China/Japan/Korea, Pi Sheng’s movable clay type (11th century), Korean movable metal type (the Prescribed Ritual Texts, 1234), and the Mongol Empire’s possession of paper, movable type, and an alphabetical script (Uigur-derived) without developing printing. Discusses King Sejong of Korea’s invention of the Hangul alphabet (1443-44). Explains why Asian cultures did not develop a printing press: complex writing systems, conservatism, wrong paper type, absence of screw-presses, and no capital markets. Covers two near-misses in Europe: Procopius Waldvogel in Avignon (1444-46), who offered to teach “the art of artificial writing” with two steel alphabets, and the Laurens Coster legend from Haarlem (the story that Coster invented printing and Gutenberg stole it, told by Hadrianus Junius in 1588).
Chapter 5: The Secret Revealed
Explains how Gutenberg’s invention probably worked. Describes the four integrated innovations: (1) the punch — a steel letter engraved in relief on the end of a steel rod; (2) the matrix — the letter punched in intaglio into a softer metal (copper); (3) the hand-held mould — an adjustable two-part device that holds the matrix at the bottom of a rectangular slot, into which molten type-metal is poured, producing a piece of type with the letter standing proud; (4) the type-metal alloy — lead with tin (to improve flow and cooling) and antimony (to harden the metal). Covers the oil-based ink (linseed oil varnish, soot, amber), the adaptation of the screw-press from wine/paper presses, the paper dampening process, and the challenge of consistent pressure. Explains Gutenberg’s departure from Strasbourg in 1444 due to the Armagnac threat, his “hidden years” (1444-1448), and his return to Mainz in 1448 with the help of a 150-gulden loan from his cousin Arnold Gelthus.
Chapter 6: In Search of a Bestseller
Describes Mainz’s financial crisis (373,000 gulden debt, bankruptcy in 1448) and Gutenberg’s return. Covers his first printed work: the Donatus (the Ars Grammatica by Aelius Donatus, a standard Latin grammar), printed in the D-K (Donatus-Kalender) type with 202 characters. Discusses the Sibylline Prophecy fragment (Sibyllenbuch/Weltgericht), a single page found in 1892, printed from D-K type, possibly an early Gutenberg product. Covers the arrival of cardinals Nicholas of Cusa and Juan de Carvajal in Mainz in December 1448 to approve the Bursfeld missal. Describes Gutenberg’s partnership with Johann Fust: two loans of 800 gulden each (1449 and 1452) at 6% interest, secured against equipment. Explains the collapse of the missal project due to the conflict between the Bursfeld Congregation’s text (backed by Rome) and the St Jakob’s text (backed by Mainz’s archbishop). Covers the 1451 Cyprus indulgence — Pope Nicholas V granted King John of Cyprus the right to produce plenary indulgences to raise money for mercenaries against the Turks, and Nicholas of Cusa ordered 2,000 indulgences prepared for sale in Frankfurt in May 1452.
Chapter 7: The Bible
Covers the 42-line Bible (B42) in detail. Describes the physical specifications: two volumes, 1,275 pages, half-folio format (30.7 x 44.5 cm), two columns per page, 42 lines per page (with the first nine folios at 40 lines, then page 10 at 41 lines), 290 different characters including 83 ligatures. Describes the production: three punch-cutters (Hans Dunne, Gotz von Schlettstadt, Hans von Speyer) working for about four months; six compositors working on three pages each, requiring approximately 46,000 characters in use at any time; three presses operating simultaneously, each with two pressmen. Covers the paper (handmade from Italy, revealed by watermarks) and vellum (about 5,000 calfskins for 30-35 copies). Print run: approximately 180 copies (135-150 paper, 30-45 vellum); 37 paper copies and 12 vellum copies survive. Mentions Paul Needham’s computer analysis (with Blaise Aguera y Arcas) revealing dozens of variants of each letter shape, suggesting Gutenberg’s type may not have been produced from punches and matrices in the conventional way. Covers the Turk Calendar (1455) printed after the fall of Constantinople (May 1453). Describes the Piccolomini letter (March 1455): Enea Silvio Piccolomini, the future Pope Pius II, writing to Cardinal Juan de Carvajal from Vienna, reports seeing quinternions (20-page sections) of the Bible at the Frankfurt fair, describes it as “extremely elegant and correct” and readable without glasses, says 158-180 copies had been printed and buyers were already ready. Discusses the design choices — justified right margin, overhanging hyphens, the golden-section proportions of the page, and the letter-spacing adjustments needed to achieve 42 lines.
Chapter 8: Colophon
Covers the Fust lawsuit of 1455. Describes the Helmasperger Notarial Instrument (6 November 1455): Fust claimed 2,026 gulden (the two 800-gulden loans plus unpaid interest and compound interest). Gutenberg argued the second 800 gulden was for “the work of the books” (das werck der bucher) and should not need to be repaid. The judgement required Gutenberg to account for funds not put to mutual use. Fust took over the Humbrechthof workshop, the presses, and the Bible. Describes Peter Schoffer’s defection from Gutenberg to Fust. Covers the Mainz Psalter (1457): 350 pages, two-colour printing (red and blue decorative capitals plus black text), the first printed colophon (attributing the work to Johann Fust and Peter Schoffer), and the first printer’s mark (two shields hanging from a twig). Describes Schoffer’s subsequent success: missals, Durandus (guide to liturgy), canon law books. Covers Gutenberg’s continued work at the Gutenberghof with D-K type: Donatus editions, calendars, the papal bull for a Turkish crusade, a single-page prayer. Describes the 36-line Bible (B36): printed in Bamberg under Albrecht Pfister, using a revised D-K type, expanded to 1,768 pages, about 80 copies (20 on vellum, 60 on paper). Covers the Catholicon (1460): a 746-page Latin dictionary and grammar by Giovanni Balbi, set in the smallest type devised to date (5 million characters, almost twice the length of the Bible), with a colophon praising Mainz and the invention of printing but anonymous about its author. Describes the 1462 sack of Mainz: the conflict between Archbishop Diether von Isenburg and his rival Adolf von Nassau, the battle of 28 October 1462, the expulsion of 800 citizens including Gutenberg and his financier Konrad Humery, and the seizure of the Gutenberghof. Covers Gutenberg’s exile in Eltville (1462-1468), the indulgence printed in 1464 using Catholicon type, the Vocabularius ex quo (1465-67), and Adolf von Nassau’s award of a pension to Gutenberg in January 1465 (2,000 kg of grain and 2,000 litres of wine per year, plus clothing and tax exemption). Gutenberg’s death on 3 February 1468, recorded by Leonhard Mengoss; burial in the church of St Francis, Mainz.
Chapter 9: Pressing to the Limits
Covers the spread of printing from Mainz to the rest of Europe after the 1462 sack. Defines incunabula (books printed before 31 December 1500) and notes the ISTC (Incunabula Short-Title Catalogue) lists almost 30,000 titles. Describes the diffusion: German printers traveled with their tools (punches, hand moulds, formes) seeking work. Strasbourg had 50 printers by 1500; by 1480, 122 towns in Western Europe had presses (50 in Italy, 30 in Germany). By 1500, 236 towns had presses, producing 15-20 million books. Covers specific cases: Heinrich Eggestein and Johann Mentelin in Strasbourg (first German-language Bible translation, banned by the archbishop of Mainz in 1485); Anton Koberger in Nuremberg (Europe’s biggest printer, 24 presses, 100 pressmen, agents across Europe); Hartmann Schedel’s Nuremberg Chronicle (1493, 1,800 illustrations, 2,500 copies in Latin and German editions). Covers Italian expansion: Konrad Sweynheym and Johann Pannartz in Subiaco (Italy’s first printed book, Lactantius, 1465); Johannes and Wendelin von Speyer in Venice (monopoly granted 1467); Nicholas Jenson (Roman typeface, first Italian Bible, 1471); Johann Numeister in Foligno (first edition of Dante’s Divine Comedy, 1472). Describes Aldus Manutius in Venice (Aldine Press, Greek classics, monopoly on Greek printing, Aristotle in five volumes 1495-98). Covers the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (1499, printed by Aldus), an architectural-erotic fantasy in an invented language, set in Poliphilus type. Discusses French printing: Ulrich Gering and Michael Friburger in Paris (1470, Sorbonne-backed). Covers William Caxton in England: learned printing in Cologne, published the Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (1471, first printed book in English), set up in Westminster in 1476, published 100 books including Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales. Ends with a postscript on Islam’s rejection of printing: despite paper, ink, alphabetical script, and knowledge of the technology (Jewish refugees printed Hebrew books in Constantinople from 1493), printing was not adopted in the Muslim world for 400 years due to the primacy of oral transmission of the Qur’an, the authority of the ijaza (chain of oral transmitters), and opposition to bida (innovation).
Chapter 10: Christendom Divided, the World United
Traces the role of print in the Reformation. Covers the shift from scribal to print culture, the rise of new specializations in publishing, the spread of scientific knowledge (Regiomontanus’s astronomical observations, Copernicus), architectural theory (Vitruvius, Palladio), cartography (Abraham Ortelius’s Theatrum orbis terrarum, 1570), the invention of the index (first printed index in Fust and Schoffer’s St Augustine, early 1460s; 83 books had alphabetical indexes by 1500), and the Polyglot Bible (Christophe Plantin, Antwerp, 1568-72, in Hebrew, Greek, Latin, Aramaic, and Syriac). The core of the chapter covers Martin Luther: his early life, education at Erfurt, fear of storms and decision to become a monk, his doctrine of justification by faith alone, his horror at Rome’s corruption during his 1511 visit, his posting of the 95 Theses (dated 31 October 1517, though Man notes the nailing-to-the-door story is likely a legend from Melanchthon’s account 30 years later). Describes the indulgence controversy: Pope Leo X’s indulgence to fund St Peter’s Basilica, Johann Tetzel’s sales campaign near Wittenberg (“even if you raped the Virgin Mary”), and Albrecht of Brandenburg’s complex financial arrangement (he borrowed 29,000 gulden from the Fugger banking family to buy the archbishopric of Mainz, to be repaid from indulgence proceeds split 50-50 with the Pope). Covers the rapid spread of Luther’s theses through printing: editions appeared in Leipzig, Basel, and Nuremberg within weeks; a third of all books printed in Germany between 1518 and 1525 were by Luther; his Address to the Christian Nobility of the German Nation sold 4,000 copies in three weeks. Covers the Leipzig Debate (1519) with Johann Eck, Luther’s excommunication (1521), the Diet of Worms (April 1521) where Luther refused to recant, his faked kidnap and seclusion at Wartburg Castle, and his translation of the New Testament into German (1522, completed in 11 weeks) and the Old Testament (1534). Discusses William Tyndale’s parallel work in English: printed his New Testament translation in Worms (1526) by Peter Schoffer the younger, 3,000 copies smuggled into England, six editions and 18,000 copies over the next three years, priced at 4 shillings (compared to 30 pounds for a hand-copied Bible). Covers the Church’s response: the Council of Trent (1545-63), the Index Librorum Prohibitorum (first published 1559, 4,000 books by its end in 1966), and the limits of censorship in the age of print.
Appendix I: The 42-Line Bible — A Possible Balance Sheet
Presents a hypothetical balance sheet based on calculations by German book historian Leonard Hoffmann. Lists costs: six presses (240 gulden), typecases and fittings (60 gulden), three years’ rent (30 gulden), heating (20 gulden), three hand moulds (60 gulden), typecasting metals (100 gulden), ink (30 gulden), paper (400 gulden), vellum (300 gulden), wages (800 gulden), Bible exemplar (80 gulden) = 2,120 gulden for the Bible alone. Adds an estimated 2,200 gulden for the second workshop (Donatus, indulgences, other jobs). Total costs including debts: approximately 4,500 gulden. Projected income: 30-45 vellum copies at 50 gulden each (1,500-2,250 gulden) plus 135-150 paper copies at 20 gulden each (2,700-3,000 gulden) = 4,200-5,250 gulden total. Concludes that the venture was technically insolvent at completion in 1455, with profitability dependent on future sales.
Appendix II: German Printers Abroad — The First Wave
Lists the first German printers in European towns, by country. Includes over 80 towns/centers: Italy (35 towns, from Subiaco 1465 to Barco 1496); France (12 towns, from Paris 1470 to Perpignan 1500); Switzerland (Geneva 1478, Rougemont 1481); Spain (17 towns, from Segovia c.1472 to Montserrat 1499); Portugal (Braga 1494, Lisbon 1495); Africa (Sao Tome 1494); Netherlands (6 towns, from Aalst 1474 to Antwerp 1500); England (London 1476, Oxford 1478); Denmark (Odense 1482); Sweden (Stockholm 1483); Bohemia-Moravia (3 towns, from Winterberg 1484 to Olmutz 1499); Hungary (Budapest 1473); Poland (Cracow 1473-74). Source: Ferdinand Geldner, Die Deutschen Inkunabeldrucker, Vol. 2, Stuttgart, 1970.

primary-sources/karrow-mapmakers-16th-ce.title: Mapmakers of the Sixteenth Century (Karrow)
primary-sources/karrow-mapmakers-16th-ce.content:
Mapmakers of the Sixteenth Century and Their Maps
Mapmakers of the Sixteenth Century and Their Maps: Bio-Bibliographies of the Cartographers of Abraham Ortelius, 1570 by Robert W. Karrow, Jr. (Chicago: Speculum Orbis Press, 1993). 888 pages. 3.3 million characters of OCR-extracted text from an Internet Archive scan.
Based on Leo Bagrow’s A. Ortelii Catalogus cartographorum, this reference work provides detailed bio-bibliographical entries for the cartographers whose maps appeared in Abraham Ortelius’s 1570 atlas Theatrum Orbis Terrarum, the first modern atlas.
Summary of Contents
Preface and Introduction
The preface explains the book’s genesis as an English-language edition and expansion of Bagrow’s 1928-1936 German catalog. Karrow examined primary sources extensively, personally examining over 90% of the original works cited. The introduction discusses the historical context of 16th-century cartography, the Ortelius atlas project, and the methods used for the biographical and bibliographical entries.
Cartographer Entries
Approximately 75 bio-bibliographical entries covering both well-known and obscure 16th-century mapmakers, including:

primary-sources/lorck-handbuch-buchdruck.title: Handbuch der Geschichte der Buchdruckerkunst (Lorck)
primary-sources/lorck-handbuch-buchdruck.content:
Handbuch der Geschichte der Buchdruckerkunst. Erster Teil (Carl Berendt Lorck, 1882)
This is a German-language encyclopedic handbook of printing history, organized by region, then by city, then by printer. It covers the origins of printing through the 19th century. The entire text is in German (late 19th-century orthography).
Summary of Contents
The handbook is divided into two main books (Erstes Buch and Zweites Buch). The first book (1450–1500) covers the invention and spread of printing. The second book (1500–1750) covers the flourishing period and decline. Each book opens with an introduction and proceeds through chapters organized by topic or geography. The volume concludes with a name/subject register and a bibliography of cited sources.
Detailed Breakdown of Contents
Book One: Invention and Spread of Printing (1450–1500)
Introduction to Book One (pages 3–10): Discusses the state of research on the invention, defines what typography is, and reviews the major literature on the history of printing up to 1880 — including works by Falkenstein, T.O. Weigel and Zestermann, A. van der Linde, Schaab, Wetter, Breitkopf, Ottley, Sotheby, Holtrop, Chatto and Jackson, Dibdin, Humphreys, De Vinne, A. Bernard, A.F. Didot, and J.P.A. Madden.
Chapter I: Prehistory of Printing (pages 11–22): Covers the earliest traces of reproduction and multiplication — impressions in stone, metal, and clay; manuscript culture and the rise of the scribal trade; illumination and rubrication; the manuscript book trade. Then covers metal engraving and woodcut; the art schools (Swabian, Franconian, Bavarian, Lower Rhenish). Includes textile printing (Zeugdruck), playing cards, and the earliest known images in metal cut (e.g., “Christ on the Cross” from the Weigel collection) and woodcut (e.g., “St. Christopher” dated 1423). Describes rubbing-prints (Reiberdrucke), one-sided (anopistographic) printing.
Provides detailed descriptions of the major xylographic works (block-books):

Ars Moriendi (12 leaves, small folio, brown ink, Mönchsschrift — the T.O. Weigel/British Museum copy described as the finest)
Historia St. Johannis / Apocalypse (3 editions with 50 illustrations, 3 with 48)
Ars Memorandi (15 crude woodcut plates with 15 text leaves)
Biblia Pauperum (Lower Rhenish origin, for the Pauperes Christi)
Speculum humanae salvationis (Lower Rhenish; only one edition with xylographic text, the rest typographic; discussed in connection with the Coster claim)
Der Entkrist (26 leaves, small folio)
Legende des heiligen Meinrad (48 xylographic leaves, octavo)
Ciromantia / Dr. Johann Hartlieb (24 leaves, printed on both sides)
Calendar of Johannes de Gamundia (c. 1470, oldest known ephemeris)
Donatus (the grammar textbook, very widely used)

Chapter II: The Invention (pages 23–36): Johannes Gutenberg’s family origins, youth, Strasbourg period (associations with Andreas Dritzehn, Hans Riffe, Andreas Heilmann; the press/mould dispute; the 1439 legal judgment), return to Mainz, the contract with Johann Fust (1450), the 42-line Bible and the 36-line Bible, Peter Schöffer’s role, Gutenberg’s later difficulties, his death, and his posthumous reputation.
Chapter III: The Spread of Printing in Germany (pages 37–54): Quick dissemination of the art. Gutenberg’s successors in Mainz. Peter Schöffer and his descendants. Ulm. Beromünster (first printing location in Switzerland). Basel. Bamberg and Albrecht Pfister. Augsburg. Nuremberg (Nürnberg). Vienna. The North: Cologne (Köln), Münster, Magdeburg, Leipzig.
Chapter IV: The Spread of Printing Abroad (pages 55–76):

Italy: Subiaco and Rome, Venice, Foligno, Milan, Florence
Spain and Portugal
France: Paris, Lyon
The Netherlands: the Histoires, Colard Mansion
England: William Caxton
Scandinavia: Denmark, Sweden
The Slavic lands, Hungary, Turkey

Chapter V: The Technique of Printing and Literary Production (pages 77–96):

Technical aspects: type-founding (Schriftgiesserei), composition (Satz), printing, proofreading
The presses, ink, book decoration
Parchment and paper
Bookbinding
Literary production: the book trade, censorship

Book Two: Flourishing Period and Decline of Printing (1500–1750)
Introduction to Book Two (pages 98–104).
Chapter VI: The Illustrating Arts in Germany (pages 105–126): German painting schools. Copper engraving and woodcut. Michel Wolgemut. Albrecht Dürer, his contemporaries and successors (Hans Burgkmair, Hans Schaeuffelein, the “Kleinmeister”). Hans Holbein the Younger. Lucas Cranach the Elder. Swiss and Alsatian artists. Discussion of “original” woodcuts by the artists themselves.
Chapter VII: Typography in Germany and the Scandinavian Countries (pages 127–158):

Nuremberg: Theuerdank, German typefaces
Augsburg: Hans Schönsperger the Elder
Frankfurt am Main: Chr. Egenolff, Sigism. Feyerabend, the Merians
Mainz: Schöffer’s successors
Tübingen: Slavic printing, Cotta
Strasbourg: illustrated printing
Basel: Johannes Froben, the Petri family, Johannes Oporinus
Zürich: Chr. Froschauer
St. Gallen: Leon. Straub
Vienna: Johann Sigriener, Hans Kohl, Johann von Gehlen
Leipzig: Melchior Lotter, Valentin Bapst
Wittenberg
The North: Berlin
Scandinavia: Denmark, Norway and Iceland, Sweden and Finland

Chapter VIII: The Printing Business and the Book Trade in Germany (pages 159–174):

Type-founding and printing typefaces
Technique of setting and printing: composing apparatus, proofreading, the press, ink
Master, journeyman, and apprentice
Bookbinding
Book trade: literary production, author-publisher relations

Chapter IX: Italy, Spain, Portugal, and South America (pages 175–192):

Venice: the Aldus family (Aldus Pius Manutius, Paulus Manutius, Aldus II). Daniel Bomberg. Mechitar
Rome: the Propaganda press
Genoa
Florence: the Giunta
Padua
Xylography: Cesare Vecellius, chiaroscuro printing, Ugo da Carpi, Count Antonio Zanetti, John Jackson
Spain and Portugal: Brocario and the Complutensian Polyglot. Madrid. Antonio Bortazar
Mexico: Johann Kromberger, Juan Pablos. Lima, Peru. Santo Domingo and others

Chapter X: France (pages 193–216):

The position of the printer. The state and the press
Xylography, livres d’heures
Anton Verard. Geofroy Tory. Jodocus Badius. Conrad Néobar
Famous printer families. The Estiennes (Stephane): Henri I, Robert I, Henri II, end of the family
Foundation of the Royal Printing Office. Ant. Vitré. Savary de Brèves
Lyon: Sebastian Gryphius, Jean de Tournes, Étienne Dolet
Type-founding. Bookbinding

Chapter XI: The Netherlands (pages 217–254):

Illustration
Christoph Plantin, his descendants, the Plantin-Moretus Museum
The Blaeu family
The Elzevirs (Elsevier family): Louis I, Matthias and Bonaventura, Isaack, Bonaventura and Abraham I, Johann and Daniel, Louis and Daniel, the end of the house, imitators
The Enschedé family and type-founding

Chapter XII: England and North America (pages 255–276):

The gradual growth of the English press: Wynkyn de Worde, Richard Pynson, Reynold Wolfe, John Day, Thomas Vautrollier, Thomas Roycroft, Samuel Palmer, Samuel Richardson
Oxford, Cambridge
The Scottish and Irish presses
Stereotyping and William Ged
Newspapers
Type-founding
North America: small beginnings. John Glover, James Franklin, Benjamin Franklin. German immigrants and their press: Christoph Sauer and his descendants

Chapter XIII: The Slavic Countries, Turkey, East Asian Countries (pages 277–288):

Poland
Russia: Moscow, St. Petersburg
Turkey: Constantinople, Ibrahim and Said Efendi
Syria
East Asia: China (Chinese block-printing method and paper manufacture)
European printing in Asia
Africa

The Coster Legend
The Haarlem/Coster claim is discussed in the context of early Dutch printing (within the Netherlands/Niederlande section). Lorck reviews the Junius account (Hadrianus Junius / Adrian de Jonghe), the alleged Costeriana, and the arguments of supporters and sceptics.
Technical Coverage
Throughout the handbook, Lorck provides descriptions of:

Paper-making
Type-founding (Schriftgiesserei): punches, matrices, moulds, metal types
The printing press and its components
Composition (setting type)
Inking (ink balls, inking slab, ink preparation)
Proofreading and correction
Bookbinding

Appendices

A. Name and Subject Register (pages 289–300)
B. Bibliography of Cited Sources (pages 301–304)

primary-sources/lowry-world-of-aldus-man.title: The World of Aldus Manutius (Lowry)
primary-sources/lowry-world-of-aldus-man.content:
The World of Aldus Manutius: Business and Scholarship in Renaissance Venice
Martin Lowry, The World of Aldus Manutius: Business and Scholarship in Renaissance Venice (Ithaca, NY: Cornell University Press, 1979). 376 pages. ISBN 9780801412141.
A scholarly monograph on Aldus Manutius (1450-1515) and the Aldine Press, examining the relationship between Renaissance scholarship and printing. Lowry analyzes the structure of the Aldine Press, its output during Aldus’s lifetime, and changes in its policies. He draws on recently discovered press copies to offer a revision of Aldus’s accepted position in the development of the printed book.
Summary of Contents
Based on the table of contents and text:
Introduction (pp. 1-8): Sets up the study’s scope and methodology.
Chapter 1 — Men of Business and Men of Letters (pp. 9-48): The Venetian printing world before Aldus. Covers the careers of John of Speyer, Nicolas Jenson, and the early Venetian printer-publishers. The economics of early printing in Venice. The relationship between capital, scholarship, and the book trade.
Chapter 2 — The Wandering Scholar (pp. 49-90): Aldus’s early life and education — his studies in Rome and Ferrara, his tutoring of the Pio princes of Carpi, his Greek studies under Guarini and Adramyttenos, and the development of his plan to print Greek classics.
Chapter 3 — Barbarigo, Torresani and Manuzio (pp. 91-128): The founding of the Aldine Press. Aldus’s financial backers (Pierfrancesco Barbarigo, Andrea Torresani), his marriage to Torresani’s daughter Maria, the merger of the Jenson-Torresani printing office with Aldus’s new press. The business structure of the firm.
Chapter 4 — The Chances of Business (pp. 129-168): The practical operations of the Aldine Press. Production methods, typefounding, paper supply, labor relations, edition sizes, pricing, distribution. The Greek type and the italic type (Francesco Griffo). Piratical competition from Lyons and elsewhere. Privileges and their enforcement.
Chapter 5 — Academic Dreams (pp. 169-208): The Aldine Academy (Neacademia) and its scholarly program. Aldus’s relationship with Greek refugee scholars. The editorial methods used to produce the Greek classics. The Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (1499) and its significance.
Chapter 6 — Authorship and Editorship (pp. 209-248): Aldus’s relationships with authors and editors — Erasmus, Bembo, Musurus, Navagero. The role of the corrector (proofreader) in the Aldine shop. The transition from scholarly editing to commercial publishing.
Chapter 7 — The Great Diffusion (pp. 249-288): The spread of Aldine books across Europe. Distribution networks, book fairs, agents. The influence of Aldine typography and format on other printers (the Estiennes, Froben, the Elzevirs). The octavo revolution and its impact.
Conclusion (pp. 289-304): Lowry’s assessment of Aldus’s place in printing history. The relationship between commerce and scholarship. The legacy of the Aldine Press.
Appendices, Bibliography, Index (pp. 305-376): Bibliographical descriptions, archival sources, and a full index.
Relevance to the Wiki
This is the single most comprehensive source on Aldus Manutius in the project. It covers much more detail than the current aldus-manutius.md entity page (which draws mainly from Putnam Vol. II and John Man). Specific topics that could enrich the wiki:

The business structure of the Aldine Press (partnership with Barbarigo/Torresani)
The Jenson-Torresani merger and the continuity of Venetian printing
The Francesco Griffo relationship and the italic type design
The Aldine Academy and its members
Distribution networks and book fairs
Piratical competition and privilege enforcement
Detailed treatment of the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili

See Also

primary-sources/nature-of-the-book-johns.title: The Nature of the Book: Print and Knowledge in the Making (Johns)
primary-sources/nature-of-the-book-johns.content:
The Nature of the Book: Print and Knowledge in the Making
Adrian Johns, The Nature of the Book: Print and Knowledge in the Making. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1998 (paperback 2000). xxi + 753 pages.
A landmark revisionist cultural history of print. Johns challenges Elizabeth Eisenstein’s thesis (in The Printing Press as an Agent of Change) that the press inherently produced fixity, standardization, and credibility. He argues instead that those qualities of print were socially constructed through contested practices among printers, authors, booksellers, readers, and the state. The book focuses mainly on England c. 1580–1720, with dense treatment of the Stationers’ Company, licensing, piracy, and the “literatory life” of London printing houses.
Raw text: nature_of_the_book_raw.txt (OCR from image-based EPUB, ~964 KB at project root).
Summary of Contents























































ChapterTitleFocus1Introduction: The Book of Nature and the Nature of the BookArgument against technological fixity; social construction of print credibility2Literatory Life: The Culture and Credibility of the Printed Book in Early Modern LondonLondon printing houses; Stationers’ Company; practices of printing3“The Advancement of Wholesome Knowledge”Licensing, censorship, regulation of the press4John Streater and the Knights of the GalaxyRepublican printer case study; Interregnum print politics5Faust and the PiratesHow the idea of a “printing revolution” was culturally constructed; piracy and authorship6The Physiology of ReadingEarly modern theories of how reading affected body and mind7Piracy and UsurpationNatural philosophy in the Restoration; Royal Society and print credibility8Histories of the HeavensFlamsteed, Newton, and the Historia Coelestis Britannica9ConclusionImplications for understanding print culture
Key Themes

































ThemeSummaryAgainst “fixity by technology”Piracy, unauthorized editions, and textual corruption were rampant; fixity came through institutions (Stationers’ Company, licensing), not the press as machine“Literatory life”Ethnography of the printing house — workshops, trade networks, author–stationer negotiationsCredibility as social achievementPrinted knowledge was trusted only when the whole production system was trustedPiracy and intellectual propertyContested authorship and proprietary claims across the periodPrint and the passionsReading as a physiological process affecting humors and passionsPolitics of natural knowledgeScientific publishing as a political act; Royal Society credibility tied to print practice
Relevance to the Wiki
Johns is the principal modern counterweight to eisenstein-printing-press-agent-of-change already in this corpus. Chapters 1–3 and 5 are most useful for:

English book-trade institutions after Caxton and de Worde (Stationers’ Company, register, patents)
How “fixity,” standardization, and credibility were argued for and against in print historiography
Material culture of the printing house (composition, proofing, house organization)
Licensing and state regulation as part of censorship-of-the-press and literary-property-and-copyright
The social construction of the “printing revolution” narrative itself (printing-revolution)

Later chapters (Restoration science, Flamsteed–Newton) sit mainly in the long seventeenth century but illuminate how early modern print credibility claims worked.
Relationship to Other Sources
