primary-sources/pearson-gutenberg-and-ar.title: Gutenberg and the Art of Printing (Pearson)
primary-sources/pearson-gutenberg-and-ar.content:
Gutenberg and the Art of Printing (Pearson)
Gutenberg and the Art of Printing by Emily C. Pearson (published 1871, Andover, Massachusetts) is a narrative biography of Johannes Gutenberg covering his life and the invention of movable type, with later chapters surveying nineteenth-century printing technology. The book runs approximately 300 pages across 25 chapters.
Summary of Contents
The book traces Gutenberg’s life from his childhood in Mainz, his exile in Strasbourg, his early experiments with block-printing and engraving, the partnership with Dritzehn (here spelled “Dritzhn”) and its dissolution through a lawsuit, the invention of movable type, the partnership with Johann Fust (called “Faust”) and Peter Schoeffer, the printing of the 42-line Bible, Fust’s seizure of the press, and Gutenberg’s final years. The final six chapters shift to a survey of nineteenth-century printing technology: typefounding, type-setting machinery, stereotyping, electrotyping, hand-presses, cylinder presses, and a closing philosophical reflection on printing.
Chapter-by-Chapter Detail
Chapter I — Strasbourg and its Cathedral. Gutenberg’s Early Life. Civil Strife. Romantic Lawsuit.
Describes Strasbourg and its cathedral. Covers Gutenberg’s birth in Mainz around 1400, his flight to Strasbourg due to political conflict between the nobility and the burghers, his banishment and loss of property, and the breach-of-promise lawsuit brought by Anna von Isemen Thur (here portrayed as a romantic summons to compel Gutenberg to fulfill his marriage promise).
Chapter II — Gutenberg in Exile. His Trade as Lapidary. Curious Law. Ancient Cuts. A Picture of a Saint. Legend. The Bible for the Poor. A Secret discovered. Gutenberg’s Experiment.
Covers Gutenberg’s exile and his trade as a lapidary (polisher of precious stones). Describes the social status of artisans in medieval Germany. Relates, through invented dialogue between Gutenberg and Anna, an examination of a playing-card that leads Gutenberg to explain wood-engraving. Includes the story of the St. Christopher woodcut (dated 1423) and the legend of St. Christopher. Discusses the Biblia Pauperum (Bible for the Poor) — a block-book of forty engraved pictures with written explanations. Anna discovers Gutenberg’s secret experiments with block-printing.
Chapter III — Ancient Books and their Materials.
A survey of the history of writing and books before printing. Covers early materials (brick, tile, shells, stone, lead), Chinese printing and papermaking, seals and stamping among the Romans, waxen tablets, bark, papyrus, parchment, paper, palimpsests, the scriptorium and monastic copyists, illuminations, the scarcity and costliness of books, Richard de Bury and his library (c. 1344), the statutes of St. Mary’s College Oxford limiting book use, chained books, and the contrast with the abundance of books in modern times.
Chapter IV — An Important Step. Engraving a Name. Engraving Pictures. Superstitions. Difficulties overcome. An Improvement. Experiment and Progress. A New Book. Cheerful Thoughts.
Gutenberg engraves Anna’s name on a wooden block and prints it on paper. He takes up the project of engraving a St. Christopher picture. Describes the search for suitable wood (apple-tree chosen), the making of tools, the improvement of printing ink (oil-based ink developed), the making of the first printer’s dabber (a sheepskin ball), and Gutenberg’s first impressions from engraved blocks.
Chapter V — Pecuniary Troubles. An Expedient. Disappointment. The Jewels. A Sale. Apprentices. Visit to the Cathedral. A New Enterprise.
Gutenberg faces financial difficulties from his experiments. He polishes jewels for the Abbot of the Cathedral to earn money. Takes on apprentices — Dritzhn (Andrew Dritzehn), Hielman, and Riffe. Visits the Cathedral library and sees block-books. Begins planning a new enterprise based on printing.
Chapter VI — Unwelcome Visitors. Unjust Demand. A Compromise. Secret Firm. A Removal. Teaching the Workmen. Block Printing. Success.
Gutenberg’s partners pressure him for results. A secret partnership is formed. The workshop is moved to a more secluded location. Gutenberg teaches his workmen the basics of block-printing. They achieve success with early block-printed products.
Chapter VII — Small Receipts. Printing the “Donatus.” “Ars Memorandi” “Ars Moriendi.” An Interesting Fact. Extract from “Ars Moriendi.”
The firm’s income is limited. They print the Donatus (a Latin grammar by Aelius Donatus), the Ars Memorandi (Art of Memory), and the Ars Moriendi (Art of Dying). An extract from the Ars Moriendi is quoted.
Chapter VIII — Effect of Gutenberg’s Books. His Times and Ours. His Books at the Cathedral. Curiosity of the Monks. Proposition of the Abbot. The “Bible for the Poor.” A Great Work well done. A Good Sale. The Canticles issued. A Difficult Undertaking. Discontent. An Accident. Discovery of Separate Types. The First Font of Movable Type. Difficulties mastered. The Great Helper.
The early printed books attract attention at the Cathedral. The Abbot proposes a project. The firm prints the Canticles. Discontent arises among the partners. An accident leads Gutenberg to the idea of separate, movable types rather than fixed engraved blocks. He produces the first font of movable type.
Chapter IX — Anna’s Disappointment. Dritzhn’s Regrets. Comfort for Anna. Gutenberg’s Progress described. The Great Enlightener. Advantages of Movable Type. Another Book. Obstacles. Criticisms. Invention. A Press contrived. New Cause of Disquiet.
Gutenberg argues the advantages of movable type over block-printing to his skeptical partners (Dritzhn and Riffe). A press is contrived. New difficulties emerge. Contains the frequently cited passage where Gutenberg explains that block-printing wastes time cutting letters that cannot be reused.
Chapter X — A Partner at the Confessional. His Death. Consequences. A Lawsuit. Thieves. Dangerous Curiosity. Destruction of Gutenberg’s Type. Curious Testimonies. Value of the Legal Document. Proof that Gutenberg was the Real Inventor. The Magistrate’s Just Judgment. Public Excitement.
One of the partners (Dritzhn) goes to confession, revealing the secret. He dies shortly after. A lawsuit ensues among the surviving partners. Includes testimony from the actual Strasbourg court depositions (Anna Schultheiss, Conrad Sachspach, Laurence Beildeck, John Dunnius the goldsmith). Gutenberg’s type is destroyed. The magistrate rules in Gutenberg’s favor.
Chapter XI — Benighted. Minstrel of the Hearth. The Black Art. A Barefoot Friar. Popular Prejudice. Hopes and Fears. Gutenberg returns to his Trade. Dissolution of the Copartnership.
Popular accusations of witchcraft and the “black art” surface against Gutenberg and his printing. Gutenberg returns to his lapidary trade. The Strasbourg partnership is formally dissolved.
Chapter XII — Congenial Quiet. Making Type again. Gutenberg issues “Absies.” Peter Schoeffer. Decides to remove to Mentz. Emotions of Gutenberg. Fraternal Sympathy. The Meeting with Faust. Gutenberg reveals his Art. A Rich Partner.
Gutenberg continues making type in quiet retirement. He issues a small work (“Absies”). Peter Schoeffer appears and becomes involved. Gutenberg decides to move to Mainz (here called “Mentz”). He meets Fust (here called “Faust”), reveals his art, and forms a new partnership with Faust as a wealthy financial backer.
Chapter XIII — The Zum Jungen. The Old Valet. A Happy Change. Going over the Process anew. Good Progress. Peter Schoeffer.
Gutenberg and his team establish the workshop at the Zum Jungen property. They review and re-establish the printing process. Peter Schoeffer joins as a skilled workman.
Chapter XIV — Working of the Press. The Medallion. An Acquisition. Experiments. A Failure. Schoeffer’s Invention. Discovery of Cast Metal Type.
Work on the press continues. Schoeffer conducts experiments. After a failure, Schoeffer discovers the method of casting metal type from matrices — cast metal type rather than individually engraved or carved letters.
Chapter XV — Schoeffer admitted to the Firm. A Grand Project. How a Bible was borrowed. The Early Press. Processes in Book-making. Ingenuity of Peter Schoeffer. Industry of the Firm. Ink. Cast Type. Three Ingenious Men. Letter-founding. Faust compliments Peter. The first Printed Page of the Bible. A Memorable Year.
Schoeffer is admitted to the partnership. The grand project of printing a Bible is conceived. A manuscript Bible is borrowed as a copy-text. Describes the early press, ink-making, and letter-founding processes. The first printed page of the 42-line Bible is produced in a memorable year (c. 1455).
Chapter XVI — Fust’s Discontent. Conspiracy against Gutenberg. The Lawsuit. Gutenberg supplanted. A New Firm. Gutenberg’s Sorrow.
Fust becomes discontented with the arrangement. A conspiracy forms against Gutenberg. Fust sues Gutenberg for repayment of loans. Gutenberg is supplanted and loses his press and types to Fust. Fust and Schoeffer form a new firm. Gutenberg is left in sorrow.
Chapter XVII — The Story of Faust’s Visit to Paris. Was it Witchcraft? Popular Excitement. Scene in a Court Room. Issue of the Psalter.
Relates the legend of Fust (Faust) traveling to Paris to sell printed Bibles, where people accuse him of witchcraft because uniform copies could only be produced by diabolical means. Includes a fictional courtroom scene. Describes the issue of the Psalter (the Mainz Psalter, 1457).
Chapter XVIII — New Friends. The Nun. Gutenberg at Work again. Printing of the “Balbus de Janua.” Other Works. A Curious Record. Death of the Great Inventor. Fadeless Laurels.
Gutenberg finds new supporters. He resumes printing and produces the Balbus de Janua (the Catholicon, a dictionary by Giovanni Balbi). Other works are mentioned. A curious record of Gutenberg is noted. Covers Gutenberg’s death and his legacy.
Chapter XIX — Fust and Schoeffer’s Success. More Books issued. An Eventful Year. Greek Type. Struck by the Plague. The Parisians and Faust’s Descendants. Schoeffer’s Death. Testimony to Gutenberg. Extension of the Art. Peculiarities of the First Printed Books. Early Printers. Piety and Chess. Education in the Olden Time. Great Enterprise. Unveiling Gutenberg’s Statue.
Covers the continued success of Fust and Schoeffer after Gutenberg’s departure. More books are issued. Greek type is introduced. Schoeffer dies. Testimonies to Gutenberg as the inventor are collected. The spread of printing to other cities is described. Discusses peculiarities of early printed books (no title pages, no page numbers, no signatures). Early printers are profiled. Covers the unveiling of Gutenberg’s statue.
Chapter XX — Modes of making Type. Varieties of Type. Cylindrical Ink-distributor. A Modern Printing Establishment. Composition Room. Cases. Proofreading.
Shifts to a description of nineteenth-century printing technology. Covers the methods of making type and the varieties of type available. Describes the cylindrical ink-distributor. Takes the reader through a modern printing establishment: the composition room, type cases, and proofreading procedures.
Chapter XXI — Type-setting by Machinery. Its Practicability. Various Machines devised. The Brown Type-setter and Distributer described. Simplicity. Reliability. Speed.
Discusses the practicability of mechanical type-setting. Surveys various machines devised for this purpose. Describes the Brown type-setter and distributor in detail: its simplicity, reliability, and speed of operation.
Chapter XXII — Stereotyping. Plaster Moulds. Planing and Bending. Correcting Stereotype Plates. Process of Electrotyping. The “Guillotine.” Ornamenting.
Describes the process of stereotyping — making plaster moulds from type forms, planing and bending stereotype plates, and correcting them. Then covers the process of electrotyping. Describes the “guillotine” machine for trimming and the ornamenting of printed pages.
Chapter XXIII — The Hand-press. Earl Stanhope’s Press. Improvements. Cylinder Presses. Press-room. Drying Room. Sewing Room. Elevator. Books for the Blind. Type, Press, and Paper invented. Catalogue of Great Exhibition. Estimate of Rapid Labor by Machinery.
Describes the hand-press and Earl Stanhope’s improved iron press. Covers cylinder presses and their advantages. Tours the various rooms of a modern printing establishment: press-room, drying room, sewing room, and the use of elevators. Mentions books printed for the blind. Notes that type, press, and paper were all invented. Cites the Catalogue of the Great Exhibition. Provides estimates of rapid labor accomplished by machinery.
Chapter XXIV — Time of the Great Invention. A First Gift. Discovery of the Alphabet. A New Era. Royal Printers. Knights of Type and Pen. A Mighty Engine. Gutenberg’s Dream. The Press mighty.
A closing philosophical chapter reflecting on the significance of Gutenberg’s invention. Discusses the timing of the invention, the alphabet as a first gift to civilization, the new era printing inaugurated, royal printers and their status, the power of the press as a “mighty engine,” and Gutenberg’s dream realized through the widespread influence of printing.

primary-sources/putnam-books-and-their-m.title: Books and their Makers during the Middle Ages, Vol. I (Putnam)
primary-sources/putnam-books-and-their-m.content:
Books and their Makers during the Middle Ages, Vol. I (Putnam)
George Haven Putnam, Books and their Makers during the Middle Ages: A Study of the Conditions of the Production and Distribution of Literature from the Fall of the Roman Empire to the Close of the Seventeenth Century, Vol. I (New York: G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1896). Covers 476-1600. Project Gutenberg eBook no. 71536, proofread by the Distributed Proofreaders team. 6,158 lines of clean text.
This volume covers the manuscript period and the first decades of printing. It is the counterpart to Vol. II (already in the wiki), which covers the later printer-publishers and the development of censorship and copyright.
Summary of Contents
Part I — Books in Manuscript. The production and distribution of books from the fall of Rome through the medieval period, covering monastic scriptoria, libraries, the rise of universities, and the commercial book trade.
Part II — The Earlier Printed Books. The Renaissance context, the invention of printing in Germany and the Netherlands, and the first printer-publishers of Italy (1464-1600).
Chapter-by-Chapter Detail
Part I: Books in Manuscript
Chapter I — The Making of Books in the Monasteries (line 828): The preservation of classical and Christian texts in monastic scriptoria. The Benedictine rule and the tradition of copying. Cassiodorus and the Vivarium. Irish monasteries and their scribal tradition (the Book of Kells, the Lindisfarne Gospels). Alcuin and the Carolingian renaissance. The scriptorium as a workshop — materials (parchment, ink, pigments), the division of labor, the cost of manuscript production.
Chapter II — Some Libraries of the Manuscript Period (line 1510): A survey of the major libraries of the Middle Ages: the Vatican Library, the library of the Sorbonne, the Medici Library, the libraries of the great monastic houses. The size and contents of these collections. How books were acquired, catalogued, and lent. The chained library system.
Chapter III — The Making of Books in the Early Universities (line 1744): The rise of the university book trade. The pecia system (the division of manuscripts into quires for simultaneous copying by multiple scribes). The stationers (stationarii) as licensed book producers. The regulation of the book trade by the universities of Paris, Bologna, and Oxford. The cost of books for students.
Chapter IV — The Book-Trade in the Manuscript Period (line 1982): The commercial production of manuscripts for sale. The rise of lay scribes and illuminators outside the monasteries. The Burgundian court library and the Flemish illuminators. Prices of books, the scale of production, the market for different kinds of texts (theology, law, medicine, romance). The transition from manuscript to print — the demand that printing would satisfy.
Part II: The Earlier Printed Books
Chapter I — The Renaissance as the Forerunner of the Printing-Press (line 2719): The intellectual and cultural conditions that prepared the ground for printing. The revival of classical learning. The growth of vernacular literature. The increase in lay literacy. The demand for texts that the manuscript system could not meet.
Chapter II — The Invention of Printing and the Work of the First Printers of Holland and Germany (line 2849): The invention of movable type. Gutenberg, Fust, and Schöffer in Mainz. The Coster claim in Haarlem. The spread of printing to Strasbourg, Cologne, Basel, Augsburg, Nuremberg, and other German cities. The economic and commercial aspects of early printing.
Chapter III — The Printer-Publishers of Italy, 1464-1600 (line 3153): The introduction of printing into Italy. Sweynheym and Pannartz at Subiaco (1464). The growth of printing in Rome, Venice, Florence, and Milan. The printer-publishers: Jenson, Aldus Manutius, the Giunti family. The Aldine Press and its innovations (italic type, octavo format, Greek classics). The business of printing in Renaissance Italy.

primary-sources/putnam-books-and-their-m.title: Books and their Makers during the Middle Ages, Vol. II (Putnam)
primary-sources/putnam-books-and-their-m.content:
Books and their Makers during the Middle Ages, Vol. II (Putnam)
Volume II of Books and their Makers during the Middle Ages: A Study of the Conditions of the Production and Distribution of Literature from the Fall of the Roman Empire to the Close of the Seventeenth Century (G. P. Putnam’s Sons, New York, 1896) covers the period from the invention of printing through the close of the seventeenth century (1500-1709).
Summary of Contents
The volume is divided into two major parts. Part II (Chapters IV-XII) surveys the principal printer-publishers of the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries—the Estiennes of Paris and Geneva, William Caxton, the Kobergers of Nuremberg, Johann Froben of Basel, Erasmus as author-client, Martin Luther as publishing phenomenon, the Plantin firm in Antwerp, and the Elzevirs of Leyden and Amsterdam. Part III (Chapters I-V) traces the development of copyright, privilege systems, and censorship across Italy, Germany, France, and England, culminating in the Copyright Act of 1709 (Queen Anne’s Act). The book is organized around the business, legal, and institutional dimensions of the book trade: markets, distribution networks, censorship mechanisms, privilege systems, book fairs, and the commercial relationship between printers, authors, and state or church authorities.
Chapter-by-Chapter Detail
Part II: The Earlier Printed Books (continued from Volume I)
Chapter IV — The Early Printer-Publishers of France (1458-1559). Opens with the failed Jenson mission of 1458 under Charles VII and the establishment of the first Paris press at the Sorbonne by Gering, Krantz, and Friburger (1469). Covers the early growth of the Paris book trade, the competitive relationship between Paris and Lyons (where printers enjoyed greater freedom from University censorship), and the rise of vernacular publishing. Treats the work of individual printers: Jodocus Badius Ascensius (his four hundred publications, the Philobiblon, the Navis Stultifera), Simon de Colines (Latin classics, Greek texts, italic type, the sixteenmo form), Giles Gourmont and the first Greek press in Paris (1507), Christianus Wechel, and Vascosanus (Typographus Regius). Includes an extensive treatment of the Estienne (Stephanus) dynasty: Henry Estienne the elder (his one hundred works, the arms of the University, press correctors), Robert Estienne’s early career (his training under Colines, the Novum Testamentum of 1524, his olive-tree device and motto, the use of Latin in his household, the practice of hanging proof-sheets in the streets for public correction), and a list of Robert’s principal publications from 1528 through 1540 (the Latin Thesaurus dictionary, editions of Cicero, Pliny, Terence, Plautus, Virgil, Horace, Quintilian, Sallust, Suetonius, Juvenal, Persius, Valerius Maximus, Lucian; four impressions of the Latin Bible by 1540; the Hebrew Scriptures in quarto; the Greek ecclesiastical writers; his appointment as Imprimeur Royal for Hebrew and Latin in 1539 and for Greek in 1540). Describes the long contest between Robert Estienne and the Sorbonne divines over his biblical corrections and marginal commentaries, the protection of Francis I, the founding of the Royal College, and the events that drove Robert to flee Paris for Geneva.
Chapter V — The Later Estiennes and Casaubon (1537-1659). Continues the Estienne story through the religious conflicts that drove the family from Paris to Geneva. Covers Robert Estienne’s flight from the Sorbonne’s censorship and his establishment of a press in Geneva (1551-1559), where he printed Calvinist works including Calvin’s Institution de la religion chrestienne. Describes the scholarly work of his son Henry Estienne (the younger): his education, his travels in Italy and Greece searching for manuscripts, his edition of the Greek New Testament (1576), his Thesaurus Graecae Linguae, his Apologie pour Hérodote, and his financial difficulties in later life. Also includes an extended section on Isaac Casaubon (87-100): his birth in Geneva, education under the Calvinist scholars, his editions of Polybius, Theophrastus, and Strabo, his work on the Greek New Testament, his removal to England under James I, his appointment as a prebendary of Canterbury, and the posthumous controversy over the state of his religious opinions at death.
Chapter VI — William Caxton and the Introduction of Printing into England (1422-1492). Covers Caxton’s apprenticeship in Bruges under Robert Large, his service as Governor of the English Nation in the Low Countries (1462-1470), his translation of the Recuyell of the Histories of Troye from French (the first book printed in English), his training under Colard Mansion in Bruges, the establishment of the first English press at Westminster (1476-1477), and his choice of texts from the Recuyell through Malory’s Le Morte D’Arthur (1485), the Golden Legend, and the Canterbury Tales. Discusses the economics of Caxton’s business: costs of types, paper, and labour; his relationship with the Burgundian court and noble patrons; his commercial methods and marketing; his role in standardising English orthography; and his successors—Wynkyn de Worde (his career, his publications, the use of illustrations), the Oxford press (Theodoric Rood, the Expositio Sancti Hieronymi of 1468, the decline of the Oxford press), and later English presses (St. Albans, the introduction of printing into Scotland).
Chapter VII — The Kobergers of Nuremberg (1440-1540). A detailed account of Anton Koberger, the greatest of the German printer-publishers, whose Nuremberg firm operated twenty-four presses simultaneously and maintained a Europe-wide distribution network. Describes Koberger’s capitalization and business methods, his agent system for sales across major European cities, his advertisement of publications at the Frankfurt fairs, his management of the risks of long-distance trade, and his practice of giving shares in important ventures to potential competitors (such as the compact with Nicholas Kessler of Basel in 1495). Includes an analysis of the Nuremberg Chronicle (1493) as a commercial venture—its financing, its production with hundreds of woodcuts by Wolgemut and Pleydenwurff, its Latin and German editions, and its marketing. Covers the decline of the firm under Koberger’s successors after his death in 1513.
Chapter VIII — Froben of Basel (1460-1528). Covers Johann Froben’s Basel press and its relationship with Erasmus, who served as editor and author. Describes Froben’s typographic standards and his role in making Basel a centre of learned publishing. Discusses his editions of the Greek and Latin Fathers (Jerome, Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine), his editions of the New Testament in Greek and Latin, his use of Holbein and Urs Graf as illustrators, the Froben imprint and device, and the continuation of the firm under his son Hieronymus Froben and nephew Nicolaus Episcopius.
Chapter IX — Erasmus and His Books (1467-1536). A biographical and bibliographical study of Erasmus as an author and publishing phenomenon. Covers Erasmus’s dealings with Aldus in Venice (the Adagia), Froben in Basel (the New Testament, the Colloquies, the Praise of Folly, the editions of Jerome, Cyprian, and Augustine), Badius in Paris, and other printers; the economics of his publications (the size of editions, pricing, profit-sharing, the twenty-four thousand copies of the Colloquies printed by Colines); his editorial methods and corrections; and the censorship troubles that shadowed his later years (the condemnations by the Sorbonne, the attacks by both Lutherans and Catholics, the imperial prohibition against his leaving the empire).
Chapter X — Luther as an Author (1483-1546). Examines Luther’s use of the printing press as an instrument of reform. Covers the pamphlet explosion of 1517-1525, the economics of Reformation printing, the role of the Wittenberg press (Melchior Lotther, Hans Lufft, Georg Rhau, Nickel Schirlentz), and the Catholic response. Describes the Flugschriften (fly-leaf literature) carried by pedlars into market-places and farmhouses, the development of a new reading public among common people, and the shift from folio and quarto to pamphlet formats. Discusses Luther’s practice of correcting proof-sheets for unauthorised reprints (to preserve textual accuracy) and his role in the development of German literary property rights. Covers the censorship systems established by both Catholic and Protestant authorities in response to the Reformation.
Chapter XI — The House of Plantin (1555-1650). A substantial treatment of Christopher Plantin’s Antwerp firm, the largest printing establishment of the sixteenth century. Describes the Polyglot Bible project (Biblia Polyglotta, 1568-1572)—its financing under the patronage of Philip II of Spain, the editorial challenges of printing the Bible in five languages (Hebrew, Greek, Latin, Chaldee, Syriac), the work of Arias Montanus as editor, and the financial catastrophe when demand fell short of expectations. Covers Plantin’s relationship with Philip II, the financial structure of the firm including the mysterious Silent Partners (possibly linked to the heresy-hunting financiers of the Spanish crown), the Plantin-Moretus dynasty after Plantin’s death in 1589, the firm’s productions in music printing (part-books by Lassus and others), botanical works, and liturgical books, and the decline of Antwerp as a publishing centre after the Spanish Fury and the siege of Antwerp (1584-1585).
Chapter XII — The Elzevirs of Leyden and Amsterdam (1587-1688). A survey of the Elzevir family firm across four generations. Covers Louis Elzevir the elder (his establishment of the business in Leyden, his early publications), Bonaventure and Abraham Elzevir (their expansion in the 1620s-1640s, their scholarly relations with the University of Leyden), and the later Elzevirs. Describes their innovations in small-format publishing—the Elzevir 12mo and 24mo classics (the series of Latin classics known as the Elzevir Republics, the Greek and Roman historians, the French authors in small format). Discusses their scholarly relations (Saumaise, Heinsius, Vossius), their role in establishing the Dutch Republic as a centre of intellectual freedom and piratical reprinting, and their practice of appropriating and reprinting the works of competitors in Germany, Italy, and France. Covers the decline of the firm after the French invasion of 1672.
Part III: The Beginnings of Property in Literature
Chapter I — Privileges and Censorship in Italy (1498-1798). A comprehensive treatment of Venetian press legislation, divided into the following subsections. Censorship (p. 352): the development of ecclesiastical and political censorship in Italy. The Earliest Legislation in Venice (p. 359): the first Venetian privilege of 1469 (John of Speyer’s monopoly for printing in Venice for five years); the earliest author’s copyright of 1486 (Antonio Sabellico’s Decades Rerum Venetiarum, indefinite term); the privilege for Peter of Ravenna’s Phoenix (1492); the privilege to Daniele Barbaro for his brother Hermolao’s Castigationes Plinii (1493, ten-year term). The Guild of Printers and Booksellers (p. 364): the organization, regulations, and competition rules of the Venetian trade guild. Copyrights in Venice (p. 369): the four classes of privilege—sweeping monopoly (one example, 1469); monopoly for a class or language (Aldus’s Greek privilege of 1495, his italic type patent of 1501); publisher’s copyright for classic authors (the third and most common class); and author’s copyright (the earliest being Sabellico, 1486). Also covers patents for improvements in printing, protection against foreign competition, the import prohibition of 1469, and the requirement that works must be printed in Venetian territory. The Inquisition (p. 371): the functioning of the Inquisition in relation to the book trade. The Index and the Book-Trade (p. 372): the Index of Prohibited Books, its development from early episcopal prohibitions through the Tridentine Index (1564) and subsequent revisions; the enforcement mechanisms (the Inquisition, the Imprimatur system, book seizures at fairs); the analysis of the Index’s impact on the book trade across Catholic Europe. The Interdict and Fra Paolo Sarpi (p. 384): the Interdict of Venice (1605-1607), Fra Paolo Sarpi’s defence of Venetian publishing freedoms, and the long contest between the Roman Church and Venetian printers. The Printers’ Guild and Press Legislation (p. 394): the guild regulations and press laws in Venice. The Last Contest with Rome (p. 401): the final struggles between Venetian publishing and Roman ecclesiastical authority.
Chapter II — Privileges and Regulations in Germany (1450-1698). Covers the German privilege system from the earliest imperial privilege (the Sodalitas Rhenana Celtica for an edition of Hroswitha’s dramas, 1501) through the end of the seventeenth century. Describes the imperial censorship system, the Frankfurt book fairs and their role in regulating the book trade, and the privileges granted by various German princes. Discusses Luther’s role in the development of literary property—his denunciations of literary piracy, his contention that the system of privileges narrowed rather than widened the conception of literary property, and his emphasis on the author’s right to preserve his text from corruption. Covers the local privileges issued by city magistracies (the Basel ordinance of 1531 protecting new editions of classic works for three years; the Nuremberg protection of Albert Dürer’s works in 1512, 1528, and 1532). Discusses the three classes of literary undertakings that imperial privileges covered: official publications (service books, school text-books, edicts, laws); first printings of works from the common stock of literature; and new works on specific subjects (where the privilege often conferred a monopoly on the subject itself, not just the specific book). Covers the distinction between privileges for books and privileges for authors (the Frankfort ordinance of 1660 distinguishing between Bücher and Autores), the imperial privilege system and its relationship to local authorities, the ecclesiastical censorship exercised by the Archbishop of Mayence and other bishops, the appointment of Doctor Jacob Össler as imperial supervisor of literature (1455), and the organization of the German book-trade through the Frankfurt book fairs. Discusses the impact of the Thirty Years’ War on German publishing.
Chapter III — Regulations for the Control and Censorship of the Printing-Press in France (1500-1700). Organized in several subsections. Conflicting Authorities (p. 437): the competing jurisdictions of Crown, Parlement, Sorbonne (Theological Faculty of the University), and the book trade guild for control over the French press. Covers the early system of permits and approvals (the first official approval in a printed book being the Tractatus Petri Nigri of 1475), the Bull of Leo X (1515) requiring ecclesiastical examination before printing. Parliament, the University, and the Book-Trade (p. 442): the roles of the Parlement of Paris (a high court of justice, not a legislature) and the University in supervising printing; the University’s claim of authority based on the printers being successors of the old University scribes; the edict of 1521 giving the University and the Faculty of Theology the right of censorship; the decrees of Parliament forbidding unapproved publication (1521-1542); the conflicts between University and Parliament. The Beginning of Legislation for the Encouragement of Literature (p. 446): the ordinance of March 7, 1537, requiring royal approval (through the royal librarian) for all books printed in any language, and establishing deposit of a copy in the Royal Library at Blois—the first step toward a national library and legal deposit. The Relations of the Crown to Literary Production (p. 456): the contest between Francis I (who used the royal influence to defend printers against theological censors) and Henry II (who placed the press under close royal supervision); the consolidation of royal control over printing after Henry II’s accession; the extension of privilege terms from five to twenty years; the replacement of University authority with Crown authority; the system of librairie under the Bourbons; and the methods by which French printers evaded censorship.
Chapter IV — The Beginnings of Literary Property in England (1474-1709). Traces English printing from Caxton through the Licensing Act and the Stationers’ Company. Covers the first English privilege (1518, to Richard Pynson for a two-year term on a specific oration), the first author’s copyright in England (1530, a seven-year term), and the first recorded English copyright dispute (c. 1530, Trevers’s unauthorized reprint of Wynkyn de Worde’s privileged work). Describes the Stationers’ Company, chartered by royal decree in 1556, serving as the organization of the London printing and publishing trade and holding authority directly from the Crown. Discusses how the Stationers’ registers served as evidence of exclusive rights to copies, with entries making no specification of term and thus implying perpetual copyright. Covers the Crown’s role in creating and protecting literary property, the King’s printers (William Faques as Regius Impressor from 1504, Richard Pynson as first to use cum privilegio), the distinction between royal privileges (for brief terms) and Stationers’ Hall entries (for indefinite terms). Discusses the Star Chamber decrees, the licensing system, and the enforcement of censorship through the Stationers’ Company. Covers the Star Chamber’s 1586 decree limiting the number of printers and presses. Discusses the Long Parliament’s ordinance requiring licensing (1643), Milton’s Areopagitica (1644) as a protest against licensing, and the lapse of the Licensing Act in 1695. Concludes with the Copyright Act of 1709 (Queen Anne’s Act), which gave statutory protection for a term of fourteen years and brought to a close the period of common-law copyright in England. Also discusses the subsequent cases of Millar v. Taylor (1769) and Donaldson v. Becket (1774) that determined the relationship between common-law copyright and the statute.
Chapter V — The Development of the Conception of Literary Property. A synthetic chapter drawing on the continental and English material presented in the preceding chapters. Traces the philosophical and legal evolution of copyright from privilege to property right across the manuscript and early print periods. Discusses the concept of copyright in the manuscript period: the control exercised by monasteries over their manuscripts as common-law property (the case of St. Columba and Abbot Finnian, c. 567, as the earliest recorded copyright dispute); the practice of selling copying privileges; the transition from manuscript to print and the need for more systematic property protection. Re-examines the four classes of Venetian privileges: (1) sweeping monopoly (John of Speyer, 1469); (2) class or language monopoly (Aldus for Greek, 1495); (3) publisher’s copyright for classic authors (the most frequent form); (4) author’s copyright (Sabellico, 1486, as the earliest in Europe). Discusses papal privileges and their limited enforceability, the restricted territorial scope of all privileges, the role of censorship as a precondition for privilege, the universality of Latin as the common literary language of Europe and its effect on the book trade and piracy, and the gradual education of European public opinion toward a recognition of literary property as a right rather than a concession. Concludes with a comparative assessment of how different European states (Italy, France, Germany, Holland, England) developed distinct approaches to literary property, with England reaching the most definite recognition through the interplay of Crown authority, Stationers’ Company practice, common law, and ultimately statute.

primary-sources/stationers-registers-arb.title: Arber — Transcript of the Registers of the Stationers' Company, Vol. I
primary-sources/stationers-registers-arb.content:
Arber — Transcript of the Registers of the Stationers’ Company, Vol. I
Edward Arber (ed.), A Transcript of the Registers of the Company of Stationers of London, 1554–1640 A.D. Volume I — Text. Privately printed, London, 1 January 1875. Reprinted New York: Peter Smith, 1950. ~33,873 lines extracted from a zip of 648 OCR’d page files. University of Illinois Library copy.
This is the first of five volumes of Arber’s Transcript. Volume I contains the earliest surviving Stationers’ Company records: Arber’s long introductory essay; the text of the Company’s Ordinances (earliest surviving printed copy, 1678–82); Arber’s notes on his editorial method; and then the full text of Register A — the Wardens’ Account Books covering 9 December 1554 through 22 July 1571 — followed by summary Cash Abstracts from 1571 through 2 August 1596. The Register A accounts are the founding primary source for the English book trade under Mary I and Elizabeth I: every apprentice presented, every freeman admitted, every book licensed, every fine levied, and every payment made by the Company is recorded year by year. Inserted into the register text, out of its chronological place, is Christopher Barker’s full 1582 Report to the Privy Council on the printing patents of 1558–1582 — the single most important document for understanding how the Elizabethan book trade actually worked. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol1_raw.txt]
Quality Assessment
OCR from a 1950 lithographic reprint of the 1875 original (University of Illinois Library copy). The body text is generally very readable. The register entries themselves are in Elizabethan English — early modern spellings, Latin-numeral money amounts (iij iiijd = 3s 4d), and abbreviated feast-day dates (e.g. “the feaste of saynt John baptest [24 June]”) — but consistently legible. Arber’s editorial footnotes appear in square brackets inline, clearly distinguishable from the primary-source text.
Artifact types:

Running headers inline — master and warden names, account date ranges (e.g. “9 December 1554–18 July 1557,” “T. Dockwray,” “J. Cawood”) repeat at the top of every page and are captured inline with the body text
Page numbers inline — both the book’s roman-numeral preliminary pages and arabic body page numbers appear as isolated lines
Library stamps in opening pages — University of Illinois library date-stamps, shelf marks, and barcode text appear in the first ~100 lines
Blank page markers — “[This page is entirely blank in the Original.]” appears occasionally
Inserted documents out of sequence — Barker’s 1582 Report is interpolated into the 3rd account (1558–59) and runs across multiple page-breaks with the header “[CHRISTOPHER BARKER’S REPORT IN DECEMBER 1582, ON THE PRINTING PATENTS OF 1558–1582.]” repeating as a running head



















































SectionLine rangeQualityFront matter, library stamps, title pages1–700Readable (with library noise)Arber’s Introduction~701–2804ReadableOrdinances of the Stationers’ Company, 1678–82~2805–4119ReadableOn the Present Transcript (editorial method)~4120–4389ReadableRegister A — Wardens’ Accounts, 1554–1571~4390–25142Readable (Elizabethan English throughout)Summary Cash Abstracts, 1571–1596~25143–33500ReadableAddendum — The Controversy of 1643–5~33500–33760ReadableCorrigenda~33775–endReadable

Contents — Section by Section
Arber’s Introduction (lines ~701–2804)
A substantial essay — the preface to the entire five-volume project — in which Arber argues for the importance of the English printer and publisher as figures equal in historical significance to the poets, statesmen, and explorers of the Elizabethan age. He names John Cawood, John Day, Henry Denham, Henry Binneman, and Christopher Barker as the representative men of the printing business, and places them beside Sidney, Spenser, Shakespeare, Burghley, Walsingham, and Drake.
He describes the great folios of the period — More’s Workes (printed by Walley, Cawood, and Tottle 1557); Becon’s Workes (Day, 1560–4); Fox’s Acts and Monuments (four editions, Day, 1563–83); Holinshed’s Chronicles (Denham 1587); Field’s edition of North’s Plutarch (1595); Hakluyt’s Voyages (Bishop, Newberry, and Robert Barker, 1599–1600) — as comparable in difficulty of production to a modern Encyclopædia Britannica.
Arber traces the history of the Company from the 1403 Brotherhood through the 1556 Charter and Elizabeth’s confirmation. He describes the five-year gap in the registers (1571–1576) where the Clerk’s book is lost. He explains his editorial system: Company members’ names are set in Clarendon type; non-members in Roman capitals. He notes that some misattributions of membership are inevitable because sheets had to be annotated as they came from the press, so later discoveries could only look backward.
The Introduction closes with a meditation on England’s Elizabethan “Golden Age” as a providential outpouring analogous to those of Israel, Greece, Rome, and Italy — framing the register as the material record of that age’s mind-world. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol1_raw.txt]

Ordinances of the Stationers’ Company, 1678–1682 (lines ~2805–4119)
The full text of the Company’s Ordinances as approved by the Lord Keeper and the Lords Chief Justices, 10 February 1682. Arber explains that all earlier manuscript Ordinances appear to have perished, and that this 1678–82 printed text — the earliest surviving — is “doubtless substantially the same” as those now lost. The Ordinances in force in 1875 were substantially the same as these.
The text covers: the constitution and powers of the Court of Assistants; election of Master and Wardens; duties of the Renter Wardens; apprenticeship and freedom rules; searches for unlicensed printing; penalties for printing contrary to Company orders; the oath of a Freeman; and the financial governance of the Hall. Approved copies signed by Richard Rainsford and Francis North. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol1_raw.txt]

On the Present Transcript (lines ~4120–4389)
Arber’s account of the editorial method. He describes the five-year labour of producing the Transcript from 2,500 manuscript pages. Key methodological points:

Company members’ names in Clarendon type; non-members in Roman capitals; the distinction is a general rule only, not always carried out with accuracy since the text had to be annotated sheet by sheet as it came from the press
Some forty thousand names appear across the five volumes; Arber could not always determine membership status in time
Example cases of misattribution: John Charlewood (not identified as a Company member until his appearance in Vol. II at a point after his earlier entries were already in print); John Wolf (apprenticed to John Day but freed in the Fishmongers’ Company, retransferred to Stationers 1583); Humphrey Toy (served as Under Warden but later found to be a Merchant Tailor)
The intent was to provide an apparatus of footnote cross-references to make the text its own interpreter

^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol1_raw.txt]

Register A — Wardens’ Accounts, 1554–1571 (lines ~4390–25142)
The primary-source core of the volume. The Wardens’ Account Book is the oldest record of the Stationers’ Company, beginning with the Master and Wardens named in the Charter and running through the 15th Annual Account ending 22 July 1571.
Structure of each annual account. Each year is headed by the names of the Master and two Wardens for that year. The account is divided into Receipts (subdivided into: Apprentices presented; Freemen and Brothers admitted; Book Entries licensed; Fines levied; Livery; Miscellaneous) and Payments (Hall dinners; setting forth men for civic shows; Gifts; Miscellaneous outgoings). Arber’s bracketed editorial notes appear throughout, identifying individuals, correcting dates, and cross-referencing other volumes.
The first account (9 December 1554 – 18 July 1557). Master: Thomas Dockwray. Wardens: John Cawood, Henry Cooke. This covers the founding years of the incorporated Company under Philip and Mary. The fee for making a freeman was 3s 4d (the Half-Noble). Early entries record Freemen being made, apprentices presented (6d per presentation), and small fines. The book entries in this first account are few — the Company was newly incorporated and the licensing system not yet fully developed. Inserted illustrative documents include: the Proclamation against Protestant books (13 June 1555); the Charter of the Company (27 September 1556); the Act of Common Council on apprentices; the Grant of Arms by Sir G. Dethick; the enrollment of the Charter in the Corporation Records (3 June 1557).
The book entry format. From the 2nd account (July 1557) onward, book entries read as follows: “To [printer’s name] to prynte [abbreviated title] and for his lycense he geveth to the howse [fee].” The typical fee was 4d for a ballad or small pamphlet, more for substantial works. Author names are given when known (often in small capitals). A single entry may cover multiple titles at a combined fee. From this point Arber’s footnotes routinely identify the work and cross-reference surviving copies.
Christopher Barker’s 1582 Report (lines ~8444–9912). Inserted out of chronological sequence into the 3rd account (10 July 1558–10 July 1559), this is the full text of Barker’s December 1582 report to the Privy Council, drawn from the Burghley papers in the British Museum. Arber calls it “hardly possible to exaggerate the importance and authority of this graphic History of English Printing during the twenty-four years which had then elapsed since Elizabeth’s accession.”
The Report surveys every printing patent granted by Elizabeth from 1558 through 1582, assessing each patent’s value, the identity of its holder or assignee, and the problems arising from the patent system. The key passage: the Marian Charter gave authority to print to all Stationers — bookbinders, booksellers, joiners, chandlers — without specifying Printers; “so that the Bookesellers being growen the greater and wealthier nomber haue nowe many of the best Copies and keepe no printing howse, neither beare any charge of letter, or other furniture but onlie paye for the workmanship.” Barker describes individual patents: Seres’s psalter and primer patent (assigned to Henry Denham); Day’s patent for the ABC and catechism; Jugge’s patent for Bibles and New Testaments; Tottle’s law-book patent; Barker’s own Queen’s Printer patent (granted 28 September 1577). He gives the practical arrangements, disputes, and sub-assignments that the formal patent grants conceal.
Elizabeth’s Injunctions of 1559 (inserted into the 4th account). Two clauses of the Injunctions are reproduced as “the first printed notice of the Company” — the founding royal acknowledgment of the Stationers’ licensing system. The Confirmation of the Charter (1 February 1560) and the Lord Mayor’s Precept creating the Company a Livery Company are inserted at the same point.
Progression of the accounts. The annual accounts run through the 15th year (22 July 1570 – 22 July 1571), with Wardens including William Seres, Richard Tottle, John Day, and Humphrey Toy at various points. The book entries grow substantially in volume from the mid-1560s onward, reflecting the expanding Elizabethan press. A note at line 25142 marks the close of the detailed annual accounts: “Here end the detailed annual Wardens’ Accounts of the Company contained in this Book.” ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol1_raw.txt]

The Gap: 1571–1576
A note at line 25142–25151 states: “There is now a gap between the 22nd July 1571 and the 20th July 1576; all our knowledge of which period will be found on the following pp. 451–474.” The Register B (kept by George Wapull the Clerk) that would have covered this period is now lost. The gap means there is no primary-source record of book entries for five years in the early 1570s — a significant lacuna covering the period of the Puritan press and early Elizabethan literary output. Register B, beginning 1576, is the subject of Volumes II and III. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol1_raw.txt]

Summary Cash Abstracts, 1571–1596 (lines ~25143–33500)
After the detailed annual accounts end, Volume I continues with summarised Cash Abstracts — annual financial summaries only — from 1571 through 2 August 1596. These give the broad receipts and payments for each year but do not list individual book entries, apprentice presentations, or freemen’s names. The receipt lines include “RECEIVED FOR LYCENCED COPPIES as doth appeare by the Register in the Clarkes booke” but the titles themselves are not given here — they are in the separate Register B (Volumes II and III). The Abstracts confirm the Company’s financial health year by year and record major exceptional items (setting forth men for civic shows, building works at the Hall, etc.). ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol1_raw.txt]

Addendum — The Controversy of 1643–5 (lines ~33500–33760)
A substantial appendix reproducing documents from a mid-17th century dispute between the Court of Assistants and a reform committee of the Company over the election and bonding of new Assistants. Includes a detailed narrative of the committee’s proceedings, the text of a Common Hall ticket issued June 1645, and a Petition to the Lord Mayor and Aldermen signed by 29 Livery members and 164 Yeomanry members on 14 June 1645. The documents debate the Company’s governance, the reform of its printing the Bible, suppression of seditious books, the Scottish Bible patent, and the importation of foreign Bibles. Beyond the period of this collection but included by Arber as illustrating the Company’s 17th-century governance. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol1_raw.txt]

Relevance to the Wiki
Arber’s five-volume Transcript is the foundational printed primary source for the English book trade after the Stationers’ Company charter (1557) through 1640: apprentices, freemen, book entries (copy registration), fines, patents, Star Chamber decrees, and Company ordinances. It anchors English material on book-trade, censorship-of-the-press, literary-property-and-copyright, and the mature London trade that followed william-caxton and wynkyn-de-worde. primary-sources/stationers-registers-arb.content:
Arber — Transcript of the Registers of the Stationers’ Company, Vol. II
Edward Arber (ed.), A Transcript of the Registers of the Company of Stationers of London, 1554–1640 A.D. Volume II — Text. Privately printed, London, 1 October 1875. Reprinted New York: Peter Smith, 1950. ~45,409 lines extracted from a zip of 906 OCR’d page files. University of Minnesota Wilson Library copy.
This is the second of five volumes of Arber’s Transcript. Volume II contains the core primary-source record of the Elizabethan book trade at its height: Register B, the Stationers’ Company’s day-by-day register from 1576 onward, organized into four distinct sections — Apprentices, Book Entries (copyright registrations), Freemen, and Fines. Book entries run from 20 July 1576 to 25 June 1595; apprentice, freeman, and fine records run to 2 July 1605. Woven throughout the register sections are major illustrative documents from state papers and Company archives: the early printing patents granted to Seres, Day, and Vautrollier; the 1582 Star Chamber case of John Day v. Roger Ward; the full John Wolf controversy documents (1582–83); the Star Chamber Decree of 23 June 1586 — described by Arber as “the greatest enactment concerning the press in the reigns of Elizabeth or James I” — and the secret 1589 report to Lord Burghley naming the authors and printers of the Marprelate tracts. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]
Quality Assessment
OCR from a 1950 lithographic reprint of the 1875 original (University of Minnesota Wilson Library copy). The register text is consistently readable throughout. The book entries are in a more standardised Elizabethan English than Volume I — the fixed formula (“Entred for his copie vnder th[e] handes of [licenser(s)], [title], [fee]”) makes entries easy to parse despite spelling variation. Arber’s editorial footnotes appear in square brackets inline.
Artifact types:

Running headers inline — master/warden names and account date ranges repeat at the top of every original page and are captured inline; also the section header “[Entrances of Copies.]” or “[Enrollments of the Freemen.]” repeats as a running head
Page numbers inline — “II. [n]” page numbers appear as isolated lines throughout
Library stamps — University of Minnesota library marks appear in the first ~90 lines
Illustrative document headers — major inserted documents are headed “[CHRISTOPHER BARKER’S REPORT…]” or “[The great Star Chamber Decree regulating printing.]” etc. repeating as running heads across multiple pages














































SectionLine rangeQualityFront matter, contents, introduction~1–3879ReadableIllustrative docs — early patents (1559–1574)~3600–3880ReadableRegister B — Apprentices (pages 31–292)~3880–16007ReadableRegister B — Book Entries / Entrances of Copies (pages 293–672)~16008–34489ReadableRegister B — Freemen (pages 673–842)~34490–43350ReadableRegister B — Fines (pages 843–864)~43351–44404ReadableRegister B — Livery and Miscellaneous (pages 865+)~44405–45409Readable

Contents — Section by Section
Introduction (lines ~603–3879)
Arber opens with an essay on the history of the word “Stationer” — its Latin and continental origins in the 13th century (Toulouse, Paris, Castile), its definition in the 1440 Promptorium Parvulorum, and its establishment in English trade. He sets out the key regulatory documents whose full texts appear in this volume and describes the framework of State Papers, Star Chamber Bills, and Company archives from which the illustrative documents are drawn. The “vital and essential documents” he identifies as foundational to understanding the 1576–1595 period are: the first Star Chamber Decree (1566); Lambarde’s draft Act for the press (1580); Thomas Norton’s letter to George Goring about John Wolf (23 October 1582); Barker’s letter to Burghley (December 1582); the Company’s complaint against Wolf (March 1583); the report on printing-presses in London (1583); the Star Chamber Decree of 23 June 1586; and the Marprelate secret report (1589).
Before the register text begins, Arber inserts the full texts of the major early patents:

William Seres’s patent for psalters and primers (8 July 1559, lines ~3600): the Letters Patent granting Seres and his son the exclusive right to print all psalters, primers, and prayer books in English and Latin; the foundation of the longest-running and most contentious monopoly in the Elizabethan book trade
John Day’s 7-year licence (11 November 1559, lines ~3709): the Letters Patent granting Day a privilege for the Cosmographical Glass and all books he might produce for seven years at his own cost, subject to pre-publication allowance — an early prototype of the later licensing system
High Commission letter to the Stationers’ Company (25 May 1560, lines ~3757): the earliest evidence of surreptitious printing — the Commissioners report that “evill desposyd persons” have “secretly taken uppon them to prynte” Seres’s privileged psalters on “pryvye presses” and direct the Wardens to seize the books and punish the offenders
Archbishop Parker’s correspondence on the Bishops’ Bible (1566–68, lines ~3849): Bishop Cox’s recommendation of Bodleigh’s Geneva Bible (9 March 1566); Parker’s notice that the revision of the Bishops’ Bible has commenced (26 November 1566); Parker’s report of the revision’s conclusion (22 September 1568); his letter presenting the first copy to Queen Elizabeth (5 October 1568) — the documentary record of the authorised Bible project that would culminate in Barker’s editions of 1568–72
Vautrollier’s patent for certain books (19 June 1574): referenced in the contents table; the grant that established Vautrollier’s printing privileges before his flight to Edinburgh

^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]

Register B — Apprentices (lines ~3880–16007)
The complete enrollment record of apprentices presented to the Stationers’ Company from 20 July 1576 (20th year of Elizabeth’s reign) through 2 July 1605. Pages 31–292 of the original volume.
Entry format. Each entry gives: the date (in Latin, by feast-day and regnal year); the master’s name (in Clarendon type if a Company member); the apprentice’s full name; his father’s name, occupation, and place of origin (including the county); the term of years; the start date (by feast day); and the fee. From 1578 onward the enrollment fee rises from 6d to 2s 6d as a note marks (line ~4736). The county-of-origin data makes these records a geographical index of where Elizabethan stationers came from — apprentices from Yorkshire, Warwickshire, Kent, Lincolnshire, and London appear in the earliest entries.
The masters named in the earliest 1576 entries include William Seres, Richard Greene, Richard Gonneld, Richard Watkins, and William Norton. As the years progress, masters such as George Bishop, Henry Denham, John Charlewood, Robert Waldegrave, Richard Field, and Humphrey Lownes appear.
This section is the primary source for the apprenticeship careers of every known Elizabethan stationer: when an individual is identified as having been apprenticed to a particular master, the entry here gives the exact date, term, and geographical origin. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]

Register B — Book Entries / Entrances of Copies (lines ~16008–34489)
The copyright registration record — the central primary source for Elizabethan literary and print history. Every book, pamphlet, ballad, and broadside entered at Stationers’ Hall for which a fee was paid is recorded here, from 20 July 1576 to 25 June 1595. Pages 293–672 of the original volume.
Entry format. The standard form from 1576 onward: “[Printer’s or publisher’s name] Entred for his copie vnder th[e] handes of [warden(s)] and [licenser], [abbreviated title], [fee].” The licenser changes across the period: in the late 1570s entries are frequently under the wardens’ hands alone, or under “the bishop of [London’s]” hand; from 1586 the Star Chamber Decree requires the Archbishop of Canterbury’s representative or a bishop alongside the Wardens for most categories of work. Fees are typically 4d for a ballad, 6d for a pamphlet or small book, and higher for substantial works.
Coverage. The 20-year span 1576–1595 covers the peak of Elizabethan literary production. Entries in these pages include:

Sidney’s Arcadia — entered by William Ponsonby, 23 August [1590]: “Receaued of him for a booke of Sir PHILIP SIDNEYS makinge intitled Arcadia: aucthorised vnder the Archbishop of CANTERBURY [his] hand” (line ~25997)
Lodge’s Penelope’s Web — entered by Edward White, 26 June 1587: “Receaued of him for printinge a booke intituled PENELOPES Webbe Aucthorised vnder the bishop of LONDONS hand” (line ~24955)
Early play texts, verse collections, chronicles, devotional works, and the full range of Elizabethan print are present

The register also shows the mechanics of transfer, conditional entry, and disputed copies: entries note “PROVIDED that ye cumpanie shall haue them at his hands,” conditional licences, and the occasional notation that a book has been withdrawn or its entry cancelled.
Embedded within this section are the major illustrative documents relevant to book-trade disputes of the period:

The Star Chamber case John Day v. Roger Ward and William Holmes (7 February–10 July 1582, lines ~38336): Day’s bill of complaint against Ward and Holmes for printing his ABC and catechism contrary to his patent; the full Star Chamber proceedings including demurrers, examinations, and the decree. The case establishes that the 1566 Star Chamber Decree was the primary legal instrument against patent infringers, and that Ward’s defence — that the patent was contrary to common law — was rejected

^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]

The John Wolf Controversy Documents (lines ~39330–39600)
The documentary record of the early 1580s crisis over unauthorized printing, centred on John Wolf (alias Wolfe), who had been apprenticed to John Day and who organized a group of journeymen printers and non-Company stationers to print patented and privileged copies in defiance of the Company’s authority.
Documents reproduced in full:

Thomas Norton’s letter to George Goring about John Wolf (23 October 1582): Norton — the barrister and government censor — reports on Wolf’s activities and the Company’s failure to contain them
The Wardens’ report to Lord Burghley that Roger Ward’s family refused to allow a search of his house (29 October 1582)
The appeal of householders using the trade of Stationers to Lord Burghley against Thomas Norton (October 1582): the journeymen printers’ side of the dispute
A similar appeal to Sir Francis Walsingham (undated, c. October 1582)
The supplication to the Privy Council of the Wardens of the Stationers on behalf of the ancients and patentees against John Wolf and his associates (c. March 1583): the Company’s formal complaint naming Wolf’s associates
The University of Cambridge’s appeal to Lord Burghley against the seizure of their printer Thomas Thomas (14 June 1583): the Cambridge press’s challenge to London Stationers’ jurisdiction outside the City
The final report of the augmented Commission from the Privy Council on the Stationers’ Company controversy (1583): the government’s resolution that settled the Wolf dispute — Wolf was eventually brought into the Company and given his own printing rights

These documents collectively show how the Elizabethan book-trade regulatory system was tested and renegotiated in the early 1580s. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]

The Star Chamber Decree of 23 June 1586 (lines ~41291–41400)
The full text of what Arber calls “the greatest enactment concerning the press in the reigns of Elizabeth or James I.” Written on vellum, this Decree — issued 23 June 1586, 28th year of Elizabeth’s reign — superseded all earlier orders and became the foundational press law for the next half-century.
Its key provisions: no person may print any book “against the fourme and meanyng” of any ordinance or statute; no press may be set up or kept except in London (plus the university towns of Oxford and Cambridge, by an earlier order); the number of presses in any printing house to be regulated by the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Bishop of London; no book to be printed until it has been “seen and perused” and allowed by the Archbishop or Bishop of London (or their nominees); a master printer who has been debarred may not exercise any branch of the trade even as a journeyman; any unlicensed books may be seized by any person whatsoever. The Act runs only for the life of the Queen.
The Decree is the direct legislative response to the Wolf controversy and to the perceived failure of the 1566 Star Chamber Decree to suppress unlicensed printing. It is the instrument that made the Archbishop of Canterbury’s imprimatur structurally necessary for all publishing — the requirement that appears in the book entries from 1586 onward. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]

The Marprelate Secret Report (lines ~41811–41870)
The full text of the secret report to Lord Burghley, dated 21 September 1589 in Burghley’s own hand, identifying the authors and printers of the Martin Marprelate tracts. Arber calls this “most valuable.”
The report identifies Robert Waldegrave as printer of the first three Marprelate books (printed in “a Dutch letter [type]” at Sir Richard Knightley’s house in Northamptonshire); names Henry Sharpe and John Hodgkins as printers of the last two books (in “a litle Romaine and Italian letter [type]”). It traces how Waldegrave’s press was searched at Easter 1588, how he saved his type “in a boxe vnder his Cloke,” brought the type to Mistress Crane’s house in London, and then to sites outside the City. It identifies the paper supply route through “a Spurrier [a maker of spurs] dwellinge about Pie Corner neere West Smythfeild.” The report also names Sir Richard Knightley and Mr Wiston as the gentlemen who harboured the press — both were later fined by the Star Chamber, though Archbishop Whitgift obtained remission of the fines. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]

Register B — Freemen (lines ~34490–43350)
The enrollment of freemen of the Company from April 1577 to July 1605. Pages 673–842 of the original volume. Each entry gives: date, freeman’s name, fee (initially 3s 4d + dinner paid), and master’s name. The fee rises progressively across the period. This section is the primary record of when each stationer took up his freedom — the moment he was legally entitled to publish (though not necessarily to print, absent a place in one of the twenty-two printing houses). ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]

Register B — Fines (lines ~43351–44404)
The record of fines levied by the Court of Assistants from 1576 to 1604. Pages 843–864 of the original volume. Entries record: date, the name of the person fined, the offence (printing without licence, breaking orders, working at an unlicensed press, etc.), and the amount. The fines section is a supplementary record to the book entries — where a book entry notes an infringement, the corresponding fine often appears here. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol2_raw.txt]
