primary-sources/stationers-registers-arb.content:
Arber — Transcript of the Registers of the Stationers’ Company, Vol. III
Edward Arber (ed.), A Transcript of the Registers of the Company of Stationers of London, 1554–1640 A.D. Volume III — Text. Privately printed, London, 1 July 1876. Reprinted New York: Peter Smith, 1950. ~40,530 lines extracted from a zip of 716 OCR’d page files. Pennsylvania State College Library copy.
This is the third of five volumes of Arber’s Transcript. Volume III contains Register C — the book entry (copyright registration) record from July 1595 to 11 July 1620, covering the last eight years of Elizabeth’s reign and the first seventeen years of James I. It also contains the Freeman list from 1605 to 31 December 1640 and the Succession of Master Printers in London 1586–1636. This is the volume most directly relevant to Elizabethan and Jacobean literary history: it contains the registration entries for Hamlet, Shakespeare’s Sonnets, Troilus and Cressida, the 1599 Bishops’ Order burning satirical books at Stationers’ Hall, the James I grant to the Company (1603), the 9 May 1615 list of Master Printers and their press allowances, and the full genealogy of London printing houses 1586–1635 tracing the succession of each of the twenty-two recognised presses. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol3_raw.txt]
Quality Assessment
OCR from a 1950 lithographic reprint of the 1876 original (Pennsylvania State College Library copy). The book entry text is consistently readable — the standard entry formula (“Entred for his copie vnder th[e h]andes of [licenser(s)], [abbreviated title], [fee]”) makes entries identifiable despite spelling variation. The supplementary sections (Freemen list, Master Printers succession) are more table-like in layout and the OCR renders them as broken columns — readable with care, but not clean prose.
Artifact types:

Running headers inline — warden names, year-period dates, and section headers (“[Entrances of Copies.]”, “[Illustrative Documents.]”) repeat on every page and appear inline
Page numbers inline — “III. [n]” page numbers appear as isolated lines throughout
Library stamps in opening pages — Pennsylvania State College library marks in first ~15 lines
Table-format OCR noise — the Freemen list and Master Printers succession are printed in multi-column tabular format; the OCR captures these as broken fragments, readable but not clean text









































SectionLine rangeQualityFront matter, contents, introduction~1–2393ReadableRegister C — court notes and misc (1596)~2394–2984ReadableRegister C — Book Entries, 1595–1620~2985–35959Readable1599 Bishops’ Order and book burning~35900–36010ReadableFreemen, 1605–1640~36813–39604Readable (table-column layout)Succession of Master Printers, 1586–1636~39605–40530Readable (table-column layout)

Contents — Section by Section
Introduction (lines ~410–2393)
Arber opens with his most provocative claim across the five volumes: that “the Press in England in the reign of Queen ELIZABETH was probably the freest in Europe; as free indeed as the political situation at that time would admit of.” He attributes this to the long administration of Lord Burghley, “who was ever on the side of light and moderation, welcomed rather than feared all honest discussion of grievances or exposure of abuses in print.” The case of John Stubbs — who had his right hand cut off in 1579 for the fervently loyal protest against the Anjou marriage — is cited as an exception to the general spirit of Elizabeth’s government.
He quotes Bacon’s praise of Elizabethan Protestant theological writing (Of the Proficience and Advancement of Learning, 1605) and Wilkins’s judgment that English sermons and treatises were “most elaborate and useful” among all European languages — arguing that the press served this achievement. He identifies the true censors as “the lording hierarchy, the Archbishops and Bishops” rather than the general clergy, and describes Laud’s imposition of Arminian theology as the product of this episcopal oligarchy.
He then turns to the practical structure: how many printing houses existed in the age of Shakespeare and Jonson? The number of acknowledged London printing houses did not materially increase in the 86 years from 1554 to 1640. The 1615 list shows 19 Master Printers; the 1634 list shows 22; the 1635 and 1636 lists show 22 and 21 respectively. The pp. 699–704 lists are described as showing this continuity. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol3_raw.txt]

Register C — Book Entries, July 1595 – July 1620 (lines ~2985–35959)
The copyright registration record for 25 years of English printing — the last eight years of Elizabeth’s reign (40th–45th years, 1595–1603) and the first seventeen years of James I (46th–64th years, 1603–1620). Pages 33–676 of the original volume.
Entry format. The standard form continues from Volume II: “[Stationer’s name] Entred for his copie vnder th[e h]andes of [licenser(s)], [abbreviated title], [fee].” The licenser named is now routinely an official appointed under the Archbishop of Canterbury — named individuals such as master Pasfield, master Murgetrod, master Harsnet, master Wilson, or master Barcham — alongside the warden. The fee remains 6d for most entries. Multiple titles entered on a single day by a single stationer are common, at 4d–6d each.
Key entries — Shakespeare and the Elizabethan stage:

Hamlet (26 July 1602, line ~10790): “Entred for his Copie vnder the handes of master PASFEILD and master waterson warden A booke called the Revenge of HAMLETT Prince [of] Denmarke as yt was latelie Acted by the Lord Chamberleyne his servantes vjd” — registered by James Roberts
Troilus and Cressida (28 January 1603, line ~19855): entered under Sir George Bucke and warden Lownes, “a booke called the history of TROYLUS and CRESSIDA vjd”
Shakespeare’s Sonnets (20 May 1609, line ~20355): “Entred for his copie vnder th[e h]andes of master WILSON and master Lownes Warden a Booke called SHAKESPEARES Sonnettes vjd” — registered by Thomas Thorpe
Merry Wives of Windsor: Arber’s footnote notes it was printed by J. Busby before the registration date; entered only when assigned to A. Johnson
King Lear: similar note at page 289 — entered by assignment rather than original registration

Key embedded documents:
List of printers who had set up contrary to the 1586 Star Chamber Decree (c. 7 July 1598, page 43): a list of names presented by the printers themselves of those who had, up to this date, established presses in violation of the Decree. A snapshot of the underground or irregular press on the eve of the 1599 book-burning.
The 1599 Bishops’ Order — books ordered burned or suppressed (1 June 1599 and 4 June 1599, lines ~35900–36010): The full text of the order signed by Archbishop Whitgift (JOHN WHITGIFT CANTUAR) and Bishop Bancroft (RICHARD BANCROFT LONDON), delivered to master Newbery, master Binge, and master Ponsonby (Wardens) at Croydon on 1 June. The Order: bans all verse satires and epigrams; directs that no plays be printed without the allowance of the Master of the Revels; bans all books of the nature of the Arcadian prose (ungodly love matters); bans all Nashe’s books and all Doctor Harvey’s books; and stipulates that no book shall be printed even with archiepiscopal signature until the Wardens have confirmed it is genuine.
Published at Stationers’ Hall on 4 June 1599 to the fourteen unprivileged printers then in business (named: John Wyndett, Gabriell Simpson, Richard Braddocke, Ffelixe Kingston, William Whyte, Raphe Blower, Thomas Judson, Peeter Shorte, Adam Islipe, Richard Ffeild, Edmond Bollifante, Thomas Creed, Edward Aldee, Valentyne Symes).
Books burnt in the hall that day:

Pygmalion (Marston)
The Scourge of Villainy (Marston)
The Shadow of Truth
Snarlinge Satires
Davies’s Epigrams
Marriage and Wyvinge
15 Foyes of Marriage

Books stayed (not burnt but called in):

Caltha Poetarum
Hall’s Satires
Willobie’s Aviso

Grant of James I to the Stationers’ Company (29 October 1603): Grant of primers, psalters, almanacks, and prognostications to the Company in perpetuity — subsequently surrendered and enlarged 8 March 1616.
Enlarged Grant of James I (8 March 1616, pages 679–682): The extended grant covering all manner of almanacks and prognostications, primers, psalters, and psalms in metre or prose, to the Company and their successors for ever. The full Latin and English text reproduced.
Gervase Markham’s promise (July 1617, page 679): Markham’s written undertaking not to write any more books on cattle, horses, or husbandry — an unusual document showing the Company enforcing a form of copyright management by requiring an author to limit his own output.
9 May 1615 list of Master Printers and their press allowances (page 699): A numbered list of 19 Master Printers, each allocated a specified number of presses. Includes Thomas Purfoot, Nicholas Oakes, Ralph Blower, George Purslow — with the number of presses each is permitted to operate. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol3_raw.txt]

Freemen, 1605–1640 (lines ~36813–39604)
A complete list of all stationers who took up their freedom of the Company from 1605 to 31 December 1640. Pages 683–688 of the original volume. The list is tabular — names, dates (month and day), and year. This section extends the Freeman record begun in Volume II (which runs to 1605) through the full Stuart period to 1640.
For any stationer active in the Jacobean or Caroline press, this is the primary record of when they were admitted as a Freeman — the formal qualification to publish in their own right. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol3_raw.txt]

Succession of Master Printers in London, 1586–1636 (lines ~39605–40530)
A series of documents tracing who held each of the twenty-two recognised London printing houses from the 1586 Star Chamber Decree through the mid-Caroline period. This is the primary source for the physical continuity of London printing capacity across fifty years.
Archbishop Abbot’s licences (pages 689): The petitions and licences by which new Master Printers were formally admitted with archiepiscopal sanction — specifically John Dawson (23 January 1621) and Miles Flesher (16 November 1624). Each petition shows the mechanism: the candidate had either served an apprenticeship and then a co-partnership with a deceased master, or had agreed for the deceased master’s “moitie” (half-share). Admission required the Archbishop’s written consent alongside the Company’s election.
Sir John Lambe’s notes on the former practice of licensing books (1636, lines ~39612): A 1636 survey by Sir John Lambe of the history of licensing, drawing on the Stationers’ Hall clerks’ books. Key findings: from the 19th year of Elizabeth (1576–77, the first year of Register B) until the 1586 Star Chamber Decree, many books were licensed by the Master and Wardens alone, some by the Master alone, some by the Archbishop and more by the Bishop of London. Lambe notes that the missing register for 1571–1576 was already lost when he made his enquiry (confirming the gap noted in Vol. I). He traces the root authority back to Elizabeth’s 51st Injunction (1559): “none shall print any booke &c. except it be licensed by ye Queenes maiestie’s writing or by [her commissioners]” — confirming this Injunction as the foundation of all Protestant press licensing. Master Kingston (then Master of the Company) testified that before the 1586 Decree “the master and wardens licensed all, And that when they had any Divinity booke of muche importance they would take the advise of some 2 or 3 ministers of this towne.”
8 October 1634 list of Master Printers — licensed and unlicensed (page 700, lines ~40057): A survey of 22 Master Printers then living, distinguishing those who had received formal archiepiscopal admission from those who had not. The unlicensed include: Adam Islip (who bought his printing house, letter, and implements from John Wolf and succeeded him — “an ancient Erection”); Felix Kingston (succeeded his father — “an ancient Erection”); Widow Aldee (succeeded her husband who was a master before the 1586 Decree); William Stansby (succeeded master Windet — “an ancient Erection”); William Jones (who farms his printing house from Widow Blore — “an ancient Erection”). The document shows that a significant number of the 22 recognised houses were “ancient Erections” — presses that predated the Decree and transmitted their legitimacy through widow succession or purchase, without formal archiepiscopal admission.
Genealogy of London printing houses, 1586–1635 (pp. 702–703, lines ~40282): A tabular genealogy tracing each of the 22 printing houses through its successive occupants from the 1586 Decree to 1635. Notable details: Robert Raworth was suppressed in 1635 for printing Venus and Adonis (a copy belonging to another stationer), but resumed printing two years later; Humphrey Lownes succeeded Short by marrying Short’s widow; Robert Young was admitted partner with Lownes in 1631 and after Lownes’s death held the house without formal admission. The document shows the 22 presses as essentially a fixed set of slots — when one master died or was suppressed, the slot was filled by succession (widow, son, partner) or by petition. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol3_raw.txt]

Relevance to the Wiki
Arber’s five-volume Transcript is the foundational printed primary source for the English book trade after the Stationers’ Company charter (1557) through 1640: apprentices, freemen, book entries (copy registration), fines, patents, Star Chamber decrees, and Company ordinances. It anchors English material on book-trade, censorship-of-the-press, literary-property-and-copyright, and the mature London trade that followed william-caxton and wynkyn-de-worde. primary-sources/stationers-registers-arb.title: Arber — Transcript of the Registers of the Stationers' Company, Vol. IV
primary-sources/stationers-registers-arb.content:
Arber — Transcript of the Registers of the Stationers’ Company, Vol. IV
Edward Arber (ed.), A Transcript of the Registers of the Company of Stationers of London, 1554–1640 A.D. Volume IV — Text. Privately printed, London, 1 May 1877. Reprinted New York: Peter Smith, 1950. ~34,464 lines extracted from a zip of 554 OCR’d page files. Pennsylvania State College Library copy.
This is the fourth of five volumes of Arber’s Transcript. Volume IV contains Register D — the book entry (copyright registration) record from 10 July 1620 to 3 November 1640, covering the last four years of James I (65th–67th years), the entire reign of Charles I to November 1640 (68th–85th years), together with Calls on the Livery and Promotions to the Assistance to 31 December 1640. This is the closing volume of the primary register text. It contains the registration entry for the Shakespeare First Folio (8 November 1623), the full documents of the George Wither war with the Stationers’ Company (1623–25), the text of the Second Star Chamber Decree on Printing (11 July 1637), Sir John Lambe’s list of printers authorised under that Decree, and a [?1614] petition of journeymen printers to Parliament. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol4_raw.txt]
Quality Assessment
OCR from a 1950 lithographic reprint of the 1877 original (Pennsylvania State College Library copy). The book entry text is consistently readable — the standard entry formula continues from Volumes II and III. The front matter and Introduction are well preserved; the supplementary sections (Livery admissions, Final Provisional List, Transfers) are more tabular in layout and the OCR captures them as broken columns, readable with care.
Artifact types:

Running headers inline — warden names, year-period dates, and section headers (“[Entrances of Copies.]”, “[Illustrative Documents.]”) repeat on every page and appear inline
Page numbers inline — “IV. [n]” page numbers appear as isolated lines throughout
Library stamps in opening pages — Pennsylvania State College library marks in first ~15 lines
Table-format OCR noise — the Livery admissions and Final Provisional List are in tabular format; OCR captures these as broken fragments





























































SectionLine rangeQualityFront matter, title pages~1–600Readable (with library noise)Introduction (pp. 9–28)~600–1775ReadableAdmissions to Clothing and Assistance (p. 29)~1776–2200Readable (table layout)Final Provisional List of Printers and Publishers (pp. 30–31)~2200–2570Readable (table layout)Notable Transfers of Books (pp. 30–31)~2570–2614ReadableCorrigenda et Addenda (pp. 31–32)~2614–2805ReadableRegister D — Book Entries 1620–1640 (pp. 33–524)~2805–33756ReadableAddendum — Journeymen Printers Abstract (pp. 525–6)~33760–33912ReadableCambridge business; Lambe’s list (pp. 527–8)~33912–34002ReadableSecond Star Chamber Decree (pp. 528–536)~34002–34464Readable

Contents — Section by Section
Introduction (lines ~600–1775)
Eight-section Introduction, the longest of the four volumes.
Section I opens with a newly discovered passage from the Life of John Bois (one of the translators of the Authorized Version of the Bible), which records that the final six revisers of the 1611 Bible — two from each of the Cambridge, Oxford, and Westminster companies — “went daily to Stationers Hall, and in Three quarters of a Year fulfilled Their Task,” receiving 30 shillings per week from the Company of Stationers. Arber uses this to trace the Company’s connection to the production of the Authorized Version, noting that the financial burden fell on Robert Barker as Queen’s Printer (not on the Company directly), and that Barker would not have begun paying the revisers before 1609 at the earliest.
Section II covers the war between George Wither the poet and the Stationers’ Company. James I had previously imprisoned Wither, but on 17 January 1623 granted him a patent giving him the monopoly on his own Hymns and Songs of the Church and — the clause the Stationers called “the sting” — requiring that no English Psalm book be sold unless bound together with Wither’s hymns. The full text of the two material clauses of the patent is reproduced. The conflict produced Wither’s Schollers Purgatory (1625), from which Arber quotes at length, including the “Character of the Honest Stationer” and the “Character of the Mere Stationer” — the second being Wither’s portrait of the bookseller as a monopolist indifferent to learning, truth, or public benefit. The embedded documents for the George Wither war appear at original pages 13–20 of this volume.
Section III gives the full text of the 1636 arbitration between master printers and journeymen printers — a 19-article Court minute settling the disputes set out in the journeymen’s petition (which is separately reproduced in the Addendum at pp. 525–6). The articles regulate: the removal of unbound workers from printing houses; the prohibition on turning over apprentices across company lines to evade the 1586 Decree; limits on the number of apprentices per master; the prohibition on standing formes except for psalters, grammars, ABCs, primers, almanacks, and prognostications; maximum impression sizes (Nonpareil: 5,000 copies; Brevier: 3,000; all other books: 1,500–2,000; not to exceed 3,000 even with the Master’s permission); and journeymen’s right to 3d per week in lieu of the customary copy of each book worked.
Section IV supplements the earlier research on the history of the Stationers’ Company name: the earliest documentary use of “Stationer” for a London citizen (1412, from Liber BROWNE in the Court of the Commissary of London); 1480 evidence from the wardrobe accounts of Edward IV showing the pre-printing Stationer craft consisted of “binders, dressers, and gilders” of manuscripts; and the 1550 will of Henry Smyth, “citizen and Stacioner of London.”
Section V describes the literary character of the period covered by this volume. Ballad entries reappear in large numbers; the 14 December 1624 Ballad Partnership created a voluntary association among the principal ballad publishers. Arber characterises this period as “the most scientific oppression to which the English people were ever subjected” — political tension made smaller stationers prefer old, non-political publications to new ones. He notes that Ben Jonson’s translation of John Barclay’s Argenis was registered on 2 October 1623 but no copy has since been seen or heard of.
Section VI closes the enquiry sustained across the four Introduction essays — the conditions under which it was possible, openly and in peace, to print and sell an English book in London.
Section VII addresses Episcopal censorship, noting that its weight must be sought in the forbidden literature of the time — specifically the Martin Marprelate tracts — rather than in the Register itself, where the Bishops’ control “was continuous, and so unquestioned that it needed not any legal process to enforce it.” The suppression of Thomas Cartwright’s Confutation of the Rhemish Testament for over thirty years, solely because the author was a Puritan, is cited. When it finally appeared in 1618, it was printed not in England but in Leyden, “owned and worked it is said by Edward Brewster, one of the self-exiled Pilgrim Fathers.”
Section VIII is Arber’s acknowledgments, and a notice of the death of Charles Childs, the printer of these volumes, on 26 December 1876. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol4_raw.txt]

Admissions to Clothing and Assistance, 1607–1638 (lines ~1776–2200)
A continuation of the Livery and Assistance admissions from Volume II (which runs to 1607). Lists new liverymen by date from 1607 through 1637, and Calls of Assistants from 1604 through 1637. Notable: the 1638 renewal of the Livery is described as “the largest renewal of the Livery at one time since the 1st July 1598” — over twenty men admitted to the Clothing and Assistance in a single session in 1638 including Hodgkinson, Leake, Rothwell, Badger, Dawson, Griffin, Clarke, and others. Calls of Assistants include William Leake and Richard Field (1604), Bankworth, Swinhowe, Matthew Lownes, and John Jaggard (1612), and others through 1637. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol4_raw.txt]

A Final Provisional List of London Printers and Publishers (lines ~2200–2570)
A continuation of the Publishers List begun in Volume V — extending the record of London printers and publishers by their date of first registered publication, from those first appearing in the Jacobean and Caroline periods (from c. 1610 to c. 1637). Names listed alphabetically within each initial letter with the date of first registered publication and the volume/page reference to the registration. This section extends the Vol. V list for stationers whose careers began after 1603. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol4_raw.txt]

Some Notable Transfers of Books (lines ~2570–2614)
A sample, described as a preview of what will be worked out systematically in Volume V, tracing the successive assignments of individual copies through the deaths and marriages of their owners. Examples: T. East’s books passing from his widow (1609) to T. Snodham, then to W. Stansby (1626), then to G. Bishop (1639); C. Knight’s books cycling through three assignments (1629, 1636, 1639) and returning to their starting point; A large portion of the Man family’s books assigned to B. Fisher (1635) and then mortgaged to B. Young (1637). These traces show the copy as a heritable and assignable asset across multiple generations. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol4_raw.txt]

Register D — Book Entries, 10 July 1620 – 3 November 1640 (lines ~2805–33756)
The copyright registration record for twenty years of English printing — the last years of James I and the full reign of Charles I to the eve of the Long Parliament. Original pages 33–524.
Entry format. The standard form continues: “[Stationer’s name] Entred for his copie vnder th[e h]andes of [licenser(s)], [abbreviated title], [fee].” Licensers named include Master Doctor Worrall, Master Cole (Warden), Master Doctor Ffeatlie, Master Doctor Goade, the Bishop of London’s chaplains, and the Master of the Revels for plays. The fee is 6d for most single entries; multiple entries in one session remain common.
Opening illustrative documents (pp. 35–38, lines ~2815–3141). The register section opens with the Scintilla, or A Light broken into darke Warehouses (London, 1641) — a rare anonymous pamphlet addressed to Parliament comparing the prices of Bibles, grammars, and school books in former times and in 1641. It surveys the King’s Printers’ Bible patents; the Cambridge University challenge (when Cambridge printed a folio Bible in 1629 at 10s rather than the London monopoly price of 12–15s, the King’s Printers immediately produced a competing edition and sold it at 5s to drive Cambridge out); and the pricing of grammars, ABCs, and almanacks under the Stationers’ Company patent. Arber’s prefatory note calls it “a remarkable testimony to the never-ending competition in the book trade; to the power of the King’s Printers, partly as patentees and partly as capitalists only.”
Key entries — Shakespeare and literary history:

Shakespeare First Folio (8 November 1623, lines ~8131–8156): “Entred for their Copie vnder the hands of Master Doctor WORRALL and Master Cole warden Master WILLIAM SHAKSPEERS Comedyes Histories, and Tragedyes soe manie of the said Copies as are not formerly entred to other men” — registered by Master Blounte (Edward Blount) and Isaak Jaggard. The sixteen plays listed: Comedies — The Tempest, The Two Gentlemen of Verona, Measure for Measure, The Comedy of Errors, As You Like It, All’s Well That Ends Well, Twelfth Night, The Winter’s Tale (fee: 7s); Histories — The Third Part of Henry VI, Henry VIII, Coriolanus, Timon of Athens, Julius Caesar; Tragedies — Macbeth, Antony and Cleopatra, Cymbeline (fee: 6d).
Ben Jonson’s translation of Barclay’s Argenis (2 October 1623): noted in the Introduction as registered but of which no copy has been found.
John Donne — sermons, devotions, and other works registered multiple times across the period (lines ~6373, 6539, 7559, 8370, 11449, 13390 and others).
Francis Bacon — multiple entries including Novum Organum, Essays, the History of Henry VII, and Historia Ventorum et Vitae et Mortis (lines ~10263, 11207, 11721, 12959, 13202 and others).
George Wither — his Motto (c. 1621), Philarete (c. 1622), Metrical Illustrations (c. 1635), and the assigned-over entries reflecting the Stationers’ attempts to control his copies.

The 68th Year (1623–24) — George Wither war: Book entries for this year occur alongside the embedded Wither war documents at pages 13–20 of the Introduction. The register entries themselves show the Stationers refusing to enter or selling round Wither’s hymn books. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol4_raw.txt]

Addendum — [?1614] Abstract of the Grievances of the Journeymen Printers (lines ~33760–33912)
Reproduced from two known copies: one in the Broadsides collection of the Society of Antiquaries (a proof with manuscript corrections), the other in the Bagford Collection (Harl. MS. 5910, fol. 137). Arber dates it to the Parliament of 1614, noting that it may have prompted the provision of £200 annually to the poor of the Company in the renewed James I Grant of 8 March 1616.
The petition is addressed to the Lords Spiritual and Temporal in the High Court of Parliament. Its central argument: the 1586 Star Chamber Decree, obtained by the masters under colour of granting the journeymen privileges and books, has been used to keep journeymen in “servile bondage all their lives” — they cannot set up their own presses (six months imprisonment without bail under the Decree), while the masters keep excessive apprentices, print by apprentice labour rather than by journeymen, raise book prices, use poor paper and bad type, and have “drawn into their own hands” all the patent books that James I’s grant was intended for the poor printers. The Stationers (booksellers) are named as the chief engrossers, who “will retail no new copies unless they be of their own” — effectively forcing printers to sell their copies at the stationers’ price or not at all. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol4_raw.txt]

Cambridge University Business (p. 527, line ~33910)
A State Papers reference (Dom. James I., Vol. 153, fol. 71) to the 1624 business of the Stationers against the Printer of Cambridge — the legal and political conflict over Cambridge University’s right to print under its royal charter, which the London Stationers consistently contested. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol4_raw.txt]

Sir John Lambe’s List of Printers for the Star Chamber Decree (July 1637, lines ~33914–34002)
From the fly-sheet of a letter addressed to himself, Sir John Lambe (Dean of the Arches) noted down those printers he considered alone worthy to be authorised under the forthcoming Decree. The list names 21 printers with Lambe’s marginal assessments of each — who is blind and rich, who has taken a partner, who reprinted The Holy Table (the forbidden book that precipitated the Decree), who prints unlawful books (“William Jones: a printer of all vnlawful bookes and therefore put out — Thomas Paine who gaue him a great Deale of mony to be partener with him may be in his roome”), and who should be replaced by a son or son-in-law. Endorsed: “note of ye 20 printer[s] for ye Star Chamber decree. Julij. 1637.” State Papers, Dom. Charles I., Vol. 364, Art. 111. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol4_raw.txt]

The Second Star Chamber Decree Concerning Printing (11 July 1637, lines ~34002–34464)
The full text of the 1637 Star Chamber Decree — the successor to the 1586 Decree and the most comprehensive press-regulation instrument of the Stuart period, in force until the Star Chamber’s abolition in 1641. Produced in court by Sir John Bankes, His Majesty’s Attorney General, on the advice of the Lord Keeper, the Archbishop of Canterbury, the Bishop of London (Lord High Treasurer), the Lord Chief Justices, and the Lord Chief Baron. Printed immediately by Robert Barker, Printer to the King.
The Decree’s key provisions include: prohibition on printing or importing seditious, schismatical, or offensive books; requirement that all books be licensed before entry into the Stationers’ Register; authority hierarchy for different categories of book (common law books: Lord Chief Justices; heraldic books: Earl Marshal; plays and entertainments: Master of the Revels; all divinity, philosophy, science, and other books: Archbishop of Canterbury or Bishop of London); no printer to print in England any book printed or allowed abroad; the number of Master Printers to be limited and confirmed by the Archbishop; no new printing house to be erected without the Archbishop’s consent; prohibition on printing houses outside London and the two universities; regulation of the number of presses per printer; strict apprenticeship limits; requirement that every book bear the printer’s name and the licenser’s name. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_vol4_raw.txt]

primary-sources/stationers-registers-arb.title: Arber — Transcript of the Registers of the Stationers' Company, Vol. V (Index)
primary-sources/stationers-registers-arb.content:
Arber — Transcript of the Registers of the Stationers’ Company, Vol. V (Index)
Edward Arber (ed.), A Transcript of the Registers of the Company of Stationers of London, 1554–1640 A.D. Volume V — Index. Privately printed, Birmingham, 15 March 1894. ~71,739 lines extracted from a zip of 404 OCR’d page files. Cornell University Library copy no. 227 of 230 sets.
This is the fifth and final volume of Arber’s five-volume Transcript. Volumes I–IV (1875–77) contain the full transcription of the actual Stationers’ Company registers — the day-by-day record of books entered for copyright, apprentices bound and freed, orders of the Court of Assistants, fines, and transfers of copy. Volume V does not repeat that register text; instead it is an index and reference companion to the whole work. It contains four distinct sections: Arber’s own introduction, a paper by the Company’s Clerk on the Company’s records and history, a master list of every publisher active 1553–1640, and a year-by-year bibliographical summary of English printed books 1553–1603. The volume closes with a general index (Index I) to persons and places across all five volumes. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_raw.txt]
Quality Assessment
OCR from a clean typeset original (1894). The text is generally very readable throughout. Artifacts:

Running headers inline — section headings (“A LIST OF LONDON PUBLISHERS, 1553-1640 A.D.,” “BIBLIOGRAPHICAL SUMMARY,” “INDEX I.,” “THE RECORDS OF THE STATIONERS’ COMPANY.,” “A TRANSCRIPT &C.”) repeat on every page and are captured inline with the body text
Page numbers inline — both the volume’s roman-numeral preliminary pages and arabic body page numbers appear as isolated lines (e.g. “V. xli.” or “257”)
Abbreviation-heavy format — the Publishers List and Bibliographical Summary use Arber’s own shorthand system (vol/page references in the form “i. 101,” “ii. 713,” format abbreviations like “s. sh. br.” = single sheet broadside, “8” = octavo, “4” = quarto, “fol.” = folio); the abbreviations key is given at lines ~992–1050
Bibliographical Summary table layout — each book entry spans multiple lines with printer address, title, author, and format interleaved; the plain-text OCR renders this without column alignment but the content is complete and identifiable









































SectionLine rangeQualityFront matter and subscription list1–207ReadableArber’s Introduction~208–1917ReadableRivington’s Paper on Company Records~1918–4120ReadableList of 847 London Publishers, 1553–1640~4121–11062Readable (abbreviation-dense)Bibliographical Summary of English Literature, 1553–1603~11063–64909Readable (entry format requires familiarity with abbreviations)Index I (persons, places, and Stationers’ Company connections)~64910–71739Readable
Contents — Section by Section
Arber’s Introduction (lines ~208–1917)
Arber introduces each of the volume’s main sections. On the List of 847 Publishers: every name is a person who either registered or transferred a book at Stationers’ Hall, or who published in London without registering. The list was checked and rechecked at a cost of nearly £100. Members of the Company appear in Clarendon type; non-members in Roman capitals. The list is a “master key to English bibliography” for the period, because almost all authorised books were printed in the metropolis (with some coming from Oxford and Cambridge presses from 1584-85 onward).
On London’s book-trade geography: Paul’s Churchyard was the focus and centre of the English book trade throughout this period. Fleet Street came second, owing to its proximity to the Inns of Court. In James I’s reign the trade began moving westward along Holborn toward Westminster. Printers had by an early date abandoned Paul’s Churchyard to booksellers, needing more room for press-work. John Day’s printing house was at Aldersgate Gate (he had his shop under the Gate); Richard Tottel’s at Temple Bar.
On the career of a London stationer: Arber traces the typical path from country apprentice to master printer. A raw country lad would be bound apprentice for enough years to complete his twenty-fourth year before being made free. Having served his time he was free to publish but not to print, since by immemorial custom there were no more than twenty-two printing houses in the City (apart from the royal printers). Vacancies arose only rarely and were filled by the Court of Assistants with the Archbishop of Canterbury’s approval. The surest path to a printing business was to marry the master’s daughter or a printer’s widow — Arber gives Richard Field marrying Vautrollier’s daughter as a canonical example, and lists three widows who each had three successive printer-husbands, the printing business passing with them each time. Short of marriage, a stationer might begin with a ballad sheet, accumulate capital publishing pamphlets, come onto the Livery, and eventually apply for one of the twenty-two masterships.
On the Bibliographical Summary: its primary object is to provide a dated list of all printers and publishers in Britain during the period, plus continental printers who produced English books or books about England. Titles are greatly abbreviated but sufficient in conjunction with author, printer/publisher, date, and format to identify any edition. The intention was to carry the summary to 1640 but circumstances prevented it; it ends at 1603. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_raw.txt]

Rivington’s Paper on the Records of the Stationers’ Company (lines ~1918–4120)
A paper read 12 December 1881 by Charles Robert Rivington, Clerk of the Stationers’ Company, to the London and Middlesex Archaeological Society; revised to 1893 for inclusion here.
History of the Company. A Brotherhood or Fellowship of Stationers existed from 1403, with Wynkyn de Worde among its early members, well before printing began. The printing trade fell naturally into their hands. In 1556, Philip and Mary granted a Charter of Incorporation. Rivington quotes the charter’s preamble in full — its stated purpose was to suppress “seditious and heretical books, rhymes, and treatises” published by “scandalous, malicious, schismatical, and heretical persons.” The first Master was Thomas Dockwray; the first Wardens John Cawood and Henry Cooke. The Charter granted the Company power to search for, seize, and destroy unlicensed books, and prohibited all printing within the realm without the Company’s licence (except by patentees). Elizabeth confirmed the Charter on 10 November 1559.
The Company’s records. The most ancient record is the first Wardens’ Account Book, beginning with the Master and Wardens named in the Charter, covering receipts and disbursements from 1554 to 1557. The first Register of Copies was long thought lost until John Northouck discovered that book entries before 1571 were in the Wardens’ Accounts. There is a gap of five years; the first separate Register of Copies begins in 1576, and from 1576 to 1881 the Registers are intact.
The Company’s halls. The Brotherhood had a hall in or near Milk Street before incorporation. By some time before 1570 they had moved to St Paul’s Churchyard. In 1611 Abergavenny House (between Amen Corner and the City Wall) was purchased for the Company. In 1666 the Hall was entirely destroyed in the Great Fire; everything was lost including the Company’s Seal, but the Registers survived, probably because they were in the Clerk’s house on Clerkenwell Green. The Hall was rebuilt by 1674.
List of Masters 1554–1881. The paper includes a complete list of Masters of the Company from the first (Thomas Dockwray) through 1881, with death dates and brief biographical notes on the more notable figures. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_raw.txt]

List of 847 London Publishers, 1553–1640 (lines ~4121–11062)
Arber’s own label: “a master key to English bibliography.” Every person who registered a book at Stationers’ Hall between 1553 and 1640 is listed, plus nearly all those known to have published in London without registering (marked with †). Company members are in Clarendon type; non-members in Roman capitals.
Format of each entry. Left column: the stationer’s initials and name. Central column: approximate period of publishing. Right columns: date and volume/page reference of first entry to that stationer; date and volume/page of last entry; names and dates of all assignments to and from that stationer (i.e. copies transferred in or out). Every entry therefore gives a quick career timeline and pointers to all relevant pages in Volumes I–IV.
What it covers. About 887 names in total, classified as: 5 patentees for books; 847 London publishers; 4 university printers (Oxford and Cambridge); 1 Dutch printer at Norwich; 6 country booksellers who published in London; and 24 authors or other persons who had books printed for them. Widows who carried on business in their own names are included. Assigns or deputies of patentees are excluded.
Sample entries visible in the text: Francis Adams, Richard Adams, Thomas Adams (noting first/last register entry dates and cross-references); Edward Aggas; Thomas Archer; John Bailey; John Barnes; Randall Bearkes; Christopher Barker (named in the introduction as an example of Clarendon-type members); Richard Tottell (similarly named). The list runs alphabetically A through Y. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_raw.txt]

Bibliographical Summary of English Literature, 1553–1603 (lines ~11063–64909)
A year-by-year catalogue of every known book printed in England (and relevant books printed on the Continent) from 1553 to 1603. This is the most substantive section of the volume — approximately 54,000 lines of text covering fifty years of English printing.
Format. Within each year, entries are grouped by printer or publisher. Each entry gives: a serial number; the abbreviated title; the author’s name; the format (fol., 4to, 8to, 16s, s. sh. br., etc.); the date; and a cross-reference to the Stationers’ register entry in Volumes I–IV where applicable. The printer’s address is given in full at their first appearance in each year (e.g. “R. T.—, Richard Tottell, dwelling at the Hand and Star [between the two Temple Gates] in Fleet street; within Temple Bar.”). The asterisk () before a publisher’s initials indicates they were also a printer at the time.
Coverage. Begins with undated books from Edward VI’s reign (1552–53) and runs continuously through 1603 (Elizabeth’s last year). The intention was to extend to 1640 but was abandoned for reasons not specified. Includes not only books produced in London but also books produced for English readers at continental presses (Geneva, Frankfurt, Antwerp, etc.). Foreign-language books by or about English people are included.
Opening entries (1553). Thomas Berthelet at the Lucrece in Fleet Street printing Erasmus; William Copland at the Rose Garland; John Day dwelling over Aldersgate; Richard Grafton within Christ’s Hospital; Reginald Wolf at the Brazen Serpent in Paul’s Churchyard; William Seres at the Hedgehog at the west end of Paul’s Church; Richard Tottel at the Hand and Star within Temple Bar. The printer addresses themselves are primary-source data on the physical geography of the Elizabethan book trade.
Scope. From the visible entries the summary includes: proclamations and statutes; Bibles and prayer books; devotional and theological works; chronicles and histories; poetry and drama; legal texts; scientific and medical works; educational books; translations from classical and contemporary European authors; maps and charts. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_raw.txt]

Index I: Persons, Places, and the Stationers’ Company (lines ~64910–71739)
A general alphabetical index to persons and places appearing anywhere in Volumes I–V of the Transcript. Each entry gives the person’s name followed by volume and page references across the five-volume set, plus (for publishers) a note of their approximate period of activity (e.g. “Published from 1579 to 1603”). Places are indexed both as locations of printing houses and as the towns from which apprentices came — the index includes, for example, a list of places in Yorkshire from which stationers came between 1576 and 1605.
A note at the end states: “It was not possible to print INDEX II, see page 215.” The intended second index (presumably a title or subject index) was never completed.
This index is the fastest way into the whole five-volume Transcript: any stationer’s name, any place, any person mentioned in the registers can be located and then followed to the relevant pages in Volumes I–IV for the full primary-source entry. ^[source: stationers_registers_arber_raw.txt]
Relevance to the Wiki
Arber’s five-volume Transcript is the foundational printed primary source for the English book trade after the Stationers’ Company charter (1557) through 1640: apprentices, freemen, book entries (copy registration), fines, patents, Star Chamber decrees, and Company ordinances. It anchors English material on book-trade, censorship-of-the-press, literary-property-and-copyright, and the mature London trade that followed william-caxton and wynkyn-de-worde. Companion reference: typographical-antiquities-ames. Modern social-history reading: nature-of-the-book-johns.

primary-sources/typographical-antiquitie.title: Typographical Antiquities (Ames / Herbert), Vol. II
primary-sources/typographical-antiquitie.content:
Typographical Antiquities: Origin and Progress of Printing in Great Britain and Ireland (Vol. II)
Joseph Ames (begun); William Herbert (considerably augmented), Typographical Antiquities: or an Historical Account of the Origin and Progress of Printing in Great Britain and Ireland. Vol. II. London: Printed for the Editor, 1786. ~37,377 lines extracted from a zip of 640 OCR’d page files. Bibliographical history of the English and Irish book trade from 1471 to 1600, organized printer by printer. This volume (the only one in the corpus zip) covers printers active in the Elizabethan period, starting at book page [685].
The work is a reference compendium, not a narrative history. Each entry gives: a brief biography of the printer, drawing on Stationers’ Company register records, court-of-assistants orders, and contemporary accounts; followed by a chronological catalogue of books known to have been printed by that printer, with exact title transcriptions, format (folio, quarto, octavo, sixteens), approximate date, and the library or private collection where a copy was located at the time of writing. Herbert substantially expanded Ames’s original 1749 compilation with new biographical material and additional book entries.
Raw text: typographical_antiquities_ames_raw.txt (~1.7 MB at project root).
Quality Assessment
OCR from a University of Virginia library copy of the 1786 printed volume. The body text is generally readable, but has several artifact types:

Long ‘s’ as ‘f’ — 18th-century typography renders the long ‘s’ as ‘f’ throughout (e.g. “ftationers” for “stationers,” “prefs” for “press”). Systematic period-typeface artifact, consistent throughout
Marginal footnotes inline — footnotes interrupt main printer entries mid-sentence in the OCR
Page headers inline — printer’s name as running header captured mid-entry
Page numbers inline — book page numbers appear as isolated numbers
Some OCR noise in borders/decorations — occasional character-noise from ornamental borders

Title transcriptions within each entry are in original Elizabethan spelling as printed on the title pages.

























SectionLine rangeQualityFront matter / title page1–64ReadablePrinter entries (pages 685–1310)65–36947Readable (long-s artifacts; footnotes inline)Index of printers36948–37377Readable
Contents — Printer Entries
This volume covers approximately 80 printers active in the mid-to-late 16th century. Entries vary greatly in length: minor figures receive a paragraph; major figures like Christopher Barker or Thomas Vautrollier receive several pages. The following are the most substantial or most relevant entries.
Richard Tottel (lines ~6766–)
Tottel was “a very considerable printer of law, and an original member of the Stationers’ company.” He dwelt in Fleet Street within Temple Bar at the Sign of the Hand and Star. He held a succession of patents for printing common law books: first granted under Edward VI (7 Edw. VI, 12 April); renewed under Philip and Mary (1 May, Pat. 2 & 3 Phil. & Mary); and extended for life under Elizabeth (12 Jan., Pat. 1 Eliz.). He served as renter 1559–60; under-warden 1561; upper warden 1567, 1568, and 1574; master 1578 and 1584. In his final years he withdrew to the country for health; the Court of Assistants noted his “continuall absence” and he was removed from the Assistantship in 1589. His career continued until 1593. The entry lists his complete known output including law reports, statutes, and Tottel’s Miscellany.
William Seres (lines ~142–)
Seres began in partnership with John Day, though Herbert notes they did not form a strict partnership and were also each “occasionally concerned with” other printers. He held a patent for psalters and primers. His entry records books printed jointly with Day and separately under his own imprint across several decades.
Henry Denham (lines ~14462–)
A substantial entry for Denham, who printed across the 1560s–80s. The books listed include a wide range of Protestant devotional, historical, and literary works.
Henry Bynneman (lines ~15696–)
Bynneman held a printing privilege covering certain categories of books including chronicles. His entry covers his output in the 1570s–80s.
Thomas Vautrollier (lines ~21394–)
Vautrollier was “a Frenchman, a scholar and printer from Paris or Rouen, who came into England about the beginning of Q. Elizabeth’s reign” and was admitted a brother of the Stationers’ Company on 2 Oct. 1564. He set up his press in Blackfriars. He printed Giordano Bruno’s works in 1584 and fled to Edinburgh thereafter, where he introduced quality printing to Scotland; he stayed there until friends interceded to obtain his pardon. He returned to London and died before 4 March 1587-8. He used the device of an anchor with two sprigs of laurel and the motto Anchora Spei. He married his daughter Jakin to Richard Field, who succeeded to his house and business. His entry lists extensive output including Beza’s New Testament, handwriting manuals, and works in French, Latin, and English across the 1570s and 1580s.
Christopher Barker (lines ~22048–)
Barker was “of an ancient family.” Elizabeth granted him “a very extensive patent” on 28 Sept. 1577 (19 Eliz.) “in consideration of his great improvement of the art of printing.” He dwelt first in Paternoster Row at the Sign of the Tiger’s Head and kept a shop in St. Paul’s Churchyard at the Sign of the Grasshopper; Herbert notes the Tiger’s Head was also the crest of Sir Francis Walsingham, “his patron.” Originally a member of the Drapers’ Company, he was translated to the Stationers on 4 June 1578, served as upper warden 1582 and 1585, and from 1588 carried on business wholly through deputies. He died 29 Nov. 1599, aged about 70. His 1582 report to the Privy Council on the state of the book trade — in which he described how booksellers “being growen the greater and wealthier nomber haue nowe many of the best Copies” — is illuminated by this career context. The entry lists his extensive Bible-printing output as Queen’s Printer.
John Charlewood (lines ~23167–)
Charlewood printed across the 1570s–80s. His entry records output including dramatic and literary works.
Robert Waldegrave (lines ~26306–)
Waldegrave’s entry records his printing output in the mid-1580s. A marginal note notes that his house was searched and his goods seized — connected to John Wolfe’s role as enforcer in the Marprelate episode. His books in this period include Protestant devotional and sermon literature.
George Bishop (lines ~26663–)
Bishop was a significant Elizabethan stationer. His entry covers multiple pages of output across the 1580s–90s, including chronicle history and legal and theological works.
John Wolf(e) (lines ~28247–)
Wolfe’s entry covers his printing output from the early 1580s, including Italian-language publications and Protestant theological works. A marginal note records that he was active “at the search of Waldegrave’s house for such [unlicensed books],” and quotes Martin Marprelate’s epithet for him: “John Woolfe (alias Machivill) most tormenting executioner of Waldegrave’s goods.”
Roger Ward (lines ~29630–)
A printer active in the later Elizabethan period. Entry records output across the 1580s–90s.
John Windet (lines ~31579–)
Windet was active in the 1580s–1600s. His entry records a range of output.
Edward Allde (lines ~32556–)
Allde was active in the later Elizabethan and early Jacobean period. His entry records output from the 1580s onward.
Richard Field (lines ~33477–)
Field was “son of Henry Field of Stratford on Avon, Tanner.” He was apprenticed to George Bishop for seven years from Michaelmas 1579, made free 6 Feb. 1586-7, and came on the livery 1 July 1598. In 1588 he married Jakin, daughter of Thomas Vautrollier, and succeeded to Vautrollier’s house and business in Blackfriars, using the same devices and printing the same copies. He was fined in May 1589 for printing a book contrary to order. His entry lists output from 1589 onward, including Puttenham’s Arte of English Poesie (1589), Ovid’s Metamorphoses, a Drake voyage account, and works in French and English across the 1590s.
Index of Printers (lines ~36948–37377)
Alphabetical index of all printers covered in this volume with their page numbers. Covers approximately 80 printers from Adams through Yetfweirt.
Relevance to the Wiki
Ames/Herbert is the classic printer-by-printer backbone for English printing after Caxton:

Biographical and imprint data for Elizabethan master printers, patents, and Stationers’ Company offices
Material for william-caxton / wynkyn-de-worde succession into the mature London trade
Concrete cases for censorship-of-the-press (Waldegrave searches, Marprelate, unlicensed printing)
Patent and privilege evidence for literary-property-and-copyright and printing-economics
Companion to the primary register transcript in stationers-registers-arber-vol1–stationers-registers-arber-vol5

primary-sources/van-netten-blaeu-review.title: Koopman in kennis. De uitgever Willem Jansz Blaeu (van Netten) — Review
primary-sources/van-netten-blaeu-review.content:
Koopman in kennis. De uitgever Willem Jansz Blaeu in de geleerde wereld (1571-1638)
Book review by Henk Nellen of Djoeke van Netten’s Koopman in kennis. De uitgever Willem Jansz Blaeu in de geleerde wereld (1571-1638) (Bijdragen tot de Geschiedenis van de Nederlandse Boekhandel; Nieuwe Reeks, dl. 15, Zutphen: Walburg Pers, 2014, 320 pp.). Published in De Zeventiende Eeuw 30 (2014) 2, pp. 270-273. In Dutch.
Summary of Contents
The review describes van Netten’s study of Willem Jansz Blaeu (1571-1638), the Amsterdam mathematician, instrument maker, cartographer, and printer-publisher. Blaeu is described as possibly the most famous Dutch printer of the seventeenth century, best known for his atlases but also for his books on mathematics, navigation, and astronomy. He worked with eminent humanists including Caspar Barlaeus, Hugo Grotius, and Gerardus Joannes Vossius.
The review highlights:

Blaeu’s printing shop “In de Vergulde Zonnewijser” on the Damrak, near competitors Willem Janssonius and Jacob Aertsz Colom
The 1637 expansion to a new, larger printing shop on the Bloemgracht with his sons Johan and Cornelis
Blaeu’s qualities: technical skill, content expertise, impressive book stock with good type and paper, clean layout, capable correctors who also assisted with indices, and an extensive distribution network
The tortoise-like slowness that gave Blaeu a poor reputation among authors — he consistently took on too much work
The competition with Janssonius and Colom, and how privileges only worked within the territory of the issuing authority
The absence of a company archive or personal letters from Blaeu, forcing the author to rely on printed works and impersonal addresses to readers
The suggestion that seventeenth-century scholarly correspondence (Vossius, Grotius) could have provided more biographical detail
The firm’s end after a devastating fire in 1672 (the rampjaar)
A correction by the reviewer: after Grotius’s death, Blaeu’s firm did publish Grotius’s Annales et Historiae in 1657

primary-sources/winship-gutenberg-to-pla.title: Gutenberg to Plantin: An Outline of the Early History of Printing (Winship)
primary-sources/winship-gutenberg-to-pla.content:
Gutenberg to Plantin: An Outline of the Early History of Printing (1926) is George Parker Winship’s survey of the origins and spread of printing in Europe from Gutenberg’s invention (c. 1440) through the era of the master printers to Christophe Plantin in Antwerp (d. 1589). Heavily influenced by Alfred W. Pollard of the British Museum.
Author: George Parker Winship (1871–1952), librarian of the Harry Elkins Widener Memorial Library, Harvard
Publisher: Harvard University Press, Cambridge, MA
Year: 1926 (second impression)
Pages: 110 (scanned page images)
Raw text: winship-gutenberg-to-plantin.txt
Scope
The book covers the first 150 years of printing in Europe (c. 1450–1600), organised chronologically and thematically. Winship describes it as “an outline aims to be a statement of facts which have in most cases long been established, with as much of the newer conclusions drawn from these facts as seems to the author reasonably certain of eventual acceptance.”
Summary of Contents
Chapter 1 — The Invention of Typography, 1440–1456. Gutenberg’s experiments in Strassburg, the Fust partnership, the 42-line Bible (1450–1456), the 1455 lawsuit, the Catholicon (1460). Indulgences of 1454–55. Gutenberg’s cost-reduction experiments (filing type bodies to fit 42 lines, saving ~5% on paper).
Chapter 2 — The Period of Development, 1460–1480. Fust & Schoeffer’s Psalter (1457) — two-color woodcut initials. The 1462 Bible with first printer’s mark. Strassburg rivals Mentelin and Rusch. The 36-line Bible, the 1448 Calendar fragment, Pfister at Bamberg with first illustrated German books (1461–62).
Chapter 3 — The Spread of Printing Throughout Germany. The 1462 sacking of Mainz disperses printers. Cologne’s textbook specialization (1,400+ titles). Chronological spread: Augsburg (1468), Nuremberg (1470), Ulm (1473), Lübeck (1474). Itinerant printers carrying only a hand-mould. Economics: paper = ~50% of cost, ~2 years to produce first book.
Chapter 4 — The Establishing of Printing as a Business. After 1480: specialization in type-founding, paper supply, and printing separate. Anton Koberger of Nuremberg — first wholesale printer/publisher. Exchange economy (books bartered sheet-for-sheet). The Nuremberg Chronicle (1493) — 1,000+ copies, 645 woodblocks, 1,809 impressions, sold across Europe.
Chapter 5 — The Printers Encounter the Renaissance. German printers cross the Alps: Sweynheym and Pannartz at Subiaco (1465) and Rome (1467) — first true roman type. Early Italian printers driven to bankruptcy by narrow market; survivors shift to practical books (military, mathematics, astrology).
Chapter 6 — Venice Becomes the Headquarters of the Book Trade. John of Speier (1469) with five-year monopoly. Nicolaus Jenson’s roman type. Venice’s advantages: cheap paper, world’s best shipping network, Italian humanist prestige. Erhard Ratdolt — decorative woodcut borders, modern title-page (1476).
Chapter 7 — Printing Reaches the Whole European World. Mainz → Basle → Lyons (vernacular popular books). Spain: Hebrew printers. First American press: Mexico City (1539, Juan Pablos), Lima (1584, Antonio Ricardo).
Chapter 8 — The First Private Presses. The Sorbonne press (1470) — three workmen from Basle. William Caxton at Bruges and Westminster: learned printing at Cologne (1471), first English book (Recuyell of the Troye Book, c. 1475), 100+ works. Wynkyn de Worde inherits (1491–1534).
Chapter 9 — The Use of Pictures. Woodcuts predate typography (playing cards, pilgrim saints, St. Christopher 1423). Block Books (Biblia Pauperum, Ars Moriendi). Albrecht Pfister: first typography + woodcut illustrations (1461–62). Augsburg leads with illustrated Bibles; Ulm produces Ptolemy (1482).
Chapter 10 — The Decade of Picture Books. 1490s boom: Basle (Ship of Fools, 1494), Venice (Malermi Bible, Hypnerotomachia Poliphili, 1499), Florence (Savonarola tracts), Paris (Book of Hours — 170 diocesan editions, 1490–1500 alone).
Chapter 11 — The Learned Printers. Aldus Manutius at Venice (from 1488) — compact cursive Greek type, Aristotle in 5 folio volumes (1495–98), revolutionary octavo Latin classics (1500–1501), italic type, anchor-and-dolphin mark. Estienne family at Paris.
Chapter 12 — The Patrons of Printing. Jean Grolier — greatest 16th-century book collector, Grolieresque bindings. Bookplates: earliest known (Hans Igler), Dürer’s plates.
Chapter 13 — Conflicting Tendencies at Paris and Geneva. The Estienne family: Henri, Robert (Thesaurus Linguae Latinae, 1532), Henri II (Greek Thesaurus, 1572). Robert’s revision of the New Testament (1528) — Sorbonne controversy, Francis I’s printing ban (1534) refused by Parlement.
Chapter 14 — The End of the Manuscript Tradition. Simon de Colines, Geofroy Tory — title-borders, initials, printer’s marks, reformed French spelling (Ç), roman type replaces black-letter.
Chapter 15 — The End of the Era of the Master Printers. Christophe Plantin at Antwerp. Antwerp supplanting Venice as commercial metropolis. Polyglott Bible (1568–1572) — 8 volumes, 4 languages, 1,200 paper + 13 vellum copies, 40 workmen, 4 presses, Philip II’s underfunding. Plantin died 1589; business to Jean Moretus; Plantin-Moretus Museum (1876).
